docs.title: What Tack is
docs.text:
Tack is a Python framework for parallel computing on CPUs and GPUs, and a toolkit for scientific data analysis and visualization built on it. You write a kernel as an ordinary Python function, and Tack compiles it for the device your arrays are on: the CPU, an Apple GPU (Metal), an NVIDIA GPU (CUDA), an AMD GPU (HIP) or an Intel GPU (Level Zero). The same filters, written that way, contour, probe and trace a simulation's data on whichever of those devices you have.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")          # or "metal", "cuda", "hip", "level_zero"


@tack.kernel
def saxpy(a, x, y, out):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):         # the parallel loop: one thread per i
        out[i] = a * x[i] + y[i]


x = tack.array(np.arange(1_000_000, dtype=np.float32))
y = tack.ones(1_000_000)
out = tack.empty_like(x)                # on the same device as x
saxpy(2.0, x, y, out)
assert out[3] == 7.0

Only the first call of saxpy compiles; later calls reuse the compiled code.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
Start from what you want to do. Each path begins with one short page and then points to the chapters it needs.

  • Write GPU code in Python

    Kernels, arrays and devices, from a first kernel to running it on a GPU.

    Start with the core · then kernels, choosing a device and complete examples

  • Analyze or visualize a dataset

    Contour, slice, clip, probe and trace a dataset you already have. For readers who know VTK or ParaView.

    Start with visualization · then extracting parts and deriving quantities. New to datasets and filters? Read the data model's first page first.

  • Connect a simulation's data

    Run filters on a simulation's own arrays, on its devices, without copies.

    Start with connecting a simulation's data · then sharing arrays and building meshes and fields

  • Scale across devices or MPI ranks

    Data in pieces, with ghost cells and global ids, over several GPUs or MPI ranks.

    Start with data in pieces · then filters over pieces and communication

Use cases shows these at more length, with the pages that show how.

docs.title: How Tack is built
docs.text:
Tack is four layers, each using only the layers below it. The guide describes them in that order, but it is not a course: start where your path starts, and follow its links down when you need them.

flowchart TB
    subgraph tack["Tack"]
        direction TB
        vis["<b>Visualization</b><br/>filters and analysis"]
        data["<b>Data</b><br/>meshes, fields, particles, AMR, pieces"]
        comm["<b>Communication</b><br/>blocks over devices and MPI ranks"]
        core["<b>Core</b><br/>kernels, arrays, devices"]
        vis -->|uses| data -->|uses| comm -->|uses| core
    end
    core --> hw["CPU · Apple Metal · NVIDIA CUDA · AMD HIP · Intel Level Zero"]
    sim["Simulation codes, PyTorch, CuPy, Warp"] <-->|"arrays, shared without copies"| core
    files["Reading and writing files:<br/>VTK, MFEM"] <-->|datasets| data
    vis -->|datasets| render["Rendering and user interfaces:<br/>VTK, ParaView, trame"]
    classDef others stroke-dasharray: 5 5
    class sim,files,render others
  • Core (tack) is the programming model: kernels with one parallel loop, device functions and device classes, arrays of scalars, vectors and matrices, reductions, scans and sorts. Arithmetic follows one written contract on every backend.
  • Communication (tack.communication) splits work into blocks, each on one device, and moves arrays between them, in one process or over MPI ranks.
  • Data (tack.dataset) holds what simulations and instruments produce: grids and unstructured meshes, polyhedra, curved cells and fields of any order, point clouds, AMR hierarchies and octrees, and datasets in pieces.
  • Visualization is about eighty filters written on the layers below. They keep VTK's names and meaning, tests compare their output with VTK's, and every one runs on every backend.

The dashed boxes are other software. Tack reads no file formats and draws nothing: VTK's readers bring data in, and VTK, ParaView or a trame application draws what Tack computes.

  • Polyhedra

  • Tetrahedra

  • An order-4 field

  • Curved cells of order 3

These are contours of one function on four kinds of cells. The cuts curve inside the order-4 and curved cells, because Tack cuts the field itself rather than a straight line between its values at the corners (gallery).

docs.title: How fast it is
docs.text: Tack's filters are Tack kernels, and they are fast on both kinds of processor. On 20 million hexahedra, point gradients take 760 ms on Tack's CPU and 23 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada, against 4,228 ms for VTK on the same 28 CPU threads. On that GPU, Tack is ahead of Viskores' C++ on 13 of the 14 filters compared. Tack is not ahead everywhere: on 5 million hexahedra, VTK's contour on the CPU is faster. Performance has the measurements.

docs.title: How Tack fits with other tools
docs.text: Tool How Tack relates to it VTK's filters Tack's filters replace VTK's where Tack has them. A VTK dataset converts to a Tack dataset and back, sharing memory where it can, and many of Tack's filters also run as VTK algorithms in a VTK pipeline. VTK still reads the files and renders. Viskores Tack takes Viskores' approach to data-parallel algorithms, written in Python instead of C++ templates. Tack also runs on Apple GPUs. ParaView and trame They draw what Tack computes, as VTK datasets. A trame application can wait for Tack's GPU work without blocking its event loop. Simulation codes Tack works on a simulation's own arrays, on its devices, through DLPack or a raw pointer, and over its MPI ranks. MFEM Tack imports MFEM meshes and solutions of any order, checked against MFEM's own evaluation of them. NumPy, PyTorch, CuPy, Warp Arrays pass both ways, through DLPack on GPUs. Tack kernels can also run on NVIDIA Warp, through a prototype backend.

docs.title: What Tack does not do
docs.text: Tack does not render, provide a user interface, or read and write file formats itself; it leaves those to VTK, ParaView and their readers. It is not a drop-in replacement for NumPy, and it has no automatic differentiation. Kernels are written in a subset of Python. Tack is not on PyPI yet, so you install it from a clone of its repository.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Install gets Tack running on your device.
  • Where to start above picks the first page for what you want to do.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
This page installs Tack and checks that it runs on your devices. It is for anyone about to use Tack for the first time. After it you have both of Tack's packages installed, with the extras for your GPU, and a check that each device compiles and runs a kernel.

Tack is not on PyPI yet, so you install it from a clone of its repository. It needs Python 3.11 or newer. There is no build step: Tack is pure Python and compiles kernels when they are first called.

git clone https://github.com/Kitware/tack.git
cd tack
uv sync --extra cpu
uv run python -c "import tack; print(tack.device('cpu'))"    # prints: cpu

These commands use uv. uv sync installs both packages into the clone's own environment: tack-core, which holds the core and communication layers, and tack-vis, which holds the data and visualization layers. Run your scripts with uv run python from the clone's directory.

docs.title: Choose the extras for your devices
docs.text:
Each backend is an extra, a named set of optional dependencies. Add the extra for each kind of device you have. Keep the cpu extra beside a GPU one, because the CPU is the default device until you choose another.

uv sync --extra cpu --extra cuda        # the CPU and an NVIDIA GPU
Device Extra What it installs What the system needs CPU cpu llvmlite nothing more Apple GPU metal pyobjc-framework-Metal macOS on Apple silicon NVIDIA GPU cuda cuda-python 13.2 or newer the NVIDIA driver, and NVRTC 13 AMD GPU hip hip-python (Linux on x86-64 only) ROCm Intel GPU level_zero nothing the Intel compute runtime: libze_loader.so and libocloc.so NVIDIA Warp (prototype) warp warp-lang and warp-simdata Warp's own requirements

The Intel extra installs nothing because Tack reaches Level Zero through system libraries, not Python packages. It exists so that the same commands work for every device.

Other extras add what some parts of Tack connect to:

Extra What it installs What it is for interop VTK 9.7.1 or newer, and PyMFEM reading and drawing data with VTK, and importing MFEM solutions mpi mpi4py 4.0 or newer running over MPI ranks; it builds against your system's MPI, so mpicc must be on your path dev pytest and the test tools running Tack's tests

PyMFEM has wheels for macOS on Apple silicon and for Linux on x86-64 only. Elsewhere the interop extra installs VTK alone.

docs.title: Install into another environment
docs.text:
To use Tack from an application's own environment, install the packages from the clone with pip. Install tack-core first, with the extras for your devices, then tack-vis, which depends on it.

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # on Windows: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -e '/path/to/tack/packages/tack-core[cpu,cuda]'
python -m pip install -e /path/to/tack/packages/tack-vis
python -m pip install 'vtk>=9.7.1'                 # optional: VTK interop

In this form interop is not an extra of either package, so install VTK and MFEM (mfem) yourself if you need them. The mpi and warp extras are extras of tack-core and tack-vis and work the same way. A plain tack-core without the cpu extra cannot run kernels on the CPU.

docs.title: Check that each device works
docs.text:
This script runs one kernel on every device Tack finds. A device works when its line says so.

import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def double(x, out):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = 2.0 * x[i]


working = []
for kind in ["cpu", "metal", "cuda", "hip", "level_zero"]:
    if tack.device_count(kind) == 0:
        print(f"{kind}: not found")
        continue
    with tack.device(kind):                      # the default device inside the block
        x = tack.arange(4, dtype=tack.f32)       # made on this device
        out = tack.empty_like(x)
        double(x, out)                           # runs where x and out are
        assert out.numpy().tolist() == [0.0, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0]
    working.append(kind)
    print(f"{kind}: works")

assert "cpu" in working

tack.device_count says 0 both when a device's software is missing and when the machine has no such device. To find out which, ask for the device itself. It raises an error that names what is missing and how to install it:

>>> tack.device("cuda")
RuntimeError: Cannot start the 'cuda' device: missing dependency.
  No module named 'cuda'
  Requires an NVIDIA GPU and the CUDA toolkit; in a clone of the repository:
    pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[cuda]'   (or: uv sync --extra cuda)

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
NVIDIA. Tack is tested with NVRTC 13, the compiler cuda-python uses to build kernels at run time. With an older NVRTC, Tack warns at the first compile, because NVRTC 12.0 miscompiled a Tack kernel. To get NVRTC 13, install the nvidia-cuda-nvrtc wheel for a CUDA version no newer than your driver's (the "CUDA Version" that nvidia-smi reports), for example pip install 'nvidia-cuda-nvrtc==13.2.*'. cuda-python finds it before a system toolkit.

AMD. The version of hip-python follows the ROCm release it binds to: 7.1.x for ROCm 7.1, 7.2.x for ROCm 7.2. The extra sets only a lower bound. If your ROCm is not the newest, install the matching version, for example pip install 'hip-python~=7.2.0'. ROCm 7.0 and 7.1 can miscompile some integer code, so use a newer ROCm if you can. Backends has the details.

Intel. Some Intel GPUs have double precision and some do not. Tack asks the device when it starts, and refuses f64 arrays on a device without it.

Apple. Apple GPUs have no double precision, so Metal has no f64. Every dataset algorithm still runs there, in single precision.

The documentation's own examples. The scripts under docs/examples/ and docs/gallery/ run from the clone with uv run python. Some need the interop extra for their figures.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Tack's visualization filters against VTK and Viskores, on the CPU and the GPU, on synthetic meshes and on real simulation data. Every Tack output is checked against VTK's before its time counts: counts, sums of positions and values, areas and volumes.

Each entry below is how many times faster Tack is: the other system's time over Tack's, so above 1× Tack is faster. Tack's time is its fresh time, which includes deriving the connectivity it needs (faces, point links) from a mesh it has not seen, since VTK and Viskores rebuild theirs on every call. The running times, fresh and warm, are at the bottom.

docs.title: Streamlines on the GPU, against Viskores
docs.text:
Viskores' streamlines on CUDA against Tack's, on the ONERA M6 wing (46.9M tetrahedra and wedges, graded toward the wing in a far field a hundred chords wide) and the aneurysm (8.7M tetrahedra), by seed count. Viskores builds its cell locator, a two-level grid, on every call; the column shows how much of its time that is. Tack's topology keeps its locator, so a later call on the same mesh reuses it. Tack is shown both ways: building a new locator each call, as Viskores does, and with the locator kept.

mesh seeds Viskores (its locator) Tack, new locator Tack, locator kept Viskores / Tack, new locator M6 wing 1 3,526 (3,059) 107 15.2 33× 17 4,143 (3,019) 188 81.5 22× 1,024 4,767 (3,041) 238 146 20× 16,384 4,705 (3,043) 197 106 24× aneurysm 1 1,714 (1,545) 31.7 3.6 54× 25 2,113 (1,539) 55.2 22.6 38× 2,000 2,887 (1,569) 88.9 60.9 32× 20,000 6,812 (1,548) 561 578 12×
  • The paths agree. On the M6, every path is the same length in both, and they lie within 1.6e-6 of each other at 17 seeds and within 3.5e-6 at 16,384. On the aneurysm the agreement is within 2.1e-6 over the first quarter at 25 seeds. At 20,000 seeds, paths through its recirculation separate further: 19,730 of 20,000 are the same length (Viskores computes in double precision, Tack in the geometry's single precision).
  • Before Tack's two-level grid (#175) it scanned the M6's crowded bins near the wing: 28–105 s on this GPU.

Machine: jura (NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada). Viskores 1.2.0 (CUDA, double precision), run through a C++ driver of its Streamline filter. Tack main at 2bbaf7e with #184, the default two-level locator (2026-10-28). Times are warm, in ms; the first call compiles.

docs.title: Real data, against VTK
docs.text:
Four datasets from production simulations, read with VTK's readers. Tack's CPU against VTK on 8 threads each, on an Apple M1 Max. Every check agrees with VTK's output.

dataset step VTK Tack VTK / Tack ONERA M6 wing, 46.9M cells (tetrahedra and wedges) density isosurface 258 81 3.2× span station (slice) 120 120 1.0× pressure gradients 1289 88 14.6× low-density cells (threshold) 107 83 1.3× outer surfaces of a fresh mesh 1122 1178 0.95× streamlines, 17 seeds, by length ³ 3900 3.6 1,083× aneurysm blood flow, 8.7M tetrahedra isosurface, slice, gradients 2.7×, 2.0×, 17× streamlines, 25 seeds ³ 3.6 1.1 3.3× LANL wildfire, 18.7M curvilinear cells plume, slice, gradients, fuel cells, surface 4.3×, 1.9×, 33×, 4.0×, 5.9× 512 pieces of a simulation's output, 5.5M voxels global ids 10,400 9,000 1.2× a layer of ghost cells 27,300 28,700 0.95×

³ Measured 2026-10-27, after the two-level grid (#175). Tack's streamlines try the cell a particle was last found in, then search its two-level cell grid, so a location near the M6's wing no longer scans thousands of cells (it was 1.0 s with one level of bins). VTK's default interpolator finds cells through the nearest point, which ends 7 of the M6's 17 paths early, inside the mesh. With VTK's cell-locator interpolator, every path runs its full length, within 3.8e-6 of Tack's, in 22.9 s.

docs.title: How these were measured
docs.text:
• One process per comparison. Tack runs in the same process as VTK (the CPU) or Viskores (the GPU), on the same mesh, and its output is checked against the other's before any timing.
  • Viskores through VTK: its filters are VTK's Viskores filters (vtkmContour and the others). On the GPU it was handed Tack's device arrays and kept its output on the device, and a trace of every run confirmed no transfers beyond sizes and counts. It ran with cudaMalloc (NO_VISKORES_MANAGED_MEMORY=1): its default, cudaMallocManaged, was 4.7–25× slower from page faults on new buffers.
  • Warm and fresh. A warm Tack run reuses the connectivity its topology keeps from an earlier filter on the same mesh; a fresh one derives it.
  • Timing. Repeated runs for a fixed budget, the median taken; Tack's timing ends with tack.sync(), since GPU launches are queued. On the Linux machine, two passes: the VTK and Tack columns take the better of the two, the Viskores column their mean (the second pass in reverse order); on the Mac, one.
  • Harness: benchmarks/vtk_compare (VTK and Tack) and benchmarks/viskores_compare (Viskores and Tack), on the meshes of benchmarks/vtk_compare/meshes.py. Point gradients against VTK (vtkGradientFilter) are a pair of vtk_compare since 0.6.1's run (#195).

docs.text:
Earlier microbenchmarks, from before October 2026

These measurements predate safe floating-point math on CUDA and Metal, the CPU threading policy's repairs, the CPU's disjoint-array variants, queued GPU launches and the CPU thread pool, all in October 2026. Their reproduce scripts time a call without tack.sync(), so their GPU columns would now time the launch rather than the kernel. They are kept as a record and have not been edited.
