docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Metal GPU vs CUDA GPU are in the same ballpark (~19-29 G elem/s) despite very different architectures. Both are memory-bandwidth limited for simple kernels, compute-limited for transcendentals.

  • CPU/NumPy gap between Mac and Linux is mostly memory bandwidth: Apple Silicon unified memory delivers ~100-200 GB/s vs ~4 GB/s effective on this DDR3 Xeon box. The CPU itself (Sandy Bridge 2012 @ 2.0 GHz, AVX1 only) also contributes to the gap.

  • FILL hits 62 G elem/s on CUDA (write-only, no reads) — close to the 4060 Ti's theoretical 288 GB/s (62G × 4 bytes = 248 GB/s).

  • sin/exp show the largest CUDA-vs-CPU speedup (34-45x) because CUDA's Special Function Units (SFUs) compute transcendentals in hardware.

  • reduce favors Metal (39G vs 26G) — likely benefiting from unified memory avoiding a writeback path for partial sums.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text: What would you use Tack for? Here are six jobs it does well. Each section says why Tack is good at the job, gives a measured result where one exists, and links to the pages that show how. The front page describes Tack as a whole.

docs.title: Analyze simulation output on the GPU you have
docs.text:
Tack's filters run on NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and Apple GPUs, and on the CPU, from the same Python script. Only the device changes: VTK reads the file, Tack filters it on the device, and VTK or ParaView draws the result. You need no build for your GPU and no second version of your script.

On an Apple M1 Max, Tack's filters on the Metal GPU are 1.5 to 154 times faster than VTK's on the CPU, on every filter compared but one. On an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada, Tack's filters on CUDA are 11 to 2,269 times faster than VTK's on 28 CPU threads. On real simulation data on the M1 Max's CPU, Tack computes the ONERA M6 wing's pressure gradients 14.6 times faster than VTK, and a wildfire simulation's gradients 33 times faster (performance).

To do it, see the visualization layer's first page, VTK for reading and drawing data, and choose a device.

docs.title: Run filters in situ, on a simulation's own arrays
docs.text:
A filter that runs inside a simulation, on its memory while it runs, is in situ. Tack works on a simulation's arrays where they already are. On the CPU or a GPU, tack.array_from_ptr wraps an existing allocation, and tack.from_dlpack takes a tensor from PyTorch, CuPy or any other library that speaks DLPack. Neither copies. A field made from such an array is read by every filter in place.

import numpy as np
import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((33, 33, 33), origin=(0, 0, 0), spacing=(1 / 32, 1 / 32, 1 / 32))
temperature = np.zeros(data.num_points, dtype=np.float32)    # the simulation's own array
values = tack.array_from_ptr(temperature, temperature.shape, tack.f32)
data.fields["temperature"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), values)

temperature[:] = data.positions()[:, 0]          # the simulation writes a step
surface = td.contour(data, "temperature", 0.5)   # Tack reads the same memory
assert np.allclose(surface.positions()[:, 0], 0.5)

On CUDA, Tack works in the same GPU context that PyTorch, CuPy and NVIDIA Warp use, so the libraries take turns on one device without switching. With Warp, Tack exchanges whole datasets with NVIDIA's warp-simdata, sharing most of their arrays. A simulation in pieces over MPI ranks keeps its pieces, and Tack runs over the same ranks. No in situ run has been timed for these pages yet.

To do it, see share arrays, connect a simulation's data and MFEM, Warp and others.

docs.title: Write your own visualization algorithm in Python
docs.text:
Tack's built-in filters are written with the same public pieces you use. A kernel of your own visits a mesh's cells, faces or points with for_each, and reads them through views, which give a cell's points and their positions, and a field's value anywhere inside a cell. carry then moves fields, ghost marks and ids from the input to your output, as the built-in filters do. Your algorithm is a Python function, so it runs on every device and needs no build.

The built-in filters show what this gives. They are Tack kernels written in Python, and on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada they are ahead of Viskores' C++ filters on 13 of the 14 compared, by up to 5.4 times (performance). One of the documentation's examples rewrites six built-in filters with public names only, and checks each result against the built-in's.

To do it, see views, write a mesh algorithm and write a filter.

docs.title: Work with higher-order and finite-element data
docs.text:
Finite-element codes store fields as polynomials inside each cell, often on curved cells. Tack keeps such data as it is. A field is continuous (H1) or discontinuous (L2) of any order, in a Lagrange, Bernstein or serendipity basis, on a geometry that may itself be curved. Filters work on the field itself. A contour or slice cuts each cell on sub-cells and places every crossing on the polynomial, so nothing is resampled onto a linear mesh first.

Tack reads MFEM meshes and solutions, and VTK's Lagrange and Bézier cells. The pictures in the MFEM gallery are MFEM's examples run through Tack. Tack's values there are checked against MFEM's own: values at random points in every element, gradients, the jumps of DG fields across faces, and integrals.

To do it, see higher-order and finite-element data and MFEM, Warp and others.

docs.title: Process big data in pieces, over MPI ranks
docs.text:
A dataset too large for one device is split into pieces, one or more on each device or MPI rank. Tack's filters run on each piece. Tack adds layers of ghost cells, numbers points and cells across pieces with global ids, and gathers pieces into one. Statistics, connected regions and streamlines work across pieces. With ghost cells in place, each piece's output is exactly its share of the output for the whole dataset. The same script runs in one process and on many ranks.

On 512 pieces of a simulation's output, numbering every point and cell takes 9.0 s against VTK's 10.4 s, and a layer of ghost cells 28.7 s against VTK's 27.3 s (performance). One limit: ghost cells do not yet carry continuous fields above order 1.

To do it, see data in pieces, filters over pieces and run under MPI.

docs.title: Compute on GPUs in Python, beyond visualization
docs.text:
Tack's core is a general programming model, and the visualization layer is one program written on it. You can write simulations, image processing or data analysis the same way. Kernels hold vectors and small matrices. Device classes let one kernel serve many data structures. Scans, sorts and segmented reductions are ready to use, and arithmetic follows one contract on every backend. The examples include heat diffusion, a particle-to-grid (MPM) simulation and tiled n-body forces, each checked against an independent reference.

Every filter on the performance page is built from these same kernels, scans and sorts.

To do it, see the core's first page, reductions, scans and sorts and the core's examples.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Install gets Tack running on your device.
  • What Tack is describes the four layers and what Tack leaves to other software.

docs.title: Communication: distributed parallelism
docs.text:
You need this layer when your data is in pieces: when you split a problem into parts, spread it over several devices, or run it over MPI ranks. The parts, called blocks, need each other's data. A stencil needs its neighbour's edge cells, and a particle needs the part that holds its position. tack.communication moves Tack arrays between blocks and combines values over them. If you contour a dataset on one device, you do not need it. Tack's own algorithms over a dataset in pieces are written on this layer and use it for you (see Data in pieces and Filters over pieces).

The layer uses only Tack's core: arrays, devices and kernels. If those are new, start with Core.

docs.title: Send a message between blocks
docs.text:
A block is one unit of distributed work, such as a part of a grid or a share of particles. Each block lives on one device and has a global id, a number unique over every process. exchange is the call every other pattern is built on. Here each of four blocks sends its id to the next block in a ring:

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * 4)                      # four blocks, World() by default

outgoing = {}
for g in blocks.local:
    after = (g + 1) % blocks.count
    outgoing[g] = {after: {"sender": tack.array(np.array([g], np.int32))}}
incoming = blocks.exchange(outgoing)                 # {destination: {source: message}}

for g in blocks.local:
    before = (g - 1) % blocks.count
    assert list(incoming[g]) == [before]
    assert incoming[g][before]["sender"].numpy()[0] == before
print(blocks, {g: list(incoming[g]) for g in blocks.local})
# Blocks(4 blocks, 4 on rank 0) {0: [3], 1: [0], 2: [1], 3: [2]}

exchange takes {source: {destination: message}}, where a message is a dictionary of names to Tack arrays. It returns {destination: {source: message}} for every block of this process. Each received array is on the destination block's device.

docs.title: One program for one process or many ranks
docs.text:
A world is the set of processes the blocks live in. tc.World() is this process alone, as in the example. tc.World(comm) spans the ranks of an mpi4py communicator, where a rank is one MPI process. Global ids run over rank 0's blocks first, then rank 1's, and so on:

flowchart LR
  subgraph rank0["rank 0"]
    b0["block 0 on cuda:0"]
    b1["block 1 on cuda:1"]
  end
  subgraph rank1["rank 1"]
    b2["block 2 on cuda:0"]
    b3["block 3 on cuda:1"]
  end
  b0 <--> b1
  b1 <--> b2
  b2 <--> b3

An algorithm written on blocks never asks which arrangement it runs on. You can develop and test it in one process, without mpiexec, and run it unchanged on hundreds of ranks. Collectives combine values in order of global id, so a floating-point sum over blocks has the same bits however the blocks are shared out. Every call on blocks is collective: every process makes the same calls, in the same order.

The model is that of DIY: blocks, links, exchanges and collectives. Tack uses plain dictionaries in place of DIY's callbacks.

docs.title: Reading path
docs.text:
Read these in order. Each page has a short example you can run in one process.

  1. Blocks and worlds: global ids, devices, the world, and which calls every rank must make.
  2. Exchange data and refresh ghosts with plans: messages between blocks, neighbours by their boxes, and a Plan built once and run every step.
  3. Route points to blocks: send each point to the block that holds it, with values, and get answers back. Particles move this way.
  4. Sort and reduce over blocks: sums, gathers and global numbering, and a sort that brings every copy of a key to one block.
  5. Run under MPI: mpi4py, a GPU per rank, GPU-aware transfers and Slurm.

The API reference for every call is in the runtime reference.

docs.title: Blocks and worlds
docs.text:
Every call in tack.communication goes through two objects. A Blocks holds this process's units of work and their devices. A World says which processes there are and moves messages between them. Before writing a computation over blocks, you decide how many blocks to make and on which devices. Each block is addressed by its global id, and its arrays live on its device. One rule says which calls every process must make.

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

world = tc.World()                         # this process alone
blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu", "cpu", "cpu"], world)
print(world, blocks)
# World(rank=0, size=1) Blocks(3 blocks, 3 on rank 0)

# One array per block, made on that block's device.
cells = {g: tack.array(np.full(4, float(g)), device=blocks.device(g)) for g in blocks.local}

# A collective: every block's value, combined over every block.
total = blocks.all_reduce({g: cells[g].sum() for g in blocks.local})
assert list(blocks.local) == [0, 1, 2] and blocks.count == 3
assert blocks.rank_of(2) == 0 and total == 4 * (0 + 1 + 2)

docs.title: A block is a unit of work on one device
docs.text:
A block is the unit you cut a problem into: a part of a grid, a share of particles, a piece of a dataset. It plays the part of a DIY block, or of one piece of a VTK partitioned dataset. Each block lives on one device, and its arrays are on that device. A global id names each block uniquely over every process.

Blocks(devices, world) makes this process's blocks, one for each entry of devices. An entry is a tack.Device or a device spec such as "cpu", "cuda:1" or "hip" (see Choose a device). Several blocks may share one device. If world is left out, it is World(), this process alone.

How many blocks to make is your choice. One block per device is the common case. More blocks than devices is useful too: an algorithm developed with four blocks on one CPU exercises every exchange it will make on four GPUs.

docs.title: Global ids number every process's blocks
docs.text:
Global ids run over every process's blocks, contiguous by process. Rank 0's blocks come first, then rank 1's, and so on, as VTK numbers the pieces of a partitioned dataset across ranks. Processes may hold different numbers of blocks. With three ranks holding one, two and three blocks:

rank blocks it holds blocks.local 0 0 range(0, 1) 1 1, 2 range(1, 3) 2 3, 4, 5 range(3, 6)

Four attributes and methods describe the numbering:

name gives blocks.local the range of this process's global ids blocks.count the number of blocks over every process blocks.rank_of(g) the rank that holds block g, for any block blocks.device(g) the device of block g, for this process's blocks only

blocks.device(g) raises ValueError for another process's block, since a process knows only its own devices. A process with no blocks is allowed: Blocks([], world) takes part in every call and holds an empty local.

docs.title: Arrays live on their block's device
docs.text:
Every array you give a call for block g must be on blocks.device(g). Make it there with device=blocks.device(g), as the example does, or with array.to_device(...). A call refuses an array on another device with a ValueError that names both.

Every array you receive for block g is on blocks.device(g) too. In one process with blocks on two GPUs, a message from a block on cuda:0 to a block on cuda:1 arrives as a copy on cuda:1. Where the destination's device can already address the sender's memory, as two blocks on one CPU can, the receiver gets the sent array itself. So a sender must not write to an array after sending it.

One process can drive several GPUs this way:

blocks = tc.Blocks(["cuda:0", "cuda:1"])          # two blocks, one per GPU

docs.title: A world is the set of processes
docs.text:
A world is the transport between processes. It plays the part of VTK's vtkMultiProcessController.

  • tc.World() is this process alone, rank 0 of 1. Its blocks may be on any of its devices, and messages between them are array copies.
  • tc.World(comm) spans the ranks of comm, an mpi4py communicator.
from mpi4py import MPI

world = tc.World(MPI.COMM_WORLD)
blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * 2, world)            # two blocks on every rank

world.rank and world.size are this process's rank and the number of ranks. Tack imports no MPI module itself. You make the communicator, and Tack communicates on a duplicate of it, so its messages never meet your application's. Make one World for a run and pass it to every Blocks. Anything with the methods Tack uses (Dup, Get_rank, Get_size, allgather, alltoall, Isend and Irecv) works in place of an mpi4py communicator.

How messages travel between ranks, staged through host memory or handed to a GPU-aware MPI as device arrays, is on Run under MPI.

docs.title: Every call is collective
docs.text:
Every call on blocks is collective: every process of the world makes it, in the same order. That includes the constructors of Blocks, Plan and Routing, which gather what every process has. It includes a process with nothing to send, which still calls exchange with an empty dictionary. A process that skips a call, or makes calls in another order, leaves the others waiting.

The calls are:

call what it does page Blocks(...) make this process's blocks this page exchange, link_by_bounds, Plan(...), Plan.run send messages, find neighbours, keep and rerun an exchange Exchange and plans Routing(...), send, reply send points to the blocks that hold them Route points all_reduce, all_gather, exclusive_scan, sort_by_key combine and sort over every block Sort and reduce

Kernels, by contrast, are not collective. Each process launches kernels on its own blocks' arrays whenever it likes, as the ghost example in Exchange and plans does between plan runs.

docs.title: Arguments are dictionaries keyed by global id
docs.text:
Every call takes and returns dictionaries keyed by global id, with entries for this process's blocks only. Naming another process's block where one of this process's is needed raises ValueError.

  • Collectives (all_reduce, all_gather, exclusive_scan), Routing and sort_by_key need an entry for every one of this process's blocks.
  • exchange and Plan need entries only for blocks that send or receive.
  • Results have an entry for every one of this process's blocks, in order of global id.

So the usual way to write a step is a dictionary comprehension over blocks.local:

counts = {g: particles[g].size for g in blocks.local}
starts, total = blocks.exclusive_scan(counts)

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• The numbering is fixed when Blocks is made. To change how many blocks a process holds, make a new Blocks, on every process.
  • Some mistakes are found on one process only, before the call communicates. That process raises, and the others wait in the call. Under MPI, end the run when a call raises, for example with comm.Abort().
  • Every exception each call raises is listed in the runtime contract.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Exchange data and refresh ghosts with plans sends arrays between blocks, the first thing most algorithms do.
  • Run under MPI puts blocks on many ranks, one GPU each.

docs.title: Exchange data and refresh ghosts with plans
docs.text:
Once a problem is cut into blocks, each block usually needs some of its neighbours' data. exchange sends any Tack arrays from any block to any block. link_by_bounds finds each block's neighbours from their bounding boxes. An exchange that repeats every step, such as refreshing ghost cells, is kept as a Plan and run again with new values.

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * 4)

# Block g covers [g, g + 1] on a line and holds g + 3 values: 10 g, 10 g + 1, ...
values = {g: tack.array(10.0 * g + np.arange(g + 3)) for g in blocks.local}
boxes = {g: ((float(g),), (g + 1.0,)) for g in blocks.local}
neighbours = blocks.link_by_bounds(boxes)
print(neighbours)
# {0: [1], 1: [0, 2], 2: [1, 3], 3: [2]}

# Each block sends its first value to the block before it, and its last value
# with a vector of its minimum, maximum and mean to the block after it.
outgoing = {}
for g in blocks.local:
    host = values[g].numpy()
    outgoing[g] = {}
    for n in neighbours[g]:
        if n < g:
            outgoing[g][n] = {"edge": tack.array(host[:1])}
        else:
            stats = [[host.min(), host.max(), host.mean()]]
            outgoing[g][n] = {"edge": tack.array(host[-1:]),
                              "stats": tack.array(stats, tack.vec3(tack.f64))}
incoming = blocks.exchange(outgoing)                 # {destination: {source: message}}

for source, message in incoming[2].items():
    print(source, {name: a.numpy().tolist() for name, a in message.items()})
# 1 {'edge': [13.0], 'stats': [[10.0, 13.0, 11.5]]}
# 3 {'edge': [30.0]}
assert incoming[2][3]["edge"].numpy()[0] == 30.0
assert incoming[2][1]["stats"].dtype == tack.vec3(tack.f64)

docs.title: Send messages with exchange
docs.text:
blocks.exchange(outgoing) delivers messages between any blocks, on any process. Its argument and its result are nested dictionaries:

  • outgoing is {source: {destination: message}}. The sources are this process's blocks. A destination may be any block, on any process, the source included.
  • A message is a dictionary of names to Tack arrays, each on the source block's device. A message may be empty.
  • The result is {destination: {source: message}}, with an entry for every one of this process's blocks, in order of global id. A block's messages are in order of source. A block that receives nothing gets an empty dictionary.

Neighbour exchanges, all-to-all exchanges and sends to a chosen block are all this one call. When it returns, every message to this process's blocks has arrived.

Arrays arrive as they were sent. Their element types and shapes are kept, so vector and matrix arrays (tack.vec3, tack.mat(2, 3)) and multidimensional arrays need no packing. Each received array is on the destination block's device. Where that device can already address the sent memory, the receiver gets the sent array itself. A sender must therefore not write to an array after sending it. Make a copy first if it must keep changing.

A structure-of-arrays array (tack.soa) cannot be sent as one array. Send its components under names of their own.

docs.title: Find neighbours by their boxes
docs.text:
Most algorithms send to neighbours, not to every block. blocks.link_by_bounds(boxes, margin=0.0) finds them from bounding boxes. boxes is {g: (lower, upper)} for this process's blocks, two corners of any one dimension. The result is {g: [neighbours]}: every block whose box overlaps or touches block g's box, grown by margin on every side.

With a margin of 0, blocks that share a face are neighbours, which is what a decomposition into abutting parts needs. With a margin of r, every block within distance r of a box is a neighbour, which is what a search radius needs. Like every call on blocks, link_by_bounds is collective: it gathers every process's boxes.

docs.title: Keep an exchange as a plan
docs.text:
Most exchanges repeat. A stencil code sends the same edge cells to the same neighbours before every step, and only the values change. A Plan keeps such an exchange: for each pair of blocks, which elements the sender reads and where the receiver writes them. You build it once and run it every step.

plan = tc.Plan(blocks, sends, receives)
plan.run(u)                                       # every step

sends is {g: {destination: indices}} and receives is {g: {source: indices}}, for this process's blocks. The indices are element indices into the block's array, as lists, NumPy arrays or integer Tack arrays on the block's device. For a multidimensional array they are flat, row-major indices. The rule that ties the two together is:

The k-th element a sender reads for a destination goes to the k-th element that destination writes from that sender.

Every send must have a receive of the same length on the other block, and the other way round. The plan checks this across every process when it is made, and raises ValueError naming the two blocks if not.

plan.run(values) gathers the sent elements, exchanges them and writes them into place:

  • values is {g: array} for every block that sends or receives.
  • {g: {name: array}} moves several arrays in one exchange. Every block must use the same names, and each name one element type on every block.
  • Received elements are written in place. Every other element is left as it was.
  • Elements move whole: for a vec3 array, an index moves three components.

A block may send to itself. This is what a periodic domain needs, where a block can be its own neighbour. What a block sends itself is read before anything is written.

docs.title: Refresh ghost rows of a periodic grid
docs.text:
The example below cuts a 24 by 16 grid into strips of rows. Each block owns its rows and stores one ghost row above and below them. The grid is periodic in y, so the last block's neighbour above is block 0. With one block, the block is its own neighbour above and below, and sends to itself.

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

NX, NY = 16, 24                                      # the whole grid's columns and rows


@tack.kernel
def diffuse(u, out):
    # Rows 0 and u.shape[0] - 1 are ghosts; x is periodic within the block.
    for i, j in tack.ndindex((1, u.shape[0] - 1), u.shape[1]):
        left = u[i, (j + u.shape[1] - 1) % u.shape[1]]
        right = u[i, (j + 1) % u.shape[1]]
        out[i, j] = u[i, j] + 0.2 * (left + right + u[i - 1, j] + u[i + 1, j] - 4.0 * u[i, j])


def row(r):
    """The flat element indices of row r of a block's array."""
    return list(range(r * NX, (r + 1) * NX))


def ghost_plan(blocks, rows):
    """Each block's first and last owned rows into the ghost rows of the blocks
    below and above it, periodic in y."""
    sends = {g: {} for g in blocks.local}
    receives = {g: {} for g in blocks.local}
    for g in blocks.local:
        below, above = (g - 1) % blocks.count, (g + 1) % blocks.count
        # What g sends, in this order: its first owned row down, its last up.
        sends[g].setdefault(below, []).extend(row(1))
        sends[g].setdefault(above, []).extend(row(rows))
        # What g receives, in the order its sources send: the block above sends
        # its first row down, into g's top ghost row; the block below sends its
        # last row up, into g's bottom ghost row.
        receives[g].setdefault(above, []).extend(row(rows + 1))
        receives[g].setdefault(below, []).extend(row(0))
    return tc.Plan(blocks, sends, receives)


def simulate(count, steps=50):
    blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * count)
    rows = NY // count                               # rows each block owns
    y, x = np.mgrid[0:NY, 0:NX]
    start = np.exp(-((x - NX / 2) ** 2 + (y - NY / 3) ** 2) / 8.0)
    u, v, owner = {}, {}, {}
    for g in blocks.local:
        u[g] = tack.array(np.pad(start[g * rows:(g + 1) * rows], ((1, 1), (0, 0))))
        v[g] = tack.zeros((rows + 2, NX), tack.f64)
        owner[g] = tack.array(np.full((rows + 2, NX), g, np.int32))
    plan = ghost_plan(blocks, rows)
    plan.run({g: {"u": u[g], "owner": owner[g]} for g in blocks.local})   # two arrays
    for step in range(steps):
        for g in blocks.local:
            diffuse(u[g], v[g])
        u, v = v, u
        plan.run(u)                                  # one array
    grid = np.concatenate([u[g].numpy()[1:rows + 1] for g in blocks.local])
    return owner, grid


owner, three = simulate(3)
print(owner[0].numpy()[[0, 1, 8, 9], 0])             # ghost, owned, owned, ghost
# [2 0 0 1]
assert owner[0].numpy()[0, 0] == 2 and owner[0].numpy()[9, 0] == 1

# One block is its own neighbour above and below: it sends to itself.
owner, one = simulate(1)
assert np.array_equal(three, one)                    # three blocks or one: the same bits

The first run of the plan moves two arrays at once. The owner array shows where each ghost row came from: block 0's bottom ghost row holds block 2's last row, across the periodic boundary, and its top ghost row holds block 1's first row. After 50 steps, three blocks and one block give the same grid, bit for bit.

Notice how ghost_plan lists the receives. When there are only one or two blocks, a block's neighbour below and above are the same block, and both rows go in one list. The receiver must list the rows in the order the sender lists them. That is why g lists what its neighbour above sends down before what its neighbour below sends up: each neighbour sends its row down first.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• A plan holds its index arrays on each block's device, so running it launches only gather and scatter kernels and one exchange.
  • Building a plan is collective, since it checks lengths across every process. Build it once, outside the time loop.
  • Plan.run raises TypeError if a name's element type differs between the sender and the receiver.
  • A plan does not know what the indices mean. Ghost cells, ghost points, shared faces and halo regions of any width are all lists of indices.
  • Every exception is listed in the runtime contract.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Route points to blocks sends values to whichever block holds a point, when you do not know the destination in advance.
  • See also Data in pieces: Tack's ghost cells for a dataset in pieces are plans like these, made for you.

docs.title: Run under MPI
docs.text:
A computation written on tc.Blocks that works in one process can run over many MPI ranks, on a workstation with mpiexec or on a cluster under Slurm with a GPU per rank. To get there, you install mpi4py, give each rank its blocks and its GPU, and choose how messages travel between ranks. A large job also keeps its compiled kernels in one bundle that every rank reads.

Only the world changes. Everything else in the program stays as it is:

from mpi4py import MPI

from tack import communication as tc

world = tc.World(MPI.COMM_WORLD)
blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * 2, world)             # two blocks on every rank

The example docs/examples/comm_ghosts.py diffuses heat along a line of 240 cells cut into six blocks. Before every step, a Plan refreshes each block's ghost cells, as in Exchange and plans. The example takes --mpi to make its world this way, and its six blocks are then shared out over the ranks. On a laptop with Open MPI 5.0, every run prints the same maximum and the same hash of the line's bytes:

$ python docs/examples/comm_ghosts.py --check
1 rank(s), 6 blocks: max 0.492189, sha256 4d622496db333f4d
$ mpiexec -n 2 python docs/examples/comm_ghosts.py --mpi --check
2 rank(s), 6 blocks: max 0.492189, sha256 4d622496db333f4d
$ mpiexec -n 3 python docs/examples/comm_ghosts.py --mpi --check
3 rank(s), 6 blocks: max 0.492189, sha256 4d622496db333f4d
$ mpiexec -n 6 python docs/examples/comm_ghosts.py --mpi --check
6 rank(s), 6 blocks: max 0.492189, sha256 4d622496db333f4d

--check also compares each run with the same kernel on one array of 240 cells, and every run passes, bit for bit.

docs.title: Install mpi4py
docs.text:
MPI is optional in Tack. The mpi extra installs mpi4py, which builds against the MPI already on your system:

uv sync --extra mpi                                  # in a clone of Tack, with your other extras
pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[mpi]'             # or, in another environment

The build needs your MPI's compiler wrapper, mpicc, on the path. On a cluster, load the MPI module first, so mpi4py links against the MPI the cluster's network uses. On a workstation, Open MPI or MPICH from the system's packages works. Tack's own continuous integration uses Open MPI from apt.

docs.title: Make a world from a communicator
docs.text:
tc.World(comm) spans the ranks of an mpi4py communicator. It is usually MPI.COMM_WORLD, but any communicator works, including one made by comm.Split. world.rank and world.size are this rank and the number of ranks.

Tack communicates on a duplicate of comm, made when the world is made. Its messages therefore never meet your application's messages, whatever tags you use. Make one World for a run and pass it to every Blocks.

Tack imports no MPI module. You import mpi4py and make the communicator, which lets you choose when MPI starts. That matters for GPUs, below.

docs.title: Share the blocks out over the ranks
docs.text:
Each rank makes only its own blocks. Global ids run over rank 0's blocks first, then rank 1's, as Blocks and worlds explains. To share a fixed number of blocks over any number of ranks, give each rank a consecutive share:

BLOCKS = 12
share = range(world.rank * BLOCKS // world.size, (world.rank + 1) * BLOCKS // world.size)
blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * len(share), world)
assert blocks.local == share                       # global id g is part g of the problem

Ranks may hold different numbers of blocks, and a rank may hold none. Collectives combine in order of global id, so results do not depend on the share-out. The rest of the program loops over blocks.local as before.

docs.title: Give each rank its own GPU
docs.text:
On a node with several GPUs, each rank usually drives one. Make that device before importing mpi4py.MPI. A GPU-aware MPI uses the device that is current when MPI starts, and importing mpi4py.MPI starts it. The rank's number on its node comes from the launcher's environment, since MPI has not started yet:

import os

import tack

# Slurm's srun sets SLURM_LOCALID; Open MPI's mpiexec sets OMPI_COMM_WORLD_LOCAL_RANK.
local_rank = int(os.environ.get("SLURM_LOCALID", os.environ.get("OMPI_COMM_WORLD_LOCAL_RANK", "0")))
device = tack.set_default_device(f"cuda:{local_rank}")

from mpi4py import MPI                             # MPI starts here, on that device

from tack import communication as tc

world = tc.World(MPI.COMM_WORLD, gpu_aware=True)
blocks = tc.Blocks([device], world)

Use "hip:N" or "level_zero:N" for AMD or Intel GPUs. A rank that moves to another device after MPI has started still works, but more slowly. With Cray MPICH on Perlmutter, such a rank's transfers within a node ran at about 7 GB/s instead of 22. Across nodes they can fail.

Under Slurm, let every rank see all of its node's GPUs and choose its own, as above. Cray MPICH copies between GPUs on one node through CUDA IPC, which needs the GPUs visible to both ranks. So bind with --gpu-bind=none, not --gpus-per-task=1:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=2
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=4
#SBATCH --gpus-per-node=4
export MPICH_GPU_SUPPORT_ENABLED=1                 # Cray MPICH: let MPI read device memory
srun --gpu-bind=none python run.py

docs.title: Choose how messages travel between ranks
docs.text:
Messages between blocks of one rank never touch MPI. Messages between ranks travel one of two ways.

  • Staged, the default. For each pair of ranks, the sender copies all the arrays of an exchange into one host buffer and sends it. The receiver copies the arrays to its blocks' devices. This works with any MPI.
  • GPU-aware, with tc.World(comm, gpu_aware=True). Tack hands MPI each array itself, through DLPack, and receives into device arrays. This needs an MPI built to read and write device memory, and saves the copies through host memory.

Some device memory cannot go to MPI as it is. CUDA's and HIP's arrays come from stream-ordered memory pools, which Cray MPICH cannot export and MVAPICH-Plus's UCX takes for host memory. For those, Tack copies each array into device memory the MPI does accept, sends that, and receives into such memory. This happens on its own. On Perlmutter's A100s with Cray MPICH, such transfers ran at 22.2 GB/s a rank within a node and 5.9 GB/s across two nodes; the measurement is recorded in vendor workarounds.

Choose GPU-aware transfers when your MPI supports them and messages are large. Stay with staging when it does not, or when you are not sure: the results are the same either way. gpu_aware=True without a communicator raises ValueError, since one process has no ranks to send to.

docs.title: Run CPU ranks side by side
docs.text:
Tack's CPU device runs kernels on a pool of threads, one per CPU the process may run on. When the launcher binds each rank to its own cores, the pools fit the node. When it does not, every rank's pool uses every CPU, and the ranks compete. Then set the number of threads per rank yourself:

TACK_CPU_THREADS=8 mpiexec -n 4 python run.py      # 4 ranks of 8 threads on 32 cores

docs.title: Keep compiled kernels for a large job
docs.text:
Each rank compiles the kernels it calls, the first time it calls them. Tack keeps compiled kernels on disk, so a later run starts warm. With thousands of ranks on a shared file system, looking up one file per kernel per rank is slow. A bundle avoids it: one file that holds every compiled kernel, which each rank reads once.

  1. Warm the cache with a small run, on one rank or a few, with TACK_CACHE=write and TACK_CACHE_DIR set to a directory of your own on scratch.
  2. Pack the directory into a bundle with TACK_CACHE_DIR=... python -m tack.cache pack.
  3. Run the job with the same TACK_CACHE_DIR. Under MPI, each rank reads the bundle and writes nothing. A kernel the bundle lacks is compiled in memory.

Keep compiled kernels between runs covers the settings, how Tack recognizes an MPI launch, and how to have rank 0 read the bundle and broadcast it.

docs.title: Check your MPI setup
docs.text:
Tack's tests run every pattern of this section on three MPI ranks, staged and GPU-aware, with CPU arrays:

uv run pytest packages/tack-core/tests/test_communication.py

Without mpi4py or mpiexec, the MPI tests are skipped. Set TACK_REQUIRE_MPI=1 to make them fail instead, so a missing MPI does not pass unnoticed.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Between ranks, an exchange first sends every rank a header with the names, element types and shapes of the arrays it will receive. The arrays follow as nonblocking sends and receives under one tag, on the world's duplicate communicator. Every request has completed when exchange returns.
  • Every call on blocks is collective. A rank that raises before a call communicates leaves the others waiting in it. In a batch job, end the run with comm.Abort() when a call raises.
  • World(comm) accepts any object with mpi4py's methods Dup, Get_rank, Get_size, allgather, alltoall, Isend and Irecv.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• See also Filters over pieces, in the layer above: Tack's filters over a dataset in pieces run over MPI ranks the same way.
  • Choose a device lists the device specs a rank can use.

docs.title: Route points to blocks
docs.text:
A probe asks for values at points anywhere in a domain, and a particle that moves must go to the block whose part of the domain it entered. In both cases a point must reach the block that holds it, and no one knows that block in advance. Routing sends each point there by a test of your own. It also sends values with the points and returns answers to where they came from. Particles move between blocks by routing in rounds. The page builds on blocks and exchanges.

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * 3)
TOLERANCE = 0.01

# Block g holds the strip g <= x < g + 1 of the rectangle [0, 3) x [0, 1).
# Its box is grown by the tolerance, so points just outside are asked too.
boxes = {g: ((g - TOLERANCE, 0.0), (g + 1 + TOLERANCE, 1.0)) for g in blocks.local}


def holds(g, points):
    """2 where block g holds a point, 1 where it is within the tolerance, else 0."""
    x = points[:, 0]
    inside = (x >= g) & (x < g + 1)
    near = (x >= g - TOLERANCE) & (x < g + 1 + TOLERANCE)
    return np.where(inside, 2, np.where(near, 1, 0))


# Each block asks about five points anywhere in the rectangle, and one outside it.
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
positions = {g: np.vstack([rng.uniform((0, 0), (3, 1), (5, 2)), [[5.0, 0.5]]])
             for g in blocks.local}
routing = tc.Routing(blocks, positions, boxes, holds)
print(routing.destination[0])
# [ 1  2  0  0  2 -1]

# Each point goes to its block, which answers with 100 times its id plus x.
arrived = routing.send()                             # {g: (points, {name: array})}
answers = {}
for g in blocks.local:
    points, values = arrived[g]
    answers[g] = {"value": tack.array(100.0 * g + points[:, 0])}
back = routing.reply(answers, like={"value": tack.f64})

expected = 100.0 * np.floor(positions[0][:, 0]) + positions[0][:, 0]
expected[5] = 0.0                                    # the point no block holds
assert np.array_equal(routing.destination[0][:5], np.floor(positions[0][:5, 0]))
assert np.array_equal(back[0]["value"].numpy(), expected)

docs.title: How a point finds its block
docs.text:
tc.Routing(blocks, positions, boxes, holds) decides where every point goes, in three steps:

  1. Each point is sent to every block whose box contains it. A box is widened by a relative slack of one millionth of its largest side, so a point on a box's face is asked of the block.
  2. Each block asked calls holds(g, points) on the points it received. The function returns one number per point: 0 where the block does not hold the point, and a positive rank where it does. True counts as 1.
  3. The point goes to the block that gave the highest rank. On a tie, it goes to the block with the lowest global id. Where every rank is 0, the point goes nowhere.

routing.destination is {g: array}: for each of block g's points, the block it goes to, or -1 where no block holds it.

The arguments are, for each of this process's blocks:

argument per block meaning positions an (n, d) NumPy array the points this block asks about; n may be 0 boxes (lower, upper), or None the region the block may hold points in; None holds nothing holds one function for every block holds(g, points) on an (m, d) float64 array, returning m ranks

Ranks let a block say how well it holds a point. In the example, a block gives 2 to a point inside its strip and 1 to a point within the tolerance outside it. A point at x = 1.005 is near block 0 and inside block 1, so it goes to block 1. A point just outside every strip, at x = 3.005, is still taken by block 2, the only block near it. Rank 2 beats rank 1 whatever the blocks' ids. Tack's cell locators rank the same way when probing a dataset in pieces: a cell that holds a point beats one that is merely close to it.

The tie rule gives every point exactly one destination. If holds returned only True and False on closed strips, a point at x = 1 would be held by blocks 0 and 1, and it would go to block 0.

Positions travel as the bits of their float64 values. The block that decides sees exactly the coordinates that were sent, on every device, so holds never disagrees with itself across a round trip.

docs.title: Send values with the points
docs.text:
routing.send(values) moves the points to their destinations, with any arrays of values that go with them. values is {g: {name: array}}: one element per point of block g, on its device. It may be left out.

It returns {g: (points, values)} for each of this process's blocks:

  • points is an (m, d) NumPy array of the points that arrived.
  • values is {name: array}, the values that came with them, on the block's device.
  • Points arrive in order of the block they came from, then in their order on that block.
  • A block that receives no points gets an empty array of points and an empty dictionary of values.

docs.title: Send answers back
docs.text:
routing.reply(answers, like) returns one answer per point to the block it came from. answers is {g: {name: array}}, one element for each point that arrived at block g, in the order send gave them. like is {name: element type}, which tells blocks that received no points what to make.

The result is {g: {name: array}}, one element for each of block g's original points, in their original order. A point that went nowhere gets zero. Call send before reply. A routing remembers what send delivered and answers in that order.

docs.title: Move particles between blocks in rounds
docs.text:
A particle that moves leaves its block. To keep each particle on the block that holds it, alternate two steps: advance every block's particles, then route them to their new blocks with their state. Each round makes a new Routing from the new positions.

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

WIDTH = 3.0                                          # x is periodic on [0, 3)
POINT = tack.vec2(tack.f64)


@tack.kernel
def move(x, velocity, dt, width):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        p = x[i] + velocity[i] * dt
        p[0] = p[0] - width * tack.floor(p[0] / width)  # wrap x into [0, width)
        x[i] = p


def holds(g, points):
    return (points[:, 0] >= g) & (points[:, 0] < g + 1)


blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * 3)
boxes = {g: ((float(g), 0.0), (g + 1.0, 1.0)) for g in blocks.local}

# Ten particles a block, each starting in its own block's strip.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x, velocity, ids = {}, {}, {}
for g in blocks.local:
    x[g] = tack.array(rng.uniform((g, 0.0), (g + 1, 1.0), (10, 2)), POINT)
    velocity[g] = tack.array(rng.uniform((-1, 0), (1, 0), (10, 2)), POINT)
    ids[g] = tack.array(np.arange(10, dtype=np.int64) + 10 * g)

for step in range(20):
    for g in blocks.local:
        move(x[g], velocity[g], 0.1, WIDTH)
    # Each particle, with its state, to the block whose strip holds it now.
    routing = tc.Routing(blocks, {g: x[g].numpy() for g in blocks.local}, boxes, holds)
    arrived = routing.send({g: {"velocity": velocity[g], "id": ids[g]} for g in blocks.local})
    for g in blocks.local:
        points, values = arrived[g]
        x[g] = tack.array(points, POINT)
        velocity[g] = values.get("velocity", tack.empty(0, POINT))
        ids[g] = values.get("id", tack.empty(0, tack.i64))

counts = [ids[g].size for g in blocks.local]
print(counts)
# [15, 9, 6]
everyone = np.concatenate([ids[g].numpy() for g in blocks.local])
assert sorted(everyone.tolist()) == list(range(30))  # every particle, once
assert all(np.all(holds(g, x[g].numpy())) for g in blocks.local)

After 20 steps the 30 particles are spread unevenly over the blocks, and each block holds exactly the particles inside its strip. The values.get calls cover a block that ends a round with no particles.

The same pattern carries any state: a particle's age, its path so far, a flag that says it left the domain. Points that go nowhere (destination -1) are dropped by send, so check routing.destination first if you need to keep them.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Routing(...), send and reply are collective. Every process makes them, in the same order, even with no points.
  • A point is asked only of blocks whose boxes contain it. A box that is too small loses points before holds sees them. Grow each box by the tolerance your holds accepts, as the first example does.
  • The points of a block may be sent to that block itself. Nothing special is needed.
  • holds runs on the host with NumPy points. To test points on the device, as a cell locator does, copy them into a Tack array inside holds and launch a kernel there.
  • Every exception is listed in the runtime contract.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Sort and reduce over blocks brings together items that share a key, such as copies of one point, when no box says where they are.
  • See also Sample and trace, in the layer above: probing and streamlines over a dataset in pieces are routing in rounds.

docs.title: Sort and reduce over blocks
docs.text:
How do you add up a value over every block, number items across all of them, or find every copy of a point that several blocks hold? Sums, extrema and counts over blocks are collectives. A global numbering is a scan. Finding every copy of a point, a key or an id is a sort, sort_by_key. Reductions, gathers and numberings give results that do not depend on how blocks are shared out. The page builds on blocks and exchanges.

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * 4)

# Block g holds 1000 + 10 g values.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
values = {g: tack.array(rng.standard_normal(1000 + 10 * g)) for g in blocks.local}

total = blocks.all_reduce({g: values[g].sum() for g in blocks.local})
lowest = blocks.all_reduce({g: values[g].min() for g in blocks.local}, op="min")
sizes = blocks.all_gather({g: values[g].size for g in blocks.local})
starts, count = blocks.exclusive_scan({g: values[g].size for g in blocks.local})
print(sizes, starts, count)
# [1000, 1010, 1020, 1030] {0: 0, 1: 1000, 2: 2010, 3: 3030} 4060

# Element k of block g is element starts[g] + k of the whole, numbered once.
numbers = {g: tack.array(starts[g] + np.arange(values[g].size)) for g in blocks.local}
assert numbers[3].numpy()[-1] == count - 1

# The sum adds the blocks' sums in order of global id, so it is exactly this.
in_order = 0.0
for g in range(blocks.count):
    in_order += values[g].sum()
assert total == in_order

# NumPy arrays combine element by element.
ranges = blocks.all_reduce({g: np.array([values[g].min(), -values[g].max()])
                            for g in blocks.local}, op="min")
assert ranges[0] == lowest

docs.title: Combine values over every block
docs.text:
Three collectives combine small values held on the host, one value per block:

call gives, on every process all_reduce(values, op="sum") the values combined by "sum", "min" or "max" all_gather(values) a list of every block's value, indexed by global id exclusive_scan(counts) ({g: offset}, total): each block's sum of the counts before it, and the sum of all

values is {g: value} with an entry for every one of this process's blocks. For all_reduce, a value is a number or a NumPy array, and arrays combine element by element. For all_gather, a value may be any small Python object that can be pickled, such as a tuple or a bounding box. For exclusive_scan, a count is an integer of at least 0.

The values are host values, not Tack arrays. Reduce each block's array on its device first, with array.sum() or a kernel (see Reductions, scans and sorts), and give the collective the result.

docs.title: Number items over every block
docs.text:
exclusive_scan is how a global numbering starts. Give it each block's count of items. Each block's offset is where its share of the numbering begins, and the total is the number of items in all. Block g then numbers its k-th item starts[g] + k, as the example does. Each item gets one number, and the numbers run from 0 to total - 1 without gaps.

When items are duplicated across blocks, as shared points are, count only the copies each block owns. The last section of this page shows how to decide who owns what.

docs.title: Results do not depend on the arrangement
docs.text:
Collectives combine values in order of global id: block 0's value, then block 1's, and so on. The order is the same whichever process holds which block. A floating-point sum over blocks therefore has the same bits on one process, on three ranks, or on six. Tack's test suite checks this, with blocks shared out over ranks in different ways.

The fixed order makes a sum reproducible, not more accurate. It is a plain sum of the blocks' values from left to right, exactly what the example's in_order loop computes.

docs.title: Match items across blocks with a sort
docs.text:
Some items have copies on several blocks: a point on the boundary between two parts of a mesh, a particle near a seam, a global id held by a ghost and by its owner. No box says where the copies are. sort_by_key brings them together:

ordered, carried = tc.sort_by_key(blocks, keys, values)

It sorts every block's keys together and cuts the global order into one range per block. Block 0 ends with the smallest keys and the last block with the largest, each block's in ascending order. The values move with their keys. Most importantly, every copy of a key ends on one block. There, the copies can be matched, counted or reduced without further communication.

The arguments are, for each of this process's blocks:

  • keys: a one-dimensional Tack array of i32, u32, i64 or u64, of the same type on every block.
  • values: {name: array}, each array with one element per key. Each name has one element type on every block. Leave values out to sort only keys; carried is then None.

The sort is stable. Equal keys keep the order of their blocks, then their order within a block. So the first copy of a key, after the sort, is the copy on the lowest block. That gives a rule for ownership that every process agrees on without asking: the lowest block that holds an item owns it.

A key is anything that is equal for copies and different otherwise: a grid index, a hash of a point's exact coordinates, a cluster label, a global id. To know where each copy came from, carry its origin as a value, for example (block << 40) | index.

docs.title: Number shared points once
docs.text:
The example below has three blocks of a 12 by 5 lattice of points. Each block holds five columns, so neighbouring blocks share a column. The sort brings each point's copies together. Each block numbers the points it then holds, a scan makes the numbers global, and an exchange sends each copy its point's number.

import numpy as np

import tack
from tack import communication as tc

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

blocks = tc.Blocks(["cpu"] * 3)
NX, NY, M = 12, 5, 4                       # points per row, rows, columns a block steps

# Block g holds lattice columns 4 g to 4 g + 4, so neighbours share a column.
# A point's key is its lattice index; in a mesh it could be a hash of its
# exact position. Its origin is (block << 40) | index on that block.
keys, origin = {}, {}
for g in blocks.local:
    i, j = np.meshgrid(np.arange(M * g, min(M * g + M, NX - 1) + 1), np.arange(NY))
    keys[g] = tack.array((j * NX + i).ravel(), tack.i64)
    origin[g] = tack.array((g << 40) | np.arange(keys[g].size), tack.i64)

# Every copy of a key lands on one block, in order of block, then index.
ordered, carried = tc.sort_by_key(blocks, keys, {g: {"origin": origin[g]} for g in blocks.local})

# On each block, a run of equal keys is one point's copies. Number the runs,
# and make the numbers global with a scan of each block's count of runs.
new_run = {}
for g in blocks.local:
    k = ordered[g].numpy()
    new_run[g] = np.diff(k, prepend=k[:1] - 1) != 0  # True where a run starts
starts, points = blocks.exclusive_scan({g: int(new_run[g].sum()) for g in blocks.local})

# Send each copy its point's number, back to the block it came from.
outgoing = {}
for g in blocks.local:
    o = carried[g]["origin"].numpy()
    number = starts[g] + np.cumsum(new_run[g]) - 1
    outgoing[g] = {}
    for source in np.unique(o >> 40).tolist():
        mine = (o >> 40) == source
        outgoing[g][source] = {"index": tack.array(o[mine] & ((1 << 40) - 1)),
                               "number": tack.array(number[mine])}
incoming = blocks.exchange(outgoing)

ids = {}
for g in blocks.local:
    host = np.full(keys[g].size, -1, np.int64)
    for message in incoming[g].values():
        host[message["index"].numpy()] = message["number"].numpy()
    ids[g] = host

print(points, "points;", sum(keys[g].size for g in blocks.local), "copies")
# 60 points; 70 copies
for g in blocks.local:
    assert np.array_equal(ids[g], keys[g].numpy())   # every copy got its point's number

The 70 copies make 60 points, each numbered once. Here the numbers equal the lattice indices, because the sort numbers points in key order and every lattice index is present. With hashed positions as keys, the numbers would be in hash order instead, which is just as good for an identity.

The bookkeeping on the host uses NumPy for clarity. On a GPU, keep it on the device with Tack's own scans and kernels.

This is the pattern behind Tack's global ids and ghost cells for a dataset in pieces. See also Data in pieces, in the layer above.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• sort_by_key is a sample sort, as DIY's is. Each block sorts its own keys on its device and sends 16 samples of them, weighted by its count. Every block then finds the same splitters, sends each range of its keys to its block, and sorts what arrives. The samples argument changes the number of samples.
  • Blocks end with about equal numbers of keys. A key repeated many times cannot be split between blocks, so heavily repeated keys can leave the blocks uneven.
  • When every block is in one process on one device, the sort joins the keys and sorts them once, with no messages. The result is the same.
  • all_gather pickles its values under MPI. Keep them small: counts, boxes, a few numbers. Move arrays with exchange.
  • The collectives raise ValueError if any of this process's blocks is missing from values. Every exception is listed in the runtime contract.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Run under MPI runs these calls over many ranks.
  • Reductions, scans and sorts covers the sorts and scans within one array, which sort_by_key uses on each block.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
The guides show how to use Tack. The contracts state what Tack promises: what is guaranteed, what the caller must ensure, and what happens when either side gets it wrong. When a guide and a contract disagree, the contract governs. When a contract and the code disagree, the discrepancy is a defect to report, not a reading to choose between.

Status

The kernel language contract is a draft under review. It was baselined at 05174e1 and last updated for the fifth numerical-semantics increment on 2026-10-03. The other three pages describe release candidate 23d6e1d. Their statements are read from the source at that hash and cite where each one lives; Backend capabilities and Runtime API were since updated for the queued GPU launches, the disk cache, debug mode and the CPU pool merged through b94af23. The hardware validation status in Conformance was recorded at 745e01f, before those changes.

docs.title: How to read a contract
docs.text:
Every statement in a contract carries one of five labels. The language contract defines the first four in its Status and interpretation section:

Label Meaning Required "An intended correctness property. A current violation is a compiler defect, including when existing examples happen to work." Current behavior "Describes the implementation without making that behavior a permanent language guarantee." Proposed "A policy this draft recommends but that needs agreement before becoming a public guarantee." Open "No portable result is promised by this draft for that case. An open decision is not permission to change existing behavior silently." Required caller constraint An obligation on the program, not on Tack. Violating it leaves the result outside the contract. Tack does not promise a diagnostic, so a missing diagnostic is not a defect.

The fifth label covers obligations that the language contract states as "access only in-bounds elements and initialized values; write only to writable storage". It is the counterpart of Required. A failed Required property is a bug in Tack. A violated caller constraint is a bug in the program, even when Tack happens to produce the expected answer.

Two more conventions apply on every contract page:

  • Errors are part of the contract. When a page says that something is rejected, it names the exception type and where the exception is raised: at decoration, at first dispatch, on every dispatch, or at inspection. It also gives the shape of the message. A rejection raised before compilation or launch leaves array storage unchanged.
  • Current behavior is not a promise. It is recorded so that you can rely on it today and so that any change to it is deliberate. Don't build a portable program on a Current behavior item when a Required item or a caller constraint covers the same ground.

docs.title: The map
docs.text:
Contract Scope Status Kernel language contract What a kernel means: supported constructs, execution and ordering, memory and aliasing, integer and floating-point semantics, reductions, workgroups, atomics and specialization identity. Regression IDs LC1–LC8 Draft under review, normative for the compiler hardening work Backend capabilities The Backend base class, the meaning of each capability attribute, the capability matrix for each backend, how launches are queued, and what each capability rejects and when Describes 23d6e1d, updated through b94af23 Runtime API Devices (tack.device, the default device, launch placement) and debug mode, arrays and their host operations, tack.sync, reductions, pointer and DLPack interop, tack.inspect, the decorators, kernel call rules, environment variables, tack.cache and exception types Describes 23d6e1d, updated through b94af23 and the device model of bba0846 Conformance and validation How each contract area is tested, which oracles the tests use, how a hardware validation is run and recorded, and the most recent status of each backend Describes 23d6e1d, with validation status recorded at 745e01f

The language contract is long because it defines semantics. The other three pages are shorter and more mechanical. They describe the surface around the language, and you can check most of their statements by reading one function.

docs.title: Contracts and the rest of the documentation
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    D["Design<br/>(why and how)"] --> C["Contracts<br/>(what is promised)"]
    C --> T["Tests<br/>(evidence)"]
    T --> V["Hardware validation<br/>(evidence per backend)"]
    G["Guides<br/>(how to use it)"] -. examples of .-> C
  • Design explains why Tack is built the way it is and how the implementation meets its contracts. For example, Specialization and Caching explains why the variant key includes baked shape constants, while the contract says only that reusing a variant must behave like a fresh compile.
  • Contracts say what is promised. They describe a mechanism only when it is observable, such as which pass raises an error.
  • Tests are the evidence. Conformance maps each contract area to its test modules. Expected values come from independent oracles, such as Python integers, NumPy, exact rationals and reference renders, and never from recording Tack's own output.
  • Hardware validation is the evidence that a backend meets the contract on a real device. A CPU run doesn't validate GPU execution, and a host-side syntax check of generated GPU source doesn't validate device behavior.
  • Guides (User's Guide and Developer's Guide) are examples. They aren't an exhaustive specification, and parts of them predate the contracts.

docs.title: Changing a contract
docs.text:
• A change to a Required item, or a decision on an Open item, changes the contract text and its tests together. The language contract says this explicitly for device assertions, and the rule applies everywhere.
  • Don't waive a failing numerical case by marking it as an expected failure. The regression baseline keeps LC1–LC8 as ordinary assertions.
  • Report a discrepancy between code and contract. Don't resolve it by editing whichever side is easier. The language contract is under human review, and changes to it go through that review.

docs.title: Backend capabilities
docs.text:
Tack compiles one kernel source for five targets, but the targets don't all offer the same things. Metal has no f64, the CPU has no workgroups, and atomics are narrower on some GPUs than ordinary arrays. This page is the contract for those differences. It covers what a backend declares, what each declaration means, what each one rejects and when, and the subset of the language that runs everywhere.

All statements describe release candidate 23d6e1d, updated for the queued launches, disk cache, debug mode and CPU pool merged through b94af23, and for the device model of bba0846. The declarations live in packages/tack-core/src/tack/runtime/backend.py (class Backend) and in the five subclasses in runtime/cpu.py, runtime/metal.py, runtime/cuda_backend.py, runtime/hip_backend.py and runtime/level_zero_backend.py. For the kernel semantics that these capabilities gate, see the kernel language contract. For the implementation story, see Backend Implementations.

docs.title: The Backend contract
docs.text: Required: every backend subclasses Backend and declares its capabilities as attributes. Callers read those attributes and don't probe for methods with hasattr or compare backend class names. Anything that can be derived is derived, so two declarations can't disagree.

docs.title: Required methods
docs.text:
Method Contract allocate_array(dtype, shape, exportable=False) Allocates backend storage and returns a DeviceBuffer. exportable=True asks for memory that Array.export_memory() can share without a copy. Only CUDA acts on the flag, and the other backends ignore it wrap_ptr(ptr, dtype, shape) Wraps existing memory as a DeviceBuffer without copying or taking ownership. What counts as ptr is backend-specific. See Pointer interop execute(kernel, args, kwargs) Compiles or reuses a variant and runs it. All five backends delegate to resolve_variant() in runtime/kernel_utils.py, which is where every capability check below runs

The base class raises NotImplementedError for all three.

docs.title: Optional methods with defaults
docs.text: Method Default Overridden by synchronize() Does nothing, which is correct for a backend whose launches complete before execute() returns. Otherwise it waits for every launch, fill and copy queued so far, and a queued launch's error is raised here. tack.sync() calls it on every backend, Device.synchronize() on one Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero, which queue launches (see Launches) fill_array(array, value) Returns False, and Array.fill fills the buffer in place CPU, which runs a fill of 256 KiB or more of its own buffers as a kernel through its dispatch, so the threads first-touch the pages cache_target() Returns None: compiled variants are not stored on disk, only lowered IR. Otherwise a string naming what compiled code depends on besides the kernel (the device, the compiler and driver versions, the compile options) all five variant_artifact(payload), load_variant(ir_func, artifact, effective_args) Raise NotImplementedError. Called only when cache_target() is not None: the picklable part of a compiled variant, and the payload rebuilt from it in another process. effective_args lets a GPU backend remake its scalar pack buffers all five memory_space(ptr) Returns "cpu", which is correct for backends whose allocations are host-addressable CUDA, HIP and Level Zero, which ask their driver. CPU overrides it with the same answer reduce_array(array, op) Raises NotImplementedError. Called only when supports_device_reductions is true Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero texture_in_hardware(shape_3d) Returns False: a Texture3D keeps a private f32 array and the generated code interpolates it in software Metal and CUDA (always True), HIP and Level Zero (per device and extent) create_texture_image(shape_3d) Raises NotImplementedError. Called only when texture_in_hardware() is true. Returns an image object with upload(array), owned by one Texture3D Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero _store_texture_shapes(ir_func, args) Records each Texture3D argument's extents on its parameter HIP and Level Zero, which clear the parameter's _is_texture flag when texture_in_hardware() is false

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Kind Meaning name declared Device type, as a device spec writes it (tack.device("cuda")) and Device.type reports it: cpu, metal, cuda, hip or level_zero ordinal declared Which of the type's devices the backend drives (Device.index). Always 0 for now display_name declared How messages spell the backend, if different from name label derived display_name or name. Use it in messages supported_dtypes declared A frozenset of the scalar types the device's arrays may have. Making an array of another type raises TypeError, and dispatch checks every array argument against this set supports_f64 derived f64 in supported_dtypes supports_device_reductions declared True when Array.sum(), min() and max() can run on the device. When false they run in NumPy on the host. It selects a path and never rejects anything supports_workgroups declared Native workgroup execution for shared, shared_like, barrier, thread_id and block_sum/block_min/block_max. It does not promise uniform participation, atomic support or safe partial workgroups supported_atomic_dtypes derived Array dtypes that support atomic_add, atomic_min and atomic_max. This is the backend's entry in ATOMIC_DTYPES (lang/atomic_support.py) intersected with supported_dtypes device_options declared Keyword options that tack.device() forwards to the constructor. tack.device() rejects any other option memory_domain derived What the backend's arrays are valid in, (name, ordinal). Level Zero adds its context handle. A backend runs kernels on another backend's arrays when the domains are equal (two CPU devices with different thread counts); arrays from two domains in one launch are refused device_memory_spaces declared memory_space() results that array_from_ptr() accepts. When the set is non-empty, every pointer must be an address (anything int() accepts) and is checked. An empty set means that the backend doesn't distinguish memory spaces and nothing is checked dlpack_refusal_note declared Text appended to the error when a DLPack import is refused, for backends whose reason the device type doesn't convey

Because supported_atomic_dtypes is an intersection, a device without f64 also loses f64 atomics. That matters on Level Zero, where supported_dtypes depends on the device.
