  2. Arrays and types: making arrays, element types, scalar arguments and casts.
  3. Kernels: the parallel loop, several dimensions, inner loops and returning a value.
  4. Control flow and math: conditions, loops, math functions and how arithmetic behaves.
  5. Device functions: helpers that kernels call.
  6. Heat diffusion: a complete simulation that puts these together.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Start with How a Tack program runs. It explains the idea that matters most when you turn NumPy code into kernels: how the work splits between Python and the device.

docs.title: Arrays and types
docs.text: Every kernel reads its inputs from arrays and writes its results into them, so arrays are where a calculation starts. You make them on a device, move values between them and NumPy, and choose their element types. A Python number passed to a kernel gets a type too, and you can predict it. Some arrays compute their values instead of storing them.

docs.title: An array from input to output
docs.text:
A tack.Array is memory on one device with a shape and an element type, much like a NumPy array that lives on the GPU. This program copies a NumPy array in, runs a kernel over it, and copies the result out:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

host = np.arange(6, dtype=np.float32).reshape(2, 3)
source = tack.array(host)                  # a copy of host, on the device
out = tack.empty(host.shape)               # new storage, values not set

@tack.kernel
def add_one(source, out):
    for row, column in tack.ndindex(source.shape[0], source.shape[1]):
        out[row, column] = source[row, column] + 1.0

add_one(source, out)
print(out.numpy())                         # [[1. 2. 3.]
                                           #  [4. 5. 6.]]
np.testing.assert_array_equal(out.numpy(), host + 1.0)

tack.array copies its input and keeps its type, here f32. tack.empty allocates an array whose values are not set. Use it when a kernel writes every value before anything reads one. out.numpy() returns a new NumPy array, a copy. Make working arrays once and reuse them across the steps of a calculation, because allocating is far slower than reusing.

docs.title: Make arrays
docs.text:
Every function that makes an array takes the shape first and the element type second, as NumPy does. Without a type, a new array is f32. A type is a Tack type such as tack.i32, or anything NumPy accepts as one, such as np.int32 or "float64".

Function Values Example tack.empty(shape, dtype) Not set tack.empty((100, 100)) tack.zeros, tack.ones Zeros, ones tack.zeros((256,), tack.i32) tack.full(shape, value, dtype) value everywhere tack.full((100,), 3.14) tack.arange(start, stop, step) A range, as NumPy's tack.arange(1, 64, 2) tack.array(values, dtype) A copy of a NumPy array or a list tack.array([1.0, 2.0]) tack.empty_like(a), zeros_like, ones_like, full_like As above, with a's shape and type tack.empty_like(source)

A new array from empty holds whatever was in memory, on every device. Write every value before you read it, or use zeros. The _like functions read only the prototype's shape and type, never its values, and the prototype can be a NumPy array or a Tack array. A dtype= argument overrides the type.

tack.array with no type keeps a NumPy array's type, so a float64 array becomes an f64 array and NumPy's default int64 becomes i64. A list of Python floats becomes f32, and a list of Python integers i32, or i64 if a value needs it. tack.asarray is the same, except that it returns a Tack array already of the type asked for as it is, without copying.

docs.title: Move values in and out
docs.text:
Values move between NumPy and Tack through three calls. tack.copyto(a, values) writes into an existing array. a.numpy() reads an array into a new NumPy array, and np.asarray(a) does the same. a.fill(value) sets every element.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = tack.empty((1024,))
tack.copyto(data, np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 1024, dtype=np.float32))
assert data.numpy()[-1] == 1.0

tack.copyto(data, 0.5)                     # a scalar fills every element
other = tack.zeros((1024,))
tack.copyto(other, data)                   # from array to array, on the device
assert np.asarray(other).max() == 0.5

data.fill(2.0)
assert data[3] == 2.0                      # read one element, as a Python float

tack.copyto is strict, like np.copyto. The values must have the array's shape or broadcast to it, and a mismatch raises ValueError. Values are converted to the array's type. Arrays have no slice assignment such as a[...] = values: build the values in NumPy and call tack.copyto, use fill, or write them in a kernel.

Reading one element with a[i], a[i, j] or a negative index is for inspecting results and for decisions in host code. On a discrete GPU each such read is a transfer of its own, so read many values with numpy(). Writing one element from the host, a[i] = x, raises TypeError, and so does iterating over an array.

On a GPU, these calls keep their place among the queued launches. A tack.copyto does not overwrite values a queued launch still reads, and numpy() waits for the launches before it. On Apple silicon the CPU and GPU share memory, so these are plain memory copies. On NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs they are transfers between host and device memory.

A zero-dimensional array holds a single value, written a[()] as in NumPy. It suits a value kernels compute and other kernels read, such as a counter:

strength = tack.empty(())
strength.fill(2.0)

@tack.kernel
def add_strength(data, strength):
    for i in range(data.shape[0]):
        data[i] += strength[()]

For a value that only the host changes between calls, pass a scalar argument instead (see Scalar arguments).

docs.title: Shape counts elements, the type describes one
docs.text:
An array's shape counts its elements. Its element type describes one element, which is a scalar, a small vector or a small matrix. A scalar array of shape (4, 3) and a vector array of shape (4,) with element type tack.vec3() both hold twelve numbers. A kernel reads a number from each element of the first and a 3-vector from each element of the second.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

velocity = tack.empty((4,), tack.vec3())       # four 3-vectors of f32
velocity.fill([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
assert velocity.shape == (4,) and velocity.size == 4
assert velocity.dtype is tack.vec3(tack.f32)
assert velocity.numpy().shape == (4, 3)        # components become the last axis

positions = tack.array(np.zeros((10, 3), np.float32), dtype=tack.vec3())
assert positions.shape == (10,)                # ten vectors
scalars = tack.array(np.zeros((10, 3), np.float32))
assert scalars.shape == (10, 3)                # thirty numbers

On the host, a vector array's components are an extra last axis: numpy() returns shape (n, 3) for n 3-vectors, and tack.copyto expects that shape. tack.array never guesses vectors from a trailing axis of three. Give the element type, and it consumes the matching trailing axes. tack.vec2, tack.vec3, tack.vec4 and tack.vec(n) describe vector types, and tack.mat2, tack.mat3, tack.mat4 and tack.mat(rows, columns) matrix types up to 4 by 4. Their components are f32 unless you name another type, as in tack.vec3(tack.i32). Vectors and matrices shows what kernels do with them.

The other properties count elements too:

f = tack.empty((4, 3))
f.size, f.ndim, len(f), f.nbytes           # 12, 2, 4, 48

v = tack.empty((4,), tack.vec3())
v.size, v.ndim, v.nbytes                   # 4, 1, 48

docs.title: Copy, convert and reshape
docs.text:
Three methods make arrays from arrays:

  • a.copy() makes a new array with its own storage.
  • a.astype(tack.f64) makes a new array of another type. A scalar type changes a vector array's component type and keeps it a vector array.
  • a.reshape(rows, columns) or a.reshape(-1) returns a view with another shape over the same storage. Nothing is copied, so writes through either are seen by both.

tack.concat([a, b, c]) joins one-dimensional arrays of one type into a new array. Memory and parallel correctness explains what to watch for when a kernel gets two views of the same storage.

docs.title: Arrays live on a device
docs.text:
Every array lives on one device, recorded as a.device. The functions above make arrays on the default device, which tack.set_default_device sets. Each also takes device=, as in tack.zeros((n,), device="cuda"), and the _like functions use the prototype's device. a.to_device("cpu") returns the array itself when that device can use its memory, and a copy otherwise.

A kernel runs on the device of its arrays. When they are on the default device, it runs there. When they are all on another device, it runs on theirs. Arrays on two devices that cannot address each other's memory raise ValueError. Choose a device covers devices in full.

Arrays can also share memory with other libraries instead of copying: tack.from_dlpack takes a PyTorch or CuPy tensor, and tack.array_from_ptr wraps a pointer a simulation hands you. Share arrays explains both.

docs.title: Scalar types
docs.text:
Tack has ten scalar types, each matching a NumPy type:

Tack NumPy Tack NumPy tack.i8 np.int8 tack.u8 np.uint8 tack.i16 np.int16 tack.u16 np.uint16 tack.i32 np.int32 tack.u32 np.uint32 tack.i64 np.int64 tack.u64 np.uint64 tack.f32 np.float32 tack.f64 np.float64

Use f32 for real numbers and i32 for indices unless you need more. f32 runs on every device, and GPUs often run it much faster than f64. Apple GPUs have no f64 at all, so with Metal as the device, making an f64 array raises TypeError. Some Intel GPUs lack it too. Choose a device says which devices have it.

docs.title: The default float type
docs.text:
f32 is the type a new array gets when nothing names one. A program that works in double precision throughout can change that once:

tack.set_default_float(tack.f64)       # tack.get_default_float() reads it

x = tack.zeros((n,))                   # f64
v = tack.empty((n,), tack.vec3())      # three f64 components
y = tack.array([0.1, 0.2])             # f64: Python floats follow it
z = tack.array(host_f32)               # f32: a NumPy array keeps its type

The setting covers empty, zeros and ones without a type, Python floats in array, full and arange, vector and matrix types without a component type, and the implicit arrays below. It is process-wide, like the default device, and arrays already made keep their type. It does not change kernels: a kernel computes in the precision of the arrays it is given.

docs.title: Scalar arguments
docs.text:
Kernels take Python numbers as arguments directly. A scalar argument is a runtime value, so calling with a new value does not compile again:

@tack.kernel
def saxpy(x, y, out, alpha):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = alpha * x[i] + y[i]

saxpy(x, y, out, 2.5)
saxpy(x, y, out, 3.0)                  # the same compiled kernel

Tack chooses a scalar's type from its value and the kernel's arrays:

  • A Python float is f32, or f64 when any array argument of the kernel is f64. So a double-precision calculation does not lose precision through its scalars.
  • A Python int is i32 when its value fits, then i64, then u64 for values above the largest i64. A value outside all three raises TypeError.
  • A NumPy scalar follows the same rules as the Python number it holds. So np.float64(2.5) is f32 in a kernel whose arrays are all f32, and np.int16(1) is i32. To choose a scalar's type yourself, cast it in the kernel (see Casts).

A kernel may take as many scalar arguments as you like. Because the type depends on the value, passing 5 and later 2**40 compiles two versions of the kernel, one for i32 and one for i64.

docs.title: Casts
docs.text:
In a kernel, float(x) converts to f32 and int(x) to i32, truncating toward zero. To convert to any other type, call the type:

@tack.kernel
def precise(x, out):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        wide = tack.f64(x[i])          # compute in double precision
        out[i] = tack.f32(wide * wide)

@tack.kernel
def high_byte(data, out):
    for i in range(data.shape[0]):
        bits = tack.u32(data[i])       # unsigned, for bit operations
        out[i] = tack.i32(bits >> 24)

Every scalar type is a cast: tack.i8() to tack.u64(), tack.f32() and tack.f64(). Integer casts keep the low bits, so tack.u8(-1) is 255. Control flow and math explains how types combine in arithmetic, and why int(floor(x)) differs from int(x) for negative numbers.

docs.title: Structure of arrays
docs.text:
A vector array stores each element's components together: x, y, z, then x, y, z. Simulations often store them apart instead, one array per component. tack.soa(x, y, z) makes a vec3 array from three existing arrays without copying them. layout="soa" makes a new one that way.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def advance(pos, vel, dt):
    for i in range(len(pos)):
        pos[i] += vel[i] * dt

x, y, z = (np.zeros(4, np.float32) for _ in range(3))     # someone else's arrays
pos = tack.soa(tack.from_dlpack(x), tack.from_dlpack(y), tack.from_dlpack(z))
vel = tack.full((4,), [1.0, 2.0, 3.0], tack.vec3(), layout="soa")

advance(pos, vel, 0.5)
assert np.allclose(y, 1.0)                     # written into their memory
assert pos.layout == "soa" and pos.components[1].size == 4
assert np.allclose(pos.numpy(), [[0.5, 1.0, 1.5]] * 4)

Kernels index a structure-of-arrays array exactly as they index an interleaved one, so the same kernel takes either layout and compiles a version for each. On the host it reads and writes as any vector array. a.components gives the component arrays back, and tack.array(a, layout="aos") copies it into one interleaved array. Two things need one buffer and so work only on the interleaved layout: an atomic at a flat component index, and exporting the whole array to another library. Its components export individually.

docs.title: Implicit arrays
docs.text:
An implicit array computes each value from its index instead of storing it. tack.arrays has them: a counting sequence, a constant, a permutation of another array, a view of part of one, a function of the index, and more. A kernel indexes them as it indexes a stored array, so a kernel written for stored arrays takes them unchanged:

import numpy as np
import tack
from tack import arrays

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def scaled(a, out, s):
    for i in range(len(a)):
        out[i] = a[i] * s

out = tack.zeros((4,))
scaled(tack.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]), out, 2.0)        # stored values
assert np.allclose(out.numpy(), [2, 4, 6, 8])

scaled(arrays.CountingArray(4, 1.0, 1.0), out, 2.0)       # 1, 2, 3, 4, computed
assert np.allclose(out.numpy(), [2, 4, 6, 8])

ids = tack.array([3, 0, 2, 1])
scaled(arrays.Permutation(ids, arrays.CountingArray(4, 0.0, 10.0)), out, 1.0)
assert np.allclose(out.numpy(), [30, 0, 20, 10])

They compose: the last call reads a permutation of a counting array. Each kind of array, and each composition, compiles its own version of the kernel, and the generated code is the expression you would write by hand. Nothing is looked up per element.

Array Value k VTK counterpart CountingArray(size, start, step) start + k * step vtkAffineArray ConstantArray(value, size) value vtkConstantArray Permutation(ids, base) base[ids[k]] vtkIndexedArray Concatenate(a, b, ...) from the part that holds k vtkCompositeArray View(base, start, size) base[start + k] Strided(values, stride, offset) values[offset + k * stride] vtkStridedArray Components(a, b, ...) a vector of a[k], b[k], ... ExtractComponent(base, c) component c of base[k] Function(func, size) func(k), a device function vtkStdFunctionArray Transform(func, base) func(base[k]) Cast(base, dtype) base[k] converted CartesianProduct(x, y, z), UniformCoordinates(...) grid points the points of a rectilinear grid or an image RandomUniform, RandomNormal random numbers

Arrays that wrap stored arrays can be written through. A store into a View or a Strided lands in the array it wraps, a store into a Permutation is a scatter, and Components writes each component to its own array. An implicit array is writable exactly when what it writes into is. A store into a computed array, such as a CountingArray, raises TypeError when the kernel compiles.

An implicit array is not a tack.Array, but it has numpy(), sum(), min(), max() and mean(), which compute its values first. Your own classes join this family by defining __getitem__ and __len__ as device functions, as Device classes shows.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Reductions. a.sum(), a.min(), a.max() and a.mean() reduce every number in an array, vector components included, and return a Python float. Reductions, scans and sorts covers them and the statistics in tack.algorithms.

Read-only arrays. An array that wraps memory Tack was given read-only, such as a read-only DLPack import, refuses tack.copyto and fill. A kernel call that passes it where the kernel may store raises ValueError before the kernel runs. Kernels read it normally.

Indexing in kernels. A kernel indexes an array with one index per dimension, grid[i, j], or one flat index in row-major order, grid[k]. Kernels has the details.

Storage. Storage is contiguous with no padding. Matrices store their rows one after another. a.scalar_dtype is the component type, a.storage_shape the shape with component axes, and a.layout is "aos" for interleaved arrays and "soa" for structure-of-arrays ones.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Kernels shows the loops that read and write these arrays.
  • Vectors and matrices shows what kernels can do with vector and matrix elements.

docs.title: Wait without blocking: asyncio
docs.text:
A program built on an event loop, such as a trame or web server or a Jupyter kernel, must not block the loop while a GPU works, or every other request waits too. Tack can wait for the device and read results back while the loop keeps running. Not every device waits off the loop, and the page says which ones do.

Two coroutines do the waiting in a worker thread, so the loop keeps running. await tack.sync_async() waits for the kernels launched so far, and await array.numpy_async() waits and then copies an array to NumPy:

import asyncio

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")     # "cuda", "metal", "hip" or "level_zero" on a GPU


@tack.kernel
def step(field, out, decay):
    for i in range(field.shape[0]):
        out[i] = field[i] * decay


async def frame(field, out):
    step(field, out, 0.5)                  # a plain call: queued on a GPU
    await tack.sync_async()                # the loop runs while the device works
    return await out.numpy_async()         # wait and copy, off the loop


async def heartbeat(ticks):
    for _ in range(3):
        ticks.append("tick")               # other work the loop keeps doing
        await asyncio.sleep(0)


async def main():
    field = tack.full(1000, 2.0)
    out = tack.empty_like(field)
    ticks = []
    values, _ = await asyncio.gather(frame(field, out), heartbeat(ticks))
    return values, ticks


values, ticks = asyncio.run(main())
np.testing.assert_allclose(values, 1.0)
assert ticks == ["tick"] * 3

docs.title: Why a read blocks the loop
docs.text:
On Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero a kernel call returns as soon as its launch is queued. The host waits only when it needs a result: when it reads an array with numpy(), indexes an element, reduces an array, or calls tack.sync(). Choose a device explains this queue.

Those waits block the thread that makes them. In an asyncio program that thread runs the event loop, so a 200 ms kernel followed by out.numpy() freezes the loop for 200 ms. The two coroutines move the wait to a thread of Tack's own, and resume your coroutine when the device is done.

Kernel calls stay plain calls. Queuing a launch takes microseconds, so there is nothing to await, and you call kernels from a coroutine as from any other code.

docs.title: Wait for the device
docs.text:
await tack.sync_async() is the asyncio form of tack.sync(). It waits until every kernel launched before the call, on every device, has finished.

  • Only earlier launches count. The point to wait for is fixed when you call it. Launches that this task or another makes while it waits are not waited for.
  • Errors arrive here. An error inside a queued launch is raised at the await, as tack.sync() would raise it. With several devices, Tack first waits for all of them, then raises the first error.

docs.title: Read an array without blocking
docs.text:
await a.numpy_async() is the asyncio form of a.numpy(). The wait for earlier launches and the copy both run in the worker thread. The result is a new NumPy array, as from numpy().

The result holds every write queued before the call. A write that another task queues while the read is in flight may or may not be in it, as with any read that runs beside writes. When one task needs another's result, order them with await: let the writer finish its launches, then start the read.

docs.title: Know which devices wait off the loop
docs.text:
device where the wait runs CUDA, HIP, Metal, Level Zero in a Tack worker thread; the loop keeps running CPU inline, and at once: CPU launches finish before the call returns Warp (prototype) inline: the loop waits

The same code is correct on every device. On the CPU there is nothing to wait for, so the coroutines return as soon as the copy is made. On Warp they block, as tack.sync() and numpy() would.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Tack's worker threads. The waits run in a pool of four threads that belong to Tack, named tack-wait, not in the loop's default executor. A busy or small default executor therefore cannot hold up a wait. More than four long waits at once queue behind each other, in order.
  • The interpreter lock. A worker thread releases Python's global interpreter lock while it waits in the driver, so the loop's other tasks run meanwhile. On CUDA, during a 490 ms kernel another task ran 436 times while one awaited sync_async, and not at all under tack.sync(). The backend implementations note has the measurements for each device.
  • GPU contexts. A worker thread makes the array's CUDA context or HIP device current itself, so you need no setup in the worker.
  • Blocking calls still work. tack.sync() and numpy() remain correct inside a coroutine. They just hold the loop while they wait.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Choose a device, for how launches are queued and when the host waits.
  • Share arrays, to hand results to another library without a copy.
  • The runtime API, for the exact behaviour of tack.sync and its asyncio form.

docs.title: Choose a device
docs.text:
A Tack program runs the same kernels on the CPU and on GPUs from Apple, NVIDIA, AMD and Intel. Once a first kernel works, the next question is where it runs. You pick a device, make it the default, and move arrays between devices. One program can also use several GPUs, ask a device what it supports, and know when a kernel call has finished.

A device is one CPU or one GPU, as a Python value. Every array lives on one device, and a kernel runs on the device its arrays live on:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def scale(x, out, factor):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = x[i] * factor


x = tack.arange(8, dtype=tack.f32)     # on the default device
out = tack.empty_like(x)               # on x's device
scale(x, out, 2.0)                     # runs where x and out are
assert str(x.device) == "cpu" and x.device == tack.get_default_device()
np.testing.assert_allclose(out.numpy(), np.arange(8) * 2.0)

# On a machine with a GPU, name it instead of the CPU:
#     tack.set_default_device("cuda")     # or "metal", "hip", "level_zero"
# and the same lines allocate on the GPU and run the kernel there.

The kernel's source does not change between devices. Tack compiles it for whichever device runs it, the first time it runs there.

docs.title: Name a device
docs.text:
tack.device(spec) returns the device that spec names. The spec is a string that names the kind of device and, for GPUs that come in numbers, which one:

spec device install extra "cpu" the CPU's cores, through LLVM cpu "metal" the GPU of an Apple silicon Mac metal "cuda", "cuda:1" an NVIDIA GPU cuda "hip", "hip:1" an AMD GPU, through ROCm hip "level_zero", "level_zero:1" an Intel GPU none: system libraries "warp" NVIDIA Warp's device (a prototype) warp

Each kind of device has its own backend: the code generator and runtime that compile kernels for it. Install Tack says what each extra needs.

Asking for the same device twice gives the same device. Its arrays and the kernels it has compiled are shared by everything that asks for it. Two devices compare equal when they are the same device, and str(device) gives its spec, such as "cuda:0".

Options make a separate device. The CPU takes num_threads, so tack.device("cpu", num_threads=1) is a second CPU device that runs every kernel on the calling thread. It shares memory with the default CPU device, so it can run kernels on CPU arrays made before it. An option a backend does not accept raises ValueError naming the ones it does.

docs.title: Set the default device
docs.text:
The default device is where arrays are allocated when you do not say, and where kernels with no array arguments run. Three calls control it:

  • tack.set_default_device("cuda") makes a device the default for the whole process, and returns it. With nothing set, the default is the CPU.
  • tack.get_default_device() returns the default device.
  • with tack.device("cuda"): makes a device the default inside the block, on the current thread only. Blocks nest, and the previous default returns when the block ends.

Every array constructor also takes device=, as a device or a spec. Every array records its device in a.device. The *_like constructors, such as tack.empty_like, allocate on their prototype's device.

Changing the default invalidates nothing. Arrays made before the change keep their device and keep working, and compiled kernels stay compiled.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def scale(x, out, factor):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = x[i] * factor


x = tack.arange(8, dtype=tack.f32)
out = tack.empty_like(x)

serial = tack.device("cpu", num_threads=1)
with serial:                        # the default inside the block
    y = tack.ones(8)                # allocated on serial
    scale(x, out, 3.0)              # serial can address CPU arrays: runs there
assert y.device == serial
assert tack.get_default_device() == tack.device("cpu")
assert x.to_device(serial) is x     # the same memory, so no copy
np.testing.assert_allclose(out.numpy(), np.arange(8) * 3.0)

docs.title: Know where a kernel runs
docs.text:
A kernel call runs on one device, chosen from its arguments:

  1. If the default device can address every array argument, the kernel runs there. This is why a one-thread CPU device made the default still runs kernels on arrays from the ordinary CPU device.
  2. Otherwise it runs on the arrays' own device. A CUDA array passed while the CPU is the default runs on its GPU.
  3. Arrays on two devices that cannot address each other's memory raise ValueError. Move one first.

a.to_device(d) moves an array. It returns the array itself when d can already address its memory, and otherwise a copy on d. Copies between two GPUs go through the host.

The array methods follow the same rule. Copies, reductions such as a.sum(), and the functions in tack.algorithms run on their input's device, whatever the default is.

docs.title: Use several GPUs
docs.text:
On a machine with several GPUs of one kind, tack.device_count("cuda") says how many there are, and tack.device("cuda:1") is the second one. The same holds for "hip" and "level_zero". The number is the one the vendor's runtime uses, so it agrees with PyTorch's numbering and with DLPack's. device_count makes no device, and it returns 0 where the backend cannot start.

A bare "cuda" or "hip" means the GPU the calling thread already uses. That is the one a framework embedding Tack has chosen, or else the first.

Each device compiles its own kernels, and the arrays of one kernel call must all be on one device. To split one problem over several GPUs, give each GPU its own arrays and launch on each. Tack's communication layer does this for you, over GPUs and over MPI ranks. See Blocks and worlds.

docs.title: Check what a device supports
docs.text:
Every backend runs the same kernel language, within what its hardware can do. A kernel that needs something a backend lacks is rejected with an error that names the kernel and the missing capability. It never runs with a different meaning.

CPU Metal CUDA HIP Level Zero Warp (prototype) f64 arrays yes no yes yes if the device has it yes Workgroups: shared memory, barriers, thread_id, block reductions no yes yes yes yes on a CUDA device Atomic array types all ten i32, u32, f32 32- and 64-bit integers, f32, f64 as CUDA i32, u32, f32 as CUDA sum, min, max on the device no: NumPy f32 f32 f32 f32 no: NumPy 3D textures in software in hardware in hardware in hardware if the device has images in hardware if the device has samplers no Iterations per launch no limit 2^32 max grid × 256 max grid × 256, at most 2^32 − 256 max group count × group size 2^31 − 1

A launch longer than its backend's limit raises ValueError naming the kernel, the count and the limit. Split such work over several calls.

In code, ask the backend rather than checking its name. backend_of takes a device, a spec, or None for the default device:

import tack
from tack.runtime.dispatch import backend_of

tack.set_default_device("cpu")
backend = backend_of(tack.get_default_device())
print(backend.name, backend.supports_f64, backend.supports_workgroups)
# cpu True False

assert backend.supports_f64 and not backend.supports_workgroups
assert tack.f64 in backend.supported_dtypes
assert tack.i64 in backend.supported_atomic_dtypes

Use this to choose between a GPU path and a portable one. The N-body tutorial runs a tiled kernel where supports_workgroups is true and a plain one elsewhere. The backend capability contract has the full matrix and what each capability rejects.

docs.title: Know when a call returns
docs.text:
On the CPU a kernel call returns when the kernel has finished. On Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero it returns as soon as the launch is queued, and the GPU runs queued launches in the order they were made. Fills and writes from the host take their place in that order too.

The host waits only when it needs a result. Reading an array waits for the launches before it: numpy(), np.asarray, indexing one element, a reduction such as a.sum(), and exporting through DLPack all wait. So does tack.sync(), which waits for every device, and device.synchronize(), which waits for one.

Most programs never call tack.sync(). You need it in two cases:

  • Timing. Without it, a GPU time measures only the queuing. See Debug and time a kernel.
  • Memory another library reads without Tack. Usually Tack handles this itself. See Share arrays.

Because launches are queued, an error inside a launch is raised at the next wait rather than at the call. In an asyncio program, the waits can run off the event loop. See Wait without blocking.

docs.title: Control the CPU's threads
docs.text:
The CPU backend compiles each kernel to native code through LLVM and runs it on a pool of worker threads, one per core. Spreading a launch over the workers costs a few microseconds, so the backend measures each kernel's cost per element and fans out only when the work is long enough to gain from it. Short launches run on the calling thread. The CPU threading design note explains how it decides.

Two settings change the thread count:

  • TACK_CPU_THREADS=4 in the environment sets it for the process.
  • tack.device("cpu", num_threads=4) makes a device with that many threads.

A count of 1 runs everything on the calling thread. That helps when profiling, and when Tack is embedded in a program that manages its own threads.

docs.title: Backend notes
docs.text:
CPU. The CPU has no workgroups, and Tack does not emulate them. A kernel that uses shared memory, a barrier, thread_id or a block reduction is rejected on the CPU before it compiles, even if that code would never run. For scratch storage private to each iteration, use tack.local_array, which works everywhere. See Use workgroups, atomics, textures and random numbers.

Metal. Apple silicon shares memory between the CPU and the GPU, but tack.array, tack.copyto and numpy() still copy values. To share storage, see Share arrays. Metal has no f64, so an f64 array cannot be made on it, and a kernel that computes in f64 is refused with the reason.

CUDA. Tack works in the GPU's primary context, the one the CUDA runtime, PyTorch, CuPy and Warp use. These libraries and Tack can therefore take turns on one thread in any order, and pass arrays to each other through DLPack. If an application already made another context current before Tack first used the GPU, Tack adopts that one instead.

Tack makes the context current on the thread that first asks for the device. Another thread that calls kernels needs the context current too. A thread on which PyTorch, CuPy or the CUDA runtime already used the GPU has it. Otherwise, in that thread, retain the primary context with cuDevicePrimaryCtxRetain and make it current with cuCtxSetCurrent, both from cuda.bindings.driver. Once a program uses two CUDA GPUs, Tack makes the right context current around every operation itself.

HIP. ROCm 7.0.2 and 7.1.1 can miscompile some integer code. Their compiler can evaluate a 64-bit signed comparison wrongly inside a long integer expression, and the kernel then returns a wrong value without an error. Use a ROCm release newer than 7.1 if you can. On 7.0 and 7.1, check integer-heavy kernels against the CPU. Go by the ROCm release, not by hiprtcVersion(), which reports 9.0 on 7.0.2.

AMD's CDNA GPUs, such as the MI300, have no texture hardware, and the MI200 cannot filter 3D textures linearly. On those, Tack samples 3D textures in software.

Level Zero. Some Intel GPUs have f64 and some do not. The backend asks the device when it starts. Atomics stay limited to i32, u32 and f32 even on a device with f64. Intel's Xe-HPC GPUs (Ponte Vecchio) have no texture samplers, so Tack samples 3D textures in software there.

A Level Zero pointer means something only in the context that allocated it. To share device arrays with VTK, start Tack with tack.interop.vtk.init_level_zero() instead of tack.set_default_device("level_zero"). It makes a device in VTK's context the default and returns it.

Warp (prototype). tack.device("warp") runs Tack kernels through NVIDIA Warp, on Warp's default device: its first CUDA GPU, else its CPU. Launches go on Warp's current stream, so a wp.ScopedStream around Tack calls applies. It lacks tack.inspect, 3D textures, device reductions, Tack's disk cache of compiled code, and launches of more than 2^31 − 1 iterations. Its interface may change.

docs.title: When a backend cannot start
docs.text:
If a backend's libraries are missing, tack.device() raises RuntimeError saying what is missing and how to install it:

RuntimeError: Cannot start the 'hip' device: missing dependency.
  No module named 'hip'
  Requires an AMD GPU with ROCm, plus hip-python; in a clone:
    pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[hip]'   (or: uv sync --extra hip)

If the device cannot be made, the previous default stays.

docs.title: Keeping an embedding program's default
docs.text: Set TACK_NO_REINIT=1 to make set_default_device keep the default once one is set. This is for programs that embed Tack beside other code that would set it again, such as an ANARI device sharing the process.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Share arrays with NumPy, PyTorch, CuPy and VTK, to bring data in and out without copying.
  • Debug and time a kernel, to measure what a device gains you.
  • The runtime API, for every argument and error of the device functions.

docs.title: Control flow and math
docs.text: Inside a kernel's parallel loop you write ordinary Python: conditions, loops and math. Each iteration can branch with if and conditional expressions, loop with for and while, and leave a loop with break or continue. That is enough for iterative per-element algorithms, such as Newton's method or a bounded search. The math functions are here too. So are the rules of integer and floating-point arithmetic, which tell you when a kernel gives the same answer as NumPy.

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
This kernel clamps each value to a range and counts the halvings that bring it below one. It uses an if, a while loop and a math function:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def clamp_and_halve(data, lo, hi, clamped, halvings):
    for i in range(len(data)):
        value = data[i]
        if value < lo:
            value = lo
        elif value > hi:
            value = hi
        clamped[i] = value

        count = 0
        v = abs(data[i])
        while v > 1.0 and count < 100:      # a cap keeps the loop bounded
            v = v * 0.5
            count += 1
        halvings[i] = count

data = tack.array(np.array([-3.0, 0.5, 9.0], np.float32))
clamped = tack.empty((3,))
halvings = tack.empty((3,), tack.i32)
clamp_and_halve(data, 0.0, 4.0, clamped, halvings)
assert clamped.numpy().tolist() == [0.0, 0.5, 4.0]
assert halvings.numpy().tolist() == [2, 0, 4]

Each iteration makes its own decisions. One iteration can take the if branch and loop four times while its neighbour does neither. On a GPU, iterations that run side by side but take different branches take longer than iterations that agree, so the cost of a branch depends on how often neighbours disagree. The result never does.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
if, elif and else work as in Python, and so do comparisons, chained comparisons such as 0 <= i < n, and and, or and not. A comparison has the value 1 when true and 0 when false.

A conditional expression, a if condition else b, evaluates only the arm it selects. and and or stop as soon as the answer is known, as in Python. Both are useful at the edges of an array, where reading past the end would be an error:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def differences(data, out):
    for i in range(len(data)):
        previous = data[i - 1] if i > 0 else data[i]     # no read of data[-1]
        out[i] = data[i] - previous

data = tack.array([1.0, 4.0, 9.0, 16.0])
out = tack.empty((4,))
differences(data, out)
assert out.numpy().tolist() == [0.0, 3.0, 5.0, 7.0]

Comparisons of vectors give one result per component. They need any or all to become a condition, as Vectors and matrices explains.

docs.title: Loops inside an iteration
docs.text:
Inside the parallel loop, for over a range and while run in order, within the iteration. range takes a start, an end and a step, and its bounds can be any value the iteration has, including values read from arrays. break leaves the nearest of these loops, and continue goes on to its next round.

A loop that stops when a calculation converges should also stop after a fixed number of rounds. A kernel cannot raise an exception from one iteration, so a value that never converges would otherwise keep its thread running:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def newton_sqrt(x, out, converged):
    for i in range(len(x)):
        value = x[i]
        guess = max(value, 1.0)
        done = 0
        if value == 0.0:
            guess = 0.0
            done = 1
        for step in range(30):                 # at most 30 rounds
            if done == 1:
                break
            better = 0.5 * (guess + value / guess)
            if abs(better - guess) <= 1e-6 * guess:
                done = 1
            guess = better
        out[i] = guess
        converged[i] = done                    # tell the host which converged

x = tack.array(np.array([0.0, 2.0, 9.0, 1e6], np.float32))
out = tack.empty((4,))
converged = tack.empty((4,), tack.i32)
newton_sqrt(x, out, converged)
np.testing.assert_allclose(out.numpy(), np.sqrt(x.numpy()), rtol=1e-6)
assert converged.numpy().all()

The converged array is how an iteration reports a failure: write a status and let host code decide what to do with it.

docs.title: Math functions
docs.text:
These functions work in kernels and device functions without importing anything. Writing from math import sqrt does no harm, and math.sqrt(x) works too.

Function Computes sqrt(x) Square root sin, cos, tan Trigonometric functions asin, acos, atan, atan2(y, x) Inverse trigonometric functions sinh, cosh, tanh Hyperbolic functions exp, exp2 e and 2 to a power log, log2, log10 Logarithms floor, ceil Rounding down and up abs Absolute value min(a, b, ...), max(a, b, ...) Smallest and largest of two or more values pow(base, exponent) Power, as base ** exponent

Each one compiles to the device's own math function. Given a vector, each applies to every component. A function computes in the precision of its argument: sqrt of an f64 is an f64. An integer argument is converted to f32 first.

Math functions have domains, and values outside them follow IEEE floating point: sqrt(-1.0) and log(-1.0) are NaN, and log(0.0) is minus infinity. Decide how your algorithm treats such values before you run it on large inputs.

docs.title: Helpers from shader languages
docs.text:
tack.math adds the small functions graphics and simulation code reaches for, with the definitions GLSL gives them:

Function Computes fract(x) x - floor(x) mix(x, y, a) x * (1 - a) + y * a clamp(x, lo, hi) min(max(x, lo), hi) saturate(x) clamp(x, 0, 1) step(edge, x) 0 below edge, 1 from it smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x) A smooth step from 0 to 1 between the edges sign(x) -1, 0 or 1 length(v), distance(a, b), normalize(v) A vector's length, a distance, a unit vector

They are device functions, so they work on scalars and vectors alike, and only kernels and other device functions can call them:

import numpy as np
import tack
from tack import math as tm

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def colour_map(data, colour):
    for i in range(len(data)):
        t = tm.clamp(data[i], 0.0, 1.0)
        colour[i] = tm.mix([0.1, 0.2, 0.8], [1.0, 0.8, 0.1], t)   # blue to yellow

data = tack.array([-1.0, 0.5, 2.0])
colour = tack.empty((3,), tack.vec3())
colour_map(data, colour)
np.testing.assert_allclose(colour.numpy()[1], [0.55, 0.5, 0.45], rtol=1e-6)

docs.title: How arithmetic behaves
docs.text:
Kernels compute in fixed-width types, as NumPy does, not with Python's unlimited integers. Most arithmetic gives what NumPy gives for the same types. These are the rules that surprise people:

Expression Result Why 7 / 2 3.5, an f32 / always divides as floating point -7 // 2 -4 // rounds down, as in Python -7 % 2 1 % takes the divisor's sign, as in Python int(-0.3) 0 int truncates toward zero int(floor(-0.3)) -1 floor rounds down first tack.i32(2147483647) + 1 -2147483648 Integers wrap at their width tack.u8(-1) 255 A cast keeps the low bits tack.i8(3) ** 5 -13 An integer power keeps the base's type, and wraps

Four of these need care in practice.

Division. Integer / gives an f32, even when you store it into an f64 array. For a double-precision quotient, cast first: tack.f64(a) / tack.f64(b). // and % on floats also round down and take the divisor's sign, like Python's.

Grid cells. To find the cell of a coordinate that can be negative, use int(floor(x)). int(x) maps both -0.3 and 0.3 to cell 0.

Wrapping. Integer +, - and * wrap at their type's width instead of growing. When two integer types meet, the result is a type that holds both ranges: i8 + u16 is i32, and i32 + u32 is i64. Mixing a signed type with u64 has no such type, so it needs an explicit cast. Use a typed constant, such as tack.constant(747796405, tack.u32), for arithmetic that must wrap at 32 bits.

Float literals. A literal such as 0.1 takes the precision of what it meets, as Python numbers do in NumPy. With an f64 array x, x[i] * 0.1 computes in f64 with the f64 nearest 0.1. Alone, or beside integers, a literal is f32. A local assigned a literal once, such as a = 0.1, behaves like the literal wherever it is read.

Floating-point results can differ between devices in their last bits. Each device has its own math library, and a compiler may fuse a multiply and an add within one expression into a single operation. No device reorders a sum or uses fast approximate math. Compare results across devices with a tolerance. The floating-point policy says exactly what is and is not guaranteed.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The kernel language contract has the complete rules. These details come up less often:

  • Shift counts must be at least zero and less than the type's width. A signed right shift copies the sign bit, and an unsigned one fills with zeros.
  • An integer divisor must not be zero. The smallest signed value divided by -1 is outside the defined domain too.
  • An integer power needs a non-negative exponent, and 0 ** 0 is 1. Cast the base to a float for negative powers: tack.f32(a) ** e.
  • Converting a float to an integer needs a finite value whose truncation fits the integer type.
  • Integer abs, min and max are exact. abs keeps its type, so the smallest signed value stays negative.
  • Floating min and max return the number when the other argument is NaN.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Device functions shows how to move a loop like Newton's method into a helper that several kernels share.
  • Vectors and matrices covers vector arithmetic, component masks and tack.select.

docs.title: Debug and time a kernel
docs.text:
A new kernel can give wrong values, crash, or run slower than it should. The first step is to check it against an independent reference, with a tolerance that suits the comparison. Debug mode then finds an index out of bounds, print shows values from inside a kernel, and the generated code shows what Tack made of your source. Timing comes last, measured so that the number means what you think.

The most common bug is an index one past the end of an array. Kernels do not check their indices, so the read quietly takes a neighbouring value. Debug mode checks every index and names the first bad one:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def forward_difference(a, out):
    for i in range(a.shape[0]):
        out[i] = a[i + 1] - a[i]           # reads a[n] at the last i


a = tack.array(np.arange(8, dtype=np.float32) ** 2)
out = tack.empty(8)

tack.set_debug(True)                       # or TACK_DEBUG=1 in the environment
try:
    forward_difference(a, out)
except IndexError as error:
    print(error)
    # Kernel 'forward_difference': a[i + 1] at ...: index 8 is outside [0, 8).
    # The access was skipped (a load gives 0).
    assert "a[i + 1]" in str(error) and "index 8 is outside [0, 8)" in str(error)
else:
    raise AssertionError("debug mode missed the bad index")
finally:
    tack.set_debug(False)

docs.title: Check a kernel against a reference
docs.text:
Start a new kernel with a small input and a result you can work out another way. Once the two agree, grow the problem and change the device. Taking these steps one at a time separates layout mistakes, unsupported operations and numerical differences, which look alike when they arrive together.

The first check should include the whole calculation: copying the input in, running the kernel, and reading the output back.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def transform(x, out):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = sqrt(abs(x[i]))


host_x = np.random.default_rng(42).normal(size=32).astype(np.float32)
x = tack.array(host_x)
out = tack.empty(32)
transform(x, out)

actual = out.numpy()
expected = np.sqrt(np.abs(host_x))
assert np.isfinite(actual).all()
np.testing.assert_allclose(actual, expected, rtol=2e-6, atol=1e-7)

Write the reference so that it states the mathematics directly. A second kernel with the same indexing would repeat the same mistake. For a stencil, a NumPy slice expression makes a good contrast with the kernel's loads one cell at a time. For a surface, check that its points lie near the level set they should and that its connectivity holds valid indices.

Every tutorial has such a check, which runs without its figure:

uv run python docs/examples/validate.py --arch cpu
uv run python docs/examples/validate.py --arch metal    # on an Apple GPU

The --arch you name must start. The checks never fall back to another device.

docs.title: Choose a tolerance
docs.text:
Compare small integer results exactly, where the arithmetic does not overflow. Floating-point results need a tolerance that allows for their precision, the order of their operations, and how sensitive the problem is.

np.testing.assert_allclose accepts an element when abs(actual - expected) <= atol + rtol * abs(expected). The absolute part matters near zero, where a relative tolerance alone accepts nothing. Keep the reference's element type explicit. An accidental float64 reference answers a different question than an f32 kernel does. For f32 inputs, a float64 reference measures the error that accumulates, but the f32 result will not match it in every bit.

Several things move the low bits legitimately:

  • Math functions such as sin and exp differ slightly between vendors' libraries.
  • A multiply and an add may be fused into one operation, which rounds once instead of twice.
  • Parallel floating-point sums by atomics can add in a different order from one run to the next.

A simulation can amplify such differences over many steps. Check an early step as well as the last, and check physical properties too, such as mass conservation, a residual or a temperature that stays in bounds.

Do not raise a tolerance to hide a difference. First rule out the usual causes: the array layout, the boundaries, initialization, conversions between types, and iterations that race on one element. Arrays and types covers the precision of literals and the integer rules, and Reductions, scans and sorts the precision of sums.

docs.title: Find an index out of bounds with debug mode
docs.text:
An index out of bounds usually shows as a crash, as wrong values near the edges of an array, or as garbage that moves when the input size changes. In a two-dimensional array, a[i, j + 1] at the last column reads the first element of the next row, so the result looks plausible.

Turn on debug mode with tack.set_debug(True), or with TACK_DEBUG=1 in the environment. TACK_DEBUG is read once, when Tack is imported. tack.set_debug(False) turns it off again.

In debug mode every array index is checked, one dimension at a time. An access out of bounds is skipped, so a load gives 0 and a store does nothing. After the launch, the call raises IndexError naming the first bad access, its source line, the index and the bounds:

IndexError: Kernel 'blur': a[i, j + 1] at blur.py:14, column 19: index 64 of
dimension 1 is outside [0, 64). The access was skipped (a load gives 0).
63 more out-of-bounds accesses in the launch were skipped too.

An access inside a device function names the function and its line. Debug mode works on every device. It is for finding bugs, not for timing. Kernels compile again with the checks, run slower, and every launch waits to finish.

docs.title: Print from a kernel
docs.text:
print works inside kernels on the CPU, CUDA and HIP. It is useful for a few iterations at a time:

import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def show(values):
    for i in range(values.shape[0]):
        if i < 2:
            print("value:", values[i])


show(tack.arange(8, dtype=tack.f32))
# value: 0.000000
# value: 1.000000

On Metal, print does nothing, since Metal has no printf. On CUDA and HIP launches are queued, so the output may appear only when the host next waits for the device. Remove print before timing. For a check that works on every device, write diagnostic values to an array and read it after the call.

docs.title: Read the generated code
docs.text:
tack.inspect compiles a kernel for the given arguments and returns the code as a string, without running it. Pass the real arguments, since their types and shapes decide what is compiled:

import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def transform(x, out):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = sqrt(abs(x[i]))


x = tack.ones(8)
out = tack.empty(8)
print(tack.inspect(transform, x, out, mode="ir"))
# Function transform(x, out):
#   ParallelFor i in [0, DimSize(x, 0)):
#     out[i] = sqrt(abs(x[i]))
source = tack.inspect(transform, x, out, mode="source")    # LLVM IR on the CPU
assert "define void" in source

There are three modes:

  • mode="ir" shows Tack's own intermediate form, the same on every device.
  • mode="source" shows what the device compiles: LLVM IR on the CPU, Metal Shading Language on Metal, CUDA C, HIP C, or OpenCL C on Level Zero.
  • mode="optimized" shows LLVM IR after LLVM's optimizations. It works on the CPU only.

Inspection applies the device's checks, so a kernel the device would reject is rejected here too, with the same message. Kernels says more about what specializes a kernel.

docs.title: Diagnose a failure by its symptom
docs.text: symptom look first at A name in device code is unknown pass the value as an argument or declare it with tack.constant; check the module the kernel was defined in An array has unexpected values or shape the NumPy shape and element type; whether it holds vectors or flat components Results change between runs two iterations storing to one element, a missing atomic, or floating-point sums by atomics Only boundary cells are wrong bounds, and the initialization of both time-step buffers: run in debug mode A crash, or garbage that moves with the input size an index out of bounds: run in debug mode The kernel is rejected on the CPU shared memory, barriers or thread_id, which need a GPU: see workgroups The kernel is rejected on Metal f64, an atomic on an unsupported type, or an array size not known when compiling Every call seems slow compilation, allocation in the loop, a read-back after every launch, or many small launches

docs.title: Time a kernel
docs.text:
Two things make a naive timing wrong. On a GPU, a kernel call returns once the launch is queued, so the clock must wait with tack.sync(). And the first call with new argument types compiles the kernel. Measure the first call and warm calls separately:

from time import perf_counter

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def transform(x, out):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = sqrt(abs(x[i]))


x = tack.array(np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=1_000_000).astype(np.float32))
out = tack.empty_like(x)                   # allocate outside the timed loop

start = perf_counter()
transform(x, out)                          # compiles, unless the disk cache has it
tack.sync()                                # wait for a queued GPU launch
first_call = perf_counter() - start

for _ in range(5):                         # let the CPU's threading settle
    transform(x, out)
tack.sync()

times = []
for _ in range(30):
    start = perf_counter()
    transform(x, out)
    tack.sync()
    times.append(perf_counter() - start)

print(f"first call {first_call * 1e3:.2f} ms, warm median {np.median(times) * 1e3:.3f} ms")
assert np.median(times) <= first_call

Keep the shape and element type fixed while you measure, since a new shape can compile a new variant. A variant is one compiled form of a kernel, for one set of argument types and shapes. On the CPU, the backend measures for itself whether worker threads help, and several warm calls let that settle. A run with one thread, tack.set_default_device("cpu", num_threads=1), separates the cost of the arithmetic from the cost of scheduling.

The first call in a process may find the kernel in Tack's disk cache rather than compile it. To time a cold compile, run with TACK_CACHE=off. See Keep compiled kernels between runs.

Measure the whole application separately, including the copies in, preprocessing, every kernel stage and the read-back, and say which costs a reported number includes. No speedup factor holds for every problem size and machine.

docs.title: Make it faster, in order
docs.text:
Try these in order, and measure after each:

  1. Keep intermediate data in Tack arrays, and read back only what you need, at checkpoints.
  2. Allocate working arrays once and reuse them. Swap time-step buffers instead of copying them.
  3. Combine independent operations on the same elements into one kernel, to save launches and temporary arrays. Keep stages that depend on each other's whole output in separate kernels.
  4. Once a measurement shows that memory traffic is the limit, consider tiling with shared memory. The N-body tutorial does this while keeping a path for the CPU.

Compare a change with identical inputs, device, shape and procedure, and run the numerical check again. The performance page records measurements of Tack against other tools.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• Debug mode and the cache. A kernel compiled in debug mode is a different kernel from the plain one. Switching modes never reuses the other's compiled code, in memory or on disk.
  • Metal source on disk. On Metal, TACK_DUMP_MSL=1 also writes each compiled kernel's source to /tmp. Other devices ignore it.
  • Compilation errors. A kernel that fails to compile reports its name, the device, and the relevant lines of the compiler's message, without the whole generated source.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Keep compiled kernels between runs, so a program's first call is fast.
  • Memory and parallel correctness, for the races behind results that change between runs.
  • The language contract, for exactly which numerical results are guaranteed.

docs.title: Device classes
docs.text:
A device class is a Python class whose objects kernels can take as arguments. An object bundles arrays, numbers and methods, and a kernel calls its methods as it would in Python. One object can replace a long list of kernel arguments. Objects of different classes let one kernel work with several data layouts. You choose which of an object's values are compiled in, and objects can hold other objects, be indexed like arrays, and have kernels as methods.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.device_class
class Stored:
    def __init__(self, values):
        self.values = values                # an array

    @tack.func
    def get(self, i):
        return self.values[i]

@tack.device_class
class Uniform:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value                  # a number

    @tack.func
    def get(self, i):
        return self.value

@tack.kernel
def add(a, b, out):
    for i in range(out.shape[0]):
        out[i] = a.get(i) + b.get(i)

x = tack.arange(5, dtype=tack.f32)
out = tack.empty((5,))
add(Stored(x), Uniform(10.0), out)
np.testing.assert_allclose(out.numpy(), [10, 11, 12, 13, 14])
add(Stored(x), Stored(x), out)
np.testing.assert_allclose(out.numpy(), [0, 2, 4, 6, 8])

add does not know whether a holds an array or a single number. Each combination of classes compiles to its own version of the kernel. In that version, a.get(i) is replaced by the method's body, so Uniform(10.0) costs no memory read at all.

docs.title: What an object brings to a kernel
docs.text:
Decorate the class with @tack.device_class and its methods with @tack.func. Tack recognizes the object by its type when you pass it, so the kernel's parameter needs no annotation. Tack then reads the object's attributes and turns each one into part of the kernel:

Attribute Example In the kernel a number on the class corners = 4 in the class body a constant, compiled in a number on the object self.nx = nx in __init__ a run-time argument an array on the object self.values = values an array argument a @tack.func method def get(self, i) inlined where it is called another device-class object self.base = base its attributes, in turn a @tack.func function self.profile = linear inlined where it is called

Inlining means that the method's body replaces each call when the kernel compiles. A method call therefore costs nothing at run time, and methods can call each other through self.

The specialization of a kernel is everything a compiled version depends on. For device classes, it includes which classes are passed, the values of their class constants, which functions their attributes hold, the element types of their arrays, and any array dimensions the kernel compiles in, as Kernels explains. A new combination compiles a new version. Run-time values, such as the numbers on an object, change nothing that is compiled, so new values reuse the compiled kernel.

docs.title: Choose constants or run-time values
docs.text:
Put a number on the class when the compiler needs it: a size, a count of corners, a fixed tile width. Put it on the object when it changes from call to call: a grid's dimensions, a coefficient, a threshold.

A size given to tack.local_array or tack.shared must be a constant, so it belongs on the class. This kernel averages the corner values of each cell of a structured grid of quadrilaterals. The corner count is a class constant, and the grid's dimensions are run-time values:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.device_class
class QuadGrid:
    corners = 4                                    # on the class: compiled in

    def __init__(self, nx, ny):
        self.nx, self.ny = nx, ny                  # on the object: run-time values

    @tack.func
    def point(self, cell, k):                      # corner k of a cell, counterclockwise
        i = cell % self.nx + (1 if k == 1 or k == 2 else 0)
        j = cell // self.nx + (1 if k >= 2 else 0)
        return i + (self.nx + 1) * j

@tack.kernel
def cell_average(cells, point_values, cell_values):
    for c in range(cell_values.shape[0]):
        ids = tack.local_array(tack.i32, cells.corners)    # needs a constant size
        total = 0.0
        for k in range(cells.corners):
            ids[k] = cells.point(c, k)
            total += point_values[ids[k]]
        cell_values[c] = total / cells.corners

for nx, ny in [(3, 2), (5, 4)]:                    # one compiled kernel for both grids
    point_values = tack.arange((nx + 1) * (ny + 1), dtype=tack.f32)
    cell_values = tack.empty((nx * ny,))
    cell_average(QuadGrid(nx, ny), point_values, cell_values)
    p = np.arange((nx + 1) * (ny + 1)).reshape(ny + 1, nx + 1)
    expected = (p[:-1, :-1] + p[:-1, 1:] + p[1:, :-1] + p[1:, 1:]) / 4
    np.testing.assert_allclose(cell_values.numpy(), expected.ravel())

The loop range(cells.corners) compiles to range(4), which the compiler can unroll. The two grid sizes reuse one compiled kernel, because nx and ny are run-time values.

A tuple works the same way, one number per entry. On the object, self.shape = (nx, ny) gives two run-time values, read as obj.shape[0] and obj.shape[1]. On the class, tile = (4, 4) gives two constants. The index must be a literal number, and len(obj.shape) is a constant.

docs.title: Write kernels as methods
docs.text:
A kernel can be a method of the class. Called on an object, it receives the object as self, so it reaches the object's arrays, numbers and methods with nothing passed in. This rasterizer draws a triangle into an RGB image:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.device_class
class Rasterizer:
    def __init__(self, n, width, height):
        self.n = n
        self.width, self.height = width, height
        self.vertices = tack.empty((n, 3), tack.vec2())
        self.pixels = tack.zeros((height, width), tack.vec3())

    @staticmethod
    @tack.func
    def edge(p, a, b):                     # uses nothing of the object
        return (p.x - a.x) * (b.y - a.y) - (p.y - a.y) * (b.x - a.x)

    @tack.func
    def inside(self, p, t):
        a, b, c = self.vertices[t, 0], self.vertices[t, 1], self.vertices[t, 2]
        return self.edge(p, a, b) >= 0.0 and self.edge(p, b, c) >= 0.0 \
            and self.edge(p, c, a) >= 0.0

    @tack.kernel
    def draw(self, shade):
        for row, column in tack.ndindex(self.height, self.width):
            for t in range(self.n):
                if self.inside([column + 0.5, row + 0.5], t):
                    self.pixels[row, column] = [shade, shade, shade]

raster = Rasterizer(1, 32, 32)
tack.copyto(raster.vertices, np.array([[[8, 8], [8, 24], [24, 8]]], dtype=np.float32))
raster.draw(0.8)
image = raster.pixels.numpy()
np.testing.assert_allclose(image[10, 10], [0.8, 0.8, 0.8])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(image[0, 0], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0])

raster.draw(0.8) is the same call as Rasterizer.draw(raster, 0.8). The kernel compiles once per class and is shared by all its objects. A device function that needs nothing from the object can be a @staticmethod. Put @staticmethod above @tack.func, and call it through self as usual.

docs.title: Derive classes and hold functions
docs.text:
A device class can derive from another. The subclass has its base's methods and class constants, and it may override either. A class can also hold a device function as an attribute and call it, which lets one class work with several interchangeable functions.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.device_class
class Fluid:
    rho_0 = 1000.0

    def __init__(self, stiffness):
        self.stiffness = stiffness

    @tack.func
    def pressure(self, rho):
        return self.stiffness * (rho / self.rho_0 - 1.0)

@tack.device_class
class Tait(Fluid):
    gamma = 7.0

    @tack.func
    def pressure(self, rho):                       # overrides Fluid.pressure
        return self.stiffness * ((rho / self.rho_0) ** self.gamma - 1.0)

@tack.kernel
def pressures(fluid, rho, p):
    for i in range(rho.shape[0]):
        p[i] = fluid.pressure(rho[i])

rho = tack.array(np.array([1000.0, 1010.0], dtype=np.float32))
p = tack.empty((2,))
pressures(Tait(100.0), rho, p)
np.testing.assert_allclose(p.numpy(), [0.0, 100 * (1.01**7 - 1)], rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-5)

@tack.func
def linear(r):
    return 1.0 - r

@tack.func
def quadratic(r):
    return (1.0 - r) * (1.0 - r)

@tack.device_class
class Smoothing:
    def __init__(self, profile, h):
        self.profile = profile                     # a device function
        self.h = h

    @tack.func
    def weight(self, r):
        return self.profile(r / self.h)

@tack.kernel
def weights(smoothing, r, w):
    for i in range(r.shape[0]):
        w[i] = smoothing.weight(r[i])

r = tack.array(np.array([0.0, 0.5], dtype=np.float32))
w = tack.empty((2,))
weights(Smoothing(linear, 1.0), r, w)
np.testing.assert_allclose(w.numpy(), [1.0, 0.5])
weights(Smoothing(quadratic, 1.0), r, w)
np.testing.assert_allclose(w.numpy(), [1.0, 0.25])

Which function an attribute holds is part of the specialization, like a class constant. Smoothing(linear, ...) and Smoothing(quadratic, ...) each compile once.

docs.title: Put objects inside objects
docs.text:
An object may hold other device-class objects as attributes, to any depth. Its methods reach theirs through the attribute, as in self.base.get(k), and a kernel can reach in too, as in arr.base.step.

flowchart LR
    K["kernel read(arr, out)"] --> P["Permuted<br/>ids: array"]
    P -- "base" --> C["Counting<br/>start, step: numbers"]
import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.device_class
class Counting:
    def __init__(self, start, step):
        self.start, self.step = start, step

    @tack.func
    def get(self, k):
        return self.start + self.step * k

@tack.device_class
class Permuted:
    def __init__(self, ids, base):
        self.ids = ids                             # an array of indices
        self.base = base                           # any object with get(k)

    @tack.func
    def get(self, k):
        return self.base.get(self.ids[k])

@tack.kernel
def read(arr, out):
    for i in range(out.shape[0]):
        out[i] = arr.get(i)

ids = tack.array(np.array([4, 3, 2, 1, 0], dtype=np.int32))
out = tack.empty((5,))
read(Permuted(ids, Counting(10.0, 5.0)), out)          # out[i] = 10 + 5 * ids[i]
np.testing.assert_allclose(out.numpy(), [30, 25, 20, 15, 10])
read(Permuted(ids, Permuted(ids, Counting(0.0, 1.0))), out)
np.testing.assert_allclose(out.numpy(), [0, 1, 2, 3, 4])

The whole tree is one argument. Every object's arrays and numbers become kernel arguments, every class constant is compiled in, and every method is inlined. So Permuted(ids, Counting(10.0, 5.0)) compiles to 10 + 5 * ids[i], the code you would write by hand. Which classes the tree holds, and where, is part of the specialization. New values reuse the compiled kernel, while another nesting compiles anew.

docs.title: Pass objects to device functions
docs.text: A device-class object, or one it holds, can be passed to a @tack.func or to another object's method. The callee then uses it as it would use self, so mean_of_two(arr, k) may call arr.get(k) or index arr[k]. Each such call gets its own copy of the callee with the object built in, so it costs nothing at run time. A method may pass on self, as in helper(self, k), or a held object, as in helper(self.base, k). The callee cannot keep the object in a local variable or return it. The indexable example below passes an object to a device function.

docs.title: Make objects indexable
docs.text:
A class becomes indexable in kernels when it defines Python's indexing methods as device functions: __getitem__ to read, __setitem__ to store and __len__ for len. A kernel then indexes the object as it would an array, and the same kernel accepts both:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.device_class
class Ramp:
    def __init__(self, n, start, step):
        self.n, self.start, self.step = n, start, step

    @tack.func
    def __getitem__(self, k):
        return self.start + self.step * k

    @tack.func
    def __len__(self):
        return self.n

@tack.func
def mean_of_two(arr, k):                           # arr: an array or an object
    return 0.5 * (arr[k] + arr[k + 1])

@tack.kernel
def midpoints(a, out):
    for i in range(len(a) - 1):
        out[i] = mean_of_two(a, i)

out = tack.empty((4,))
midpoints(tack.arange(5, dtype=tack.f32), out)     # a stored array
np.testing.assert_allclose(out.numpy(), [0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5])
midpoints(Ramp(5, 1.0, 0.5), out)                  # an indexable object
np.testing.assert_allclose(out.numpy(), [1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 2.75])

@tack.device_class
class Image:
    def __init__(self, values, nx, ny):
        self.values = values
        self.shape = (nx, ny)                      # two run-time values

    @tack.func
    def __getitem__(self, k):                      # k is a vector of two indices
        return self.values[k[0] + self.shape[0] * k[1]]

    @tack.func
    def __setitem__(self, k, v):
        self.values[k[0] + self.shape[0] * k[1]] = v

@tack.kernel
def bump(image):
    for i, j in tack.ndindex(image.shape[0], image.shape[1]):
        image[i, j] += float(i + 10 * j)

values = tack.zeros((6,))
bump(Image(values, 3, 2))
np.testing.assert_allclose(values.numpy(), [0, 1, 2, 10, 11, 12])

The two calls of midpoints compile to two versions of one kernel. One reads the array directly, and the other inlines __getitem__. Nothing in the kernel marks a as either.

Several indices, as in image[i, j], arrive as one vector, so __getitem__(self, k) reads k[0] and k[1]. image[i, j] = v calls __setitem__. image[i, j] += v calls __getitem__ and then __setitem__, and evaluates the index once. len(obj) may be the parallel loop's bound; it is evaluated when the kernel launches, like an array's length. An object held by another is indexed the same way, as in self.base[k].

The implicit arrays of tack.arrays are built this way, which is why every kernel can index them. See Arrays and types.

docs.title: Loop over an object
docs.text:
A class can say what a loop over it runs through. __tack_iterate__ names one to three of its numbers on the object, fastest first, and a kernel then loops over the object itself:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.device_class
class Grid:
    __tack_iterate__ = ("nx", "ny")

    def __init__(self, nx, ny):
        self.nx, self.ny = nx, ny

    @tack.func
    def flat(self, c):
        return c[0] + self.nx * c[1]

@tack.kernel
def label(cells, out):
    for c in cells:                                # c[0] runs fastest
        out[cells.flat(c)] = 100 * c[1] + c[0]

out = tack.empty((6,), tack.i32)
label(Grid(3, 2), out)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(out.numpy(), [0, 1, 2, 100, 101, 102])

With one name, for c in cells is for c in range(cells.nx), and c is an integer. With two or three names, it is a tack.ndindex over them, and c is the vector of indices with c[0] running fastest. As the kernel's parallel loop, it launches in that shape, so recovering the indices costs no division. Because the object's methods receive c as it comes, one kernel can serve a class that loops in one dimension and another that loops over a grid.

docs.title: Organize an application around state
docs.text:
Use a device class when several kernels share the same arrays and parameters. The Physarum tutorial gathers its agents' positions and headings into one object, initializes them with a kernel written as a method, and passes the object to three simulation stages. Class constants describe the sensing model, and the object's numbers and arrays describe one particular simulation.

The QuadGrid example above shows the other common use: one algorithm, several storage layouts. A second class with the same point method, reading an explicit connectivity array, would run the same cell_average kernel on an unstructured mesh. See also Data, whose mesh views follow this pattern.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Instance numbers that shadow class constants. A number set on the object with the same name as a class constant replaces it, and stays compiled in. Setting anything other than a number under that name removes the constant, as a subclass attribute does.

Allocation sizes. A run-time value as a tack.local_array size may compile on the CPU, but GPU compilers refuse it. Use a class constant, a literal, a tack.constant or an array dimension so the kernel runs on every device.

Function attributes. Assigning another function to an existing object's attribute takes effect at the next call, which compiles a version for it if needed.

Rules for nesting. An object may not hold itself, directly or through others.

Rules for indexable objects. A store into an object without __setitem__ is refused when the kernel compiles. So is an atomic on an indexable object, which has no memory of its own to update. The methods run only in kernels. On the host, Python calls __len__ to decide whether an object is true, so test an indexable object with is None, not if obj:.

Define classes once. Define device classes at module level. A class defined inside a function is a new class on every call, so each call compiles anew. Its compiled versions are released when the class is garbage-collected.

Host cost. Each call walks the object tree on the host to gather its arguments. Each level of nesting adds a few microseconds to a call, about 4 µs a level on the CPU backend of an M1 Max. The compiled code pays nothing. Specialization and caching explains what a call costs and why.
