docs.text:
• Reductions, scans and sorts are the library algorithms that accept arrays and indexable objects alike.
  • Memory and parallel correctness explains what kernels may safely read and write when many iterations run at once.
  • The Physarum tutorial builds a whole simulation around one device class.

docs.title: Device functions
docs.text: When the same few lines appear in several kernels, move them into a device function. A device function is a helper that kernels call, a Python function decorated with @tack.func. Tack inlines it into every kernel that calls it, so splitting a kernel into named pieces costs nothing at run time. A device function can return several values, take arrays and use small scratch arrays. Helpers can live in modules of their own and be shared between kernels.

docs.title: Write a device function
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.func
def lerp(a, b, t):
    return a + t * (b - a)

@tack.kernel
def blend(src, dst, out, t):
    for i in range(len(out)):
        out[i] = lerp(src[i], dst[i], t)

src = tack.zeros((4,))
dst = tack.array([4.0, 8.0, 12.0, 16.0])
out = tack.empty((4,))
blend(src, dst, out, 0.25)
assert out.numpy().tolist() == [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]

Tack inlines a device function: when it compiles blend, it copies the body of lerp into the kernel in place of the call. There is no call at run time, so splitting a kernel into helpers costs nothing.

Because it is inlined, a device function takes the types of the values each call passes. The same lerp works on f32 and f64 numbers, on integers, and on vectors, compiled separately for each. Calling a device function from Python, outside a kernel, raises RuntimeError. Write a NumPy version for host code when you need one, which also makes a good reference to test against.

A device function contains what a kernel's loop body can contain: arithmetic, conditions, loops, math functions, and calls to other device functions. It may return early, outside a loop:

@tack.func
def side(x):
    if x < 0.0:
        return -1
    return 1

Every return of a function must give values of the same kind: all scalars of compatible types, or all vectors of one width.

docs.title: Return several values
docs.text:
A device function can return a tuple, which the caller unpacks:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.func
def to_cartesian(r, theta):
    return r * cos(theta), r * sin(theta)

@tack.kernel
def convert(r, theta, x, y):
    for i in range(len(r)):
        x[i], y[i] = to_cartesian(r[i], theta[i])

r = tack.array([1.0, 2.0])
theta = tack.array(np.array([0.0, np.pi / 2], np.float32))
x, y = tack.empty((2,)), tack.empty((2,))
convert(r, theta, x, y)
np.testing.assert_allclose(x.numpy(), [1.0, 0.0], atol=1e-6)
np.testing.assert_allclose(y.numpy(), [0.0, 2.0], atol=1e-6)

The values can be scalars, vectors and matrices in any mix, and the targets can be local variables or array elements. A ray tracer's hit function might return a distance, a normal and a colour:

@tack.func
def closest_hit(origin, direction):
    ...
    return distance, normal, colour          # a scalar and two 3-vectors

@tack.kernel
def shade(origins, directions, depth, normals):
    for i in range(len(depth)):
        depth[i], normals[i], colour = closest_hit(origins[i], directions[i])

A device function may return another call's result as it is, with return closest_hit(o, d). A local name may hold such a result until it is unpacked, as in hit = closest_hit(o, d) and then depth, normal, colour = hit. Using that name as a single value raises UnsupportedSyntaxError.

docs.title: Call device functions from device functions
docs.text:
Device functions call each other, to any depth, and all of it is inlined into the kernel:

@tack.func
def square(x):
    return x * x

@tack.func
def length3(x, y, z):
    return sqrt(square(x) + square(y) + square(z))

Tack finds the function a call names the way Python would, at the place the call is written. So you can import a device function from another module, call it as module.function, or import it under another name, and two modules can each define a square without interfering. A device function defined inside another Python function, and returned from it, works too.

Tack resolves these names the first time it compiles the kernel, and the compiled kernel keeps the inlined body. Binding a name to a different function afterwards does not change a kernel already compiled. Make the kernel again to pick up the change.

docs.title: Pass arrays
docs.text:
A device function can take arrays and index them as a kernel does. The array is the caller's array, not a copy, so a store through it changes the caller's data:

@tack.func
def load_or(data, i, default):
    value = default
    if 0 <= i < len(data):
        value = data[i]
    return value

Vectors and matrices, in contrast, are passed as values. Changing a vector argument inside the function changes the function's copy only.

A device function can also take a texture and sample it, and a device class and call its methods. See Workgroups, atomics, textures and random numbers for textures.

docs.title: Use small scratch arrays
docs.text:
Sometimes one iteration needs a few values at a time: the weights of a cell's points, or a short list to sort. tack.local_array(dtype, size) gives each iteration a small array of its own. On a GPU it lives in the thread's registers or private memory, and on the CPU on the thread's stack. Its values are not set, so write each element before reading it.

Pass a local array to a device function, and the function fills it in place. That lets a helper produce several values at once without returning them:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

ORDER = tack.constant(4)

@tack.func
def powers(w, x):                       # fills w with 1, x, x**2, x**3
    p = 1.0
    for k in range(ORDER):
        w[k] = p
        p *= x

@tack.kernel
def polynomial(x, coefficients, out):
    for i in range(len(x)):
        w = tack.local_array(tack.f32, ORDER)
        powers(w, x[i])
        total = 0.0
        for k in range(ORDER):
            total += coefficients[k] * w[k]
        out[i] = total

x = tack.array([0.0, 1.0, 2.0])
coefficients = tack.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0])     # 1 + x**3
out = tack.empty((3,))
polynomial(x, coefficients, out)
assert out.numpy().tolist() == [1.0, 2.0, 9.0]

The size must be known when the kernel compiles. It can be a literal, a tack.constant, a device class's class constant, or an expression of these and the array dimensions the kernel reads, such as 2 * data.shape[1]. A scalar argument cannot be a size, because its value is known only at the launch. Keep local arrays small, a few dozen elements at most: a GPU has little private memory per thread.

tack.local_array_like(array, size) makes a local array of array's element type, so one kernel serves f32 and f64 inputs:

PAIR = tack.constant(2)


@tack.kernel
def row_energy(data, out):
    for row in range(data.shape[0]):
        scratch = tack.local_array_like(data, PAIR * data.shape[1])
        for column in range(data.shape[1]):
            x = data[row, column]
            scratch[PAIR * column] = x
            scratch[PAIR * column + 1] = x * x
        total = 0.0
        for column in range(PAIR * data.shape[1]):
            total += scratch[column]
        out[row] = total

Here the size, PAIR * data.shape[1], depends on the input's width, so an input of another width compiles another version of the kernel.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
What a device function cannot do, each refused with UnsupportedSyntaxError when the kernel compiles:

  • return inside a loop. Record the result in a local variable, break, and return after the loop.
  • Call itself, directly or through another function. Rewrite the recursion as a loop, with a local array as the stack if it needs one.
  • Call an ordinary Python function, or a function passed in as an argument. Every call must name a @tack.func that Tack can find when it compiles.
  • Read a Python variable from around it. As for kernels, use tack.constant for fixed values, and arguments for everything else.

Device classes take this further: an object whose methods are device functions, whose arrays and parameters kernels read, and whose class constants are compiled in.

docs.text:

  • Device classes groups device functions with the data they work on.

docs.title: Core examples
docs.text:
These six tutorials each build a complete program with Tack's core: arrays, kernels, device functions and classes, atomics, scans and workgroups. Once a first kernel works, they show the pieces working together in a real program. Each one opens with the question it answers, develops the program from its data layout to its host loop, and ends with a check of the result. None needs datasets or visualization.

Every tutorial runs on the CPU and on any GPU, and checks itself against an independent reference:

uv run python docs/examples/heat.py --arch cpu --check
uv run python docs/examples/heat.py --arch cuda --check      # or metal, hip, level_zero

docs.title: Heat diffusion on a plate
docs.text: How do you step a simulation on a grid, when each cell's new value depends on its neighbours' old ones? Two hot spots on a cold plate spread and fade. Each time step is one stencil kernel that reads an old array and writes a new one, and the host swaps the two between steps. This is the first simulation to read: it needs only kernels and two-dimensional arrays. Read the tutorial.

docs.title: Advecting coloured dye
docs.text: How do you move a field through a flow, sampling between grid points? A blob of coloured dye rotates in a velocity field. Every output cell traces back along the flow to where its colour came from and interpolates the old colours there. It uses arrays of RGB vectors and a device function for the interpolation. Read the tutorial.

docs.title: Agents that follow a trail
docs.text: How do many agents read and write one shared grid without racing each other? Agents sense a trail, turn toward it, move, and deposit more of it, while the trail diffuses and fades. The agents are a device class, their starting places and turns come from random numbers, and their deposits are atomic adds. Moving, depositing and diffusing are separate kernels, so no kernel reads the trail while another writes it. Read the tutorial.

docs.title: Marching squares: count, scan, write
docs.text: How does a kernel write an output whose size it does not know in advance, in a fixed order? A contour of a circle comes out of a grid of samples, with zero, one or two segments per cell. One kernel counts each cell's segments, an exclusive scan turns the counts into offsets, and a second kernel writes each cell's segments at its offset. The pattern fits any output with a count known per input item. It uses a scan and local arrays. Read the tutorial.

docs.title: A particle-to-grid simulation
docs.text: How do particles hand their momentum to a grid and take it back? A block of fluid falls under gravity, simulated with the material point method. Particles carry the material's state, and a temporary grid exchanges momentum between them each step. It uses arrays of 2×2 matrices, weights over a 3×3 stencil, and atomic adds into a two-dimensional grid. Read the tutorial.

docs.title: Tiled N-body forces
docs.text: How do GPU threads share data through fast memory, while the same program still runs on the CPU? Each body sums the gravitational pull of every other body. A plain kernel does it on every device. A tiled kernel loads positions into shared memory 256 at a time and uses barriers, and the program picks it on devices with workgroups. Read the tutorial.

docs.title: Run the tutorials
docs.text:
Each script is shown in full at the end of its tutorial and can be downloaded from there. Run them from the repository root, after installing Tack from source:

  • --arch names the device: cpu, metal, cuda, hip or level_zero. The device must start. The scripts never fall back to another.
  • --check runs a smaller problem and compares it with a NumPy reference or with properties the answer must have. It is a correctness check, not a benchmark.
  • --output heat.png saves the tutorial's figure. Figures need VTK, which uv sync --extra interop installs, or add it for one run with uv run --with vtk python docs/examples/heat.py --output heat.png.

uv run python docs/examples/validate.py --arch cpu runs every tutorial's check on one device. The figures on this page were made on the CPU. A GPU draws the same pictures, though its numbers can differ in the low bits, as Debug and time a kernel explains.

The heat example adapts one of Tack's own examples. Dye, the trail-following agents, marching squares and MPM adapt public Taichi examples, and N-body adapts NVIDIA Warp's tile example. Each tutorial links its original and says what it changed. The adapted Taichi and Warp scripts keep their Apache-2.0 license, and the others use Tack's BSD-3-Clause license. See the notices.

docs.text:

  • Debug and time a kernel, to check and measure your own version of a tutorial.
  • For examples on meshes and fields, see the Visualization layer's examples.

docs.title: How a Tack program runs
docs.text: A Tack program is a Python program in which some functions are compiled for a device. Turning NumPy code into such a program raises a few questions. Which parts run on the device, and which in Python? How does a calculation split into kernels, and in what order does the device run them? Why is one call slow, because it compiles, when the next is fast? The answers shape how you write a simulation's time loop and give a kernel the values it needs.

docs.title: Host code and device code
docs.text:
A program has two kinds of code. Host code is ordinary Python. It makes arrays, prepares input with NumPy, decides which kernels to call, runs the time loop and reads the results. Device code is the body of a @tack.kernel function, or of a @tack.func function a kernel calls. Tack reads that source and compiles it for the device. On the CPU, device code is compiled too. It does not run in the Python interpreter.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel                                   # device code: compiled
def scale(x, out, factor):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = factor * x[i]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)                 # host code: Python and NumPy
values = rng.random(1000, dtype=np.float32)
x = tack.array(values)
out = tack.empty_like(x)
for factor in (0.5, 2.0):
    scale(x, out, factor)                      # one launch per call
    assert np.allclose(out.numpy(), factor * values)

Device code is a part of Python made for numbers. It has arithmetic, if, for and while, math functions, small vectors and matrices, and calls to other device functions. It has no Python objects, lists or dictionaries, no NumPy calls and no file operations. Do those in host code and hand the kernel arrays. Kernels and Control flow and math describe what device code can contain. The kernel language contract gives the exact rules.

Task In host code In device code Make storage tack.empty, tack.zeros, tack.array Small scratch arrays with tack.local_array Read values a.numpy(), or a[i] for one element a[i], grid[row, column] Write values tack.copyto(a, values), a.fill(value) a[i] = value Repeat work A Python loop that calls kernels One parallel for per kernel, with ordinary loops inside Reuse code A Python function A @tack.func function Wait for the device tack.sync(); reading an array also waits Not needed

docs.title: A call is one launch over a range
docs.text:
A kernel has exactly one parallel loop: a for directly in its body. Calling the kernel launches it. The device runs every iteration of that loop, each on its own thread on a GPU, or spread over the cores on a CPU. Iterations run in any order, and many at once.

That is why each iteration must write its own outputs. In the first example, iteration i writes out[i] and nothing else, so no order of the iterations gives a different answer. Two iterations that write the same element, or one that reads what another writes, give answers that depend on timing. Memory and parallel correctness shows the patterns that stay correct: one writer per output, reading neighbours from a separate array, and gathering instead of scattering.

Loops inside the parallel loop are ordinary loops. They run in order, within one iteration. A row sum gives each row an iteration and walks the columns inside it:

@tack.kernel
def row_sums(matrix, sums):
    for row in range(matrix.shape[0]):         # parallel: one iteration a row
        total = 0.0
        for column in range(matrix.shape[1]):  # in order, within the row
            total += matrix[row, column]
        sums[row] = total

A local variable such as total belongs to its iteration. It does not carry values between iterations.

docs.title: Split dependent stages into separate kernels
docs.text:
Many calculations have stages: compute every force from the current positions, then move every particle. The second stage needs the first one finished everywhere. Within one launch nothing guarantees that, because the iterations run in any order. Put each stage in its own kernel and call them in order:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def compute_force(pos, force):
    for i in range(pos.shape[0]):
        force[i] = -pos[i]                     # a spring pulling toward zero

@tack.kernel
def integrate(pos, vel, force, dt):
    for i in range(pos.shape[0]):
        vel[i] += dt * force[i]
        pos[i] += dt * vel[i]

n = 1000
pos = tack.array(np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, n, dtype=np.float32))
vel = tack.zeros((n,))
force = tack.empty((n,))

for step in range(100):                        # Python runs the time loop
    compute_force(pos, force)
    integrate(pos, vel, force, 0.01)

assert np.abs(pos.numpy()).max() < 1.0          # every particle swung back

Tack keeps calls in program order. Each launch sees everything the launches before it wrote. Each host access to an array, such as numpy(), tack.copyto, reading one element or a sum, sees everything launched before it. So integrate sees the whole force array, and the check after the loop sees the last step.

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Python
    participant D as Device
    P->>D: compute_force (queued)
    P->>D: integrate (queued)
    Note over P: Python continues at once on a GPU
    D->>D: runs the launches in order
    P->>D: pos.numpy()
    D-->>P: waits for the launches, then copies

On the CPU, a call returns when the kernel has finished. On a GPU, a call returns as soon as the launch is queued, and Python goes on while the device works. Reading an array waits for the launches before it. The program above behaves the same either way, and you manage no streams or events. Call tack.sync() to wait for every launch on every device. You need it to time a kernel, and when another library reads memory Tack wrote. Choose a device says how each device queues and waits, and Wait without blocking shows how to wait from an asyncio event loop.

GPU programmers may know tack.barrier(), which waits for the other threads of one workgroup. It does not wait for the whole launch, so it cannot replace a second kernel. See Workgroups, atomics, textures and random numbers.

docs.title: Give a kernel the values it needs
docs.text:
A kernel sees only its arguments, the constants you declare, and the device functions it calls. It does not see the Python variables around it. Reading a module-level gravity = 9.8 in a kernel raises NameError, with the line and a suggestion. Choose how to supply each value by how often it changes:

Kind of value How to supply it Example A number that changes between calls A scalar argument integrate(pos, vel, force, dt) A number fixed for the program tack.constant GRAVITY = tack.constant(9.8) State the kernels read and write An array argument positions, a grid, a counter Several arrays and parameters that belong together A device class a particle system object

A scalar argument is a runtime value: a new value runs the same compiled code. A constant is compiled in, like a literal. Rebinding its Python name later does not change a kernel already compiled. Kernels shows constants, and Device classes shows how an object gathers arrays and parameters for a solver.

docs.title: What compiles once and what compiles again
docs.text:
The first call of a kernel compiles it, and later calls reuse the compiled code. Tack keeps one compiled form, a variant, for each combination of the things the generated code depends on. A call that differs in one of them compiles another variant. A call that differs only in values reuses one.

Compiles a new variant Reuses the variant An array of another element type (f32 to f64, f32 to vec3) New values in the same arrays An argument that was a scalar becomes an array, or the reverse A new scalar value of the same type A scalar of another type, such as an integer too large for i32 Another length of a one-dimensional array used as the loop's bound An array dimension the kernel uses inside its body, such as a row length Another number of rows in a two-dimensional array A device class's class constants or its structure A device class's instance numbers

The dimensions are the case to watch. A dimension that sets only the parallel loop's range is passed to the launch. A dimension used inside the body becomes a number in the generated code. Indexing grid[row, column] uses the row length to find the element, so grids of different widths compile separately. Kernels shows how to avoid this when it matters.

For a simulation this means: allocate the working arrays once, before the time loop, and update them in place. The first step compiles every kernel, and every later step only launches. Tack also keeps compiled variants on disk, so the next run of the program starts warm. Editing a kernel, a device function it calls, or a constant compiles it again. See Keep compiled kernels between runs.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The compilation steps. On the first call with a new combination of argument kinds, Tack takes five steps.

  1. It reads the decorated function's source and checks it uses only what device code supports.
  2. It translates it into Tack's intermediate representation, inlining every device function it calls.
  3. It fills in the argument types and the array dimensions the body uses, and works out the type of every expression.
  4. It generates code for the device: LLVM IR on the CPU, Metal Shading Language, CUDA C, HIP C, or OpenCL C for Level Zero.
  5. It compiles it with the device's compiler, and launches it.

LLVM and the vendors' compilers optimize the generated code. tack.inspect shows the intermediate representation and the generated code without running the kernel. See Kernels. The design notes explain the compilation pipeline and what goes into a variant.

Threads on the CPU. The CPU backend decides per kernel whether a launch is worth spreading over its threads, by timing the kernel on the ranges it runs. Small launches of cheap kernels run on the calling thread. The first few calls of a kernel include this measuring. The CPU threading design note describes the policy.

Overlapping arrays on the CPU. When no array a kernel writes overlaps another of its arrays, the CPU compiles a variant that lets LLVM assume so. A call that passes overlapping arrays, such as two views of one buffer, uses a second variant that does not. Both give the same results.

docs.text:
• Arrays and types explains the arrays every kernel reads and writes, and the types of scalar arguments.
  • Kernels covers the parallel loop in full: several dimensions, inner loops and returning a value.

docs.title: Keep compiled kernels between runs
docs.text:
A kernel compiles the first time it is called with new argument types and shapes. Tack keeps what it compiles on disk, so the next process that calls the same kernel loads it instead of compiling it again. The cache is on by default and needs no code. You need the rest of this page only to find where the cache lives, move it, limit it or turn it off, or use it in an MPI job on a shared file system.

This example runs one small program twice, each time in a new process, with the cache in a directory of its own. The first run compiles and stores the kernel. The second finds it on disk:

import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

program = '''
import sys
import tack
import tack.cache

tack.set_default_device("cpu")
tack.cache.configure(directory=sys.argv[1])


@tack.kernel
def scale(x, out, factor):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = x[i] * factor


x = tack.ones(8)
scale(x, tack.empty_like(x), 2.0)
print(tack.cache.stats().get("variant_hit", 0))
'''

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    script = Path(folder) / "scale.py"
    script.write_text(program)
    cache = str(Path(folder) / "cache")
    runs = [subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(script), cache], capture_output=True,
                           text=True, check=True).stdout.split()[-1] for _ in range(2)]
assert runs == ["0", "1"]          # compiled the first time, loaded the second

docs.title: What the cache saves
docs.text:
A first call has two parts: Tack's own work on the kernel's Python source, and the device's compiler. The cache keeps the results of both, so a warm start skips both. These are first calls of contour on a small grid, a visualization filter that compiles many kernels, in a new process:

machine and device cache off cache warm Apple M1 Max, CPU 445 ms 31 ms Apple M1 Max, Metal 1.1 s 31 ms NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada, CUDA 1.15 s 72 ms Intel Max 1100, Level Zero 5.1 s 145 to 190 ms AMD MI210, HIP 6.9 s 37 ms

On CUDA most of the cold time is the vendor's compiler, and on Level Zero and HIP nearly all of it is. That is why Tack keeps each device's compiled code, and not only its own intermediate form.

docs.title: Change where and how it caches
docs.text:
Three environment variables control the cache. They are read when the first kernel compiles:

variable meaning TACK_CACHE_DIR Where entries are kept. The default is ~/Library/Caches/tack on macOS, $XDG_CACHE_HOME/tack or ~/.cache/tack on Linux, and %LOCALAPPDATA%\tack\Cache on Windows. TACK_CACHE write looks entries up and stores new ones, the default. read looks up but never stores. bundle reads only the directory's bundle file, the default under MPI. off turns the cache off. TACK_CACHE_SIZE The most the entries may take, such as 500M or 2G in binary units, or unlimited. The default is 1G.

tack.cache.configure sets the same from Python, over the environment. It takes effect at the next kernel compiled:

import tempfile

import tack
import tack.cache

tack.set_default_device("cpu")
folder = tempfile.mkdtemp()                   # a directory only you can write

tack.cache.configure(directory=folder, mode="write", max_size="4G")
directory, mode, rank = tack.cache.settings()
assert str(directory) == folder and mode == "write" and rank is None
assert tack.cache.size_limit() == 4 * 2**30

tack.cache.configure(mode="off")              # no cache for this process
assert tack.cache.settings()[1] == "off"

The directory must belong to you and be writable by nobody else, since its entries hold code that Tack will run. Tack refuses a directory that fails this, with a warning, and compiles without the cache.

docs.title: Know when an entry is used
docs.text:
Two things are stored for each kernel. One is the kernel after Tack has translated its Python source, before it is specialized for argument types. The other is each compiled variant: one compiled form of the kernel, for one set of argument types and shapes.

An entry is used only when everything it was made from is unchanged. That means the kernel's source, every device function and constant it uses, the classes it is given, the argument types and shapes, the Tack version, and the device with its compiler and driver. So editing a kernel, a device function it calls, a tack.constant it reads or a device class it is given makes the next process compile again. So do upgrading Tack and moving to another machine. A damaged or partly written entry is ignored, and the kernel compiles.

Debug mode is part of the key. A kernel compiled with bounds checks is a different kernel, so switching modes never mixes the two.

docs.title: Keep it to a size
docs.text:
The entries of every Tack version share one limit, TACK_CACHE_SIZE. Each Tack version, and each edit of a Tack checkout, keeps entries of its own, and those of a version you no longer run would otherwise stay for good. Past the limit, a process that stores entries deletes the least recently used ones until 90% of the limit is left. Loading an entry marks it as used, so the kernels you run stay.

The directory is checked at most once an hour, by all processes together, never once per kernel. The cache can therefore briefly exceed its limit.

The command line shows and manages the cache:

python -m tack.cache info                  # settings, entries and size
python -m tack.cache prune                 # keep to the limit now
python -m tack.cache prune --max-size 200M # ...or to another limit
python -m tack.cache clear                 # this Tack version's entries
python -m tack.cache clear --all           # every version's entries

clear --all deletes only what the cache made, so the directory may hold other files too. The same operations are tack.cache.describe, tack.cache.prune and tack.cache.clear in Python.

docs.title: Use the cache in an MPI job
docs.text:
On a parallel file system such as Lustre or GPFS, thousands of ranks each looking up a file per kernel load the file system's metadata servers, as thousands of ranks importing Python do. A bundle avoids it: one file that holds every entry, which each rank reads once.

  1. Warm up. Run the job's kernels once, on one rank or in a small job, with TACK_CACHE=write and TACK_CACHE_DIR set to a directory of your own on scratch.
  2. Pack the directory into a bundle:
TACK_CACHE_DIR=/scratch/me/tack-cache python -m tack.cache pack
  1. Run the job with the same TACK_CACHE_DIR. Under MPI the default mode is bundle. Each rank reads the bundle once, and never looks up or writes a file per kernel. A kernel the bundle lacks compiles in memory, as it would without a cache.

Tack recognizes an MPI launch from the launcher's environment variables: Open MPI, MPICH, Intel MPI, MVAPICH2, Cray PALS and ALPS, and Slurm's srun. A launch of one task counts as no MPI. So does a Slurm batch script itself, so a warm-up run on the script's own line, without srun, stores entries as it would on a workstation.

To have only rank 0 read the bundle and broadcast it to the others, call tack.cache.load_bundle(comm=MPI.COMM_WORLD) on every rank before the first kernel, with mpi4py's communicator. It is collective, and returns the number of entries read. If rank 0 cannot use the bundle, because there is none, it is damaged, or it is not your own, rank 0 warns why and every rank compiles its kernels.

With TACK_CACHE=write under MPI, only rank 0 stores entries and the other ranks read. Concurrent writers are safe, but the bundle is the better path for a large job. Run under MPI covers the rest of an MPI job's setup.

docs.title: Time a cold compile
docs.text: With the cache on, the first call in a process may load a kernel rather than compile it. To time a cold compile, run with TACK_CACHE=off. See Debug and time a kernel.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• What each device stores. The CPU stores object code, and Metal its generated source. CUDA stores PTX, which the driver compiles for the GPU when it loads. HIP stores the code object, machine code for the GPU's architecture. Level Zero stores the GPU's native code, which loads without compiling, and the SPIR-V it was made from, used if a driver update or another stepping of the GPU refuses the native code. The Warp prototype stores only Tack's part, and Warp's own cache keeps its compiled code.
  • Safe writes. Entries are written to a temporary file and renamed into place, so a reader never sees a partial one. Each entry carries a checksum.
  • Bundles and the size limit. Bundles are neither counted against the limit nor deleted by pruning. You make and remove them by hand.
  • The counters. tack.cache.stats() returns this process's counts of hits, misses and writes, as the first example reads.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Debug and time a kernel, to measure first calls and warm calls.
  • Run under MPI, for MPI jobs on clusters.
  • The tack.cache reference, for every function's arguments.

docs.title: Kernels
docs.text: A kernel is a Python function, decorated with @tack.kernel, whose outermost loop runs in parallel on a device. The kernels of a typical simulation or image calculation are built from a few parts, and each has a section below. The parallel loop comes first, then its forms over two or three dimensions and the ordinary loops inside it. Array dimensions, constants and a returned value follow, and the last section shows the code Tack generates. The page builds on how a program runs.

docs.title: The parallel loop
docs.text:
Every kernel has exactly one parallel loop. It is a for statement directly in the kernel's body, and each of its iterations runs on its own GPU thread, or in a share of the CPU's threads:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def fill(data, value):
    for i in range(len(data)):
        data[i] = value

data = tack.empty((1000,))
fill(data, 3.0)
assert np.all(data.numpy() == 3.0)

The loop's range sets how many iterations a launch runs. It can be a scalar argument, range(n), an array dimension, range(data.shape[0]), or len(data), the length of the first dimension. A start and a step work too, as in range(1, n - 1) and range(0, n, 2).

The loop must be at the top of the body, not inside an if or another loop. A kernel with no parallel loop, or with two, raises UnsupportedSyntaxError naming the line and column. Two independent loops belong in two kernels.

docs.title: Code before the loop
docs.text:
Statements before the parallel loop may run more than once per launch: once per GPU thread, or once per share of the CPU's work. So they may only assign local variables, read arrays and declare scratch arrays. Every iteration starts from the values they set:

@tack.kernel
def scale(x, out, k):
    s = 2.0 * k                    # computed before the loop, read by every iteration
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = x[i] * s

A store to an array, an atomic or a print before or after the loop raises UnsupportedSyntaxError, with the remedy: move it into the loop.

docs.title: Work that must run in order
docs.text:
Some calculations are a recurrence, where each value needs the one before it. Run them in a parallel loop of one iteration, with an ordinary loop inside:

@tack.kernel
def cumulative_trapezoid(rho, e, n, dx):
    for _ in range(1):                 # one iteration: the loop below runs in order
        e[0] = rho[0] * dx * 0.5
        for i in range(1, n):
            e[i] = e[i - 1] + (rho[i - 1] + rho[i]) * dx * 0.5

This uses one thread of the device, so keep it for short or rare work. A running sum over a large array is a scan, which Reductions, scans and sorts computes in parallel.

docs.title: Loops over two or three dimensions
docs.text:
tack.ndindex makes a parallel loop over a grid. Each iteration gets one index per dimension, the slowest first:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def smooth(u, out):
    for i, j in tack.ndindex((1, u.shape[0] - 1), (1, u.shape[1] - 1)):
        out[i, j] = 0.25 * (u[i - 1, j] + u[i + 1, j] + u[i, j - 1] + u[i, j + 1])

u = tack.array(np.arange(16, dtype=np.float32).reshape(4, 4))
out = tack.zeros((4, 4))
smooth(u, out)
print(out.numpy())
# [[ 0.  0.  0.  0.]
#  [ 0.  5.  6.  0.]
#  [ 0.  9. 10.  0.]
#  [ 0.  0.  0.  0.]]
assert out.numpy()[1, 1] == 5.0 and out.numpy()[0, 0] == 0.0

Each argument of ndindex is a size, such as u.shape[0], or a (start, end) pair. The pairs here visit the interior of the grid and leave the boundary alone, as a stencil needs. Sizes and pairs can be mixed. An empty or reversed pair gives no iterations. The launch runs the product of the extents, here 2 times 2.

ndindex takes two or three dimensions as one parallel loop. It writes the index of a two-dimensional grid as (row, column), matching NumPy's [row, column] and its (height, width) shapes.

docs.title: Ordinary loops inside the parallel loop
docs.text:
Loops inside the parallel loop are ordinary loops. Each iteration runs them in order, on its own:

@tack.kernel
def row_sums(data, out):
    for row in range(data.shape[0]):          # parallel: one iteration a row
        total = 0.0
        for column in range(data.shape[1]):   # in order, within the row
            total += data[row, column]
        out[row] = total

An inner loop's bounds may be anything the iteration computes, including values read from arrays. That is how a kernel walks lists of different lengths, stored one after another with an offsets array, as VTK stores a cell's points:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def sum_segments(offsets, data, sums):
    for c in range(sums.shape[0]):
        total = 0.0
        for i in range(offsets[c], offsets[c + 1]):
            total += data[i]
        sums[c] = total

offsets = tack.array([0, 3, 4, 8])                 # three lists: 3, 1 and 4 long
data = tack.array(np.arange(8, dtype=np.float32))
sums = tack.empty((3,))
sum_segments(offsets, data, sums)
assert np.allclose(sums.numpy(), [3.0, 3.0, 22.0])

Inner loops take range with a start, an end and a step, and while. Control flow and math covers while, break and continue.

docs.title: Index arrays
docs.text:
An array takes one index per dimension, grid[i, j], or a single flat index in row-major order, grid[k], as a NumPy array's ravel() would number it. Indexing with another number of indices raises TypeError when the kernel is called, naming the line. Without that check, grid[i, j] on a three-dimensional array would silently read some other element.

A vector of integers supplies one index per component, so grid[cell] is grid[cell[0], cell[1]] when cell is a 2-vector. Vectors and matrices introduces vectors.

docs.title: Array dimensions inside a kernel
docs.text:
a.shape[k] and len(a) work anywhere in a kernel: in conditions, in arithmetic and in indices, not only as the loop's range. The dimension's number must be written as a literal, as in x.shape[0]. A variable d in x.shape[d] raises UnsupportedSyntaxError, because the shape is read when the kernel compiles.

@tack.kernel
def reverse(x, out):
    for i in range(x.shape[0]):
        out[i] = x[x.shape[0] - 1 - i]

Where a dimension appears decides whether the kernel compiles again for another shape. A dimension used only as the parallel loop's range is passed to the launch, so one compiled kernel serves every length. A dimension used inside the body is compiled in as a number. The reverse above therefore compiles once per array length. A two-dimensional index such as grid[row, column] uses the row length to find the element, so grids of different widths compile separately too.

Compiling the dimension in lets the compiler simplify the arithmetic around a known size, and for a simulation that keeps its arrays it costs nothing after the first step. When the shapes change often, pass the length as a scalar argument instead, which is a runtime value:

@tack.kernel
def reverse(x, out, n):            # one compiled kernel for every n
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = x[n - 1 - i]

docs.title: Declare constants
docs.text:
A kernel does not see the Python variables around it. If it did, a module-level dt = 0.01 could change after the kernel compiled, and the kernel would silently keep the old value. Reading such a name raises NameError. Declare a fixed value with tack.constant instead:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

DT = tack.constant(0.01)
GRID = tack.constant(128)

@tack.kernel
def step(x, v):
    for i in range(GRID):
        v[i] = v[i] * (1.0 - DT)
        x[i] += v[i] * DT

x = tack.zeros((GRID,))                # the host uses the same names
v = tack.ones((GRID,))
step(x, v)
assert np.allclose(x.numpy(), 0.99 * 0.01)

The kernel reads DT as if it were the literal 0.01. A constant is still a Python number, so host code uses it too, as tack.zeros((GRID,)) does. Constants work from other modules (from params import DT) and inside device functions. math.pi, math.e and math.tau work without declaring them.

A second argument gives a constant a type. That matters for integer arithmetic that must wrap at a width, and for double-precision values:

MULTIPLIER = tack.constant(747796405, tack.u32)   # x * MULTIPLIER wraps at 32 bits
TENTH = tack.constant(0.1, tack.f64)              # exactly the double nearest 0.1

A tuple of numbers declares a vector constant, and a tuple of equal-length tuples a matrix constant:

SUN = tack.constant((0.5, 0.5, 0.0))
ROTATE = tack.constant(((0.0, -1.0), (1.0, 0.0)))

In a kernel they are a vector and a matrix. On the host they index like tuples, and np.asarray(SUN) gives an array to compute with.

A constant is fixed where you declare it, and arithmetic on constants gives plain numbers. So declare a derived value again, as in H = tack.constant(1.0 / (GRID - 2)). Binding the name to another constant later does not change a kernel already compiled. For a value that changes between calls, pass an argument.

docs.title: Return a value
docs.text:
A kernel whose last statement is return, after the parallel loop, hands a value back to Python. The return annotation names its type: -> int for i32, -> float for f32, or any Tack type such as -> tack.f64.

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def count_above(values, count, threshold) -> int:
    for i in range(len(values)):
        if values[i] > threshold:
            tack.atomic_add(count, 0, 1)
    return count[0]

values = tack.array(np.array([0.1, 0.9, 0.7, 0.2], np.float32))
count = tack.zeros((1,), tack.i32)
live = count_above(values, count, 0.5)
assert live == 2 and isinstance(live, int)        # a Python int

The returned expression is evaluated once, after the loop has finished. It may read arrays, arguments, constants and variables assigned before the loop. It may not read a variable the loop assigns, which has one value per iteration. The cost is one tiny extra launch and the transfer of one number.

tack.atomic_add adds to an element safely when many iterations add to the same one. It returns the element's value before the addition, which gives each iteration a slot of its own. That makes a common pattern: append the values that pass a test to an output array, and return how many there are.

@tack.kernel
def compact_positive(values, out, count, n) -> int:
    for i in range(n):
        if values[i] > 0.0:
            slot = tack.atomic_add(count, 0, 1)
            out[slot] = values[i]
    return count[0]

Reset the counter before each call, and give the output room for every input:

values = tack.array(np.array([-2, 1, -0.5, 3, 0, 2], dtype=np.float32))
out = tack.empty(values.shape)  # capacity for every input
count = tack.empty((1,), tack.i32)
count.fill(0)
length = compact_positive(values, out, count, values.size)
result = out.numpy()[:length]
# Arrival order is unspecified: compare the values after sorting.
assert length == 3 and isinstance(length, int)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(np.sort(result), np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=np.float32))

The returned length is exact, but the order of the appended values is not fixed, so compare them sorted. When the order matters, count, scan and write instead, as marching squares does. Workgroups, atomics, textures and random numbers covers atomics in full.

docs.title: See the generated code
docs.text:
tack.inspect compiles a kernel for the arguments you give it and returns the code as a string, without running it:

import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def saxpy(x, y, out, a):
    for i in range(len(x)):
        out[i] = a * x[i] + y[i]

x, y, out = tack.empty((1024,)), tack.empty((1024,)), tack.empty((1024,))
ir = tack.inspect(saxpy, x, y, out, 2.0, mode="ir")
print(ir)
# Function saxpy(x, y, out, a):
#   ParallelFor i in [0, DimSize(x, 0)):
#     out[i] = ((a * x[i]) + y[i])
assert "ParallelFor" in ir
source = tack.inspect(saxpy, x, y, out, 2.0, mode="source")
assert "fmul" in source                           # LLVM IR on the CPU
Mode Shows "ir" Tack's intermediate representation, after inlining "source" The code given to the device's compiler: LLVM IR on the CPU, Metal Shading Language, CUDA C, HIP C, or OpenCL C for Level Zero "optimized" LLVM IR after LLVM's optimizations. CPU only; other devices raise ValueError

Pass the same arguments a call would get, because the types and dimensions the code is compiled for come from them. Inspection makes the same checks as a call, so arguments a call would refuse raise here too. The code is for the device the call would run on, chosen from the arguments' arrays as a call chooses. To see another device's code, pass arrays made on it, such as tack.empty((n,), device="cuda").

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
The exact rules of the kernel language are in the kernel language contract: which Python constructs are accepted, the order in which expressions are evaluated, and what may and may not run outside the parallel loop. Two of them come up in practice:

  • A local variable assigned before the parallel loop and reassigned inside it gets a fresh copy in each iteration. Iterations never see each other's values.
  • A break that leaves the parallel loop itself is refused, because the iterations are not in sequence. break and continue work in inner loops.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Control flow and math covers conditions, inner loops and the math functions kernels can call.
  • Device functions shows how to factor a kernel's body into helpers.
  • Heat diffusion is a complete stencil simulation built from these pieces.

docs.title: Memory and parallel correctness
docs.text:
A kernel's iterations run at the same time, in no promised order. In NumPy, every operation finishes before the next begins. In a kernel, thousands of iterations share the same arrays at once, and the answer must not depend on their order. Writing such kernels comes down to knowing which iteration owns each output. From that follows when a kernel needs a second array, an atomic or a scan. Tack checks some of this for you, and the page says what it leaves to you.

The question to ask of every kernel is this: which iteration writes each output, and what can it read while other iterations are writing? This smoothing step answers it with two arrays. Every iteration reads only the old array and writes only its own element of the new one:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def smooth(old, new):
    for i in range(old.shape[0]):
        left = old[i - 1] if i > 0 else old[i]
        right = old[i + 1] if i < old.shape[0] - 1 else old[i]
        new[i] = 0.25 * left + 0.5 * old[i] + 0.25 * right

start = np.array([0, 0, 4, 0, 0], dtype=np.float32)
old = tack.array(start)
new = tack.empty_like(old)
for step in range(2):
    smooth(old, new)
    old, new = new, old                 # swap the names, not the data

expected = start.copy()
for step in range(2):
    padded = np.concatenate([expected[:1], expected, expected[-1:]])
    expected = 0.25 * padded[:-2] + 0.5 * padded[1:-1] + 0.25 * padded[2:]
np.testing.assert_allclose(old.numpy(), expected)

Had smooth written into old itself, iteration i might read a neighbour that another iteration had already smoothed, and the result would change from run to run.

docs.title: Ownership decides correctness
docs.text:
There are two shapes of parallel work, and they need different tools.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Gather["Gather: each output has one writer"]
        a1[input] --> o1[output i]
        a2[input] --> o1
        a3[input] --> o1
    end
    subgraph Scatter["Scatter: several writers share an output"]
        p1[iteration p] --> g1[output k]
        p2[iteration q] --> g1
        p3[iteration r] --> g1
    end

In a gather, an iteration reads as many inputs as it likes and writes one output that no other iteration writes. A row sum, a stencil and a particle interpolating from a finished grid are gathers. They need no synchronization, only inputs that do not change during the launch.

In a scatter, several iterations add into the same output. Particles depositing mass onto a grid are a scatter. They need an atomic update, or a reorganization, such as a sort, that turns the scatter into a gather.

Tack does not prove that a kernel is free of such conflicts. A kernel that compiles may still have two iterations write the same element. The sections below are the patterns that keep it correct.

docs.title: Know where each element is
docs.text:
A scalar array of shape (height, width) stores height * width values in row-major order: the last index varies fastest, as in NumPy's default. In a kernel, image[row, column] is the same value as image[row * width + column].

flowchart LR
    A["shape (2, 3)"] --> B["a[0,0] a[0,1] a[0,2] | a[1,0] a[1,1] a[1,2]"]
    B --> C["offsets 0 1 2 | 3 4 5"]

A vector or matrix array stores each element's components together, and then moves to the next element. An RGB image is stored R, G, B of pixel (0, 0), then of pixel (0, 1), and so on. Its shape counts pixels, and numpy() appends the component dimension.

Allocation One element is numpy() gives tack.empty((h, w)) one f32 per pixel (h, w) tack.empty((h, w), tack.vec3()) one RGB vector per pixel (h, w, 3) tack.empty((n,), tack.mat2()) one 2×2 matrix per particle (n, 2, 2)

Choose one indexing convention and keep it. The introductory grid examples use (height, width) and [row, column]. The dye tutorial uses (width, height) and [x, y] to match its coordinate arithmetic, and transposes for image output. Both are valid, but data written in one convention and read in the other comes out transposed.

docs.title: Give each output one writer
docs.text:
This kernel is correct even though it updates its input in place:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def scale(data, factor):
    for i in range(data.shape[0]):
        data[i] *= factor

data = tack.array(np.arange(4, dtype=np.float32))
scale(data, 2.0)
np.testing.assert_allclose(data.numpy(), [0, 2, 4, 6])

Iteration i reads and writes only element i, so no other iteration can see its work half done. The same reasoning covers a velocity update in which each particle reads finished forces and writes only its own velocity.

docs.title: Read neighbours from a stable input
docs.text:
A stencil reads the old values around each element. Updating the same array lets one iteration read a neighbour that another has already changed. Use two arrays, as in the first example, and swap them between steps with old, new = new, old. The swap changes which Python name refers to which array; it copies nothing. Both arrays need the same shape and element type.

Write every element that the next step will read, the boundary included. A new array's contents are unspecified, so an element no kernel wrote holds whatever was in memory. If a kernel writes only the interior, fill the border of both arrays first. tack.zeros makes an array that starts at zero, and fill sets an existing one. The heat tutorial develops this pattern in two dimensions.

Some in-place numerical schemes are valid, such as red-black updates in two separate calls. They need an argument specific to the algorithm, and two arrays are the safe default.

docs.title: Remember that views share storage
docs.text:
reshape returns a view, a second array over the same memory. copy makes independent storage:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

grid = tack.zeros((4, 4))
flat = grid.reshape((16,))              # the same memory, seen as 16 elements
independent = grid.copy()               # new memory

@tack.kernel
def number(a):
    for i in range(a.shape[0]):
        a[i] = float(i)

number(flat)
np.testing.assert_allclose(grid.numpy()[1], [4, 5, 6, 7])       # written through the view
np.testing.assert_allclose(independent.numpy()[1], [0, 0, 0, 0])

Passing grid and flat as two arguments does not give a kernel two buffers. Tack keeps each iteration's own reads and writes in program order, even through two views of one memory. That does not make two iterations' conflicting accesses safe. A stencil's output must be a separate allocation, not a view of its input. Arrays shared with other libraries can overlap in the same way; Share arrays covers them.

docs.title: Scatter with atomics
docs.text:
When several iterations add into one element, a plain += can lose contributions. Two iterations may both read the old value, add, and store, so one addition disappears. tack.atomic_add makes each such update indivisible:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def deposit(cell_of, mass, grid_mass):
    for p in range(cell_of.shape[0]):
        tack.atomic_add(grid_mass, cell_of[p], mass[p])

cell_of = tack.array(np.array([0, 2, 2, 1, 2], dtype=np.int32))
mass = tack.array(np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], dtype=np.float32))
grid_mass = tack.zeros((3,))                # atomics add to what is there
deposit(cell_of, mass, grid_mass)
np.testing.assert_allclose(grid_mass.numpy(), [1, 4, 10])

An atomic makes one update indivisible. It does not order the rest of the kernel, and it does not make other reads see the update. So finish the scatter in one kernel and read the grid in the next. The Physarum and MPM tutorials separate their stages this way.

Floating additions arrive in whatever order the iterations run, so a floating sum built by atomics can change in its last bits from run to run. Integer sums are exact. When you need the same bits every run, sort by destination and reduce each run instead, with sort_by_key and reduce_by_key from Reductions, scans and sorts.

docs.title: Claim slots, or count, scan and write
docs.text:
An atomic's return value is the element's value just before the update. That lets each iteration claim a unique slot in an output list:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def append_large(values, out, count):
    for i in range(values.shape[0]):
        if values[i] > 2.5:
            slot = tack.atomic_add(count, 0, 1)     # the old count is this iteration's slot
            out[slot] = values[i]

values = tack.array(np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], dtype=np.float32))
out = tack.empty((5,))                              # room for every input
count = tack.zeros((1,), tack.i32)
append_large(values, out, count)
length = count[0]                                   # reads one element
np.testing.assert_allclose(np.sort(out.numpy()[:length]), [3, 4, 5])

The order of the appended items is not specified, which is why the check sorts them. The counter must start at zero, and the output must have room for every item that might be appended. An atomic neither allocates memory nor checks the index it produces.

When the order matters, or the output size is not known in advance, use count, scan and write instead. One kernel counts each input's outputs, exclusive_scan turns the counts into offsets and returns the exact total, and a second kernel writes each input's outputs at its offset. Reductions, scans and sorts shows it, and the marching squares tutorial builds an algorithm on it.

docs.title: Move data between the host and a device
docs.text:
Every array belongs to the device it was made on, shown by a.device. A kernel runs on its arrays' device. Changing the default device does not move existing arrays, and they keep working where they are. a.to_device(d) copies one to another device. Choose a device explains devices.

tack.copyto and numpy() copy whole arrays between NumPy and Tack. They copy even on the CPU and Metal, where the host can address the memory. On the host, a[i] reads one element. On CUDA, HIP and Level Zero that is one transfer per read, so keep it out of inner loops. Host code cannot write an element; use tack.copyto, fill or a kernel.

On a GPU a kernel call returns once the launch is queued. Every host read first waits for the launches before it, so reads always see finished work. How a Tack program runs explains the queue.

Arrays borrowed from another library through array_from_ptr or DLPack share that library's memory. Keep the owner alive while Tack uses the memory. Read-only memory cannot be passed to a kernel that may write it. Share arrays has the rules.

docs.title: What Tack checks, and what it leaves to you
docs.text:
Mistake What happens two iterations write one element without an atomic not detected; the result may change from run to run an index outside an array not checked; the result is undefined, except in debug mode reading an element no one wrote not detected; the value is whatever was in memory a read-only array passed where the kernel stores refused at the call arrays on two devices in one call refused at the call

Debug mode finds bad indices. tack.set_debug(True), or the environment variable TACK_DEBUG=1, compiles every kernel with a check on each array access. A call with an access outside its array raises IndexError naming the first one. Debug and time a kernel shows how to use it.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Negative indices. On the host, a negative index counts from the end, as in NumPy. In a kernel it does not: an index must lie within the array.

Vector atomics. An atomic on a vector or matrix element updates each component with its own atomic. The element is not updated as one indivisible whole.

Atomic types. Not every device supports atomics of every element type. Metal and Level Zero support atomics on i32, u32 and f32. CUDA and HIP add i64, u64 and f64, and the CPU supports every type. Support for f64 arrays does not imply f64 atomics. Workgroups, atomics and textures has the table.

Atomics are not fences. Atomics are relaxed. They make one update indivisible among the iterations of a launch on one device, and order nothing else.

The language contract states these rules precisely, and the memory and aliasing notes explain why they are what they are.

docs.title: Reductions, scans and sorts
docs.text:
Many parallel programs need the same few steps between their own kernels: add up an array, turn counts into offsets, sort by a key, or combine the values of each group. Tack has ready-made versions of these steps that run on the device. Use them instead of copying an array to NumPy for a sum, a cumsum or an argsort. The page also says which of their results are reproducible.

import numpy as np
import tack
from tack.algorithms import exclusive_scan, std

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = tack.array(np.array([3.0, 1.0, 4.0, 1.0, 5.0], dtype=np.float32))
assert data.sum() == 14.0                     # a Python float
assert data.max() == 5.0
assert abs(std(data) - np.std([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])) < 1e-6

counts = tack.array(np.array([2, 0, 3, 1], dtype=np.int32))
offsets = tack.empty((4,), tack.i32)
total = exclusive_scan(counts, offsets, 4)    # offsets[i] = counts[0] + ... + counts[i - 1]
assert total == 6
np.testing.assert_array_equal(offsets.numpy(), [0, 2, 2, 5])

The sum and maximum are methods of every array. The standard deviation and the scan come from tack.algorithms, which runs them as kernels on the device that holds the arrays.

docs.title: Choose the right tool
docs.text:
You want Use Returns one number from an array a.sum(), a.min(), a.max(), a.mean() a Python float a statistic var, std, norm, absmax, count_nonzero, dot, histogram a Python number; histogram an array running sums, or offsets from counts exclusive_scan, inclusive_scan the total, and the sums in your output array a sorted order argsort, sort_by_key, gather new arrays one value per run of equal keys unique, reduce_by_key new arrays one value per segment of a CSR layout segment_reduce, segment_scan, segment_broadcast, segment_ids arrays a sum inside a kernel, over a workgroup tack.block_sum, block_min, block_max a value in every lane

import tack does not load tack.algorithms. Import its functions as in the examples, or import tack.algorithms first.

Everything here runs on every backend, except the block reductions, which need a GPU. The algorithms take stored arrays and the implicit arrays of tack.arrays alike. For example, exclusive_scan(tack.arrays.CountingArray(n), offsets, n) scans 0, 1, 2 and so on without storing them.

docs.title: Reduce an array to one number
docs.text:
a.sum(), a.min(), a.max() and a.mean() reduce every scalar component of the array, whatever its shape or element type. There is no axis argument. A vector array of n elements of type vec3 reduces 3 * n components. The result is always a Python float, also for integer arrays.

The CPU reduces with NumPy. The GPU backends reduce f32 arrays on the device and read back one value.

What crosses to the host

On a GPU, a reduction of any element type other than f32 copies the whole array to the host and reduces it with NumPy, on every call.

The accumulator depends on the element type.

Element type sum() adds in min(), max() f32 f32 exact f64 f64 exact signed integers i64, wrapping modulo 2^64 exact unsigned integers u64, wrapping modulo 2^64 exact

Converting the sum to a Python float can round integer sums past 2^53. mean() divides the returned sum by the number of components, in double precision.

docs.title: Compute statistics
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import tack
from tack.algorithms import count_nonzero, dot, histogram, norm, var

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

values = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], dtype=np.float32)
data = tack.array(values)
assert abs(var(data) - np.var(values)) < 1e-6          # population variance
assert abs(norm(data) - np.linalg.norm(values)) < 1e-5
assert norm(data, ord=1) == 21.0
assert dot(data, data) == 91.0
assert count_nonzero(data) == 6

counts, edges = histogram(data, bins=3, range=(0.0, 6.0))
np.testing.assert_array_equal(counts.numpy(), [1, 2, 3])   # counts stay on the device
np.testing.assert_allclose(edges, [0, 2, 4, 6])            # edges are NumPy
Function Computes var(data), std(data) the population variance and standard deviation norm(data, ord=2) the Euclidean norm; ord=1 the sum of absolute values; ord=float("inf") the largest absmax(data) the largest absolute value count_nonzero(data) the number of nonzero components, exact as a Python int dot(a, b) the sum of a[i] * b[i] histogram(data, bins, range) the counts per bin as an i32 array, and the edges as NumPy

Each function takes an optional n, the number of elements to read in flat order. A negative n, or one larger than an array, raises ValueError.

The statistics compute in f64 if an input is f64, and otherwise in f32. Integer inputs convert before any product, so dot of two i32 arrays holding 100000 gives 10^10 rather than an overflow. Each statistic forms its terms in a temporary array and reduces it as a.sum() or a.max() would. Their accuracy and host traffic are therefore those of the array reductions above.

histogram differs from numpy.histogram in one way. Values below the range are counted in the first bin and values above it in the last, where NumPy drops them. Details has the rest of its rules.

docs.title: Turn counts into offsets with a scan
docs.text:
A prefix scan turns a list of numbers into running sums. exclusive_scan writes, at position i, the sum of the inputs before i. inclusive_scan includes input i itself. Both return the total.

The classic use is stream compaction, in three steps. A kernel counts what each input will write, a scan turns the counts into write offsets and the total into the output's size, and a second kernel writes each input's output at its offset:

import numpy as np
import tack
from tack.algorithms import exclusive_scan

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def count_positive(values, counts):
    for i in range(values.shape[0]):
        counts[i] = 1 if values[i] > 0.0 else 0

@tack.kernel
def write_positive(values, offsets, out):
    for i in range(values.shape[0]):
        if values[i] > 0.0:
            out[offsets[i]] = values[i]

values = tack.array(np.array([0.5, -1.0, 2.0, -3.0, 4.0, 0.0], dtype=np.float32))
n = values.size
counts = tack.empty((n,), tack.i32)
offsets = tack.empty((n,), tack.i32)

count_positive(values, counts)
total = exclusive_scan(counts, offsets, n)
positive = tack.empty((total,))
write_positive(values, offsets, positive)
np.testing.assert_allclose(positive.numpy(), [0.5, 2.0, 4.0])   # in input order

Unlike claiming slots with an atomic counter, the output keeps the inputs' order and has exactly the right size. The marching squares tutorial builds a whole contouring algorithm this way.

Some options cover common needs:

  • Wide offsets. The scan adds in the output's element type. Keep the counts i32 and make the offsets i64 when the total may pass 2^31 − 1.
  • CSR offsets. exclusive_scan(counts, offsets, n, close=True) also writes the total at offsets[n], so offsets needs n + 1 elements. Compressed sparse row (CSR) offsets of this kind describe variable-length groups, as in the next section.
  • No wait. Returning the total reads it from the device, which waits for the queued work on a GPU. Pass total=False when you need only the offsets. The scan then returns None and stays queued.
  • In place. exclusive_scan(a, a, n) is correct.

Only the first n elements are read and written. Integer results are exact, apart from wrapping at the output's width, and identical on every backend and every run.

tack.algorithms also has copy(src, dst, n) and fill_value(dst, value, n), single kernels that copy or fill the first n elements.

docs.title: Sort and group by key
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import tack
from tack.algorithms import argsort, gather, reduce_by_key, sort_by_key, unique

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

keys = tack.array(np.array([5, 3, 5, 1], dtype=np.int32))
values = tack.array(np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], dtype=np.float32))

order = argsort(keys)                              # stable: equal keys keep their order
np.testing.assert_array_equal(order.numpy(), [3, 1, 0, 2])
np.testing.assert_allclose(gather(values, order).numpy(), [4, 2, 1, 3])

sorted_keys, sorted_values = sort_by_key(keys, values)
distinct, sums = reduce_by_key(sorted_keys, sorted_values)    # op="sum", "min" or "max"
np.testing.assert_array_equal(distinct.numpy(), [1, 3, 5])
np.testing.assert_allclose(sums.numpy(), [4, 2, 4])
distinct, counts = unique(sorted_keys)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(counts.numpy(), [1, 1, 2])

argsort returns the permutation that sorts the keys, and gather applies it. sort_by_key sorts keys and carries values along. unique and reduce_by_key walk the runs of equal keys, giving one key and one count or one reduced value per run. All of them return new arrays.

Sorting is how unstructured data gets what a structured grid has for free. The pattern is always the same: make a key per item, sort, then walk the runs. This example inverts a mesh's connectivity, from the points of each cell to the cells around each point:

import numpy as np
import tack
from tack.algorithms import exclusive_scan, sort_by_key, unique

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Three triangles; connectivity lists each cell's points, cell_of each entry's cell.
connectivity = tack.array(np.array([0, 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 3, 4], dtype=np.int32))
cell_of = tack.array(np.repeat(np.arange(3, dtype=np.int32), 3))

points, cells = sort_by_key(connectivity, cell_of)     # entries grouped by point
point_ids, counts = unique(points)                     # each point and its cell count
offsets = tack.empty((point_ids.size + 1,), tack.i32)
exclusive_scan(counts, offsets, point_ids.size, close=True)

# The cells around point p are cells[offsets[p]:offsets[p + 1]].
o, c = offsets.numpy(), cells.numpy()
np.testing.assert_array_equal(c[o[2]:o[3]], [0, 1, 2])   # point 2 is in every triangle
np.testing.assert_array_equal(c[o[4]:o[5]], [2])

The same pattern finds a mesh's boundary faces, which appear once after sorting, and merges duplicate points.

Keys and order. Sort keys are i32, u32, i64 or u64; other key types raise TypeError. The sort is stable, so equal keys keep their original order and their values keep theirs. Values may be any element type. The permutation is i32 up to 2^31 − 1 elements and i64 beyond; argsort(keys, index_dtype=tack.i64) asks for i64 at any size.

Runs. unique and reduce_by_key need equal keys next to each other, which sorting guarantees. They work on any key type that supports !=, floats included. They return each run's first key in order of appearance, so the unsorted input [7, 7, 2, 2, 7] gives [7, 2, 7].

Reproducible results. The sort gives the same permutation on every backend and every run. reduce_by_key reduces each run on one thread, in element order, so its floating sums are the same on every run and equal a sequential sum. Very long runs make that one thread the slowest.

docs.title: Reduce segments of a CSR layout
docs.text:
Variable-length groups, such as each cell's points, each point's cells or the rows of a sparse matrix, are often stored as one flat array of values and CSR offsets. Segment k is values[offsets[k]:offsets[k + 1]], and there are offsets.size - 1 segments. The segmented operations work on that layout directly, with no keys:

import numpy as np
import tack
from tack.algorithms import segment_broadcast, segment_ids, segment_reduce, segment_scan

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

values = tack.array(np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], dtype=np.float32))
offsets = tack.array(np.array([0, 2, 2, 6], dtype=np.int32))    # segment 1 is empty

sums = segment_reduce(values, offsets)                  # op="min", "max" or "mean"
np.testing.assert_allclose(sums.numpy(), [3, 0, 18])
np.testing.assert_allclose(segment_reduce(values, offsets, op="mean").numpy(),
                           [1.5, np.nan, 4.5])
np.testing.assert_allclose(segment_scan(values, offsets).numpy(), [1, 3, 3, 7, 12, 18])
np.testing.assert_allclose(segment_broadcast(sums, offsets, 6).numpy(), [3, 3, 18, 18, 18, 18])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(segment_ids(offsets, 6).numpy(), [0, 0, 2, 2, 2, 2])
Function Gives segment_reduce(values, offsets, op) one value per segment segment_scan(values, offsets, inclusive=True) running sums that restart at every segment; op="min" or "max" for running extremes segment_broadcast(segment_values, offsets, n) each segment's value on each of its elements segment_ids(offsets, n) each element's segment number, -1 outside every segment

Empty segments. An empty segment reduces to the empty= argument. By default that is 0 for a sum, NaN for a floating mean, and the type's greatest or least value for min and max. empty="keep" leaves the output as it was, which needs an out= array you filled.

Long and short segments. A segment of up to 256 elements is reduced by one thread, in element order. A longer one is cut into chunks of 256 that are combined afterwards. So many short segments cost one pass, and one huge segment costs a few launches rather than one thread walking it all.

Reproducible results. Floating sums are grouped by those fixed chunks, so they are the same bits on every backend and every run. A long segment's sum is then not exactly the sequential one. segment_reduce(..., ordered=True) sums each segment in element order, one thread per segment, as reduce_by_key does. Vector values reduce component by component.

docs.title: Reduce inside a kernel on a GPU
docs.text:
On a GPU, iterations run in workgroups of 256 lanes that can share memory. tack.block_sum(v), tack.block_min(v) and tack.block_max(v) combine one f32 value from every lane of a workgroup, and give every lane the result. They save a separate pass when each workgroup needs its own partial result.

The CPU has no workgroups and refuses any kernel that uses them. This example runs the kernel where it can and shows the refusal on the CPU:

import numpy as np
import tack
from tack.runtime.dispatch import get_backend

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

@tack.kernel
def group_sums(data, partial):
    for i in range(data.shape[0]):
        s = tack.block_sum(data[i])         # every lane of the group gets the same s
        if tack.thread_id() == 0:
            partial[i // 256] = s           # one lane writes the group's result

data = tack.ones((1024,))                   # a multiple of 256
partial = tack.empty((4,))
if get_backend().supports_workgroups:
    group_sums(data, partial)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(partial.numpy(), [256, 256, 256, 256])
else:
    try:
        group_sums(data, partial)
    except RuntimeError as error:
        assert "does not support workgroup execution" in str(error)
    else:
        raise AssertionError("the CPU ran a block reduction")

With for i in range(n), workgroup g holds iterations 256 * g to 256 * g + 255, and tack.thread_id() is the lane's position in it. Three rules apply:

  • f32 only. Cast other values first: tack.block_sum(tack.f32(x)).
  • Complete workgroups. The iteration count must be a multiple of 256, or the call raises ValueError before anything runs. Tack does not pad. Pad the data with the reduction's identity, such as 0.0 for a sum.
  • Every lane takes part. The reduction must not sit under a condition that depends on the loop index, an array value or thread_id(). To leave values out, have every lane contribute the identity instead: tack.block_sum(x if x > 0.0 else 0.0). Conditions on scalar arguments are fine.

The reduction includes its own barriers, so it needs no tack.barrier() around it. Workgroups, atomics and textures explains workgroups in full.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Repeatability. Integer results and extremes are exact everywhere. Floating sums differ by family:

Operation CPU GPUs f32 a.sum(), mean(), and statistics on f32 NumPy the last bits can change from run to run other a.sum() and statistics NumPy NumPy, after a copy to the host scans the same on every run the same on every run reduce_by_key, segment_* the same bits everywhere the same bits everywhere block_sum combined with atomic_add not available the last bits can change from run to run

The GPUs combine their workgroups' f32 partial sums with atomics, in the order the workgroups finish, which is why those sums vary. The contract promises an error bound, not reproducibility, for array sums on any backend. Compare floating sums with a tolerance.

Scans of floating values match np.cumsum bit for bit up to 4096 elements on the CPU and 2048 on GPUs. Beyond that, each chunk starts from the sum of the earlier chunks' totals, so the last bits can differ from np.cumsum.

NaN, infinity and empty arrays. A NaN anywhere makes sum(), min() and max() return NaN. Infinities add by ordinary floating addition, so inf + -inf is NaN. min() of 0.0 and -0.0 is -0.0 and max() is 0.0, in either order. On an empty array sum() is 0.0, mean() is NaN, and min() and max() raise ValueError. var and std of nothing are NaN; norm, absmax and dot of nothing are 0.0. count_nonzero counts NaN as nonzero and -0.0 as zero.

Histogram bins. A value's bin is int((x - lo) * (1 / width)), computed in the data's precision and clamped to the first and last bins. A value equal to hi lands in the last bin, as in NumPy. Without range, the range is the data's minimum and maximum, and equal ones become lo to lo + 1. bins must be at least 1, and the range must be finite with lo at most hi. NaN, and values so far outside the range that their bin does not fit a 32-bit integer, land in a backend-dependent bin; filter them first. Counts are exact while they fit an i32.

Copy and fill. copy converts into the destination's type by the kernel language's rules, so floats truncate toward zero and integers wrap. fill_value converts its value the same way, so 300 fills a u8 array with 44. Neither checks n against the arrays. array.fill(value), by contrast, fills the whole array and converts as NumPy does. copy_with_offset(src, dst, offset, n) writes dst[offset + i] = src[i]; import it with from tack.algorithms.copy import copy_with_offset.

When calls return. A call that returns a Python value, such as a reduction, a statistic or a scan's total, waits for the work it reads. On GPUs, a scan with total=False, a sort or a segmented operation may return before the device finishes. The next read of an array waits for it, as How a Tack program runs explains.

The language contract states the reduction rules precisely, and the parallel execution notes explain how the scans and sorts are built.

docs.title: Share arrays with NumPy, PyTorch, CuPy and VTK
docs.text:
Data usually comes from somewhere else: a NumPy script, a PyTorch model, a simulation's own GPU memory, a VTK pipeline. The question is how to get it into Tack kernels and the results back out, and when a copy can be avoided. Tack shares memory with other libraries through DLPack. It can also wrap a raw pointer from a simulation, and it exchanges arrays with VTK.

There are two ways in. A copy gives Tack its own array, independent of the source. A shared array uses the source's memory, so a write through either side is seen by the other:

import numpy as np
import tack

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.kernel
def add_one(a):
    for i in range(a.shape[0]):
        a[i] = a[i] + 1.0


host = np.zeros(4, dtype=np.float32)

copied = tack.array(host)          # Tack's own copy
add_one(copied)
assert host[0] == 0.0              # the source is unchanged

shared = tack.from_dlpack(host)    # the same memory, no copy
add_one(shared)
assert host[0] == 1.0              # the kernel wrote into the NumPy array

view = np.from_dlpack(shared)      # and back out, still no copy
add_one(shared)
assert view[0] == 2.0

docs.title: Decide whether to copy or share
docs.text:
A copy is the simple choice. It suits a first program, and data that arrives once or rarely. Sharing saves the copy, and with it time and memory. In exchange, both libraries must agree on four things: the device the memory is on, its layout, how long it lives, and whether Tack may write to it.

to copy share bring data in tack.array(x), tack.copyto(a, x) tack.from_dlpack(x), tack.array_from_ptr(ptr, ...) take results out a.numpy(), np.asarray(a) np.from_dlpack(a), torch.from_dlpack(a), cupy.from_dlpack(a) exchange with VTK vtk_to_dataset, dataset_to_vtk vtk_to_array, array_to_vtk

docs.title: Copy values in and out
docs.text:
tack.array(x) makes a new array holding a copy of x: a NumPy array, a sequence, or another Tack array. It keeps a NumPy array's element type unless you pass dtype=. tack.copyto(a, x) copies x into an existing array, converting to its element type and broadcasting as np.copyto does. a.numpy() and np.asarray(a) copy an array into a new NumPy array.

A vector or matrix array's components become trailing NumPy dimensions. An array of 100 vec3 elements reads back with shape (100, 3), and tack.array(points, tack.vec3()) reads a (100, 3) NumPy array as 100 vectors. Arrays and types covers element types and shapes.
