docs.title: CPU — LLVM through llvmlite
docs.text:
Initialization. CPUBackend.__init__ (runtime/cpu.py) chooses the thread count from TACK_CPU_THREADS, or else _physical_core_count(), which asks each platform for physical cores rather than logical processors. It creates the variant cache and, at the first fan-out, reaches the process's thread pool: the pool JIT'd from LLVM IR in cpu_pool.py, or a ThreadPoolExecutor with TACK_CPU_POOL=python, on Windows, or where the pool cannot be made (CPU Threading Policy). With TACK_CPU_MALLOC=1 on Linux it also tells glibc to keep freed pages. There is no device to select. allocate_array returns uninitialized NumPy storage, first touched by the kernel that writes it.

Compilation. _compile_kernel generates an llvmlite.ir module with generate_llvm_ir, parses and verifies it with llvm.parse_assembly and mod.verify(), then optimizes and JIT-compiles:

  • _create_target_machine() targets the default triple with llvm.get_host_cpu_name(), the host's feature string, and opt=3.
  • _optimize_module() runs the new pass manager's O3 pipeline (create_pipeline_tuning_options(3)) with loop vectorization, SLP vectorization, loop unrolling and loop interleaving enabled.
  • The code joins a shared MCJIT engine (cpu_pool.shared_jit, a new one every MODULES_PER_ENGINE (32) modules), under an entry name made unique (unique_name: the process's random tag and a serial number), since kernels of one name would otherwise share an address there. Once the code is made the engine drops the module's IR (remove_module). An engine of its own cost about 950 KB a variant, mostly its memory manager's sections and state; shared, about 75 KB. Each variant keeps its engine alive, so an engine goes with the last of its variants.

No fast-math flags are emitted, so floating-point semantics follow Numerical Semantics. The entry point is looked up by kernel_entry_name() (codegen/identifiers.py), which prefixes tack_kernel_ and encodes the name, because llvmlite's symbol lookup needs ASCII and a kernel must not collide with a libm function.

Calling convention. The generated function is

void tack_kernel_<name>(T0* array0, T1 scalar1, ..., int64 __loop_start__, int64 __loop_end__)

Arrays are pointers, scalars are passed by value, and the parallel loop runs over [__loop_start__, __loop_end__). CompiledKernel builds a ctypes.CFUNCTYPE for this signature once, with c_void_p for each array. bind() marshals the array addresses (NumpyBuffer.address, computed once per array) and scalars once per dispatch; call_range() then runs each chunk with its own bounds, because chunks run concurrently. The JIT'd pool does not call through ctypes at all: cpu_pool.chunk_wrapper JITs, once per compiled kernel and under a lock, a __tack_chunk(pack, start, end) that loads the arguments from 8-byte slots (pack_args) and calls the kernel at its address.

Disk cache. set_object_cache captures the object code MCJIT emits, and variant_artifact stores it after a header and the entry's unique name (_STORED); load_variant adds it to the shared engine with add_object_file, which takes about 0.4 ms and runs neither LLVM's optimizer nor its code generator. The name is unique across processes too, so code stored by two processes loads into one engine.

Launch. Whether a dispatch runs serially or fans out across the pool is decided by measurement, not a fixed threshold; CPU Threading Policy describes it in full. A second compiled variant may exist per specialization, with noalias array pointers, for calls whose arrays are proven not to overlap — see Memory and Aliasing.

Features. supports_workgroups is false, so kernels using shared memory, barriers, local thread IDs or block reductions are rejected before compilation. Textures are sampled in software: LLVMCodeGen emits the trilinear interpolation inline over the texture's private copy of its array, with the extent baked in as constants. Reductions use NumPy on the host — the data is already there. Loop indices are 64-bit.

docs.title: Metal
docs.text:
Initialization. MetalBackend.__init__ (runtime/metal.py) raises ImportError if pyobjc-framework-Metal is missing, takes MTLCreateSystemDefaultDevice() (RuntimeError if there is none), and creates one command queue. There are no options.

Compilation. _compile_kernel generates MSL with generate_msl_source, compiles it with newLibraryWithSource_options_error_ using an MTLCompileOptions whose fastMathEnabled is false, looks up the entry function, and builds a compute pipeline state. Any of the three steps failing raises RuntimeError; a library failure includes the MSL source. Setting TACK_DUMP_MSL (a boolean flag read by dispatch.env_flag, so 0, false, no and off leave it off) writes the source to /tmp/tack_<entry>.msl.

Arguments. Array pointers go into one argument buffer — the mechanism that makes overlapping arrays legal in MSL, explained in Memory and Aliasing. f64 never reaches the generator in normal dispatch, because it is not in supported_dtypes; MSLCodeGen also raises TypeError for an f64 parameter on its own, since Apple GPUs do not implement double precision.

Launch. The threadgroup width is min(pipeline.maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup(), 256). The grid is exactly loop_end threads (dispatchThreads_threadsPerThreadgroup_), so the last threadgroup may be partial and the kernel needs no bounds guard. Each dispatch encodes a compute pass into the backend's open command buffer (_open_batch), under the backend's batch lock, and returns. The buffer is committed every _BATCH (64) launches, with at most _IN_FLIGHT (4) committed ones outstanding; synchronize() commits the open one and waits for all of them, and a command-buffer error raises RuntimeError there, at the next host access, rather than at the launch's call. Each launch owns what it reads: a fresh argument buffer, its packed scalars in a buffer of their own (_Uniforms), and references to its arrays until it completes. A launch that binds memory handed outside Tack (_shared: an exported or wrapped buffer) completes before returning. An empty range returns before encoding anything. The loop index is declared long but initialized from [[thread_position_in_grid]], which Metal types as uint, so one dispatch covers at most 2³² iterations; check_launch_size() refuses a longer one against _MAX_LAUNCH with ValueError before encoding.

docs.title: CUDA
docs.text:
Initialization. CUDABackend.__init__ (runtime/cuda_backend.py) calls cuInit(0) and cuDeviceGet(0). If a context is already current on the calling thread — an embedding application such as an AMReX simulation made one — Tack adopts it. Otherwise it retains the device's primary context (cuDevicePrimaryCtxRetain), which the CUDA runtime and the libraries on it (PyTorch, CuPy, Warp) use: until 2026-10 Tack created its own with cuCtxCreate, and its next launch after one of those libraries made the primary context current failed with CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE (found comparing with Warp). Either way the context gets a _ContextToken that counts the backends sharing it and records whether Tack owns it; when an owned context's last backend goes away, a primary context is released (others may hold it) and any other destroyed, and buffers allocated in it are marked dead first. Memory and Aliasing explains why.

One thread's context

The context is current on the thread that made the device (the first tack.device("cuda"), whichever call made it). The launch path does not make it current on other threads, so a thread that dispatches must first call cuCtxSetCurrent with the backend's context, or its launch fails with CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_CONTEXT.

Compilation. _compile_ptx compiles with NVRTC using exactly these options, the module constant _NVRTC_OPTIONS, which the disk cache's target also names:

Option Why --ftz=false keep denormals rather than flushing to zero --prec-div=true IEEE-rounded division --prec-sqrt=true IEEE-rounded square root --fmad=true allow multiply-add contraction, which the contract permits; the generator emits a product outside a sum as __fmul_rn/__dmul_rn, since NVRTC also fuses across statements --extra-device-vectorization let NVRTC vectorize more aggressively

--use_fast_math is never passed. No target architecture is given, so NVRTC emits PTX for its default virtual architecture and the driver JIT-compiles that PTX in cuModuleLoadData. A compile failure raises RuntimeError with the NVRTC log and the source; the program is destroyed on both paths.

The first compile in a process checks nvrtcVersion and warns if NVRTC is older than 13 (runtime/nvrtc_version.py). NVRTC 12.0 miscompiled tack-examples' lattice Boltzmann example on an H100 (density off by up to 1.6e-2; 2.3e-6 with 13.2), and was not reduced to a kernel, so there is no workaround to apply. It also left the compiling thread in the C locale, which _compile_keeping_thread_locale undoes. The check runs at the first compile rather than when the device is made, so a machine without NVRTC fails where it did before.

Launch. Block size is WORKGROUP_SIZE (256, from lang/workgroup_participation.py) and the grid is (loop_end + 255) // 256 blocks. The kernel receives the loop end as a long long __n__ parameter and begins

long long i = (long long)blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
if (i >= __n__) return;

Locals and loop indices are long long. The built-ins are 32-bit unsigned, so blockIdx.x is widened before the multiply; a 32-bit product would wrap once a launch reached 2³² threads. At initialization the backend reads CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_MAX_GRID_DIM_X, and a launch of more than that many blocks of 256 is refused by check_launch_size() with ValueError. Arguments are passed as a ctypes array of pointers to argument values, and the launch is queued on the context's stream (_ContextToken makes one per context, with cuStreamCreate, on first use) and returns. An empty range returns before launching, since cuLaunchKernel rejects an empty grid. Buffers are stream-ordered: cuMemAllocAsync and cuMemFreeAsync on that stream, from the device's default memory pool with its release threshold raised, so freed memory is handed back out without a device round trip, and an array dropped while a queued launch still uses it is freed after that launch. A device without memory pools (a GPU in TCC mode on Windows) allocates with cuMemAlloc instead; since cuMemFree waits for the whole device, a dropped buffer is queued on its context and freed once the stream is idle, at the next allocation or sync (_free_dropped). from_numpy, fill and the allocation's zeroing are queued in order with the launches; to_numpy and read_range queue their copy and wait with cuStreamSynchronize.

Disk cache. The PTX NVRTC made is stored with the entry name, the parameter layout and the scalar pack layout, and loaded with cuModuleLoadData; load_variant makes the pack arrays anew from the call's arguments, since they are device memory of the process.

Export. allocate_array(..., exportable=True) returns an ExportableCUDABuffer, allocated through the virtual memory management API (cuMemCreate / cuMemMap) so it can be shared as an OS handle; see Interoperability.

docs.title: HIP
docs.text:
Initialization. HIPBackend.__init__ (runtime/hip_backend.py) calls hipInit(0) and uses the current device from hipGetDevice(). Tack does not create or destroy a context; the HIP runtime manages it. The backend then asks whether the device has texture hardware at all (hipDeviceAttributeImageSupport) and, if so, the smallest of its maximum 3D texture extents.

Compilation. _compile_code_object creates a hipRTC program and compiles it with the options in _HIPRTC_OPTIONS, which is one: -ffp-contract=on. hipRTC's default is clang's for HIP, -ffp-contract=fast, which fuses a multiply into an add or subtract in a later statement; on AMD GPUs it did so where the product had another use, so one variable held two values (with p = k * 0.2, p - p came out as the product's rounding error instead of zero), and a contour of a computed array took finite values for infinite ones. on fuses only inside one expression, which is what the contract permits. hipRTC targets the current device by default, and no unsafe or relaxed math option is requested. The result is a code object loaded with hipModuleLoadData. The disk cache stores that code object, machine code for one architecture, with the entry name, parameter and scalar pack layouts, and load_variant remakes the pack arrays from the call's arguments. HIPCodeGen (codegen/hip_gen.py) is the CUDA generator with two overrides: it prepends #include <hip/hip_runtime.h>, and it spells the texture handle hipTextureObject_t (_TEXTURE_OBJECT_TYPE), because hipRTC rejects CUDA's cudaTextureObject_t.

Launch. Identical geometry to CUDA — 256-thread blocks, a ceiling-divided grid, the same 64-bit index, guard and locals — through hipModuleLaunchKernel, queued as on CUDA. HIP has no context object to hold the stream, so it belongs to the device (_Queue, a blocking stream made on first use, so it stays ordered with the null stream), and each buffer keeps a reference to it. Buffers come from hipMalloc through a cache of dropped arrays' buffers (buffer_cache.BufferCache, by capacity class, at most a quarter of the device): every use of a buffer is queued on the one stream, so a dropped array's work runs before its buffer's next array's, which is what a stream-ordered pool promises, without a hipFree (which waits for the device) per array. ROCm 7.1.1's pool (hipMallocAsync, its release threshold raised) slowed with every allocation it had made -- over the 512 eta pieces' global ids from 63 to 600 µs a call, 2.7 ms when trimmed after each step, where hipMalloc stayed at 17 µs -- and stalled that port for two hours (illyad, 2026-10-27); TACK_HIP_ALLOCATOR=pool still selects it. A host write from pageable memory is queued behind the launches; measured on ROCm 7.1, HIP stages a small one (16 KB) before from_numpy returns and waits for the stream before a large one (4 MB), so either way the array gets what the array held when the call returned (test_hip_async.py). The launch limit (_query_max_launch) is the device's maximum gridDim.x times 256, capped at 2³² − 256, because the dispatch packet on AMD GPUs holds the grid's total work-item count in 32 bits.

hip-python 10 is a compatibility package over rocm.bindings (PyPI's newest, so the extra's lower bound resolves to it), and four things moved: no hip.LONG_VERSION (VERSION instead; _HIP_PYTHON_VERSION reads either), no hip.chip (the runtime library for the ctypes waits comes from rocm.bindings.util.paths.get_library_path, _runtime_library), a function whose first C parameter is an output struct allocates and returns it, (err, struct), instead of taking it (hipPointerGetAttributes, hipGetDeviceProperties; _call_with_output reads which from the binding's signature); and a struct's character arrays (hipDeviceProp_t.name, gcnArchName) are str, not bytes (_text). Before this, importing LONG_VERSION failed, so HIP read as unavailable and every HIP test skipped. With them the suite passes on hip-python 10.0 against ROCm 7.1.1 (MI210, 2026-10-15) as on 7.2.2.

Known toolchain defect. ROCm 7.0.2's device compiler (AMD clang 20, embedded in hipRTC's comgr) miscompiles one generated integer expression at -O1 and above: a 64-bit signed -253 < -1 inside the full expression evaluates false. The generated source is free of undefined behavior (UBSan under clang and gcc, -O0 to -O3) and is correct on CUDA and under ROCm's clang 23, so it's a compiler defect and not a code generation one. It depends on the surrounding expression, so Tack doesn't try to avoid it. ROCm 7.1.1, still AMD clang 20, does the same: on an MI210 (gfx90a) the generated kernel, built by hipcc into a host program with no Tack involved, gives the right answer at -O0 and the wrong one at -O1 to -O3. test_integer_expression_differential.py marks that one case as a strict expected failure when the HIP runtime reports ROCm 7.0 or 7.1 (hipRuntimeGetVersion()). hiprtcVersion() can't identify the release: it reports 9.0 on ROCm 7.0.2. A fixed toolchain reports XPASS, and the mark is then removed.

docs.title: Level Zero
docs.text:
Initialization. LevelZeroBackend.__init__ (runtime/level_zero_backend.py) loads libze_loader.so through ctypes and calls zeInit(0). Without options it takes the first driver and that driver's first device and creates its own context. With external_context={"driver", "device", "context"} it adopts all three handles from another library instead — see Interoperability. _query_device then reads:

Query Used for zeDeviceGetProperties deviceId, passed to ocloc -device; the device name zeDeviceGetComputeProperties maxGroupSizeX and maxTotalGroupSize, which cap the group size, and maxGroupCountX, which with it bounds one launch zeDeviceGetImageProperties maxImageDims3D, and maxSamplers > 0 as "has texture samplers" zeDeviceGetModuleProperties fp64flags != 0 adds f64 to supported_dtypes zeDeviceGetCommandQueueGroupProperties the first queue group with the compute flag

supported_dtypes is assigned on the instance, shadowing the class attribute, so supports_f64 follows the device automatically. _create_queues makes the backend's queue: one asynchronous immediate command list, to which every launch, fill and copy is appended, each followed by a barrier (_ordered) that keeps them in program order. A driver without zeCommandListHostSynchronize (API 1.6) gets a synchronous immediate list instead, every append completing at once. The list, and each kernel's argument state, are shared by every dispatch on the backend, and Level Zero forbids using them from two threads at once, so a reentrant _launch_lock is held around every launch, native reduction and host copy.

Compilation. OpenCL C from generate_opencl_source is compiled to SPIR-V in process by _compile_to_spirv, which calls oclocInvoke in libocloc.so with

compile -spv_only -device 0x<deviceId> -options "-cl-std=CL2.0 -cl-fp32-correctly-rounded-divide-sqrt" -file kernel.cl

and passes the source from memory, null-terminated, because ocloc treats in-memory sources as C strings. The options are the module constant _OCLOC_OPTIONS. The .spv output is handed to _create_module, which calls zeModuleCreate as ZE_MODULE_FORMAT_IL_SPIRV with build flags _MODULE_BUILD_FLAGS (the same OpenCL options, _OPENCL_OPTIONS); a failure raises RuntimeError with the module build log and the source. zeKernelCreate then returns the kernel handle. When the source uses double, the generator adds #pragma OPENCL EXTENSION cl_khr_fp64 : enable.

The cost of ocloc. Compilation on this backend is dominated by libocloc itself. Measured on an Intel Data Center GPU Max 1100 on 2026-10-04, idle, an ocloc call took about 191 ms regardless of kernel size, against 0.2 ms for zeModuleCreate; llvmlite on the CPU backend compiled the same kernel shapes in 21–55 ms. The floor is startup inside the library, not code generation. The disk cache is what avoids it: a variant is stored as the native binary IGC made at zeModuleCreate (zeModuleGetNativeBinary) beside the SPIR-V, and loaded as ZE_MODULE_FORMAT_NATIVE, about 0.2 ms a module in a new process; a binary the driver refuses loads from the SPIR-V instead (counted as native_refused). SPIR-V alone still went through IGC at zeModuleCreate, about 50 ms a kernel, unless the driver's own persistent cache, which lives outside TACK_CACHE_DIR and is off or unwritable on many clusters, held the result. The cache target therefore names the device and its IP version (which names its stepping), the driver, ocloc's version and options, the module build flags and f64 support. With the disk cache off, a device made with options recompiles the same sources, because the in-memory variant cache belongs to a backend instance; the plain tack.device("level_zero") is one backend for the process, so switching the default away and back keeps its variants.

Launch. The group size is min(256, maxGroupSizeX, maxTotalGroupSize). Each argument is set with zeKernelSetArgumentValue, followed by the loop end as a 64-bit __n__; the kernel starts with long i = (long)get_group_id(0) * (long)get_local_size(0) + (long)get_local_id(0); if (i >= __n__) return;, because this driver's get_global_id(0) wraps at 2^32 (see Parallel execution). Dispatch appends the launch with ceil(loop_end / group_size) groups to the queue, followed by a barrier, and returns; the kernel's arguments are captured when the launch is appended, so the next call may set its own. The host waits with zeCommandListHostSynchronize where it reads an array or calls tack.sync(). Ordering by barriers was chosen over an in-order list (ZE_COMMAND_QUEUE_FLAG_IN_ORDER): on driver 25.05.32567 an in-order list, immediate or regular, cost about 130 µs of device time per kernel, a barrier about 5. from_numpy queues a copy of a private snapshot of the array, so the caller may change it at once; host memory a queued copy or fill reads is held until the next wait, which comes early past 1024 objects or 256 MiB. Arrays are freed with zeMemFreeExt's deferred policy, after the work queued so far, where the driver has the extension; otherwise freeing waits for the queue. An empty range returns first; a negative count would wrap as an unsigned group count. The group count is a ctypes uint32 array that truncates rather than rejects, so a launch of more than maxGroupCountX groups is refused by check_launch_size() first.

LevelZeroBackend.__del__ intentionally does nothing: Level Zero cleanup at interpreter shutdown can crash because the driver may already be unloaded.

docs.title: Launches are queued
docs.text:
The CPU's dispatch returns once the range has run. The four GPU backends queue a launch and return: Metal into the open command buffer, CUDA on one stream per context, HIP on one stream per device, Level Zero on one asynchronous immediate command list. Waiting after every launch kept Python from preparing launch n + 1 while launch n ran, and for short launches the host side was most of the call: on Metal a wait cost about 0.3 ms; a contour of a million cells on an RTX 4060 Ti went from 9.6 to 7.1 ms, about the host cost of its 31 launches alone; on an Intel Max 1100 a hundred small launches went from 8.7 to 2.6 ms.

  • Order. Launches, fills and host-to-device copies on one backend run in the order they were made. On CUDA, HIP and Level Zero from_numpy and fill are queued with the launches; Metal's MetalBuffer methods wait for every live Metal backend's launches (_synchronize_all) before touching the shared memory.
  • Waits. The host waits where it reads an array (to_numpy, read_range and so host indexing, reductions), where memory leaves Tack (share(), below), after each launch in debug mode (its check reads the errors array), at Device.synchronize(), and at tack.sync(), which calls every live backend's synchronize(). A launch's error surfaces at the next wait rather than at its call.
  • Lifetimes. An array Python drops while a queued launch still uses it outlives that launch: CUDA and HIP allocate and free in stream order, Level Zero frees with the driver's deferred policy, and a Metal launch holds references to its arrays until it completes.
  • Memory outside Tack. A wrapped pointer (wrap_ptr, so array_from_ptr and DLPack imports), a DLPack export and Metal's export_memory() mark the buffer shared (DeviceBuffer.share()): the export waits for the queued launches, and every later launch that binds a shared buffer completes before it returns, because the other library may read the memory with no Tack call in between. CUDA's export_memory() of an ordinary array waits, then copies it once into exportable memory. CUDA, HIP and Level Zero also complete a launch that samples a hardware texture, whose image could otherwise be destroyed before the launch read it.

test_cuda_async.py, test_hip_async.py and test_level_zero_async.py cover order across launches and fills, per-launch scalars, host writes while the queue is busy, dropped temporaries, waits and shared buffers; test_metal.py covers Metal's order across batches, per-launch scalars and host writes.

docs.title: How each backend queues and waits, as measured
docs.text:
The measurements behind each backend's queue and waits, kept from the developer notes:

  • CUDA: CUDABuffer holds a stream-ordered device pointer (cuMemAllocAsync on the context's stream, freed with cuMemFreeAsync, so a temporary dropped while a queued launch still uses it is freed after that launch, and the driver's pool, with its release threshold raised, hands memory back out without a round trip). Every launch, fill and copy goes through that one stream (_ContextToken.queue()) in order and returns once queued; to_numpy, read_range and reductions wait for the stream (_drain) and then copy: a copy to pageable host memory waits inside the driver with the context held, so no other thread could launch meanwhile (one launch per 910 ms wait on an H100, driver 595), while a thread in cuStreamSynchronize holds nothing a launch needs (511 launches at 43 µs); from_numpy and fill queue and return; tack.sync() is a stream synchronize, and a launch's error surfaces at the next wait. A launch's scalar upload is a pageable cuMemcpyHtoDAsync, staged by the driver; behind a long kernel the staging ring fills after about 510 queued launches and the next upload waits for the kernel. A buffer handed outside Tack (wrap_ptr, DLPack export, share()) completes every launch that uses it before the launch returns, and so does a texture launch, since its image could be destroyed before a queued launch read it. See test_cuda_async.py.
  • HIP: HIPBuffer holds a stream-ordered device pointer, as CUDA's does: one blocking stream per device (_Queue, _queue() in hip_backend.py; ordered with the null stream), memory from hipMalloc through a cache of dropped arrays' buffers (BufferCache; TACK_HIP_ALLOCATOR=pool for the stream-ordered pool). Launches, fills and copies are queued on it and return; to_numpy, read_range, reductions and tack.sync() wait on an event recorded after the queued work (_StreamMarker, _wait_stream), through ctypes on the runtime library (_runtime), never hipStreamSynchronize: hip-python's wrappers hold the GIL while the runtime waits (another thread ran 6 times during a 357 ms wait, 353 through ctypes), and ROCm 7.1's stream synchronize holds the stream, so another thread's launch on it took the whole wait (350 ms; 60 µs waiting on an event). A copy to pageable host memory waits inside hipMemcpyAsync the same way, so a read waits on an event first (about 8 µs idle). A launch's error surfaces at the next wait. A host write from pageable memory may be queued: HIP stages a small one before returning and waits for the stream before a large one (16 KB staged, 4 MB waited, ROCm 7.1). wrap_ptr, DLPack export (share()) and texture launches complete before returning. A device without memory pools falls back to hipMalloc/hipFree. See test_hip_async.py.
  • Level Zero: L0Buffer holds a device pointer (zeMemAllocDevice). Every launch, fill and copy is appended to the backend's one asynchronous immediate command list (_queue) and returns once queued, each followed by a barrier (_ordered), which keeps program order: Intel's in-order lists (ZE_COMMAND_QUEUE_FLAG_IN_ORDER) cost about 100 µs of device time per kernel on driver 25.05, a barrier about 5. to_numpy, read_range and reductions queue a copy and a marker under _launch_lock and wait on the marker's event outside it (_ListMarker), so other threads launch meanwhile; tack.sync() is zeCommandListHostSynchronize; from_numpy copies the array privately and queues; copies to the device up to 16 MiB and from it up to 64 KiB go through pooled USM host memory (_HostStaging, guarded by _launch_lock), since from pageable memory Intel's driver does not return from appending one (to the device up to 4 MiB, from it up to 1 KiB, driver 25.05) until the queue drains, which made a launch's scalar upload wait for the kernels before it; host memory a queued copy or fill reads is held (_hold) until the next wait (a marker releases the holds before it), which comes early past 1024 objects or 256 MiB. Arrays are freed with zeMemFreeExt(DEFER_FREE), after the work queued so far (_free; without the extension, wait then free). share(), wrap_ptr, DLPack export and textures complete their launches before returning, as on CUDA. A driver without zeCommandListHostSynchronize gets a synchronous list. See test_level_zero_async.py.
  • asyncio (runtime/aio.py, optional): await tack.sync_async() and await array.numpy_async() wait in one of Tack's worker threads (tack-wait, 4) and resume the coroutine, so an event loop (trame, Jupyter, a server) keeps running while the device works; kernel calls stay plain calls. A backend opts in with Backend.async_marker() -- an object whose blocking wait() covers every launch queued so far and raises a launch's error: CUDA records a blocking-sync event on the context's stream (_StreamMarker), Metal commits the open batch and waits on the last command buffer (_CommandBufferMarker), Level Zero appends a barrier signalling a host-visible event from the backend's pools, reset and reused after the wait (_ListMarker, _take_event), HIP records a blocking-sync event on the device's stream and waits through ctypes (_StreamMarker) -- and buffers with DeviceBuffer.waits_off_thread and thread_binding() (CUDA makes its context current in the worker, _BoundContext; HIP makes the buffer's device current, _BoundDevice). Without a marker (the CPU) the wait is inline: correct, and the loop simply waits. The mark is taken at the call, so launches queued later are not waited for. cuda-bindings releases the GIL in cuEventSynchronize: during a 490 ms kernel another task ran 436 times awaiting sync_async and 0 times under tack.sync(); Level Zero's ctypes calls release it too (311-384 times during a 685 ms kernel on a Max 1100); hip-python's do not, hence HIP's ctypes waits (1353 times during a 1.45 s kernel on an MI210). See test_asyncio.py.

docs.title: Scalar arguments on the GPU
docs.text:
The CPU passes scalars by value. The four GPU backends instead run pack_scalars (lang/ir_pack_scalars.py) on a copy of the variant's IR in their build callback: every scalar parameter is replaced by a load from a small array, one array per scalar dtype (__pack_f32__, __pack_i32__, ...), marked _is_scalar_pack. The pass was written for Metal, whose kernels have a limited number of buffer bindings; packing makes the count one per scalar type instead of one per scalar, and the other GPU backends share the code path.

On CUDA, HIP and Level Zero the pack arrays are allocated once, when the variant is built (_create_pack_arrays in runtime/kernel_utils.py), and stored in the variant's payload. Each dispatch writes the new values with _update_pack_arrays, a host-to-device copy queued after the launches before it, so a queued launch still reads the values it was given. Metal keeps no pack arrays: each launch copies its values into a new buffer (_Uniforms) that the launch owns, since a shared pack rewritten for the next call could change under a launch that has not run yet. Changing a scalar's value therefore never recompiles. The loop range is resolved from the unpacked IR, because packing rewrites the parameter list that the range expression refers to.

Since the pack arrays belong to the variant, two threads dispatching the same variant at once would each write their arguments into the same buffers, and a launch could run with the other call's scalars. Reproduced on CUDA with four threads, 248 of 400 dispatches computed with another thread's scalars. CUDA and HIP therefore hold KernelVariant.dispatch_lock from the pack update until the launch is queued, so different variants still dispatch concurrently; uncontended, the lock cost about 0.25 µs against a 95 µs CUDA dispatch. Level Zero takes its backend-wide _launch_lock instead (see Level Zero). Metal launches own their argument buffer and scalars and encode one at a time under the backend's batch lock. The CPU binds arguments per call and takes no lock.

docs.title: Textures
docs.text:
tack.texture3d(array, shape) creates a Texture3D (lang/array.py) holding a copy of the array; in a kernel, tex.sample(u, v, w) interpolates trilinearly at normalized coordinates, where 0 and 1 are the centers of the first and last texels. Hardware samplers put texel centers at (i + 0.5) / N, so every hardware path rewrites each coordinate to (u * (N - 1) + 0.5) / N.

Storage. The texture copies its array when it is created, on every backend, and tex.update() copies it again; writes to the array in between don't reach it. The copy is storage the texture owns, in tex._storage. Backend.texture_in_hardware(shape_3d) chooses it: where the answer is true, create_texture_image() returns a backend image object (MetalTextureImage, CUDATextureImage, HIPTextureImage or L0TextureImage) whose upload(array) does the copy; otherwise the texture allocates a private f32 array and update() copies into it with the device copy kernel. Only one extra copy is held per texture. Images are built eagerly and updated in place, so their texture objects stay valid, and they free their device objects when the texture is collected (CUDA's only while its context is alive). At dispatch, bind_textures() (runtime/kernel_utils.py) replaces each Texture3D argument with its storage, never its array. No compiled kernel caches texture objects.

Backend Hardware path Software fallback when CPU none always Metal MTLTexture (3D, R32Float), filled by a blit from the array's buffer; sampler(normalized, linear, clamp_to_edge) never CUDA 3D CUDA array (one 32-bit float channel) filled with cuMemcpy3D; texture object with linear filtering, clamp, normalized coordinates never HIP hipMalloc3DArray + hipMemcpy3D; texture object as on CUDA the device reports no image support, or an extent exceeds its 3D texture limit Level Zero zeImageCreate (3D, 32-bit float), filled through a host staging allocation; CLK_NORMALIZED_COORDS_TRUE \| CLK_ADDRESS_CLAMP_TO_EDGE \| CLK_FILTER_LINEAR maxSamplers == 0 (Xe-HPC), or an extent exceeds maxImageDims3D

The fallback decision changes the generated code, so HIP and Level Zero ask texture_in_hardware() again in their own _store_texture_shapes, passed to resolve_variant, which runs before the variant key is built. The texture and the variant therefore agree on which storage is bound. Falling back clears the parameter's _is_texture flag and the generator emits a software trilinear helper over the texture's private array instead. tack.inspect calls the same hook, so it shows the code dispatch compiles.

CDNA parts — gfx940/941/942, the MI300 family — have no texture hardware, and hipRTC refuses tex3D outright there ("The image/texture API not supported on the device"), which is why HIP asks hipDeviceAttributeImageSupport rather than assuming. Xe-HPC similarly has no samplers; filtered image reads would be driver-emulated.

Why a snapshot on every backend. Hardware samplers read an image, not the array, so on those paths a texture is a copy whatever Tack does. The only portable rule is therefore that a texture is a copy everywhere, taken at points the program chooses: at creation and on update(). Owning the image in the texture, rather than caching it in a compiled kernel under the array's device address, means no texture is ever handed another's image (a new array that reuses a freed array's address, or a second texture over the same array, gets its own copy), and the image is released with its texture. The images are single-channel 32-bit float, so texture3d() rejects non-f32 arrays rather than reinterpreting them, and it rejects shapes whose W*H*D differs from the array's size, which the copies would read past. render_volume() calls update() before each render, since the mixed-scene path tracer reads the volume's array directly. test_texture_snapshot.py pins these rules.

docs.title: Device reductions
docs.text: Array.sum(), min() and max() call backend.reduce_array() when supports_device_reductions is true and otherwise reduce with NumPy on the host. All four GPU backends implement reduce_array only for f32 arrays, using a source from array_reduction_source(dialect, op) (codegen/reductions.py): a 256-lane tree in each group, followed by unordered atomic accumulation of the partial results. Any other dtype falls back to NumPy, as does Level Zero when the device's group-size limits are below 256. CUDA, HIP and Level Zero pass the element count as a 64-bit argument and check it with check_launch_size(). Metal's kernel holds the count in 32 bits, so Metal reduces an array of 2³² or more elements with NumPy over its shared buffer. An empty array returns 0.0 for sum and raises ValueError for min and max on every backend. The ordering and accuracy promises are in the contract.

docs.title: Workarounds and why they exist
docs.text: Generated code and runtime calls shaped around a vendor defect, each with the vendor and version it was found on and the test that guards it, are recorded in Vendor workarounds, so that each can be retired when a fix ships.

docs.title: Compilation Pipeline
docs.text:
This page follows one kernel call from Kernel.__call__ to a running native kernel. For each stage it names the module and function responsible, what the stage takes in and hands on, the invariants it establishes, and what it rejects. It is the "how" behind the kernel language contract. The companion page Specialization and Caching covers the cache key in depth.

The pipeline has three tiers with very different lifetimes, and most of the design follows from keeping them apart:

Tier Built Keyed by Lives in IR template Once per lowering specialization vector widths, texture extents, template structure Kernel._ir / Kernel._ir_cache Compiled variant Once per variant key argument types and categories, baked-in shapes, … the backend's _cache Dispatch Every call — nothing is retained

A warm call touches only the third tier and the key derivation that leads to it, and a call whose argument signature was seen before skips the key derivation too (_fast_resolve; see Specialization and Caching). Validation, lowering, the IR passes, verification, code generation and native compilation run only when something new is needed, and the first two tiers are also kept on disk across processes (the disk cache), so a new process may load both instead of building them.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    call["Kernel.__call__<br/>(lang/kernel.py)"] --> exec["backend.execute()"]
    exec --> rv["resolve_variant()<br/>(runtime/kernel_utils.py)"]
    rv --> fast{"signature seen before?<br/>(_fast_resolve)"}
    fast -- yes --> launch
    fast -- no --> args["classify arguments:<br/>templates, vectors, textures"]
    args --> getir{"Kernel.get_ir():<br/>IR template cached?"}
    getir -- no --> dir{".ir entry on disk?"}
    dir -- yes --> store
    dir -- no --> tr["template_rewrite<br/>(device-class args only)"]
    tr --> val["source_validation<br/>validate_source()"]
    val --> ast["ast_transform<br/>transform_kernel()"]
    ast --> vlow["verify_ir('lowered')"]
    vlow --> store["store IR template"]
    store --> key
    getir -- yes --> key["derive variant key<br/>(_KeyProbe, shape_signature,<br/>arrays_disjoint on CPU)"]
    key --> hit{"variant cached?"}
    hit -- no --> dvar{".variant entry on disk?"}
    dvar -- "yes: backend.load_variant" --> cache
    dvar -- no --> clone["clone_ir(template)"]
    clone --> passes["resolve → infer → check types →<br/>localize scalars → atomics/workgroups →<br/>optimize (verify after each)"]
    passes --> build["backend build callback:<br/>[GPU: clone + pack_scalars] →<br/>annotate_types → codegen → native compile"]
    build --> cache["store KernelVariant"]
    cache --> launch
    hit -- yes --> launch["per-dispatch checks, loop range,<br/>bind arguments, launch"]

docs.title: Stage 1: entry
docs.text:
Kernel (packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/kernel.py). The @tack.kernel decorator only captures the function. Kernel.__init__ reads its source with read_source (lang/func.py, a wrapper around inspect.getsource), dedents it and parses it with ast.parse. Nothing is validated or lowered at decoration time. If the source cannot be read (a function created by exec(), a bare REPL, or python -c before Python 3.13), read_source raises RuntimeError at once, naming the function and chaining the OSError. A kernel is compiled from its source text, so there is nothing to fall back on. @tack.func reads device functions through the same helper.

Kernel.__call__ asks tack.runtime.dispatch.launch_backend(name, args) which backend runs the launch: the default device's (get_backend(), the CPU if none was chosen) when it can address every array argument (an equal Backend.memory_domain) or there are none, otherwise the arrays' own device's. Arrays in two memory domains raise ValueError naming both. A @tack.device_class argument's arrays decide only when no plain array does, and resolve_variant checks them all against the chosen backend (check_devices, on the slow and the fast path). It then calls backend.execute(self, args, kwargs). Every backend's execute begins with resolve_variant() in packages/tack-core/src/tack/runtime/kernel_utils.py and passes it a backend-specific build callback. The CPU backend also passes specialize_disjoint=True. HIP and Level Zero pass their own store_texture_shapes, because their texture lowering depends on the device.

Kernel.__call__ is also where errors get the kernel's name. It translates them by exception type:

Raised inside the pipeline Reaches the caller as UnsupportedSyntaxError unchanged (it already names the kernel and source position) TypeError TypeError("Kernel '<name>': …"), chained to the original. A message that already starts with the kernel's name (argument count, backend dtypes, atomic targets) keeps it, so the name appears once other RuntimeError, including NotImplementedError and IRVerificationError RuntimeError("Kernel '<name>' failed on <BackendClass>: …"), chained, with any inner Kernel '<name>': prefix removed. A message containing "compilation failed" is shortened to its error: lines anything else (NameError, ValueError, …) unchanged

docs.title: Stage 2: argument classification
docs.text:
resolve_variant first rejects keyword arguments with NotImplementedError, which Kernel.__call__ reports as a RuntimeError. It then classifies the positional arguments. This runs on every dispatch:

  • _detect_template_args finds @tack.device_class objects (anything with a true _device_class attribute) and records their parameter indices.
  • _expand_template_args removes them and appends each template's array attributes and then its runtime (instance) scalars, each group sorted by attribute name, taking templates from the highest index down. This order matches the parameters that rewrite_templates appends, which is what lines the expanded argument tuple up with the IR's parameter list.
  • _detect_vector_arrays_from_args maps parameter names to _vector_n for tack.Array with a vector element dtype arguments. _detect_texture_arrays maps parameter names to Texture3D.shape_3d.

docs.title: Stage 3: the IR template
docs.text:
Kernel.get_ir(vector_arrays, template_args, texture_arrays, debug) returns the lowered, verified IR for this lowering specialization. Vector widths, texture extents, template objects and debug mode change what the frontend emits (scalarized component loads, sampling code, inlined method bodies, constants, bounds checks), so each combination gets its own template:

  • with no vectors, textures or templates, and debug mode off, the single Kernel._ir;
  • otherwise Kernel._ir_cache[key], with key = Kernel._make_cache_key(vector_arrays, template_args, texture_arrays, debug).

Lookups are lock-free. A miss takes the module-level _transform_lock (an RLock) and checks again before building, so concurrent first calls lower a template once. Building is Kernel._lower, which asks the disk cache (disk_cache.lowered) for a .ir entry first and otherwise runs _verified_transform: transform_kernel(...) followed by verify_ir(function, 'lowered'). A template that fails verification raises before it is stored, so it is never cached, in memory or on disk.

In debug mode (tack.set_debug(True) or TACK_DEBUG=1) lowering wraps each array access's flat index in an IRBoundsCheck, which is -1 when an index is out of bounds, after recording the first violation in a hidden errors array; leading and flat extents are IRArrayExtent loads from a hidden extents array, so no extent is compiled in. The two hidden array parameters (__tack_errors__, __tack_extents__) follow the kernel's own; dispatch appends them per thread (runtime/debug_bounds.py). The helpers are in lang/ir_bounds.py.

docs.title: 3a. Template rewrite
docs.text:
For @tack.device_class arguments, rewrite_templates in packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/template_rewrite.py works on a deep copy of the kernel's Python AST, before any IR exists. classify_template_attrs sorts the object's public attributes three ways:

  • class-level numeric attributes become ast.Constants (compile-time constants);
  • instance numeric attributes and Array attributes become synthetic parameters;
  • @tack.func methods are resolved with self removed, into a map local to this transformation.

Generated method calls carry a _tack_template_call marker, so a user function that happens to share the generated spelling stays distinct. Synthetic names are reserved with fresh_name against every name in the kernel and its methods. The IR and the code generators never see a template object. The rewrite rules are in Template System.

docs.title: 3b. Source validation
docs.text:
transform_kernel constructs a KernelTransformer. Its visit_Module calls validate_source() (packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/source_validation.py) on the kernel's FunctionDef before lowering a single statement. _SourceValidator is an allow-list visitor. Its generic_visit rejects every AST node type not in _SUPPORTED, and dedicated visitors handle the constructs whose support depends on context. Among other things it rejects:

  • parameters that are not plain positional ones, and default values;
  • non-numeric constants, except docstrings and print labels;
  • expression statements that are not calls, and keyword arguments;
  • barrier() used as a value, and barrier()/thread_id() with arguments (an atomic may be a value: the element's old value);
  • for/while with else, and literal zero or negative range steps;
  • break out of the parallel loop, and continue outside a loop;
  • return in a kernel, and return inside a loop in a device function. A kernel's final return, with a return annotation, is split off before validation (Kernel._split_result) into a one-thread epilogue kernel that stores the value in a hidden one-element array;
  • calls that are neither a statically bound @tack.func nor a kernel intrinsic (resolved through CallBindings, below).

Each rejection raises UnsupportedSyntaxError, a NotImplementedError and so also a RuntimeError. The message names the kind (Kernel or Device function), the function, the construct, and its line and column in the captured, dedented source.

Validation exists because lowering is selective. Before it, the transformer silently dropped statements it had no case for: an assert vanished from the IR without a diagnostic (contract regression LC4). Validating the original source, rather than relying on the transformer's own fallbacks, also catches constructs the transformer would never visit, such as statements after a return in a device function. See the source contract.

docs.title: 3c. AST transform
docs.text:
KernelTransformer (packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/ast_transform.py, with its parts in lang/lowering/) lowers the validated AST to the tree of nodes defined in packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/ir.py. The decisions that matter for the rest of the pipeline are these:

  • Loops. The kernel body's one for … in range(...) becomes the single IRParallelFor, normalized to start at zero. A kernel without one, a second one, or one inside a top-level if or while raises UnsupportedSyntaxError at the definition or the loop (_visit_parallel_for). A nonzero start or a step is moved into the body as i = start + idx * step, because every backend launches its grid over [0, n) and never sees the start (regression LC5). Nested loops become IRSequentialFor, and their range arguments are captured into temporaries so they are evaluated once, on entry. tack.ndindex(a, b) or (a, b, c) becomes one parallel loop that keeps its dimensions (dims, extents), which each backend binds from a launch of that shape; workgroup kernels and four or more dimensions use a loop over the product with the indices recovered by // and % in the body (lang/parallel_dims.py).
  • Array indexing. f[i, j] linearizes to i * IRDimSize(f, 1) + j. f.shape[k] and len(f) lower to IRDimSize. A dimension index that is not a literal is rejected.
  • Vectors. Vector expressions are scalarized into per-component names (_component_name), and a vector-array load expands into one load per component.
  • Evaluation order. _visit_ordered and _capture_value hoist the statements produced by expression-level inlining (_pre_stmts). When a later operand has side effects, they capture earlier operands into temporaries first. Together they preserve left-to-right evaluation.
  • Statements outside the loop. _visit_body checks each statement lowered outside the parallel loop with _check_outside_parallel_loop. An array or array store, atomic, barrier, block reduction or print there raises UnsupportedSyntaxError at its source position, since such statements may run any number of times per launch. The check runs on the lowered statement, so effects arriving through inlined device functions, template methods, vector stores or tuple unpacking are caught too, and nested bodies are checked first, so the position is the innermost statement's. See Parallel Execution.
  • continue. _mark_outermost_continues flags each continue that belongs to the parallel loop, so code generators end the iteration rather than the kernel (regression LC8).
  • Unbound names. _check_names_bound raises NameError when a name is read but never bound. The message gives the source position and, if the read came from an inlined device function, its name. Kernels do not capture Python values from the enclosing scope.

KernelTransformer.visit turns any NotImplementedError raised during lowering into an UnsupportedSyntaxError with the kernel name and the node's position, so the transformer's own refusals read like the validator's.

docs.title: 3d. Device-function binding and inlining
docs.text:
CallBindings (packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/call_bindings.py) answers "what does this call name refer to?" statically. A bare name is looked up in the defining function's closure cells and then in its globals. An attribute is followed only through module objects (vars(module)), never by evaluating a property or an arbitrary expression. A name that the function assigns, or binds as a parameter, is dynamic and shadows any outer binding.

A name that resolves to a Func is a device function to inline. An unbound bare name, or a name bound to the same-named object in builtins, math or tack, is an intrinsic; lowering then decides whether it knows it. Anything else raises NotImplementedError ("not a statically bound @tack.func or a supported kernel intrinsic"), which surfaces as UnsupportedSyntaxError.

_inline_func_body then works through these steps:

  1. Build CallBindings for the callee's namespace, and validate its original FunctionDef with validate_source(kind='Device function').
  2. Reject arity mismatches (TypeError) and recursion (_active_funcs).
  3. Allocate fresh names for parameters, locals and return slots.
  4. Restructure returns with _structure_returns, so every return is the last statement on its path. Statements after an if that returns are copied into its branches (regression LC7).
  5. Rename the body with _NameRenamer, which also turns each return into assignments to the result slot or slots.
  6. Emit parameter assignments (__<func>_<param>_<N>__ = <arg>), except for textures and shared or local arrays, which are aliased directly.
  7. Lower the renamed body with the callee's bindings active.

Bindings are consulted when an IR template is built. A cached template keeps the inlined bodies, so rebinding a device function later does not update existing kernels. The contract asks callers to recreate the kernel instead.

docs.title: 3e. Fresh names and identifier encoding
docs.text:
Every generated name (__eval_N__, __step_idx_N__, inlined locals, template parameters, vector components, scalar packs, localized scalars) comes from fresh_name in packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/ir_names.py. It appends a deterministic suffix until the spelling is unused. The IR therefore keeps Python's own names and never collides with a user binding.

Target-language spelling is a separate, later concern, handled in packages/tack-core/src/tack/codegen/identifiers.py:

  • kernel_entry_name encodes the kernel name for every backend. That includes LLVM: llvmlite's symbol lookup needs ASCII, and a kernel must not collide with a libm symbol.
  • The GPU generators call rename_gpu_bindings. It returns a codegen-only copy (transform_ir(..., copy_nodes=True)) in which every binding is tack_var_ plus an injective encoding. ASCII identifiers keep a readable form with _ and Z escaped; everything else becomes UTF-8 hex.

No vendor keyword lists are consulted. A parameter called float or threadIdx is simply encoded.

docs.title: 3f. Lowered verification
docs.text: verify_ir(function, 'lowered') checks the newly built tree (see the verifier table). Its failures are compiler bugs rather than user errors. It runs once per IR template.

docs.title: Stage 4: variant key derivation (every dispatch)
docs.text:
Before any of this, resolve_variant tries the dispatch fast path (_fast_resolve): when the call's signature (_call_signature, read off the arguments) was seen before on this backend and kernel, it reuses the template expansion plan and the variants that call resolved, decides disjointness, runs the per-call checks of stage 6 and returns. Calls with keyword arguments, arguments the signature cannot describe, and every call in debug mode take the steps below, the slow path, which records what it resolved for the next call (details).

With the template in hand, resolve_variant takes these steps:

  1. It calls check_workgroup_support on the template. Backends that declare supports_workgroups return at once. On the CPU, the set of workgroup primitives the kernel uses is memoized on the template (_workgroup_features), and using any of them raises NotImplementedError.
  2. It infers argument types on a _KeyProbe, a stand-in carrying a fresh list of _ProbeParams, by running infer_param_types and the backend's store_texture_shapes on it. The template's own parameters are not written to. Otherwise two threads dispatching the same kernel with different dtypes could read each other's annotations between write and read, and fetch a variant compiled for the other call's types.
  3. It computes shape_signature(template, name_to_array) and, on the CPU, arrays_disjoint(template, effective_args).
  4. It builds the key with kernel_variant_key and looks it up in the kernel's slot of backend._cache.

What goes into the key, and why, is the subject of Specialization and Caching.

docs.title: Stage 5: variant construction (miss only)
docs.text:
On a miss, resolve_variant first asks the disk cache for a .variant entry (_stored_variant): its post-pass IR and the backend's artifact, rebuilt by backend.load_variant, skip everything below, and a damaged or unloadable entry is ignored. Otherwise it runs the common passes on a private copy, and afterwards stores the new variant on disk (_store_variant) when the backend has a cache_target(). The order matters: each step relies on annotations an earlier one established, and each verification boundary rechecks the whole tree.

# Step Function Establishes Rejects 1 Copy clone_ir(template) a private, fully independent IR graph — 2 Resolve resolve_ir (lang/ir_resolve.py) every IRDimSize outside the parallel loop's end becomes a constant, following @tack.func array aliases; shared_like/local_array_like dtypes and texture extents are filled in unknown array: RuntimeError verify_ir(…, 'resolved') 3 Infer infer_param_types (lang/type_inference.py), store_texture_shapes type_annotation, _is_array, _is_texture and _texture_shape on every parameter wrong argument count or unsupported argument type: TypeError verify_ir(…, 'inferred') 4 Check types check_dispatch_types every array dtype is in backend.supported_dtypes TypeError naming the kernel, parameter, dtype and backend 5 Localize scalars _localize_outer_scalars (runtime/kernel_utils.py) a scalar parameter, or a local bound before the loop, that the loop body assigns to becomes a fresh local, seeded at the top of each iteration (regression LC6) — verify_ir(…, 'localized') 6 Atomics check_atomic_support, check_atomic_alignment (lang/atomic_support.py) each atomic target is a global array parameter of a dtype the backend supports, and suitably aligned TypeError (target or dtype), ValueError (alignment) 7 Workgroups (GPU) check_workgroup_participation, check_workgroup_launch (lang/workgroup_participation.py) collectives sit in provably uniform control flow; records whether the variant needs full 256-lane groups ValueError 8 Optimize optimize_ir (lang/ir_optimize.py) conservative copy propagation only — verify_ir(…, 'optimized') 9 Record ir_func.disjoint_arrays = disjoint the CPU no-overlap promise, for codegen — 10 Build the backend's build(ir_func, effective_args) see below backend compiler errors

Scalar localization runs after inference because it needs _is_array. It runs before packing because packing rewrites every read of a scalar parameter into a load from the pack buffer, so on GPU an assignment to that name would otherwise be lost. Outer locals are renamed for a different reason: on the CPU the statements before the loop run once per chunk, so without a per-iteration copy an iteration's assignment would carry into the next iteration of its chunk. The rename deliberately skips the parallel loop's end, which must keep naming the parameter for host evaluation.

Copy propagation is the only Tack-level optimization. Loop-invariant code motion and common-subexpression elimination were removed because they lacked memory and control-flow safety analysis. An invariant address is not an invariant value, and hoisting out of a zero-trip loop changes behavior (regression LC1). LLVM and the vendor compilers still optimize the generated code. IR Passes describes each pass in detail.

docs.title: The backend build callback
docs.text:
Backend Build steps Code generator Native compilation CPU annotate_types → verify_ir('typed') generate_llvm_ir (codegen/llvm_gen.py) llvm.parse_assembly and verify(), O3 pipeline, MCJIT, get_function_address Metal clone_ir → pack_scalars → verify_ir('packed') → annotate_types → verify_ir('typed') generate_msl_source newLibraryWithSource_options_error_ (fast math off), then a compute pipeline CUDA same as Metal generate_cuda_source NVRTC → PTX → cuModuleLoadData HIP same as Metal generate_hip_source hipRTC → code object Level Zero same as Metal generate_opencl_source oclocInvoke → SPIR-V → zeModuleCreate

GPU backends pack scalars on another clone. Packing rewrites the parameter list, and dispatch needs the unpacked IR to evaluate the launch range against the original arguments. KernelVariant.ir keeps the pre-packing IR's skeleton (_launch_skeleton: name, parameters, and the parallel loop with its bounds but no body), once the variant is stored to disk; the bodies were most of what variants held, tens of megabytes for a high-order filter's kernels. The payload holds the compiled kernel, the pack_info, and on CUDA, HIP and Level Zero the pack buffers, which are allocated once per variant (Metal makes a buffer of a launch's scalars per launch). The CPU annotates the variant's IR in place, since nothing else reads it. In debug mode annotate_types ends with ir_bounds.guard_accesses, which skips each access whose checked index is negative: a load yields a zero of its type, and a store or atomic runs under if index >= 0.

Annotation (annotate_types in lang/ir_type_annotate.py) can still reject a program: a negative literal integer exponent and a non-f32 block reduction both raise TypeError. Code generators re-check atomic support and workgroup participation on their own input, because direct generation can receive IR that no dispatch prepared.

The finished KernelVariant(ir, payload, requires_full_workgroups, atomic_targets, written_arrays, has_textures) is stored under its key. written_arrays lists the index and name of each array argument the kernel may store to (all of them when a store can't be traced), and the variant carries its own dispatch_lock. If any step raised, nothing is stored. The next call retries the variant (and fails the same way) rather than finding it cached in a broken state.

docs.title: Stage 6: dispatch (every call)
docs.text:
On a hit or a miss, resolve_variant ends with the checks that depend on this call's values. When the variant needs full workgroups, check_workgroup_launch requires the logical count to be a multiple of 256. check_atomic_alignment checks the alignment of the current atomic targets' storage, and check_writable_arrays refuses a read-only array (from array_from_ptr without writable=True, or a read-only DLPack import) bound to a parameter in written_arrays, with ValueError. The backend then takes over:

  1. It evaluates the launch count with _get_loop_range(variant.ir, args). This interprets the parallel loop's end against the arguments, with a texture standing for its source array; it understands constants, scalar parameters, IRDimSize, and + - * // over those. GPU backends return without launching when the count is not positive, and refuse a count past what one grid can index with check_launch_size() (ValueError).
  2. It replaces each Texture3D argument with the storage the texture owns, its hardware image or private array (bind_textures).
  3. On GPU, it writes the scalar values into the cached pack buffers (_update_pack_arrays) and appends those buffers to the argument list. CUDA and HIP do this and the launch under the variant's dispatch_lock, Level Zero under its backend _launch_lock; Metal copies the values into a buffer the launch owns.
  4. It launches. The CPU backend chooses between a serial call and its thread pool (see CPU Threading Policy) and returns once the range has run; GPU backends queue a grid and return (see Backend Implementations). In debug mode Kernel.__call__ then reads the errors array, which waits for the launch, and raises IndexError for a recorded violation.

docs.title: Verification at pass boundaries
docs.text:
verify_ir(function, stage) in packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/ir_verify.py is a read-only check of one IRFunction. Every stage runs the structural checks, and later stages add more. A failure raises IRVerificationError (a RuntimeError) that names the kernel, the stage, the node kind and the structural path, for example function.body[0].body[2].value.

Stage Called from Adds (all) — every node is a registered kind in a valid role (statement, expression, parameter); required attributes are present; names are nonempty; operators come from the known sets; constants are numeric; no cycles; parameter names are unique; exactly one top-level IRParallelFor, starting at constant 0; no array store, atomic, block reduction, barrier or print outside it; sequential loops sit inside it; break targets a sequential loop; each continue's outermost flag matches its loop; no IRReturn; every name read is bound somewhere in the function lowered kernel._verified_transform nothing further; a shared_like allocation may still lack its dtype resolved resolve_variant, inspect no IRDimSize or IRAttribute outside the parallel loop's end; allocation dtypes are ScalarTypes; texture extents are three positive integers inferred resolve_variant, inspect every parameter has a ScalarType and a boolean _is_array; every array load, store and atomic names an array parameter, an allocation, or a pointer copy of one localized resolve_variant, inspect rechecks the above after scalar localization optimized resolve_variant, inspect rechecks the above after copy propagation packed GPU _build_variant, inspect no scalar parameter remains typed every _build_variant, inspect every scalar expression outside the host-evaluated loop end has a ScalarType dtype; comparisons, Boolean operations and not have i32; every assignment has a storage type or is a pointer copy

The verifier deliberately does not prove definite assignment: its binding check asks whether a name is bound anywhere in the function, not on every path. Nor does it prove bounds safety, race freedom, barrier uniformity, alias safety of future optimizations, or numerical equivalence. Those remain the job of the contract tests, the differential tests and hardware validation (see Conformance and Validation).

docs.title: Why verification runs only on misses
docs.text: Verification walks the entire tree several times per variant, and for large kernels such as the path tracer it is a noticeable part of cold compilation. What it checks is a property of the IR, and a cached variant's IR does not change, so re-verifying on a hit would re-prove a fact already established for the same tree. The warm path therefore performs no verification walks, and its cost does not grow with kernel size. The price is paid once, on the first call of each variant. Verifying incrementally, instead of rechecking everything at each boundary, is a possible future saving that would keep every boundary's guarantees.

docs.title: IR ownership: templates are immutable
docs.text:
The template returned by get_ir() is shared by every dispatch of every variant built from it. Passes mutate IR in place: resolve_ir replaces IRDimSize nodes with constants, inference writes annotations onto parameters, and packing rewrites the parameter list. Running them on the template had two failure modes, both seen before the current design:

  • Consumed nodes. Once the first call had resolved a 2-D array's row stride into a literal, no IRDimSize remained for a second shape to resolve. The IR itself was stale, not only the compiled code.
  • Published annotations. Annotations written onto shared parameters were visible to concurrent dispatches computing their keys.

So the template is treated as immutable. The only writes it ever receives are memoized facts derived from its source alone (_shape_deps, _written_params, _written_flags, _workgroup_features), which do not depend on any call's arguments. All mutation happens on copies made by clone_ir.

docs.title: clone_ir rather than copy.deepcopy
docs.text:
clone_ir in packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/ir_traversal.py produces the same result as a deep copy, faster for this kind of data:

  • Registered IR node types (the keys of CHILD_FIELDS) are plain attribute containers. Cloning one is object.__new__(kind) plus a cloned __dict__, which skips deepcopy's generic __reduce_ex__ reconstruction for every node.
  • Every attribute is copied, including pass annotations and metadata, not only the structural children. A clone is a complete, independent graph.
  • One identity memo spans the whole graph, so shared nodes stay shared and cycles are preserved rather than duplicated. The sharing is real: an ndindex dimension node appears both in the loop's end and in its extents, and a range's start both in an extent and in the body.
  • ScalarType instances keep their identity, because type maps compare by identity. This matches ScalarType.__deepcopy__. Other metadata falls back to copy.deepcopy with the same memo, and a keep-alive list stops object ids from being reused during the copy.

Structural cycles are still invalid IR. clone_ir copies them faithfully and the verifier rejects them. Adding a node type with __slots__ or a custom copy protocol would mean revisiting this fast path.

The other two traversal primitives share CHILD_FIELDS, so all three agree on what a child is and fail loudly (TypeError: Unknown IR node) on an unregistered kind:

  • walk_ir(root) yields nodes in preorder and raises ValueError on a cycle.
  • transform_ir(root, rewrite, copy_nodes=False) rewrites children in postorder, in place. With copy_nodes=True it shallow-copies each node first, which is how rename_gpu_bindings makes its codegen-only copy.

docs.title: Inspection
docs.text: tack.inspect(kernel, *args, mode=...) (packages/tack-core/src/tack/lang/inspect_kernel.py) runs the same pipeline without the cache and without a launch. _prepare_ir clones the template and runs resolve, infer, the backend's _store_texture_shapes, check_dispatch_types, localize, the atomic and workgroup checks, optimize and annotate, with the same verification stages, so it rejects what dispatch would and makes the same texture decision. For mode="source" on a GPU backend it then packs and re-annotates (packed, typed). On the CPU it computes the disjoint-arrays bit for the given arguments, so the LLVM it shows is the variant those arguments would run. mode="optimized" is the CPU module after O3; on other backends it raises ValueError once the kernel's own checks have passed. Inspection never populates the variant cache.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• Specialization and Caching: the variant key and cache lifetime.
  • Principles: translate-or-reject, specialization, and correctness by default.
  • Developer's Guide: AST Transform, IR, IR Passes, Codegen.

docs.title: CPU Threading Policy
docs.text:
Every CPU dispatch makes one decision before it runs: execute the loop range on the calling thread, or split it into chunks and fan them out over a persistent thread pool. This page explains how that decision is made, why, and what is and is not promised about it.

The whole policy lives in packages/tack-core/src/tack/runtime/cpu.py: per-kernel state on CompiledKernel, decision and measurement code on CPUBackend, entered through CPUBackend._dispatch. The runtime chapter and the backends guide carry short versions.

In one paragraph

The backend compares two measured costs: how long this kernel takes per element when run serially, and how long it costs to wake the pool. Both are estimated continuously from real dispatches and folded into a per-kernel integer threshold (parallel_min_elems), so the decision is one integer comparison. Because each estimate can only be refreshed by one kind of dispatch, the policy periodically runs the other kind on purpose, so a wrong decision in either direction is eventually re-measured. Every path executes each loop index exactly once, so the decision affects speed only.

docs.title: What a fan-out costs
docs.text:
CPUBackend._parallel_execute divides [start, end) among the backend's num_threads threads (see "A thread count per launch" below for the alternative that was tried). Arguments are marshalled once per dispatch (CompiledKernel.bind); only the loop bounds differ between chunks.

The chunks run through one of two pools. The default is the pool in cpu_pool.py: a small program in LLVM IR, built with llvmlite.ir and JIT'd beside the kernels, whose N - 1 detached pthreads each wait on their own mailbox, a launch count (spinning for a while, then sleeping: on a futex on Linux, on os_sync_wait_on_address on macOS 14.4 and later, and elsewhere in nanosleep polls that back off to a millisecond). macOS used to poll, and every launch then waited for its slowest sleeper: the policy measured a 1 ms fan-out, kept mid-size launches serial, and the pool made the dataset filters 1.3–2.6× slower than the executor on an M1 Max; blocking on an address, its fan-out measured 73 µs. A fan-out is one ctypes call: pool_run posts to workers 0 .. k - 2, wakes those of them that sleep, runs as worker k - 1 itself and leaves the rest asleep, so a launch of two on a pool of sixteen costs two wake-ups (4.4 µs hot on a 2 GHz Xeon, against 11 when every worker was woken) and the k threads of every launch are the same k. Workers are not pinned to cores. Pinning was tried and dropped (2026-10-14): on a two-socket Xeon it was parity on 8 threads of 8 cores and a loss on 16 (every worker pinned: a 1M contour 33 ms against 19; one per core: still behind unpinned on most filters), and on a 28-core EPYC it lost 5-9% on the dataset filters, because a pinned worker cannot move off a busy core. The workers and the caller claim chunks from a shared counter (GRAIN per worker, each at least MIN_CHUNK elements) and run them through a wrapper JIT'd once per kernel that loads the arguments from 8-byte slots, and the workers never touch Python. Claimed rather than assigned because the dispatch waits for its slowest worker: with one equal chunk each, a worker the scheduler put on the sibling hyperthread of a busy core ran 1.7× slower and a compute-bound kernel over a million cells took 29 or 50 ms from run to run; claiming, it takes fewer chunks and the run takes 38 ms every time. Each worker reports the time and the elements it ran, which is what the rate and floor bookkeeping below reads. The pool is one per process (CPool.get), sized by the CPUs the process may run on (its affinity mask on Linux, the performance cores on Apple silicon), or by the first backend's thread count if that is larger; a dispatch uses as many of its threads as its backend has, and a backend asking for more threads than the pool has falls back to the executor. The pool's launch state is one set of JIT'd globals, so a run holds CPool._txn from the call through the read of its report: two Python threads fanning out at once otherwise ran each other's function and argument pack. A pool whose workers cannot all be started is dismantled, its workers joined, before the backend falls back. TACK_CPU_POOL=python selects the other pool, a ThreadPoolExecutor with one call_range task per chunk, which is also the fallback on Windows or when the JIT'd pool cannot be made.

What a fan-out costs differs by an order of magnitude between the two. Through the executor every worker wakes, takes the GIL to reach its ctypes call and takes it again to return, and the handoffs serialize: about 60 µs per worker on a 2 GHz Xeon (490 µs for eight, 1.2 ms after an idle gap of 2 ms or more, when the cores have entered C6); _calibrate_fan_out's docstring records 223 µs on the 10-core Apple silicon machine the policy was first written on (August 2026). Through the JIT'd pool it is 3–5 µs hot and about 100 µs after an idle gap (the C-state exit). Either way the policy measures the pool it uses and a fan-out pays only when the serial run it replaces takes meaningfully longer; with the JIT'd pool that is far more often. Measured on the Xeon, the dataset filters at a million cells went from a median 1.05× to 1.9× on eight threads.

docs.title: Why no fixed threshold works
docs.text:
The module docstring records the crossover — the range above which a fan-out wins — for three f32 kernels on that machine:

Kernel body Character Crossover out[i] = x[i]*2 + 1 memory bound ~4,000,000 sqrt(..) + sin(..) ~10 flop/element ~130,000 20-iteration inner loop ~120 flop/element ~4,000

The break-even moves by three orders of magnitude with arithmetic intensity, so any element count is wrong for most kernels. The original policy threaded every range above 1024 elements, below all three: for the memory-bound kernel a 65,536-element dispatch took 30.7 µs serially and 262.3 µs threaded, and threading won only at 4,194,304 elements (559 µs against 485 µs).

A threshold in elements also silently encodes the thread wake-up cost and timer resolution of the machine it was chosen on. So the module writes down no thresholds in elements or nanoseconds, only ratios — how much margin to demand, how much of a sample to trust, how far one sample may move an estimate — which carry across machines.

docs.title: What a wrong decision costs
docs.text:
Error What happens Size Over-eager: fanned out, serial would have won The dispatch pays a whole fan-out to save less than that Up to ~10x slower per dispatch in the measurement above, on every dispatch while the estimate stays wrong Under-eager: ran serially, parallel would have won Speedup not taken Bounded by the serial run; near the crossover, small by definition

The asymmetry shapes the design. Where the policy must err, it errs toward serial: estimates that are too high are distrusted, estimates that are too low are believed, and priors for the fan-out cost are pessimistic.

docs.title: Two paths, one crossover
docs.text:
With serial rate r_s (ns per element), fan-out cost F, and aggregate parallel rate r_p (ns per element of the whole range when fanned out):

serial ≈ n · r_s      parallel ≈ F + n · r_p      crossover n* = F / (r_s − r_p)

CPUBackend._min_elems stores the crossover scaled by a margin M:

parallel_min_elems = max(2, int(F · M / rate))
    rate = r_s − min(r_p, 0.9 · r_s)

The rate keeps r_p because real kernels do not divide perfectly. The removed policy v1 (see History) used rate = r_s: it assumed perfect division of the work, parallel ≈ F + T_serial / P, and drops r_p. Its margin of 2.0 (_PARALLEL_BREAK_EVEN) covers the break-even factor P / (P − 1) for any thread count. But real kernels do not reach speedup P: the effective speedup P_eff = r_s / r_p ranged from 1.5 to 9.2 across the kernels measured in the module's comments, and the margin v1 really applies is M · (1 − 1/P_eff). For a bandwidth-bound kernel with P_eff ≈ 1.5 that is 0.67 — below break-even, so the fan-outs it permits near the crossover lose.

Until a fan-out has measured it, r_p is 0.0 and the rate is r_s, so "not measured yet" needs no special case. The 0.9 · r_s clamp keeps the denominator positive when a noisy r_p approaches r_s, and caps the threshold at ten times the serial-rate-only one for the same inputs.

The floor is two elements, the fewest a fan-out can split; above it the costs decide, and a range shorter than the thread count leaves the threads it does not need idle (the pool's workers claim chunks from a counter, the executor's take one element each). It was the thread count, which kept chunks at one element or more when a fan-out split its range into one chunk a thread, and ran fewer dear elements than threads serially on every call: 17 streamlines on the ONERA M6 wing took 30 ms a call on jura's 28 threads, against 7-12 ms on 8 (2026-10-27). An unmeasured kernel, or a one-thread backend, gets _NEVER (1 << 62).

docs.title: The margin
docs.text:
Case _margin() default clamp(1 + _MARGIN_K · cv, _MARGIN_MIN, _MARGIN_MAX) = clamp(1 + 1.3 · cv, 1.0, 2.5) TACK_CPU_MARGIN set that value

A margin insures against mis-estimates, so it is sized by how unreliable the estimates currently are. cv is a smoothed relative deviation of new fan-out samples from the stored estimate (_update_fan_out_knot; weight _CV_SMOOTHING = 0.10, one sample capped at _CV_SAMPLE_CAP = 3.0). _margin()'s docstring records why: on one machine, a quiet run wanted the smallest margin tried while a loaded run needed at least 1.5.

Before any fan-out sample has been compared, cv is 0 and the margin is 1.0. (v1 used a constant 2.0, _PARALLEL_BREAK_EVEN.)

docs.title: One integer compare on the hot path
docs.text:
