@on_inputs_device
def segment_reduce(values, offsets, op="sum", out=None, empty=None, ordered=False):
    """Each segment's reduction: ``out[k]`` is the sum (``op="min"``, ``"max"``,
    ``"mean"``: the least, the greatest, the sum over the count) of
    ``values[offsets[k]:offsets[k + 1]]``, for the ``size(offsets) - 1`` segments,
    in ``values``' element type (a vector's componentwise). An empty segment
    gets ``empty``: by default 0 for a sum, NaN for a floating mean, and the
    type's greatest or least -- an infinity for floats -- for min and max;
    ``empty="keep"`` leaves its ``out`` as it is (a point with no cells keeps
    what the caller put there).

    Floating sums group by chunks of 256 elements, the same on every backend
    and run; ``ordered=True`` sums each segment in element order, one thread a
    segment, as ``reduce_by_key`` does (a long segment is then one thread's
    loop). Integer sums wrap at the values' width; min and max are exact either
    way. Returns ``out`` (made if not given)."""
    if op not in _OPS:
        raise ValueError(f"op is one of {', '.join(_OPS)}, not {op!r}")
    nseg = _segments(offsets)
    n = size_of(values)
    _check(offsets, nseg, n)
    kind = element_type(values)
    if out is None:
        out = tack.empty((nseg,), kind)
    elif size_of(out) < nseg:
        raise ValueError(f"out has {size_of(out)} elements for {nseg} segments")
    if not nseg:
        return out
    # One element of the values' type, a vector's every component the identity.
    keep = 1 if isinstance(empty, str) and empty == "keep" else 0
    identity = tack.full((1,), _identity(op, kind, None if keep else empty), kind)
    if ordered:
        _reduce_ordered(values, offsets, 0, offsets, 1, _OPS[op], out, identity, keep, nseg)
        return out
    long_flags = tack.empty((nseg,), tack.i32)
    long_count = tack.zeros((1,), tack.i32)
    _reduce_short(values, offsets, _OPS[op], _CHUNK, out, identity, keep, long_flags,
                  long_count, nseg)
    starts, stops, ids, nlong = _long(offsets, long_flags, long_count, nseg)
    if nlong:
        # The long segments' sums (a mean's too, divided as they are placed).
        total = _OPS["sum"] if op == "mean" else _OPS[op]
        long_out = tack.empty((nlong,), kind)
        _reduce(values, starts, 0, stops, 0, nlong, n, total, long_out, identity)
        _scatter_long(ids, starts, stops, long_out, _OPS[op], out, nlong)
    return out

Each segment's prefix sums (op="min", "max": running least or greatest), restarting at every segment: out[i] for i in segment k is the reduction of values[offsets[k]:i + 1] (inclusive), or of values[offsets[k]:i] with zero at the segment's first element (an exclusive sum; exclusive is for sums). Elements outside every segment are left as they are. out may be values. Floating sums group by chunks of 256 elements, the same on every backend and run. Returns out.

@on_inputs_device
def segment_scan(values, offsets, op="sum", inclusive=True, out=None):
    """Each segment's prefix sums (``op="min"``, ``"max"``: running least or
    greatest), restarting at every segment: ``out[i]`` for ``i`` in segment ``k`` is
    the reduction of ``values[offsets[k]:i + 1]`` (``inclusive``), or of
    ``values[offsets[k]:i]`` with zero at the segment's first element (an
    exclusive sum; exclusive is for sums). Elements outside every segment are
    left as they are. ``out`` may be ``values``. Floating sums group by chunks of
    256 elements, the same on every backend and run. Returns ``out``."""
    if op not in _OPS:
        raise ValueError(f"op is one of {', '.join(_OPS)}, not {op!r}")
    if not inclusive and op != "sum":
        raise ValueError("an exclusive scan is a sum's: op='sum'")
    nseg = _segments(offsets)
    n = size_of(values)
    _check(offsets, nseg, n)
    if out is None:
        out = tack.empty((n,), element_type(values))
    elif size_of(out) < n:
        raise ValueError(f"out has {size_of(out)} elements for {n} values")
    if nseg and n:
        long_flags = tack.empty((nseg,), tack.i32)
        long_count = tack.zeros((1,), tack.i32)
        _scan_short(values, offsets, _OPS[op], 1 if inclusive else 0, _CHUNK, out, long_flags,
                    long_count, nseg)
        starts, stops, _, nlong = _long(offsets, long_flags, long_count, nseg)
        if nlong:
            _scan(values, starts, 0, stops, 0, nlong, n, _OPS[op], inclusive, out)
    return out

@on_inputs_device
def segment_broadcast(segment_values, offsets, n, out=None):
    """Each segment's value spread over its elements: ``out[i] = segment_values[k]``
    for every ``i`` in segment ``k``, ``out`` of ``n`` elements (elements outside
    every segment left as they are). The inverse of ``segment_reduce``'s
    placement: per-segment results back to the elements. Returns ``out``."""
    nseg = _segments(offsets)
    _check(offsets, nseg, n)
    if size_of(segment_values) < nseg:
        raise ValueError(f"{size_of(segment_values)} values for {nseg} segments")
    if out is None:
        out = tack.empty((n,), element_type(segment_values))
    _spread(segment_values, offsets, nseg, n, out, 0)
    return out

@on_inputs_device
def argsort(keys, n=None, index_dtype=None):
    """Stable permutation that sorts the first ``n`` keys ascending.

    ``keys`` is an ``i32``, ``u32``, ``i64`` or ``u64`` array.  Returns a
    new array ``perm`` of ``n`` elements with ``keys[perm[0]] <=
    keys[perm[1]] <= ...``; equal keys keep their original order.  ``n``
    defaults to the whole array and may be zero.  ``perm`` is ``i32``, or
    ``i64`` past ``2**31 - 1`` elements or when ``index_dtype`` asks.
    """
    _key_width(keys)
    n = _count(n, keys)
    indices = _index_dtype(n, index_dtype)
    perm = tack.empty((n,), indices)
    if n == 0:
        return perm
    _iota(perm, n)
    if n == 1:
        return perm

    flip = 0 if keys.dtype in (tack.u32, tack.u64) else 1 << (keys.dtype.bits - 1)
    mapped = tack.empty((n,), tack.u64)
    map_keys = _map_keys_32 if keys.dtype.bits == 32 else _map_keys_64
    map_keys(keys, mapped, flip, n)

    # The passes needed depend on the spread of the keys, not their width.
    # The base is the smallest mapped key, so digits above the spread are
    # all zero and those passes can be skipped.
    base, largest = _key_range(mapped, n)
    spread = largest - base
    passes = (spread.bit_length() + _RADIX_BITS - 1) // _RADIX_BITS
    if passes == 0:
        return perm  # every key is equal: the identity is the stable order

    from tack.runtime.dispatch import get_backend

    mapped_b = tack.empty((n,), tack.u64)
    perm_b = tack.empty((n,), indices)
    if get_backend().supports_workgroups:
        # Tiles sorted into the second buffers, then scattered back: the
        # pass's result is where its input was.
        ntiles = (n + _TILE - 1) // _TILE
        counts = tack.empty((_RADIX * ntiles,), tack.i32)
        offsets = tack.empty((_RADIX * ntiles,), indices)
        starts = tack.empty((_RADIX * ntiles,), tack.i32)
        for p in range(passes):
            shift = p * _RADIX_BITS
            _sort_tiles(mapped, perm, mapped_b, perm_b, counts, starts, base, shift, n,
                        ntiles)
            exclusive_scan(counts, offsets, _RADIX * ntiles, total=False)
            _scatter_tiles(mapped_b, perm_b, mapped, perm, offsets, starts, base, shift, n,
                           ntiles)
        return perm
    nchunks = (n + _CHUNK - 1) // _CHUNK
    counts = tack.empty((_RADIX * nchunks,), tack.i32)
    offsets = tack.empty((_RADIX * nchunks,), indices)
    src_keys, src_perm, dst_keys, dst_perm = mapped, perm, mapped_b, perm_b
    for p in range(passes):
        shift = p * _RADIX_BITS
        _count_digits(src_keys, counts, base, shift, n, _CHUNK, nchunks)
        exclusive_scan(counts, offsets, _RADIX * nchunks, total=False)
        _scatter_digits(src_keys, src_perm, dst_keys, dst_perm, offsets,
                        base, shift, n, _CHUNK, nchunks)
        src_keys, dst_keys = dst_keys, src_keys
        src_perm, dst_perm = dst_perm, src_perm
    if src_perm is not perm:
        copy(src_perm, perm, n)
    return perm

Sort the first n keys ascending, carrying values along.

Returns (sorted_keys, sorted_values) as new arrays of n elements; sorted_values is None when no values are given. The sort is stable, so equal keys keep the order of their values. See argsort for the key dtypes.

@on_inputs_device
def sort_by_key(keys, values=None, n=None):
    """Sort the first ``n`` keys ascending, carrying ``values`` along.

    Returns ``(sorted_keys, sorted_values)`` as new arrays of ``n``
    elements; ``sorted_values`` is ``None`` when no values are given.  The
    sort is stable, so equal keys keep the order of their values.  See
    ``argsort`` for the key dtypes.
    """
    arrays = (keys,) if values is None else (keys, values)
    n = _count(n, *arrays)
    perm = argsort(keys, n)
    sorted_keys = gather(keys, perm, n)
    sorted_values = None if values is None else gather(values, perm, n)
    return sorted_keys, sorted_values

def gather(src, indices, n=None):
    """New array ``out`` with ``out[i] = src[indices[i]]`` for ``i < n``.

    ``indices`` is an integer array; ``n`` defaults to its size.  The
    output has ``src``'s dtype.  Indices must lie in ``[0, src.size)``.

    if n:

@on_inputs_device
def unique(sorted_keys, n=None):
    """The distinct keys of a sorted array and how often each occurs.

    ``sorted_keys`` must have equal keys adjacent (sorted, or grouped).
    Returns ``(keys, counts)``: ``keys`` is a new array of the same dtype
    holding each distinct key once, in order of first appearance, and
    ``counts`` the run lengths, an index array (see ``argsort``).  Works for any
    dtype that supports ``!=``.
    """
    n = _count(n, sorted_keys)
    offsets, nruns = _run_offsets(sorted_keys, n)
    keys = tack.empty((nruns,), element_type(sorted_keys))
    counts = tack.empty((nruns,), offsets.dtype)
    if nruns:
        _gather(sorted_keys, offsets, keys, nruns)
        _run_lengths(offsets, counts, nruns)
    return keys, counts

Reduce the values of each run of equal keys to one value.

sorted_keys must have equal keys adjacent, as for unique; values is any array with at least n elements. op is "sum", "min" or "max". Returns (keys, reduced): the distinct keys and a new array of values' dtype with one entry per key. @on_inputs_device
def reduce_by_key(sorted_keys, values, n=None, op="sum"):
    """Reduce the values of each run of equal keys to one value.

    ``sorted_keys`` must have equal keys adjacent, as for ``unique``;
    ``values`` is any array with at least ``n`` elements.  ``op`` is
    ``"sum"``, ``"min"`` or ``"max"``.  Returns ``(keys, reduced)``: the
    distinct keys and a new array of ``values``' dtype with one entry per
    key.  Each run is reduced serially in element order, so the result is
    exact for integers and reproducible for floats; integer sums wrap at
    the values' width.
    """
    reducer = _REDUCERS.get(op)
    if reducer is None:
        raise ValueError(f"op must be one of {', '.join(_REDUCERS)}; got {op!r}")
    n = _count(n, sorted_keys, values)
    offsets, nruns = _run_offsets(sorted_keys, n)
    keys = tack.empty((nruns,), element_type(sorted_keys))
    reduced = tack.empty((nruns,), element_type(values))
    if nruns:
        _gather(sorted_keys, offsets, keys, nruns)
        reducer(values, offsets, reduced, nruns)
    return keys, reduced

docs.title: Communication between blocks
docs.text: tack.communication moves data between blocks -- units of work with global ids, each on a device, such as the pieces of a partitioned dataset -- and combines values over them. World() is this process; its blocks may be on any of its devices. The User's Guide's Communicate Between Blocks builds algorithms on it step by step, and the Runtime API contract says what it guarantees.

docs.title: tack.communication.World
docs.text:
World(comm=None, *, gpu_aware=False)

The processes blocks live in, and how messages move between them.

World() is this process alone (rank 0 of 1): its blocks may be on any of its devices, and a message reaches its destination as copies of its arrays on the destination block's device -- the arrays themselves when that device can already address them.

World(comm) spans the ranks of comm, an mpi4py communicator (or anything with its Dup, Get_rank, Get_size, allgather, alltoall, Isend and Irecv). Tack communicates on a duplicate, so its messages never meet the application's; make one World for a run. Messages between ranks are staged through host memory, or with gpu_aware=True passed to MPI as the arrays themselves (through DLPack), for an MPI that reads and writes device memory. Where a backend says the MPI may not take an array's memory as it is (the stream-ordered pools of CUDA and HIP, which Cray MPICH cannot export and MVAPICH-Plus's UCX takes for host memory), the array goes as a device copy in memory the MPI does take, and arrives in such memory. Tack imports no MPI module: the caller makes the communicator.

A GPU-aware MPI uses the device that is current when MPI starts. Make the rank's device first, with tack.device("cuda:N"), and only then import mpi4py.MPI, which starts MPI. A rank that moves to another device afterwards loses Cray MPICH's CUDA IPC between ranks on a node (7 GB/s a rank against 22 on Perlmutter's A100s), or fails across nodes. CUDA IPC also needs every rank to see its node's GPUs (Slurm's --gpu-bind=none, not --gpus-per-task=1), each rank taking its own by local rank.

def __init__(self, comm=None, *, gpu_aware=False):
    self.gpu_aware = bool(gpu_aware)
    if comm is None:
        if gpu_aware:
            raise ValueError("gpu_aware applies to messages between ranks; "
                             "World() is one process")
        self._comm = None
        self.rank, self.size = 0, 1

exchange(outgoing)

Send messages between blocks and return what each block received.

outgoing is {source: {destination: message}}: for blocks on this rank, a message, a dict of names to Tack arrays on the source block's device, for any block. The result is {destination: {source: message}} for every block on this rank, in order of global id, with an empty dict where nothing came; each message's arrays are on the destination block's device.

A message's arrays belong to the receiver afterwards: where the destination's device addresses the source's memory, they are the sent arrays themselves, so a sender must not write to what it sent.

Source code in packages/tack-core/src/tack/communication/_blocks.py 
def exchange(self, outgoing):
    """Send messages between blocks and return what each block received.

    ``outgoing`` is ``{source: {destination: message}}``: for blocks on this
    rank, a message, a dict of names to Tack arrays on the source block's
    device, for any block. The result is ``{destination: {source: message}}``
    for every block on this rank, in order of global id, with an empty dict
    where nothing came; each message's arrays are on the destination block's
    device.

    A message's arrays belong to the receiver afterwards: where the
    destination's device addresses the source's memory, they are the sent
    arrays themselves, so a sender must not write to what it sent.
    """
    self._local_keys(outgoing, "exchange()")
    messages = []
    for source in sorted(outgoing):
        device = self._backend(source)
        for destination in sorted(outgoing[source]):
            self._check_gid(destination, "a message's destination")
            message = outgoing[source][destination]
            _check_message(message, source, destination, device)
            messages.append((source, destination, message))
    incoming = {gid: {} for gid in self.local}
    for source, destination, message in self.world._exchange(messages, self.rank_of, self.device):
        incoming[destination][source] = message
    return {gid: dict(sorted(received.items())) for gid, received in incoming.items()}

    are small Python objects (over MPI they are pickled)."""

values ({gid: number or NumPy array}, every block on this rank) combined over every block by op ("sum", "min" or "max").

def all_reduce(self, values, op="sum"):
    """``values`` (``{gid: number or NumPy array}``, every block on this rank)
    combined over every block by ``op`` (``"sum"``, ``"min"`` or ``"max"``).

    Values combine in order of global id, the same order whichever rank
    holds which block, so a floating-point sum has the same bits however
    the blocks are assigned."""
    if op not in _OPS:
        raise ValueError(f"all_reduce() takes op 'sum', 'min' or 'max', not {op!r}")
    every = self.all_gather(values)
    if not every:
        raise ValueError("all_reduce() over no blocks has no value")
    scalar, array = _OPS[op]
    result = every[0]
    for value in every[1:]:
        both_numbers = not isinstance(result, np.ndarray) and \
            not isinstance(value, np.ndarray)
        result = scalar(result, value) if both_numbers else array(result, value)
    return result

def exclusive_scan(self, counts):
    """Each block's offset, the sum of the counts of the blocks before it:
    ``({gid: offset}, total)`` for the blocks on this rank, from ``counts``
    (``{gid: int}``, every block on this rank) -- where each block's share of
    a global numbering starts."""
    every = self.all_gather(counts)
    for gid, count in enumerate(every):
        if not isinstance(count, (int, np.integer)) or count < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"exclusive_scan() takes counts that are integers of at "
                             f"least 0; block {gid}'s is {count!r}")
    starts = np.concatenate(([0], np.cumsum(every, dtype=np.int64)))
    return {gid: int(starts[gid]) for gid in self.local}, int(starts[-1])

link_by_bounds(boxes, margin=0.0)

Each block's neighbours: {gid: [other gids]} for the blocks on this rank, every block whose box overlaps or touches its box grown by margin on every side.

boxes is {gid: (lower, upper)} for every block on this rank, two corners of equal length. Blocks that share a face touch, so a margin of 0 finds the neighbours of a decomposition into abutting pieces; a margin of r finds every block within r.

Source code in packages/tack-core/src/tack/communication/_blocks.py 
def link_by_bounds(self, boxes, margin=0.0):
    """Each block's neighbours: ``{gid: [other gids]}`` for the blocks on this
    rank, every block whose box overlaps or touches its box grown by
    ``margin`` on every side.

    ``boxes`` is ``{gid: (lower, upper)}`` for every block on this rank, two
    corners of equal length. Blocks that share a face touch, so a margin of
    0 finds the neighbours of a decomposition into abutting pieces; a margin
    of ``r`` finds every block within ``r``."""
    if margin < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"link_by_bounds() takes a margin of at least 0, not {margin}")
    for gid, box in boxes.items():
        lower, upper = (np.asarray(corner, float) for corner in box)
        if lower.shape != upper.shape or lower.ndim != 1:
            raise ValueError(f"block {gid}'s box needs two corners of equal length, "
                             f"not {box!r}")
        if (lower > upper).any():
            raise ValueError(f"block {gid}'s box has a lower corner above its upper "
                             f"one: {box!r}")
    every = self.all_gather({gid: tuple(np.asarray(c, float) for c in box)
                             for gid, box in boxes.items()})
    dims = {len(lower) for lower, _ in every}
    if len(dims) > 1:
        raise ValueError(f"link_by_bounds() needs boxes of one dimension, not {sorted(dims)}")
    lower = np.array([box[0] for box in every]).reshape(self.count, -1)
    upper = np.array([box[1] for box in every]).reshape(self.count, -1)
    links = {}
    for gid in self.local:
        near = np.all((lower <= upper[gid] + margin) & (lower[gid] <= upper + margin), axis=1)
        near[gid] = False
        links[gid] = [int(g) for g in np.flatnonzero(near)]
    return links

docs.text:
Plan(blocks, sends, receives)

Which elements each block sends to which, and where the receiver puts them: an exchange kept for reuse, as ghost values are refreshed from their owners.

sends is {gid: {destination: indices}} and receives {gid: {source: indices}}, for blocks on this rank of blocks: the element indices a block reads for each destination, and those it writes from each source, in matching order. Indices are integer Tack arrays on the block's device, or anything numpy.asarray makes integers of. Every send must have a receive of its length on the other block, and the other way round; this is checked across ranks when the plan is made. A block may send to itself, as a piece in a periodic box is its own neighbour: what it sends is gathered before anything is written.

Source code in packages/tack-core/src/tack/communication/_plan.py 
def __init__(self, blocks, sends, receives):
    self.blocks = blocks
    blocks._local_keys(sends, "Plan's sends")
    blocks._local_keys(receives, "Plan's receives")
    self._sends = _indices(blocks, sends, "sends", "destination")
    self._receives = _indices(blocks, receives, "receives", "source")
    counts = blocks.all_gather({gid: (
        {other: idx.size for other, idx in self._sends.get(gid, {}).items()},
        {other: idx.size for other, idx in self._receives.get(gid, {}).items()})
        for gid in blocks.local})
    for gid in blocks.local:
        sent, received = counts[gid]
        for other, count in sent.items():
            theirs = counts[other][1].get(gid, 0)
            if theirs != count:
                raise ValueError(f"block {gid} sends {count} elements to block {other}, "
                                 f"which receives {theirs} from it")
        for other, count in received.items():
            theirs = counts[other][0].get(gid, 0)
            if theirs != count:
                raise ValueError(f"block {gid} receives {count} elements from block "
                                 f"{other}, which sends {theirs} to it")

Copy each sent element of values into its place on the receiving block.

values is {gid: array} -- or {gid: {name: array}} to move several arrays in one exchange -- with an entry for every block on this rank that sends or receives; each array is on its block's device, and an array and its counterparts on other blocks have one element type. Received elements are written in place; the others are left as they were.

def run(self, values):
    """Copy each sent element of ``values`` into its place on the receiving block.

    ``values`` is ``{gid: array}`` -- or ``{gid: {name: array}}`` to move
    several arrays in one exchange -- with an entry for every block on this
    rank that sends or receives; each array is on its block's device, and an
    array and its counterparts on other blocks have one element type. Received
    elements are written in place; the others are left as they were."""
    blocks = self.blocks
    if len({isinstance(entry, dict) for entry in values.values()}) > 1:
        raise TypeError("Plan.run() takes an array for every block or a dict of "
                        "arrays for every block, not both")
    named = {gid: entry if isinstance(entry, dict) else {"values": entry}
             for gid, entry in values.items()}
    blocks._local_keys(named, "Plan.run()")
    needed = sorted(set(self._sends) | set(self._receives))
    missing = [gid for gid in needed if gid not in named]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"Plan.run() needs values for blocks {missing}, which send or "
                         f"receive")
    for gid in needed:
        for name, array in named[gid].items():
            if not isinstance(array, Array):
                raise TypeError(f"Plan.run() moves Tack arrays; block {gid}'s {name!r} "
                                f"is a {type(array).__name__}")
            if array._backend.memory_domain != blocks._backend(gid).memory_domain:
                raise ValueError(f"block {gid}'s {name!r} is on {array.device}, not on "
                                 f"the block's device {blocks.device(gid)}")
    names = {gid: sorted(named[gid]) for gid in needed}
    if len({tuple(n) for n in names.values()}) > 1:
        raise ValueError(f"Plan.run() needs the same names on every block, not "
                         f"{sorted({tuple(n) for n in names.values()})}")

    outgoing = {}
    for gid, destinations in self._sends.items():
        outgoing[gid] = {}
        for destination, indices in destinations.items():
            message = {}
            for name, array in named[gid].items():
                message[name] = gather(array, indices)
            outgoing[gid][destination] = message
    incoming = blocks.exchange(outgoing)
    for gid, sources in self._receives.items():
        for source, indices in sources.items():
            message = incoming[gid][source]
            for name, array in named[gid].items():
                received = message[name]
                if received.dtype != array.dtype:
                    raise TypeError(f"block {source} sent {name!r} as {received.dtype}, "
                                    f"and block {gid} holds {array.dtype}")
                scatter(received, indices, array)

docs.title: tack.communication.Routing
docs.text:
Routing(blocks, positions, boxes, holds)

Where each point goes: the lowest block that holds it.

positions is {gid: points} for every block on this rank, an (n, d) host array of coordinates each (n may be 0); boxes {gid: (lower, upper)} for every block on this rank, None for a block that holds nothing. A point is asked of every block whose box holds it (with a relative slack of 1e-6), and holds(gid, points) -- called by the block asked, with the points it was asked about as an (m, d) float64 host array -- says how well it holds each: 0 not at all, or a rank (True is 1). The point goes to the block of the highest rank, the lowest such block on a tie: a locator that holds a point beats one only within its tolerance. Coordinates travel as their f64 bits in u64 arrays, which every device stores, so a block decides on exactly the points it was given.

destination is {gid: array}, each point's block, or -1 where no block holds it. send moves values with the points to their destinations, and reply returns values from there to where the points came from.

Source code in packages/tack-core/src/tack/communication/_route.py 
def __init__(self, blocks, positions, boxes, holds):
    self.blocks = blocks
    blocks._every_local(positions, "Routing's positions")
    blocks._every_local(boxes, "Routing's boxes")
    self._positions = {g: _points(positions[g]) for g in blocks.local}
    every = blocks.all_gather({g: None if boxes[g] is None else
                               tuple(np.asarray(c, np.float64) for c in boxes[g])
                               for g in blocks.local})

    # 1. Each point to every block whose box holds it.
    asked = {}
    for g in blocks.local:
        x = self._positions[g]
        asked[g] = {}
        for d, box in enumerate(every):
            if box is None or not len(x):
                continue
            lower, upper = box
            slack = 1e-6 * max(float(np.max(upper - lower)) if len(upper) else 0.0, 1.0)
            inside = np.all((x >= lower - slack) & (x <= upper + slack), axis=1)
            rows = np.flatnonzero(inside)
            if len(rows):
                message = _bits(x[rows], blocks.device(g))
                message["slot"] = tack.array(rows.astype(np.int64), tack.i64,
                                             device=blocks.device(g))
                asked[g][d] = message
    questions = blocks.exchange(asked)

    # 2. Each block says which it holds.
    answers = {}
    for g in blocks.local:
        answers[g] = {}
        for origin, message in questions[g].items():
            held = np.asarray(holds(g, _unbits(message))).astype(np.int32).reshape(-1)
            answers[g][origin] = {"slot": message["slot"],
                                  "held": tack.array(held, tack.i32,
                                                     device=blocks.device(g))}
    replies = blocks.exchange(answers)

    # 3. The highest rank takes it, the lowest block on a tie (replies come
    # in order of block, so a later one must rank strictly higher).
    self.destination = {}
    for g in blocks.local:
        n = len(self._positions[g])
        destination = np.full(n, -1, np.int64)
        best = np.zeros(n, np.int32)
        for d, reply in replies[g].items():
            slots = reply["slot"].numpy()
            rank = reply["held"].numpy()
            better = rank > best[slots]
            destination[slots[better]] = d
            best[slots[better]] = rank[better]
        self.destination[g] = destination
    self._arrivals = None

send(values=None)

Move values ({gid: {name: array}}, an element per point, on the block's device; may be omitted) with the points to their destinations. Returns {gid: (positions, {name: array})} for every block on this rank: what arrived there, the points as an (m, d) host array and the values on the block's device, in order of origin block and then of the points there. reply answers in that order.

Source code in packages/tack-core/src/tack/communication/_route.py 
def send(self, values=None):
    """Move ``values`` (``{gid: {name: array}}``, an element per point, on the
    block's device; may be omitted) with the points to their destinations.
    Returns ``{gid: (positions, {name: array})}`` for every block on this
    rank: what arrived there, the points as an ``(m, d)`` host array and the
    values on the block's device, in order of origin block and then of the
    points there. ``reply`` answers in that order."""
    blocks = self.blocks
    values = values or {g: {} for g in blocks.local}
    outgoing, self._order = {}, {}
    for g in blocks.local:
        outgoing[g] = {}
        for d in np.unique(self.destination[g][self.destination[g] >= 0]).tolist():
            rows = np.flatnonzero(self.destination[g] == d)
            device = blocks.device(g)
            message = _bits(self._positions[g][rows], device)
            message["slot"] = tack.array(rows.astype(np.int64), tack.i64, device=device)
            indices = tack.array(rows.astype(np.int64), tack.i64, device=device)
            for name, array in values.get(g, {}).items():
                if not isinstance(array, Array):
                    raise TypeError(f"Routing.send() moves Tack arrays; block {g}'s "
                                    f"{name!r} is a {type(array).__name__}")
                message["value." + name] = gather(array, indices)
            outgoing[g][int(d)] = message
    incoming = blocks.exchange(outgoing)
    arrived = {}
    self._arrivals = {}
    for g in blocks.local:
        parts = list(incoming[g].items())               # in order of origin
        self._arrivals[g] = [(origin, m["slot"], m["slot"].size) for origin, m in parts]
        x = (np.concatenate([_unbits(m) for _, m in parts]) if parts
             else np.zeros((0, self._width()), np.float64))
        names = sorted({k for _, m in parts for k in m if k.startswith("value.")})
        joined = {}
        for name in names:
            pieces = [m[name] for _, m in parts]
            joined[name[len("value."):]] = pieces[0] if len(pieces) == 1 \
                else tack.concat(pieces)
        arrived[g] = (x, joined)
    return arrived

reply(values, like)

Send values -- {gid: {name: array}}, an element for each point that arrived at the block (send's order) -- back to where the points came from. Returns {gid: {name: array}} for the blocks on this rank, an element per point of the block's positions, zero where the point had no destination. like is {name: element type}, for blocks none of whose points were taken.

Source code in packages/tack-core/src/tack/communication/_route.py 
def reply(self, values, like):
    """Send ``values`` -- ``{gid: {name: array}}``, an element for each point
    that arrived at the block (``send``'s order) -- back to where the points
    came from. Returns ``{gid: {name: array}}`` for the blocks on this rank,
    an element per point of the block's ``positions``, zero where the point
    had no destination. ``like`` is ``{name: element type}``, for blocks
    none of whose points were taken."""
    if self._arrivals is None:
        raise ValueError("Routing.reply() answers what Routing.send() delivered: "
                         "send first")
    blocks = self.blocks
    outgoing = {}
    for g in blocks.local:
        outgoing[g] = {}
        start = 0
        for origin, slots, count in self._arrivals[g]:
            indices = tack.array(np.arange(start, start + count, dtype=np.int64),
                                 tack.i64, device=blocks.device(g))
            message = {"slot": slots.to_device(blocks.device(g))}
            for name in like:
                message["value." + name] = gather(values[g][name], indices)
            outgoing[g][origin] = message
            start += count
    incoming = blocks.exchange(outgoing)
    out = {}
    for g in blocks.local:
        n = len(self._positions[g])
        out[g] = {}
        for name, dtype in like.items():
            array = tack.zeros((n,), dtype, device=blocks.device(g))
            for _, message in incoming[g].items():
                scatter(message["value." + name], message["slot"], array)
            out[g][name] = array
    return out

docs.text:
sort_by_key(blocks, keys, values=None, samples=16)

Sort the keys of every block, carrying values along: block 0 ends with the smallest keys, the last block with the largest, each block's ascending.

keys is {gid: array} and values {gid: {name: array}}, for every block on this rank: one-dimensional i32, u32, i64 or u64 keys of one type on every block, and values of the keys' length, each name of one element type everywhere, all on the block's device. Returns (keys, values) in the same form (values None if not given), on the same devices.

Every copy of a key ends on one block, so equal keys can be grouped where they land; heavily repeated keys can leave blocks uneven. The sort is stable: equal keys keep the order of their blocks, then their order within a block. A sample sort, as DIY's: each block sorts its own keys and sends samples of them, weighted by its count, from which every block finds the same count - 1 splitters; each block sends each range to its block, and sorts what arrives.

Source code in packages/tack-core/src/tack/communication/_sort.py 
def sort_by_key(blocks, keys, values=None, samples=16):
    """Sort the keys of every block, carrying ``values`` along: block 0 ends with the
    smallest keys, the last block with the largest, each block's ascending.

    ``keys`` is ``{gid: array}`` and ``values`` ``{gid: {name: array}}``, for every
    block on this rank: one-dimensional ``i32``, ``u32``, ``i64`` or ``u64`` keys of
    one type on every block, and values of the keys' length, each name of one
    element type everywhere, all on the block's device. Returns ``(keys,
    values)`` in the same form (``values`` None if not given), on the same
    devices.

    Every copy of a key ends on one block, so equal keys can be grouped where
    they land; heavily repeated keys can leave blocks uneven. The sort is
    stable: equal keys keep the order of their blocks, then their order within
    a block. A sample sort, as DIY's: each block sorts its own keys and sends
    ``samples`` of them, weighted by its count, from which every block finds the
    same ``count - 1`` splitters; each block sends each range to its block, and
    sorts what arrives.
    """
    blocks._every_local(keys, "sort_by_key()")
    given = values is not None
    values = {gid: {} for gid in blocks.local} if values is None else values
    blocks._every_local(values, "sort_by_key()'s values")
    for gid in blocks.local:
        _check(blocks, gid, keys[gid], values[gid])
    kinds = blocks.all_gather({gid: (keys[gid].dtype, {name: v.dtype for name, v in
                                                       values[gid].items()})
                               for gid in blocks.local})
    if len({repr(kind) for kind in kinds}) > 1:
        raise TypeError(f"sort_by_key() needs one key type and the same values, of one "
                        f"type each, on every block, not {sorted({repr(k) for k in kinds})}")

    ordered, carried, picks = {}, {}, {}
    for gid in blocks.local:
        perm = argsort(keys[gid])
        ordered[gid] = gather(keys[gid], perm)
        carried[gid] = {name: gather(v, perm) for name, v in values[gid].items()}
        n = ordered[gid].size
        m = min(samples, n)
        at = ((np.arange(m) + 0.5) * n / max(m, 1)).astype(np.int64)
        chosen = gather(ordered[gid], tack.array(at, tack.i64, device=blocks.device(gid)))
        picks[gid] = (chosen.numpy(), n)
    splitters = _splitters(blocks.all_gather(picks), blocks.count)
    if _in_one_place(blocks):
        return _sorted_in_one_place(blocks, ordered, carried, splitters, kinds, given)

    outgoing = {}
    for gid in blocks.local:
        n = ordered[gid].size
        bounds = [0, *search_right(ordered[gid], splitters).tolist(), n]
        outgoing[gid] = {}
        for destination in range(blocks.count):
            start, count = bounds[destination], bounds[destination + 1] - bounds[destination]
            if count:
                message = {"keys": take(ordered[gid], start, count)}
                for name, v in carried[gid].items():
                    message["values." + name] = take(v, start, count)
                outgoing[gid][destination] = message
    incoming = blocks.exchange(outgoing)

    sorted_keys, sorted_values = {}, {}
    for gid in blocks.local:
        runs = list(incoming[gid].values())             # in order of source block
        device = blocks.device(gid)
        key_type, value_types = kinds[gid]
        joined = _joined([run["keys"] for run in runs], key_type, device)
        perm = argsort(joined)
        sorted_keys[gid] = gather(joined, perm)
        sorted_values[gid] = {
            name: gather(_joined([run["values." + name] for run in runs], dtype, device), perm)
            for name, dtype in value_types.items()}
    return sorted_keys, (sorted_values if given else None)

def addresses_dlpack(self, device_type: int, device_id: int) -> bool:
    """Whether this backend can wrap a DLPack tensor on ``(device_type,
    device_id)`` without copying, so `from_dlpack` may put it here. By
    default by the backend's name (``lang/dlpack.py``'s
    ``_DEVICE_BACKENDS``) and, for a type with several devices, its ordinal.
    The Warp backend answers for the one device it drives."""
    from tack.lang.dlpack import _DEVICE_BACKENDS
    return self.name in _DEVICE_BACKENDS.get(device_type, ()) and (
        not self.multi_device or self.ordinal == device_id)

Allocate a single-channel f32 3D texture image.

Only called when texture_in_hardware() is True. The result is owned by one Texture3D: it exposes upload(array), which copies the array into it, and frees the device objects when collected.

Source code in packages/tack-core/src/tack/runtime/backend.py 
def create_texture_image(self, shape_3d):
    """Allocate a single-channel f32 3D texture image.

    Only called when `texture_in_hardware()` is True. The result is
    owned by one `Texture3D`: it exposes ``upload(array)``, which copies
    the array into it, and frees the device objects when collected.
    """
    raise NotImplementedError(
        f"{self.label} backend has no hardware textures")

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
This page is the source of truth

Tack has five backends, and a sixth as a prototype (Warp), and the details differ in ways that matter. This table is the canonical one — the README and the guides link here rather than restating it, because a capability table copied into three places drifts, and this one has.

docs.title: The five
docs.text:
Backend Codegen Runtime compiler Dispatch Buffer CPU llvm_gen.py → LLVM IR llvmlite JIT ctypes call, thread pool NumpyBuffer Metal msl_gen.py → MSL Metal API (pyobjc) compute pipeline MetalBuffer CUDA cuda_gen.py → CUDA C NVRTC → PTX cuLaunchKernel CUDABuffer HIP hip_gen.py → HIP C hipRTC hipModuleLaunchKernel HIPBuffer Level Zero opencl_gen.py → OpenCL C libocloc → SPIR-V zeCommandListAppendLaunchKernel L0Buffer Warp (prototype) warp_gen.py → @wp.kernel Python Warp wp.launch on Warp's current stream WarpBuffer (wp.array)

hip_gen.py is a few statements: it subclasses the CUDA generator and swaps the #include and the texture handle type (hipTextureObject_t), because HIP device code otherwise uses CUDA's syntax. opencl_gen.py also extends the CUDA generator, but overrides considerably more — OpenCL C spells address spaces, thread indices, barriers and math differently, and the wrong spelling still compiles as C.

docs.title: Launches and the disk cache
docs.text:
A kernel call returns The disk cache stores CPU when the kernel has finished object code Metal once queued in a command buffer, committed every 64 launches MSL source CUDA once queued on a stream PTX, compiled by the driver at load HIP once queued on a stream the code object Level Zero once queued on an asynchronous immediate command list the native binary, and the SPIR-V to fall back on Warp (prototype) once queued on Warp's current stream nothing: Warp's own kernel cache keeps the compiled code

A queued launch is waited for where the host reads an array or calls tack.sync(), and its errors surface there. A launch that uses memory shared with another library (DLPack export, array_from_ptr) completes before the call returns. See Backends in the User's Guide and The Kernel Cache.

Debug mode (tack.set_debug(True) or TACK_DEBUG=1) checks every index on all five.

docs.title: Scalar types
docs.text:
i8/u8 i16/u16 i32/u32 i64/u64 f32 f64 CPU ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ Metal ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ CUDA ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ HIP ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ Level Zero ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ⚠️ Warp (prototype) ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

Metal has no f64 — Apple GPUs do not implement double precision, so this is a hardware fact rather than a gap in Tack.

Level Zero decides at runtime. Some Intel parts implement f64 and some do not, so the backend queries zeDeviceGetModuleProperties when the device starts and builds its supported set from the answer. Ask the backend rather than assuming:

from tack.runtime.dispatch import get_backend
tack.set_default_device("level_zero")
print(get_backend().supports_f64)

supports_f64 is derived from supported_dtypes rather than stored separately, so the two cannot disagree.

docs.title: Workgroup execution
docs.text:
supports_workgroups is false on CPU and true on Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero, and on Warp's CUDA devices (not its CPU). Shared memory, barriers, local thread indices and block reductions require this capability. CPU rejects such kernels before compilation or execution; use local_array / local_array_like for private scratch storage instead.

Collectives require complete 256-lane groups and conservatively proven uniform participation. Smaller Metal pipeline/Level Zero device limits and partial collective grids are rejected. Shared/thread-ID kernels without collectives retain partial-grid support. The flag itself describes the execution model and does not certify participation or atomics. See the workgroup contract.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
Tack is not on PyPI yet. In a clone of the repository, each backend is an extra of tack-core (uv sync --extra cuda does the same as the line below):

pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[cpu]'          # llvmlite
pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[metal]'        # pyobjc-framework-Metal
pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[cuda]'         # cuda-python; needs the NVIDIA driver
pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[hip]'          # hip-python; needs ROCm
pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[level_zero]'   # installs nothing — see below
pip install -e 'packages/tack-core[warp]'         # warp-lang: the prototype Warp backend

Two of these need a word; the Warp backend is described in Backends.

HIP. hip-python's version tracks the ROCm release it binds to — 7.1.x against ROCm 7.1, 7.2.x against 7.2 — so the extra sets a lower bound rather than a pin. A system on a different ROCm wants it spelled out:

pip install 'hip-python~=7.2.0'

It ships manylinux x86_64 wheels only, so the dependency carries a platform marker and is skipped elsewhere. hip-python 10, a compatibility package over rocm.bindings, works too: it is what the lower bound installs today, and Tack runs on it against ROCm 7.1.

Level Zero. The extra is deliberately empty. Level Zero is reached through ctypes to libze_loader.so (the Level Zero runtime) and libocloc.so (the Intel offline compiler, part of intel-opencl-icd) — system libraries, not Python packages. The extra exists so the name stays valid.

docs.title: Asking a backend what it can do
docs.text:
Backends declare their capabilities rather than being probed with hasattr:

from tack.runtime.dispatch import get_backend

be = get_backend()
be.name                       # 'cpu', 'metal', 'cuda', 'hip', 'level_zero'
be.label                      # how to spell it in a message
be.supported_dtypes           # the frozenset dispatch checks array arguments against
be.supports_f64               # derived from the above
be.supports_device_reductions # whether .sum()/.min()/.max() run on device
be.device_memory_spaces       # what memory_space() must return for a pointer

See Backend for the full contract.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
This page defines every term the documentation uses, once. It is for readers who meet a word they do not know, and for readers who know VTK, ParaView or Viskores and want the word they already use. Each entry gives a definition, the counterparts in VTK, ParaView and Viskores, and the page that explains the term in full. The terms are grouped by Tack's four layers and listed alphabetically within each.

Two words mean something different in ParaView. A block here is a unit of distributed work, not one block of a multiblock dataset; that is a piece. A view here is how a kernel sees a dataset, not a render view.

A dash means there is no direct counterpart.

docs.title: array
docs.text:
A tack.Array: memory on one device, with a shape and an element type. The elements are scalars, small vectors or small matrices.

VTK: vtkDataArray · ParaView: an array · Viskores: ArrayHandle

Explained in arrays and types.

docs.title: atomic
docs.text:
An operation (tack.atomic_add, atomic_min, atomic_max) that updates one array element so that threads writing it at the same time lose no update. It returns the element's old value, which lets a thread claim a slot.

VTK: std::atomic in vtkSMPTools code · ParaView: — · Viskores: AtomicArray

Explained in workgroups, atomics, textures and random numbers.

docs.title: backend
docs.text:
The code generator and runtime for one kind of device. Tack has five: the CPU, Metal, CUDA, HIP and Level Zero, and NVIDIA Warp as a prototype.

VTK: a vtkSMPTools backend · ParaView: — · Viskores: a device adapter

Explained in choose a device. The backends reference lists what each supports.

docs.title: device
docs.text:
A backend made a value, such as tack.device("cuda:0"). It is where arrays live and kernels run. Every array records its device, and a kernel runs where its arrays are.

VTK: — · ParaView: — · Viskores: a device adapter tag and device id

Explained in choose a device.

docs.title: device class
docs.text:
A class decorated with @tack.device_class, whose objects a kernel takes as arguments. Its methods are compiled into the kernel, and its arrays and numbers become the kernel's arguments.

VTK: — · ParaView: — · Viskores: an execution object (ExecutionObjectBase)

Explained in device classes.

docs.title: device function
docs.text:
A function decorated with @tack.func, which kernels call. It is inlined into each kernel that calls it.

VTK: — · ParaView: — · Viskores: a VISKORES_EXEC function · CUDA: a __device__ function

Explained in device functions.

docs.title: implicit array
docs.text:
An array whose values are computed from its index or from other arrays, not stored: a constant, a count, uniform coordinates, a permutation. The module tack.arrays holds them, and kernels index them like any array.

VTK: vtkImplicitArray (vtkConstantArray, vtkAffineArray) · ParaView: — · Viskores: fancy array handles (ArrayHandleConstant, ArrayHandleCounting, ArrayHandleUniformPointCoordinates)

Explained in arrays and types.

docs.title: kernel
docs.text:
A Python function decorated with @tack.kernel, with one parallel loop. Tack compiles it for a device when it is first called, and each iteration of the loop runs as its own thread.

VTK: — · ParaView: — · Viskores: a worklet · CUDA: a kernel

Explained in kernels.

docs.title: launch
docs.text:
One call of a kernel over its loop's range. On a GPU a launch is queued and the call returns before it finishes. Reading an array or calling tack.sync() waits for it.

VTK: — · ParaView: — · Viskores: invoking a worklet · CUDA: a kernel launch

Explained in how a Tack program runs.

docs.title: variant
docs.text:
One compiled form of a kernel, for one set of argument types and, where the kernel's code depends on them, array shapes. A call with a new combination compiles a new variant. Later calls reuse it.

VTK: — · ParaView: — · Viskores: a template instantiation, made when the C++ is built

Explained in how a Tack program runs.

docs.title: workgroup
docs.text:
The threads of a GPU launch that share fast on-chip memory and wait for each other at barriers. The CPU has no workgroups.

VTK: — · ParaView: — · Viskores: — · CUDA: a thread block

Explained in workgroups, atomics, textures and random numbers.

docs.title: block
docs.text:
One unit of distributed work, on one rank and one device, such as one piece of a dataset. Blocks are numbered over all ranks by a global id, which is not a dataset's global ids.

VTK: — · ParaView: the part of the data one server process holds (not a multiblock's block) · Viskores: a DIY block · DIY: a block

Explained in blocks and worlds.

docs.title: plan
docs.text:
A Plan: the sends and receives between blocks, worked out once and run every step. Refreshing ghost values after each time step is the usual use.

VTK: — · ParaView: — · Viskores: —

Explained in exchange and plans.

docs.title: rank
docs.text:
One MPI process. A rank holds one or more blocks.

VTK: a process of a vtkMultiProcessController · ParaView: one pvserver process · Viskores: an MPI rank

Explained in blocks and worlds.

docs.title: routing
docs.text:
Sending points to the blocks that hold them, with values that travel with the points, and answering them in their order. Routing does it, for example to probe a dataset in pieces.

VTK: — · ParaView: — · Viskores: —

Explained in route points to blocks.

docs.title: world
docs.text:
The processes that work together: World() for one process, or World(comm) for the ranks of an MPI communicator. The same code runs in either.

VTK: vtkMultiProcessController · ParaView: the server's processes · Viskores: the communicator EnvironmentTracker holds

Explained in blocks and worlds.

docs.title: AMR dataset
docs.text:
An AMRDataSet: levels of structured boxes, each level finer than the one before it, with finer boxes covering parts of coarser ones. It is block-structured adaptive mesh refinement.

VTK: vtkOverlappingAMR · ParaView: an AMR dataset · Viskores: —

Explained in AMR hierarchies and octrees.

docs.title: cell
docs.text:
One element of a mesh, such as a tetrahedron, a hexahedron or a polyhedron. Its corners are points.

VTK: a cell · ParaView: a cell · Viskores: a cell (its shape a CellShapeTag)

Explained in cells and meshes.

docs.title: cell data
docs.text:
A field with one value per cell, constant inside each cell. In Tack it is a Constant field.

VTK: cell data · ParaView: cell data · Viskores: a field with cell association

Explained in fields and where values live.

docs.title: Constant
docs.text:
The space of fields with one value per cell, constant inside the cell. A Constant field is cell data.

VTK: cell data · ParaView: cell data · Viskores: cell association

Explained in fields and where values live.

docs.title: dataset
docs.text:
A DataSet: a topology, a geometry and fields. An image, an unstructured mesh and a point cloud are all datasets.

VTK: vtkDataSet · ParaView: the output of a source or filter · Viskores: viskores::cont::DataSet

Explained in the data layer's first page.

docs.title: field
docs.text:
A Field: values with a meaning. It holds an array of values, the space that says how they define a function, and a physical unit.

VTK: a data array with its association (point or cell) · ParaView: an array · Viskores: viskores::cont::Field

Explained in fields and where values live.

docs.title: geometry
docs.text:
The field that gives a dataset's positions. On an image it is computed from an origin and a spacing; on an unstructured mesh it is stored.

VTK: vtkPoints, or an image's origin and spacing · ParaView: the points · Viskores: a CoordinateSystem

Explained in topology and geometry.

docs.title: ghost cells
docs.text:
Cells copied from neighbouring pieces into a piece, so that filters on the piece see across its boundary. Ghost marks say they belong to another piece.

VTK: ghost cells (vtkGhostCellsGenerator) · ParaView: the Ghost Cells filter · Viskores: ghost cells

Explained in data in pieces.

docs.title: ghost marks
docs.text:
Bits for each point and each cell that say a copy is owned by another piece, or that a cell or point is hidden. Tack uses VTK's bits, so marks pass both ways unchanged.

VTK: vtkGhostType · ParaView: vtkGhostType · Viskores: the ghost cell field

Explained in data in pieces.

docs.title: global ids
docs.text:
Numbers for points and cells that are unique over all the pieces of a dataset. Copies of one point in two pieces have the same global id.

VTK: GlobalIds (vtkGenerateGlobalIds) · ParaView: the Global Point And Cell Ids filter · Viskores: —

Explained in data in pieces.

docs.title: H1
docs.text:
The space of continuous fields, whose values at shared nodes belong to every cell around them. It has any order. At order 1 an H1 field is point data.

VTK: point data; the point data of Lagrange cells · ParaView: point data · Viskores: point association · MFEM: H1_FECollection

Explained in fields and where values live and higher-order and finite-element data.

docs.title: higher order
docs.text:
Fields or geometry that are polynomials of order 2 or more inside each cell. A geometry of higher order makes curved cells.

VTK: Lagrange and Bézier cells; cell grids · ParaView: the same · Viskores: —

Explained in higher-order and finite-element data.

docs.title: L2
docs.text:
The space of discontinuous fields. Each cell holds its own values, of any order, so values may jump across a face. Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) solutions are L2 fields.

VTK: a discontinuous cell-grid attribute · ParaView: the same · Viskores: — · MFEM: L2_FECollection

Explained in fields and where values live and higher-order and finite-element data.

docs.title: octree
docs.text:
An OctreeDataSet: adaptive refinement by trees, in which each refined cell splits into eight children (four in 2D), down to leaves of different sizes.

VTK: vtkHyperTreeGrid · ParaView: a hyper tree grid · Viskores: —

Explained in AMR hierarchies and octrees.

docs.title: origin
docs.text:
The point a dataset's positions are stored relative to. It is three double-precision numbers, so positions far from zero stay accurate when they are stored in single precision.

VTK: — · ParaView: — · Viskores: —

Explained in coordinates, units and time.

docs.title: piece
docs.text:
One part of a dataset split for distribution over devices or ranks. A PartitionedDataSet holds a rank's pieces.

VTK: a partition of a vtkPartitionedDataSet · ParaView: a partition · Viskores: a partition of a PartitionedDataSet

Explained in data in pieces.

docs.title: point
docs.text:
A node of a mesh, the corner of one or more cells. Point clouds have points and no cells.

VTK: a point · ParaView: a point · Viskores: a point

Explained in cells and meshes.

docs.title: point data
docs.text:
A field with one value per point, interpolated linearly inside each cell. In Tack it is an H1 field of order 1.

VTK: point data · ParaView: point data · Viskores: a field with point association

Explained in fields and where values live.

docs.title: set
docs.text:
A Set: a selection of points, cells, faces or edges, made from their ids or from flags. A dataset can keep named sets.

VTK: a vtkSelection, or a list of ids · ParaView: a selection · Viskores: —

Explained in build meshes and fields.

docs.title: space
docs.text:
Where a field's values live and how they define a function inside each cell. H1, L2 and Constant are spaces.

VTK: a field's association (point or cell); the basis of a cell-grid attribute · ParaView: the association · Viskores: a field's association

Explained in fields and where values live.

docs.title: topology
docs.text:
How points join into cells, without positions. A structured topology is a grid of cells numbered by their index; an unstructured one stores each cell's points.

VTK: the cells of a vtkUnstructuredGrid, or an image's extent · ParaView: — · Viskores: a CellSet

Explained in topology and geometry.

docs.title: unit
docs.text:
A field's physical unit, such as "m/s". A dataset's spatial unit is its geometry's. Filters carry units to their outputs and derive the units of new quantities.

VTK: the UNITS_LABEL of an array's information · ParaView: — · Viskores: —

Explained in coordinates, units and time.

docs.title: algorithm
docs.text:
A function that takes a dataset first and returns something new: a dataset, a field or values. It never changes its input. An algorithm that returns a dataset is a filter.

VTK: a filter (vtkAlgorithm) · ParaView: a filter · Viskores: a filter

Explained in the visualization layer's first page. The algorithms reference lists them all.

docs.title: carry
docs.text:
Moving fields, ghost marks and global ids from a filter's input to its output. td.carry does it from a description of where each output point and cell comes from.

VTK: vtkDataSetAttributes::CopyData and InterpolateAllocate · ParaView: — · Viskores: a filter's mapping of fields onto its output

Explained in write a filter.

docs.title: filter
docs.text:
An algorithm that returns a new dataset, such as contour or clip.

VTK: a filter · ParaView: a filter · Viskores: viskores::filter::Filter

Explained in the visualization layer's first page.

docs.title: in situ
docs.text:
Running analysis inside a simulation while it runs, on its memory and its devices, instead of on files it writes.

VTK: in situ through Catalyst · ParaView: Catalyst · Viskores: in situ through Ascent

Explained in connect a simulation's data.

docs.title: locator
docs.text:
A search structure that finds the cell holding a point (CellLocator) or the points near a point (PointLocator). A topology keeps the locator it builds, so later searches reuse it.

VTK: vtkCellLocator, vtkStaticCellLocator, vtkStaticPointLocator · ParaView: — · Viskores: CellLocatorTwoLevel, PointLocatorSparseGrid

Explained in sample and trace.

docs.title: pathline
docs.text:
The path of one particle through a velocity field that changes in time. Pathlines follows particles over a dataset's steps.

VTK: vtkParticlePathFilter · ParaView: the Particle Path filter · Viskores: the Pathline filter

Explained in steps over time.

docs.title: streakline
docs.text:
The line made by all the particles released from one point over time, as dye released into a flow. Streaklines makes them.

VTK: vtkStreaklineFilter · ParaView: the Streak Line filter · Viskores: —

Explained in steps over time.

docs.title: streamline
docs.text:
A path through a velocity field that does not change in time. td.streamlines traces them from seed points.

VTK: vtkStreamTracer · ParaView: the Stream Tracer filter · Viskores: the Streamline filter

Explained in sample and trace.

docs.title: view
docs.text:
How a kernel sees a dataset's cells, faces, points or fields. A view is a device class that holds a dataset's arrays and answers in mesh terms: a cell's points, their positions, a field's value inside a cell. It is not a render view.

VTK: a vtkCell, and vtkDataSet methods such as GetCellPoints · ParaView: — · Viskores: the arguments of a WorkletVisitCellsWithPoints

Explained in views.

docs.title: Kernel language contract (draft)
docs.text:
This is the draft contract for compiler hardening, updated for the 0.6.0 release on 2026-10-28. It defines the intended portable kernel model, identifies known violations, and separates decisions still open for discussion. It is not a claim that the current implementation satisfies every requirement below. The baseline was reviewed at 05174e1.

Tack is a language for numerical kernels expressed using Python syntax. Its goals are predictable numerical results, portable CPU/GPU execution, and a compiler small enough to maintain. It does not implement arbitrary Python, provide autograd, or replace NumPy's general-purpose array API.

docs.title: Status and interpretation
docs.text:
• Required means an intended correctness property. A current violation is a compiler defect, including when existing examples happen to work.
  • Current behavior describes the implementation without making that behavior a permanent language guarantee.
  • Proposed means a policy this draft recommends but that needs agreement before becoming a public guarantee.
  • Open means no portable result is promised by this draft for that case. An open decision is not permission to change existing behavior silently.

Known defects are listed under Regression baseline. This draft governs the hardening work where older guides disagree. The guides remain useful examples, but are not an exhaustive semantics specification.

docs.title: Source and supported constructs
docs.text:
Required: the frontend must either translate a construct according to its defined semantics or reject it with a diagnostic. Silently dropping a statement, operand, or control-flow effect is not acceptable. Diagnostics identify the construct, kernel or device function, and source location. The frontend validates original source before lowering, including unreachable statements in device functions. Locations currently refer to the captured, dedented source, rather than absolute file coordinates.

The current language surface includes the following families. Inclusion does not imply that every Python use of the syntax is supported or that all corner cases have been validated.

Family Kernel surface Boundary Values Numeric literals, scalar parameters, array loads, local variables, tack.constant names (scalars, vectors, matrices), vectors and matrices up to 4×4 Fixed-width Tack types, not arbitrary Python objects. Assigning to a scalar parameter makes it a per-iteration local (LC6). Vectors and matrices are scalarized; see Vectors and matrices Arithmetic Arithmetic, comparisons, Boolean expressions, explicit casts, listed math builtins, @ on vectors and matrices Numerical and evaluation rules below. Comparisons and Boolean expressions of vectors act per component Assignments Local assignment, augmented assignment, array stores, tuple assignment to names, array elements and components Storage and ordering rules below Control flow range, tack.ndindex over sizes or (start, end) pairs, nested sequential loops, while, if/elif/else, conditional expressions, break, continue One top-level parallel loop; statements outside it only bind locals, load arrays and declare arrays Composition @tack.func inlining, returning one or several values (or another call's several values); a kernel's trailing return; @tack.device_class templates, passed to @tack.funcs and methods as well as to kernels, with inheritance, device functions held as attributes or under @staticmethod, kernels as methods, and indexing through @tack.func __getitem__, __setitem__ and __len__ (obj[i], obj[i] = v, obj[i] += v, len(obj); several indices as one vector; instance tuples of numbers read as obj.shape[k] with a literal k) Static source transformation, not arbitrary Python calls. A return ends the function on its path; one inside a loop is rejected (LC7) Storage Scalar arrays, vector arrays, matrix arrays, local arrays, shared memory, 3D textures Backend capability restrictions apply Parallel primitives Atomics, barriers, thread index, block reductions Workgroup requirements below

Python exceptions, try, context managers, generators, and runtime Python object manipulation are outside this baseline and rejected. So are imports, assertions (LC4), nested definitions, comprehensions, annotated assignments, keyword/starred arguments, and unsupported operators. Docstrings and pass are explicit no-ops. Parameter annotations and decorators remain host metadata; ordinary positional parameters without defaults are supported. Kernels do not capture numerical values from the enclosing Python scope: reading a name that is not a parameter and is never assigned raises NameError with the kernel (or inlined device function) and source position. The exception is explicit: a name bound to a tack.constant in the function's globals or closure, or reached as an attribute of a module, reads as that constant's value, a literal fixed where the constant was declared. Untyped, it follows the literal rules; declared with a dtype, it is that literal under the corresponding cast. A parameter or local of the same name shadows it. A kernel reads the constant its name was bound to when the kernel was first lowered. math.pi, math.e and math.tau read as literals in the same way. A for loop's variable is a binding that ends with its loop: reading the name after the loop, before it is assigned again, raises NameError with the read's position (Python would give the last value iterated; copy it to another name inside the loop instead). Sibling loops may share a variable, and the name may be assigned as an ordinary local afterwards. Local and shared arrays are storage, not values: binding another name to one (view = tmp) is rejected, while indexing it or passing it to a device function is supported. Supporting device assertions later would require changing this contract and its rejection test together. Barriers are statement-only; an atomic is a statement or an expression whose value is the element's old value.

Required: device-function binding. A static @tack.func call resolves to the function object bound in the defining kernel or device function's Python globals or closure. Imported aliases and module-qualified calls are supported. Each nested callee uses its own defining namespace; arguments use the caller's namespace. Importing another module with a same-named function must not change either cold or cached compilation. Local names and parameters shadow external callable bindings; runtime function values and ordinary Python callables are rejected rather than resolved by name. Resolution follows module dictionaries only and does not evaluate object properties or arbitrary Python expressions. Recursive device calls are rejected with a source diagnostic.

Template methods retain their original defining bindings after self resolution. Generated method calls use a transformation-local map and a source marker, so a user function with the same generated spelling remains distinct. No process-wide device-function registry participates in validation or lowering. Static bindings are consulted when an IR specialization is first built; cached IR preserves the inlined bodies. Rebinding a callable afterward is not a supported way to update compiled kernels; recreate the kernel to capture changed bindings.

Required: identifier preservation. Python-legal parameter, local, loop, allocation and kernel names retain their binding identity even when they are target-language keywords, builtins or compiler helper names. GPU code generation encodes every binding into a dedicated namespace and all backends use a shared encoding for kernel entry lookup, including Unicode names. Generated lowering temporaries, vector components, template parameters and packed scalar buffers allocate fresh spellings before code generation. These internal spellings are not a public ABI; argument order and resource binding indices stay unchanged.

Current behavior: kernels are compiled from inspectable source; a bare REPL or dynamically generated function may not provide that source. Kernel arguments are positional. A kernel whose last statement is return expr, with a return annotation naming the type (-> tack.f32, -> float for f32, -> int for i32), gives the host that value: after the launch, a one-thread epilogue kernel runs the statements outside the parallel loop and stores the expression into a hidden one-element array of that type, which the call reads and returns as a Python number. The expression may read arrays, arguments, constants and locals bound outside the loop, not a local the loop assigns. A kernel without one returns None. Device functions can return supported scalar, vector or tuple values for inlining.

docs.title: Execution and ordering
docs.text:
Required: the portable baseline has one top-level parallel range or ndindex iteration space. Each iteration owns its local variables. There is no defined order among different parallel iterations. Algorithms must avoid conflicting cross-iteration memory accesses unless they use the appropriate supported synchronization or atomic operation.

Required: the parallel loop is a for statement directly in the kernel body. A kernel without one, with a second one, or with one nested in a branch or while is rejected with a source diagnostic. Statements outside the parallel loop, before or after it, may be evaluated any number of times per launch: once per GPU thread, and on CPU once per chunk, threading probe or timing sample. They may therefore only assign local variables, load arrays, and declare shared or local arrays, which is unobservable however often it runs. Stores to arrays, atomics, barriers, block reductions and print there are rejected with the kernel or device function and source position, including inside top-level branches and while loops and when they arrive through an inlined @tack.func or template method. Every parallel iteration starts from the values those statements bind; an iteration that reassigns such a local does not change what another iteration sees.

Within one iteration, statements and nested sequential loops obey program order. A load observes an earlier store to the same location by that iteration, absent a conflicting access from another iteration. This holds across loop iterations, conditionals, and inlined device-function bodies. An empty sequential loop does not execute its body. See LC1.

Required: scalar operands and function arguments evaluate from left to right. Inlined calls retain their original execution position. and and or short-circuit; a conditional expression evaluates only its selected arm. Chained comparisons stop at the first false comparison and evaluate the middle operands' effects once. Ordinary assignment evaluates its value before its store index. Augmented assignment evaluates its index once and reads the old value before evaluating the right-hand side. A tuple assignment evaluates its whole right-hand side and then assigns its targets from left to right, so a subscript target's index sees the names assigned before it and not those after. A vector assignment evaluates every component of its right-hand side before it assigns any: v = v.cross(w) and a[i] = a[i].cross(b[i]) read the old components, including when the arrays read and written share storage. Sequential range arguments are evaluated once before entering the loop, including when its body changes a bound or step variable.

The top-level range(start, end) executes exactly the indices in [start, end), and no iteration when that interval is empty or reversed. Backends launch their grids from zero, so the frontend moves a nonzero start into the body; the length of the interval remains a per-dispatch value and does not specialize the compiled kernel. See LC5.

Required: every index of the interval executes, however long it is, or the launch is refused before anything runs. CUDA and HIP compute the iteration index in 64 bits from the block and thread numbers, and Level Zero from the work-group number (get_group_id), because Intel's get_global_id wraps at 2^32. A launch longer than one grid of the backend can index raises ValueError naming the kernel, the count and the limit. CUDA admits its device's maximum gridDim.x times 256 iterations; HIP also at most 2^32 - 256, because the AMD dispatch packet holds the work-item count in 32 bits; Metal 2^32, the range of its uint thread position; Level Zero its device's maximum group count times the workgroup size.

Early exits must preserve the defined control flow. continue ends the current iteration of its nearest enclosing loop, including the top-level parallel one, where it skips the rest of that iteration only (LC8). This frontend rejects break from the parallel loop: there is no ordered prefix of parallel iterations to stop. A kernel return anywhere but as the last statement is rejected. Positive range steps are supported, and literal zero or negative steps are rejected. A dynamic step must be positive; runtime validation of that caller constraint remains open. Cross-iteration communication requires further validation before joining the portable baseline. Outer launch bounds must be resolvable from host arguments and array metadata.

Required: optimizations preserve the observable behavior of every defined, race-free program, whether or not a current example uses that pattern. In particular, an invariant address does not make the stored value invariant. Moving a computation must also respect whether it executes at all; moving a load out of a zero-trip loop can introduce an invalid access. When a pass cannot establish safety, it must leave the computation in place.

Current implementation: Tack performs conservative copy propagation, retaining assignments and replacing only subsequent uses when neither the copy nor its source is rebound anywhere in the kernel. One kernel-wide assignment summary, including loop and allocation bindings, is reused in nested blocks. This deliberately leaves some block-local copies to the backend compiler instead of recounting every subtree. Custom load hoisting and CSE are disabled until memory and control-flow analyses can establish their safety. LLVM and the vendor compilers still perform their own optimizations.

docs.title: Memory and aliasing
docs.text:
Arrays (kernel arguments that are tack.Arrays) are typed, shaped storage associated with a backend. A new array holds unspecified contents until a kernel, tack.copyto or fill writes them; tack.zeros, ones and full make filled arrays. A subscript of an array gives one index per dimension, or a single flat, row-major index; a vector of integers stands for one index per component. Binding an array whose number of dimensions differs from the number of indices a kernel gives it raises TypeError at the call, naming the source position. Indices are not checked against the array's extents, except in debug mode (below). An array view or an imported pointer can share storage with another array. Host code reads one element with f[i, j] (a Python number, or a NumPy array of a vector or matrix element) and may not write one; DeviceBuffer.read_range defines the copy, which is a slice of host-visible memory on CPU and Metal and a copy of just the element on CUDA, HIP and Level Zero. Object identity does not establish that two arrays have different backing allocations. Callers must keep external storage alive for its use and must pass, in one launch, arrays in one device's memory; a launch runs on that device (the default device when it can address them).

Required: support overlapping array arguments by default, preserving program order within each iteration. This includes passing the same array twice and passing distinct views over the same storage. It does not make cross-iteration data races valid. LC2 tests this policy. LLVM array parameters carry no noalias promise; CUDA/HIP and OpenCL array pointers carry no __restrict__ or restrict promise. Metal loads array pointers from one argument buffer, so overlapping arrays are not passed as separate device-buffer kernel arguments.

Disjoint-storage specialization (CPU). The CPU backend may compile a second variant whose array pointers carry noalias, and uses it only for calls it has checked. The check runs on every dispatch and compares the byte ranges of the array arguments, never Python object identity: a call qualifies when no array the kernel stores to, directly, atomically, or through an inlined device function, shares a byte with any other array argument. Arrays that are only read may overlap each other. Calls that do not qualify run the variant without the promise, so the overlap policy above is unchanged and the two variants must agree on every race-free program. The qualification is part of the compiled-variant key. test_disjoint_arrays.py covers the analysis, partial overlaps of imported storage, the generated signatures, and switching between overlapping and disjoint calls.

Textures. tack.texture3d(array, shape=(W, H, D)) copies the array's data when it is created, on every backend. Later writes to the array, whether kernel stores, tack.copyto, or external and DLPack writes, are not visible to the texture until tex.update() copies the array again; sampling after that call sees the array's data as of the call. The copy belongs to the texture: a hardware image on CUDA, Metal, HIP with image support and Level Zero with samplers, otherwise a private array that generated code interpolates in software. It is released with the texture, and is never looked up by device address, so one texture cannot be served another's data. The array must be f32 with exactly W·H·D elements, x varying fastest; only interp='linear' is implemented, and other modes are rejected. test_texture_snapshot.py covers this on every available backend.

Required caller constraints for this baseline: access only in-bounds elements and initialized values; write only to writable storage. Dispatch refuses a read-only array (array_from_ptr's default, or a DLPack import flagged read-only) bound to a parameter the kernel may store to or update atomically; when a store cannot be traced to a parameter, every array argument counts as written. That is a check of the binding, not of accesses: writable arrays aliasing read-only storage are not detected. Indices are not checked, and an out-of-bounds access has no defined result. Debug mode (tack.set_debug(True) or TACK_DEBUG=1) is the exception: it checks every index of every array access against its extent, one dimension at a time (so a[i, j + 1] past the last column is caught even when its flat index lands inside the array), skips an access outside it (a load gives 0, a store or atomic does nothing), and makes the call raise IndexError naming the first such access; see the runtime API.
