Point clouds, curves, surface meshes, OpenFOAM polyMesh and boundary patches, CGNS sections of linear elements (one shape, MIXED, NGON_n and NFACE_n), EnSight parts of one kind, corner-point grids (inactive cells hidden) and FLASH axisymmetric data (an AMRDataSet of revolved boxes) are taken as they are: their arrays become Tack's, CGNS's 1-based and MIXED connectivities read lazily (see "models imported as they are"). Every other model goes through warp-simdata's to_vtk_data_model first. Image data becomes a uniform grid (offset from its extent), a structured grid a structured topology over its points, polydata of polygons or polylines a polygonal or polyline topology (vertices alone become vertex cells; a mix of kinds is refused: split it first), and an unstructured grid an unstructured topology, or a polyhedral one when it has polyhedra. NODE fields become H1 fields and ELEMENT fields Constant ones. The dataset must be on the device Tack's Warp device drives.

Source code in packages/tack-vis/src/tack/interop/warp.py 
def from_simdata(ds):
    """A warp-simdata dataset (or ``DatasetCollection``) as a Tack ``DataSet`` (or
    ``PartitionedDataSet``) on the Warp device, sharing its arrays.

    Point clouds, curves, surface meshes, OpenFOAM polyMesh and boundary
    patches, CGNS sections of linear elements (one shape, MIXED, NGON_n and
    NFACE_n), EnSight parts of one kind, corner-point grids (inactive cells
    hidden) and FLASH axisymmetric data (an ``AMRDataSet`` of revolved boxes)
    are taken as they are: their arrays become Tack's, CGNS's 1-based and MIXED
    connectivities read lazily (see "models imported as they are"). Every
    other model goes through warp-simdata's ``to_vtk_data_model`` first. Image data becomes a uniform grid (``offset`` from its extent), a structured
    grid a structured topology over its points, polydata of polygons or
    polylines a polygonal or polyline topology (vertices alone become vertex
    cells; a mix of kinds is refused: split it first), and an unstructured grid
    an unstructured topology, or a polyhedral one when it has polyhedra. NODE
    fields become H1 fields and ELEMENT fields Constant ones. The dataset must
    be on the device Tack's Warp device drives.
    """
    sd = _simdata()
    from warp_simdata.data_models.vtk import (
        image_data,
        polydata,
        structured_grid,
        unstructured_grid,
    )
    from warp_simdata.data_models.vtk.conversion import to_vtk_data_model

    from tack.arrays import ConstantArray, UniformCoordinates
    from tack.dataset import (
        PartitionedDataSet,
        PolygonalTopology,
        PolyhedralTopology,
        PolylineTopology,
        UnstructuredTopology,
    )
    from tack.dataset.dataset import grid_topology

    if isinstance(ds, sd.DatasetCollection):
        pieces = ds.datasets
        if any(not piece.has_field(name) for name in ds.get_field_names() for piece in pieces):
            # Fields of the collection itself: its VTK conversion hands them out.
            pieces = to_vtk_data_model(ds).datasets
        return PartitionedDataSet(from_simdata(piece) for piece in pieces)
    device = tack.device("warp")
    from warp_simdata.data_models.flash import axisymmetric as flash_model
    if ds.data_model is flash_model.DataModel:
        return _flash_amr(ds, device)
    with device:
        direct = _direct_topology(ds, device)
        if direct is None:
            more = _more_direct(ds, device)
            if more is not None:
                topology, geometry, ghosts = more
                return _with_fields(ds, topology, geometry, device, ghosts)
    if direct is not None:
        return _with_fields(ds, *direct, device)
    ds = to_vtk_data_model(ds)
    handle, kind = ds.handle, ds.data_model.DatasetHandle
    if kind is image_data.DatasetHandle:
        lo = np.asarray(handle.extent_min, np.int64)
        dims = np.asarray(handle.extent_max, np.int64) - lo + 1
        spacing = np.asarray(handle.spacing, np.float64)
        start = np.asarray(handle.origin, np.float64) + lo * spacing
        topology = grid_topology(dims.tolist(), offset=lo.tolist(), device=device)
        geometry = UniformCoordinates(dims.tolist(), start, spacing, np.eye(3), device=device)
    elif kind is structured_grid.DatasetHandle:
        lo = np.asarray(handle.extent_min, np.int64)
        dims = np.asarray(handle.extent_max, np.int64) - lo + 1
        topology = grid_topology(dims.tolist(), offset=lo.tolist(), device=device)
        geometry = from_warp(handle.points)
    elif kind is polydata.DatasetHandle:
        def present(offsets):
            return offsets is not None and offsets.shape[0] > 1
        kinds = [k for k in ("verts", "lines", "polys") if present(getattr(handle, f"{k}_offsets"))]
        if len(kinds) > 1:
            raise ValueError(f"polydata of {' and '.join(kinds)} together has no one Tack "
                             "topology: split it by kind first")
        n = ds.get_num_nodes()
        kind = kinds[0] if kinds else "verts"
        offsets = getattr(handle, f"{kind}_offsets")
        points = getattr(handle, f"{kind}_connectivity")
        offsets = from_warp(offsets) if present(offsets) else np.zeros(1, np.int32)
        points = from_warp(points) if present(getattr(handle, f"{kind}_offsets")) \
            else np.zeros(0, np.int32)
        with device:                        # host arrays among them go to the Warp device
            if kind == "polys":
                topology = PolygonalTopology(offsets, points, num_points=n)
            elif kind == "lines":
                topology = PolylineTopology(offsets, points, num_points=n)
            else:
                count = (len(offsets) if isinstance(offsets, np.ndarray) else offsets.shape[0]) - 1
                if points.shape[0] == count:
                    # One point each: every cell a VTK_VERTEX, an implicit array stored
                    # nowhere, as Tack's own point clouds' (uniform_cells).
                    types = ConstantArray(1, count, dtype=tack.u8)
                else:
                    # Poly-vertices among them (VTK_POLY_VERTEX, 2): a type per cell.
                    counts = np.diff(offsets.numpy() if isinstance(offsets, Array) else offsets)
                    types = np.where(counts == 1, 1, 2).astype(np.uint8)
                topology = UnstructuredTopology(types, offsets, points, num_points=n)
        geometry = from_warp(handle.points)
    elif kind is unstructured_grid.DatasetHandle:
        n = ds.get_num_nodes()
        types = from_warp(handle.cell_types)
        present = _present_types(types)
        if 42 in present:
            with device:                    # its new arrays on the Warp device
                topology = _polyhedra_from_simdata(handle, PolyhedralTopology, n)
        else:
            topology = UnstructuredTopology(types, from_warp(handle.cell_offsets),
                                            from_warp(handle.cell_connectivity), num_points=n)
        geometry = from_warp(handle.points)
    else:
        raise TypeError(f"no Tack topology for warp-simdata's {kind.__name__}")
    return _with_fields(ds, topology, geometry, device)

docs.title: Dataset API
docs.text:
tack.dataset, in the tack-vis package. This page describes the API as it stands; the Visualization Guide develops the model, mesh construction, field spaces, filters, mesh kernels and complete pipelines with checked examples. For why it is shaped this way and how it got here, see the design records: Dataset API and Polyhedra. They are history; this page is the current state. What is missing is listed with each part, and under Settled, and open. Each algorithm's and class's signature and parameters are in Algorithms and Data Model.

import tack.dataset as td
from tack.dataset import algorithms as alg

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
• A DataSet is a topology, named fields and named sets.
  • A topology is cells and the entities derived from them: faces, edges and points, and which cells lie on each side of a face.
  • A Field is a space and its values.
  • A space says where values live and how they are interpolated, if at all. It is built on a topology and owns its layout.
  • The geometry is a field, so point positions are data like any other. It is kept apart from the named fields, as data.geometry. Its values are relative to the dataset's origin, three doubles on the host (Origins and point clouds).
  • Kernels run over an iteration domain (cells, faces, edges or a face set) through for_each. That makes one launch per group of like entities, and each field argument becomes a view specialized to the group.
data = td.rectilinear_grid(np.linspace(0, 1, 11), np.linspace(0, 1, 11), [0.0, 1.0])
x = data.positions()
data.fields["height"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), scalars(x[:, 2] + 0.25 * x[:, 0]))
gradient = alg.gradients(data, data.fields["height"])     # a field on the cells

Here scalars stands for any function that puts a host array in a tack.Array.

docs.title: Import path migration
docs.text: The package is tack.dataset (previously tack.data). Change import tack.data as td to import tack.dataset as td, and use tack.dataset.<submodule> for direct imports. Existing td.DataSet, td.Field, spaces, topologies and algorithm calls keep their names and signatures. The shorthand td means Tack datasets.

docs.title: Topologies
docs.text:
There are two kinds. Shape-based topologies have cells of fixed shapes, each with a reference element: counts, tables and shape functions are compile-time constants. Polyhedral topologies have cells that are lists of faces of any size, with no reference element. They are separate paths that share everything else: spaces without a basis, fields, sets, for_each, the face conventions, and a common set of methods on cell views. topology.reference_cells says which kind a topology is.

Topology Built from Kind UnstructuredTopology(types, offsets, connectivity, num_points=None, id_dtype=None) VTK cell types and point rows, of the linear shapes (vertex to pyramid) shape-based StructuredTopology(point_dims, id_dtype=None, offset=None), usually through rectilinear_grid(x, y, z) grid dimensions; cells addressed by (i, j, k); offset, the grid index of its first point in a larger grid (VTK's extent's start: split's pieces, an image whose extent starts elsewhere) shape-based PolyhedralTopology(face_offsets, face_points, cell_offsets, cell_faces, cell_face_sides, num_points=None, id_dtype=None) faces stored once, as point rings wound out of side 0; each cell a list of faces, with the side (u8, 0 or 1) it is on polyhedral, 3D PolyhedralTopology.from_cell_faces(cells, num_points, positions=None, orient=False, id_dtype=None) each cell's own face rings, as VTK and most readers give them; copies of a face matched by point set polyhedral, 3D PolygonalTopology(loop_offsets, loop_points, num_points=None, id_dtype=None) each polygon's loop of points polyhedral, 2D PolylineTopology(line_offsets, line_points, num_points=None, id_dtype=None) each polyline's chain of points, two or more; a chain may close polyhedral, 1D

num_points exists because a dataset may have points that no cell uses.

Implicit topology arrays. An UnstructuredTopology's types, offsets and connectivity may each be an implicit array from tack.arrays, kept as it is and computed where it is read, as Viskores' single-type cell sets keep theirs:

  • the types of cells all of one shape, a ConstantArray (u8);
  • the offsets of cells all of one size, a CountingArray with that size as its step;
  • the connectivity of cells that each have their own points (vertex cells, a 2D contour's lines), a CountingArray too.

uniform_cells(shape_id, count, id_dtype) in tack.dataset.topology makes the first two. Filters whose output cells are all one shape give them: contour and slice (triangles, or lines in 2D), tetrahedralize, triangulate, extract_edges, the point extractions and probe's vertex cells (all three implicit), and threshold, extract_cells, extract_geometry and mask of a topology of one shape. A topology of one shape groups its cells without a histogram of their types. Everything else reads them as it reads stored ones; numpy() computes them on the host.

dataset_to_vtk hands them over as VTK's own: a ConstantArray of types becomes the cell type given as a number (VTK keeps it as a vtkConstantArray), a CountingArray a vtkAffineArray. vtk_to_dataset takes VTK's constant and affine arrays back as ConstantArray and CountingArray.

docs.title: Ids
docs.text:
Every id a topology stores or derives has one integer type, topology.id_dtype (also data.id_dtype): point and cell ids, offsets, faces, edges, point links, and the orders and keys that sort them. It is i32 unless the topology:

  • is asked for i64 (id_dtype=tack.i64);
  • is built from i64 fields;
  • or is too large for i32: an id, an offset or a derived array past 2^31 − 1 entries (a mesh's edges number up to twelve per cell).

Asked for i32, a topology too large for it raises, so a valid mesh's ids (each below num_points) are never wrapped. Arrays from NumPy or VTK (whose ids are 64-bit) take the narrowest type that holds them. Kernels specialize on their fields' types, so the same kernels serve both, and an i32 mesh pays nothing for the i64 path.

A filter's output keeps its input's type, or takes i64 when the output can be too large for i32 (a hexahedron tetrahedralizes into 24 connectivity entries), so a pipeline that starts in i64 stays there. Sort keys are tuples of ids, never ids packed into one integer, so 64-bit ids sort as 32-bit ones do.

On GPUs without 64-bit atomics (Metal, Level Zero), CellLocator's search from the cells refuses a dataset of more than 2^30 − 1 cells (it ranks a point's candidate cells up to twice the cell count in an atomic minimum); the search from the points uses no atomics, and everything else works there.

pytest --ids=i64 runs the dataset tests with every topology in i64.

docs.title: Derived entities
docs.text:
• topology.faces() and topology.edges() are derived on the device by sorting, the first time they are asked for, and then kept.
  • Faces are codimension 1 of the cells of the highest dimension (topology.dimension): a 3D mesh's faces are polygons, a 2D mesh's are its edges, on the shape path as on the polygonal one. A 2D cell's faces go round it (VTK counts none). A mesh mixing dimensions takes its faces from its top-dimensional cells alone.
  • On a 2D mesh face_geometry gives each edge's normal in the plane of its side 0's cell, pointing out of it, and its length as its "area"; face_centers its midpoint. net_flux, divergence, perot, jump and upwind_flux then work on 2D meshes as on 3D ones.
  • A mesh of line cells (a 1D grid's, or VTK lines) has no faces yet: a line's would be its end points, which are not derived, so faces() and everything built on it (face_geometry, extract_surface, side traces, jump, upwind_flux, ...) raise NotImplementedError. A polyline topology's have them.
  • A cell of no volume (a hexahedron whose points coincide, a grid of spacing 0), or a face or polygon of no area, has measure 0, its centroid at the mean of its points, and normals of zero length, so upwind_flux through it is 0. What divides by the measure has no value there: its gradients, flow_quantities and perot are NaN.
  • A polyline topology's faces are the chains' ends, one per point that chains end at: side 0 is the first chain ending there (in cell order), side 1 the second, and the normal runs along side 0's chain, out of it, with an "area" of 1. A vertex has no winding, so any two chains meeting end to end are consistent. Three or more ending at one point (a branch) have no faces: faces() refuses them, as a polygonal topology's refuses an edge of three polygons, while everything that does not need faces still works.
  • A face's points are wound out of its side 0. Side 1 is the cell on the other side, or none (-1) on the boundary.
  • Each cell knows, per local face, the face's id and which side of it the cell is on.
  • On a polyhedral topology the faces are given, not derived, and keep their given numbering.
  • Unstructured, polyhedral and polyline topologies also derive each cell's distinct points, sorted (cell_points(), CSR (offsets, point_ids)), for point data.

docs.title: Converting and checking
docs.text:
Function What it does as_polyhedra(data) a 3D shape-based dataset as polyhedra, carrying its fields as_polygons(data) a 2D shape-based dataset as polygons check_winding(data) of polyhedra or polygons, a cell Set of the cells whose faces do not wind consistently; empty when all is well (a shape's faces come from its table) orient(topology) turns around faces wound into their only cell from_cell_faces(..., orient=True) repairs input whose faces or cells are inconsistently wound, then turns each connected piece outward by the sign of its total volume topology.validate() checks the arrays a topology is built from, on their device, reading back a few integers: offsets start at 0, never run backwards and end at their members' length; every id is within its range (points; faces, for polyhedra; sides 0 or 1); an unstructured topology's types are linear shapes with their point counts. Raises ValueError saying what is wrong and how often, or returns the topology

Winding comes from the input, not from geometry. Inconsistent input is refused unless the caller asks for the repair.

A topology is not checked when made: a bad id is read, or written, out of bounds by whatever uses it first. Call validate() on input you did not make, or turn on debug mode (tack.set_debug(True), TACK_DEBUG=1), which checks every topology's ids when it is made -- before a polygonal or polyline topology derives anything from them -- along with every kernel's array accesses.

docs.title: Spaces
docs.text:
Space Values Interpolated Topologies H1(data, order=1) one per point, shared by the cells around it; order 2 adds one per edge and quad face; order p (basis=) p - 1 per edge, (p - 1)^2 per quad face, (p - 1)^d per cell yes, continuous order 1 on all; order 2 on tetrahedra, hexahedra, voxels, wedges, triangles, quads and pixels; any order on segments, quads, pixels, hexahedra and voxels, and on triangles, tetrahedra and wedges with nodes="equispaced" ((p - 1)(p - 2)/2 per triangle face, (p - 1)(p - 2)(p - 3)/6 per tetrahedron, (p - 1)^2 (p - 2)/2 per wedge) L2(data, order=1) each cell's own copies: order 1 one per corner, order 0 one per cell; order may be an array, one order per cell; a tensor basis' values in blocks or cell-fastest (layout=, by device by default) yes, discontinuous shape-based Constant(data) one per cell yes, constant in the cell all Values(data, on, oriented=False) one per point, edge, face or cell: data about the entity, with no basis no all SideTraces(data) per face, per side, per face point; made by project into it through the face's shape shape-based, 3D
  • Identity. A space is interned on its topology: H1(data) is the same object every time, so fields on it share its layout. Two spaces with different parameters are different objects.
  • Size. Every space knows its size. A field of the wrong length, or a field from another topology, is refused.
  • Continuity follows from where the values live (MFEM's model): values on shared entities are continuous, and values owned per cell are not.
  • Oriented face values. oriented=True is for a quantity measured along the face's normal, such as a normal flux. Anything that turns a face around (threshold, orient) negates such values. Plain face values (an area, an id) are left alone.

Attributes: topology, size, on (the entity kind the values are indexed by), interpolated, and order where it applies.

docs.title: Moving a field between spaces
docs.text:
project(data, field, space) gives field in another space of the same topology, as a new field. Values on points or cells count as order-1 H1 and Constant, as source and as target.

Into Each value is Exact when H1 (order 1 or 2) the mean, over the cells around the node, of the source evaluated there the source is continuous: a lower order comes across exactly Constant, order-0 L2 the source's average over the cell: its integral over the measure (average="nodes": the mean of its nodes, as vtkPointDataToCellData) the source is constant in the cell order-1 L2 (or an order per cell) the source's value at each corner (the cell's average at order 0) the source's order is at most 1 SideTraces each side's value from its cell always

Where cells disagree -- cell data, DG data -- the H1 mean is VTK's averaging (vtkCellDataToPointData). Sums run in a fixed order. Scalars or vectors; floating point. Values on faces or edges have no basis and are refused. On polyhedra, polygons and polylines only cell and point values project, each into the other.

Unused points retain their values when the source is H1 (or values on points). Cell or DG sources give unused points zero, since no cell contributes there.

project is the one way to move a field: into H1(data) for point values, Constant(data) for one value per cell, L2(data) for each cell's own copies, SideTraces(data) for each side's value at the faces.

docs.title: A field from a function of position
docs.text:
interpolate(data, function, space, dtype=None) is the field in space whose values are function at the space's nodes. function is a @tack.func of a world position (a 3-vector of the geometry's type) that returns a scalar or a vector; dtype is what it returns, data.dtype by default (dtype=tack.vec3() for 3-vectors).

@tack.func
def temperature(x):
    return x.x * x.x + 2.0 * x.y

data.fields["t"] = td.interpolate(data, temperature, td.H1(data, order=2))
Space Its nodes H1 the points; at order 2 also edge middles, quad face centers and cell centers; at order p the products of the 1D nodes on each edge, quad face and cell order-1 L2 each cell's corners Constant, order-0 L2, Values(data, "cells") each cell's parametric center Values(data, "points") the points
  • Node positions come from the geometry as they are needed (a curved geometry's included) and are never stored.
  • A node shared by several cells is evaluated once, by the first cell that has it (cells in group order). Which cell writes each node is kept on the space, so a changed geometry is seen. A discontinuous (L2) geometry gives a shared node the first cell's position.
  • A point no cell uses takes function at its own position when the geometry is H1, and zero when it is L2.
  • A polynomial of the space's order on straight cells is represented exactly; anything else gets the space's nodal interpolant.
  • On polyhedra, polygons and polylines only point values (H1 of order 1, Values(data, "points")) interpolate, from an H1 geometry.

docs.title: Fields and arrays
docs.text:
Field(space, values): the values are a tack.Array with a scalar or vector element dtype, or an implicit array from tack.arrays (in tack-core). An array's shape counts coefficient values; its dtype controls components. The space supplies their mesh association and basis. The implicit arrays, all in tack.arrays, are indexable in any kernel as a stored array is (a[k], len(a)), not only through a field:

Array Value k VTK Viskores ConstantArray(value, size, dtype=None, device=None) value, a scalar or a vector vtkConstantArray ArrayHandleConstant CountingArray(size, start=0, step=1, dtype=None) start + step * k vtkAffineArray ArrayHandleCounting CartesianProduct(x, y=(0.0,), z=(0.0,), device=None) a rectilinear grid's point, from three axes vtkStructuredPointArray ArrayHandleCartesianProduct UniformCoordinates(dims, origin, spacing, direction=None) an image's point, origin + direction @ (ijk * spacing) vtkStructuredPointArray ArrayHandleUniformPointCoordinates Permutation(ids, base) base[ids[k]] vtkIndexedArray ArrayHandlePermutation Concatenate(a, b, ...) the arrays end to end vtkCompositeArray ArrayHandleConcatenate Strided(values, stride, offset=0, size=None) values[offset + stride * k] of a scalar field vtkStridedArray ArrayHandleStride View(base, start, size) base[start + k] -- ArrayHandleView ExtractComponent(base, c) component c of base[k] -- ArrayHandleExtractComponent Components(a, b, ...) two to four scalar arrays as a vector -- ArrayHandleCompositeVector Function(func, size, dtype=tack.f32, width=None) func(k), a @tack.func vtkStdFunctionArray ArrayHandleImplicit Transform(func, base, dtype=None, width=None) func(base[k]) -- ArrayHandleTransform Cast(base, dtype) base[k] converted -- ArrayHandleCast RandomUniform(size, seed, low, high), RandomNormal(size, seed, mean, stddev) draws from tack.random, a pure function of k and seed -- ArrayHandleRandomUniformReal, ...StandardNormal

An array's operands are any arrays -- implicit, or device fields -- so they compose to any depth: Permutation(ids, Concatenate(field, CountingArray(...))) is an array. Every algorithm takes one unchanged: a field's view holds it as a nested template (tack.device_class objects may hold others) and reads array.get(k), which inlines to the expression one would write by hand. A composed array therefore costs nothing per value beyond what it computes; each level of nesting costs about 8 us per kernel launch on the host. VTK's vtkStdFunctionArray runs a C++ function on the CPU; a Function or Transform is a @tack.func, so it runs in the kernel on every backend. materialize(array) stores one, by a kernel; to_host reads one back. A NumPy array is refused as values: copy it with tack.array(host, dtype=...) first.

uniform_grid(dims, origin, spacing, direction=None) is a dataset on UniformCoordinates, as rectilinear_grid(x, y, z) is on a CartesianProduct; sources.wavelet and sources.tangle are uniform grids. The VTK interop reads and writes vtkImageData as uniform grids, direction matrix included. A size of 1 adds no cells, in any position: (1, 3) is a line of three points along y, as (3, 1) is along x. A grid with no axis of two or more points has no cells: (1, 1, 1) is one point, and a size of 0 makes it empty. Their topology is then an UnstructuredTopology without cells, and the VTK interop still writes them as vtkImageData (or vtkRectilinearGrid).

Geometry. DataSet(topology, geometry, fields=None, sets=None, dtype=tack.f32) takes the geometry as an H1 or L2 field of 3-vectors, or as positions per point (any array of 3-vectors), which become an H1 field. It is kept apart from fields: data.geometry returns it, assigning data.geometry replaces it (checked as the constructor checks it), and data.positions() gives the positions on the host. Algorithms move it with the cells; it is never among the fields they carry or select. An L2 geometry pulls cells apart without changing the topology. A geometry of order 2 is curved.

Fields. data.fields holds the fields by name and space: two fields may share a name in different spaces, as VTK's point and cell arrays do (Fields that share a name).

data.fields["p"] the one field called "p"; KeyError where two share the name data.fields["p", td.Constant], data.fields["p", space] the field of that name in a kind of space, or in that space data.fields["p"] = f f is the one field called "p", replacing every other data.fields["p", space] = f f beside the fields of that name in other spaces, replacing the one in its own "p" in data.fields, ("p", td.H1) in data.fields whether any field matches list(data.fields), dict(data.fields) the keys: each name, or (name, space) for a name fields share; every key finds its field, and DataSet(fields=...) takes them back data.fields.named("p"), data.fields.entries() every field called "p"; each field with its name

An algorithm's field argument, and each entry of a filter's fields=, is a Field, a name, or (name, space); in fields=, a name selects every field of that name.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Field(space, values, unit=None): unit is the values' physical unit, a string kept in unyt's canonical spelling ("m/s", "m*s**-1" and "m/s^1" are one unit; "1" is "dimensionless"), or None for unknown. The spatial unit is the geometry's, data.unit, and origin is in it. Kernels never see a unit. See Coordinates, Units and Time.

Field(..., unit=), field.unit the values' unit, or None DataSet(..., unit=), data.unit the spatial unit, the geometry field's; uniform_grid, rectilinear_grid and point_cloud take unit=, point_cloud also units={name: unit} OctreeDataSet(..., units={name: unit}), octree.unit, octree.units the fields' units, and the roots' spatial unit convert(data, unit, field=None) a Field in unit (a new field in the same space), or a dataset with its geometry (origin scaled in double precision; images stay images) or a named field in unit, scaled and offset on the device Statistics.unit, .weight_unit, .unit_of(name) the field's and the weights' units, and each statistic's (variances in the square, sum times the weights') interpolate(..., unit=) the function's values' unit, which its code does not say quantities as parameters lengths ("10 cm", (0.1, "m"), a unyt or pint quantity) converted to the spatial unit, isovalues and thresholds to the field's, step sizes to the particles' time unit; a mass, density or velocity given as one quantity brings its unit (see Units and quantities reference) tack.dataset.units canonical, conversion (factor and offset), same, compatible, common, derived (products of powers), delta (degrees Celsius to kelvin for differences), named (Pa*m**3 as J); the registry is unyt's plus ftUS, the US survey foot

Filters that keep a quantity keep its unit (everything carry takes along, project, values_at_centers, traces, magnitude, means, centres in the spatial unit); those that compute one derive it (gradients, products, measures, fluxes, statistics, deposits, SPH, particle times: the table in Units and quantities reference). Positions in two known spatial units do not meet: probe's points, pieces, AMR boxes and octree probes refuse them. The VTK interop maps each array's UNITS_LABEL.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
Tack holds no series of steps: a simulation in situ, or a reader's loop, hands filters one step at a time, and each step is a dataset at its time.

DataSet(..., time=, time_unit=), data.time, data.time_unit the step's time, a double on the host or None, in a unit of time or None kept by every filter, as the origin and spatial unit are (carry, keep_marks, drop_marks, to_device); probe gives back its target's refused pieces of a PartitionedDataSet and boxes of an AMRDataSet at two times (compared in one unit); an octree's time is its roots' VTK vtkDataObject::DATA_TIME_STEP both ways; VTK has no time unit tack.dataset.temporal filters fed one step at a time (update(data), which returns the step's output), keeping copies of what they need of earlier steps (copy=False keeps references); a PartitionedDataSet streams piece by piece RunningStatistics(fields) per point or cell over the steps so far: <name>_mean, _variance (population), _min, _max (Welford, f64 where the device has it); count; one mesh over the steps (remesh first) TimeDerivative(fields, copy=True) <name>_dt, the backward difference since the previous step, in the field's unit over the time unit; None on the first step; one mesh, increasing time Advection(field, seeds=None, integrator="rk4", step_size=None, copy=True) particles through the steps, the velocity linear in time between the kept previous step and this one (each probed in its own mesh, over ranks where pieces are); update returns them (seed, source, release, time, status); inject(points, time=None) releases more at any time extend_paths(paths, particles) joins a step's particles onto the paths so far, by seed: polylines through each particle's points in time Pathlines(field, seeds, ...), Streaklines(field, seeds, releases=1, ...) the current pathlines every step; the line of each seed's released particles, newest first

See Streaming Steps.

docs.title: Origins and point clouds
docs.text:
A position is data.origin + value: the origin is three floats kept in double precision on the host ((0.0, 0.0, 0.0) unless set), the value the geometry's, in tack.f32 or, on a device that has it, tack.f64. Kernels see only the values, so coordinates far from zero keep their precision: single precision resolves 0.25 m at 4,000 km, a LiDAR survey's eastings, but a millimetre within a few kilometres of an origin. LAS files store scaled integers and an offset for the same reason.

DataSet(..., origin=), data.origin set it; assigning it moves every point (the values stay) data.world_positions() origin + positions(), a float64 host array; positions() stays the values data.rebased(origin) the same world positions relative to another origin: each value moved by the difference of the origins, taken in double precision, added in the geometry's type. An image stays an image, its corner moved in double precision (a raster at survey coordinates, rebased near it, holds its points exactly); a rectilinear grid moves its axes; other implicit geometry becomes positions per point point_cloud(positions, fields=None, origin=None, dtype=tack.f32) a dataset of one implicit vertex cell per point (types, offsets and connectivity stored nowhere), fields as point data. Host positions are world positions, taken relative to origin in double precision; without one, float64 positions get the lower corner of their box rounded down, others zero. A Tack array of 3-vectors is relative to origin already. Floating-point fields take dtype, integer fields (a classification, intensities) keep their type; tack.f64 is refused on a device without it

Filters keep it: an output dataset has its input's origin (through carry, keep_marks and drop_marks), as to_device, split, ghost_cells and merge_pieces do. Lengths, areas, gradients and normals do not depend on it. What takes or gives absolute positions converts on the host in double precision:

  • Implicit functions are given in world coordinates. Plane, Sphere, Cylinder, Box and Planes move their parameters by the origin exactly (implicit.relative_to); another object with a value is evaluated at the value plus the origin, added in the geometry's type.
  • probe points and advect/streamlines seeds given as host arrays are world positions; a dataset's points (a target, advect's particles) are its own, relative to its origin, and moved by the difference of the origins; a Tack array of seeds is relative to the data's origin.
  • point_elevation's points are world positions. interpolate's function is called with world positions (the value plus the origin, in the geometry's type).
  • transform moves the origin by the map, in double precision, and applies only its linear part to the values. cylindrical and spherical convert world positions, and give an origin of zero.
  • The VTK interop: vtk_to_dataset(..., origin=) takes VTK's points, an image's origin and a rectilinear grid's lines relative to it in double precision; dataset_to_vtk writes world positions (double-precision points where the origin is not zero).
  • Position-valued fields (cell_geometry(...).centroid, a field holding positions) are relative to the dataset's origin, as its geometry is.
  • CellLocator.find takes positions relative to the dataset's origin.

Pieces whose positions are compared or moved between them must share one origin: ghost_cells, generate_global_ids, merge_pieces, connected_components, probe and advection over a PartitionedDataSet refuse two (partitioned.common_origin, over every rank); rebased puts a piece on another. An image's own origin (UniformCoordinates) is separate from the dataset's and computed in the geometry's type.

docs.title: Finding points near points
docs.text:
PointLocator(data, bin_size=None, points_per_bin=4) puts the points in uniform bins over their box (about points_per_bin a bin, cubes along the axes they span) and sorts them by bin, each bin in index order (buckets.bucket_order), as VTK's vtkStaticPointLocator. Nothing is atomic, so every query visits the same points in the same order every time, and distances are compared with each product rounded on its own (squared_length, which no backend fuses), so the neighbours within a radius and the k nearest are the same on every backend; reported distances agree to rounding. Like CellLocator, it records its geometry (serves) and is refused once Tack has written the positions; the filters below use the one the topology keeps (cached_point_locator) unless given one.

locator.neighbors(radius, points=None) every point within radius (inclusive) of each query, CSR (offsets, ids); the queries are the points themselves, each leaving itself out, unless points (a host array of world positions, or a Tack array relative to the origin) are given locator.nearest(k, points=None) the k nearest (any k; up to 32 kept in private arrays, more in the output's rows), (ids, squared_distances), each (m, k), nearest first, ties by index; -1 where the points run out. Rings of bins outwards until the k-th distance lies within those searched locator.grid() the sorted points and the grid as a device class, for one's own kernels: span(x, r), cell(x), bin(i, j, k), first(b), end(b), point(s), offset(p, x) (point p less x, to its nearest image in a periodic box)

PointLocator(..., periodic=box) takes a periodic box in world coordinates (a side, the box from zero; three sides; or (lower, upper) corners), as a cosmology simulation's: the bins tile the box exactly, points outside it wrap in, and every distance is to a point's nearest image. A search radius must stay under half the box (check_radius). The point filters below take periodic= and pass it on; without one, nothing changes (it is compiled out).

docs.title: Point cloud filters
docs.text: voxel_downsample(data, size, keep="centroid") one point per occupied voxel of side size (or three sides) anchored at the points' lower corner: the voxel's centroid (new points: floating-point fields averaged, integer fields its first point's; ghost marks dropped), its first point, or its point nearest the centroid (input points, in input order, fields and marks kept). Voxels by a stable sort, each reduced in index order: the same bits run to run, and the same voxels and kept points on every backend. VTK's vtkVoxelGrid fits a whole number of bins to the box, so its voxels are not exactly size; PDAL's filters.voxeldownsize is this outliers(data, radius=, min_neighbors=) marks (outlier, u8) points with fewer than min_neighbors others within radius, with each point's count (neighbors): VTK's vtkRadiusOutlierRemoval, the same points outliers(data, k=, deviations=1.0) marks points whose mean distance to their k nearest is more than deviations standard deviations above the mean of those means, with each one (mean_distance): PCL's test; VTK's vtkStatisticalOutlierRemoval has the same mean and deviation and also removes points that far below the mean. Marked, not removed, as PDAL marks (class 7): threshold_points(out, "outlier", 0, 0) keeps the rest surface_normals(data, consistent=True) a surface's polygons wound alike (each region as its first cell) and its unit normals: cell_normals (Newell's) and normals at the points (the cells' summed, made unit), as VTK's vtkPolyDataNormals without splitting; a non-orientable surface is refused point_normals(data, k=None, radius=None, viewpoint=None, direction=(0, 0, 1)) each point's unit normal from the covariance of its k nearest points (itself included) or those within radius: the eigenvector of the least eigenvalue, in closed form; signed toward viewpoint (a world position) or along direction (up). Zero with fewer than three neighbours, or on a line. VTK's vtkPCANormalEstimation agrees within 0.1° connected_components(data, radius=, min_size=None) with radius, points within it of each other connect too: on a point cloud, Euclidean clusters (VTK's vtkEuclideanClusterExtraction, one to one) and friends-of-friends halos with the linking length. The radius hook walks the locator's bins (nothing stored per pair, each pair once). min_size makes regions of fewer points -1 and numbers the rest again deposit(data, grid, field=None, reduce=None, method="nearest", per_volume=False) points onto an axis-aligned image: into the cell holding each ("nearest", a field on the cells) or onto its corners by trilinear weights ("cic", cloud in cell, on the points), as Viskores' particle density filters and yt. Counts without a field; with one, "sum", "mean", "count", and for "nearest" "min" and "max" (a LiDAR surface model: the highest return per cell of a 2D image). Empty cells hold 0, or NaN for means and extrema; per_volume divides by the cell's volume. Points outside are left out. Each target reduced in point order, by a sort: the same bits run to run; counts, minima and maxima the same on every backend, sums and means to rounding sph_interpolate(particles, target, fields=None, kernel="cubic", smoothing_length="h", mass="mass", density="density", normalize=False, dimension=3) SPH values at a target's points (a dataset, or world positions as vertex cells): sum_j (m_j / rho_j) A_j W(r, h_j), each particle reaching to its kernel's support (the scatter form), with shepard, the sum of (m / rho) W; normalize divides by it. Kernels "cubic", "quartic", "quintic", "wendland", VTK's, normalized in 1 to 3 dimensions (the Wendland kernel from 2); within float rounding of vtkSPHInterpolator. Smoothing length, mass and density are point fields or numbers; integer fields are not interpolated sph_density(particles, kernel="cubic", smoothing_length="h", mass="mass") each particle's density by the SPH sum with its own smoothing length (the gather form, SPLASH's), itself included

docs.title: Cosmology halos
docs.text:
Dark matter halos are friends-of-friends groups, connected_components(particles, radius=linking_length, min_size=..., periodic=box), and halo_catalog describes them. Ported from Viskores' cosmotools and ParaView's LANL halo finder, with what they lacked: per-particle masses, softening, periodic boxes, an applied minimum size (Viskores stores it and never uses it), and the pruned most-bound-particle search on every large halo.

halo_catalog(particles, region="point_region", mass=1.0, velocity=None, center="mbp", softening=0.0, G=1.0, periodic=None) one point per halo (labels of region >= 0), at its most bound particle or centre of mass, with halo, count, mass (per-particle masses or one number), com, mbp (the index of the particle of least potential -G sum m / sqrt(r^2 + softening^2)), potential, radius (the farthest particle from the point), and with velocity its mass-weighted mean and one-dimensional dispersion. Each halo is unwrapped about its first particle in a periodic box, and its points put back in. The MBP is exact: halos up to 2048 particles sum every pair; larger ones use Viskores' MxN pruning, tightened by bounding each particle against each far bin's box rather than bin against bin (on a concentrated halo of 40,000, 3% are summed exactly instead of 69%). The catalogue shares the particles' origin; every sum runs in particle order

docs.title: Point clouds in pieces
docs.text:
A point cloud in pieces (a PartitionedDataSet of point_clouds, on one origin) works as a mesh in pieces does: filters over neighbours run per piece on pieces with copies of their neighbours' points, and the algorithms whose answer needs every piece take the partitioned dataset.

ghost_points(pds, radius=None, k=None, periodic=None, around=None, fields=None) each piece with copies of the other pieces' points it needs appended, vertex cells marked DUPLICATECELL at points marked DUPLICATEPOINT, owned where they came from. With radius, every point within radius of the piece's box, found by the boxes in one exchange (around, a piece for each, widens a piece's box to its own piece's points: the targets sph_interpolate resamples onto there). With k, exactly the points among an owned point's k nearest: each point's k nearest in its own piece bound the true distance, a point whose ball reaches another piece's box asks that piece for its k nearest, and the best are fetched. In a periodic box a copy across a face is an image, moved by the box's side, so the pieces are ordinary clouds: run filters on them without periodic. Fields, sets and global ids come along, and update_ghosts refreshes copies from their owners per piece, after ghost_points point_normals, outliers' radius test, sph_density (then update_ghosts(pds, "density")), sph_interpolate onto around's pieces: each owned point (and each target) gets the whole's answer connected_components(pds, radius=, min_size=None, periodic=None) each piece labelled with copies within radius, each copy's region joined to its owner's: the whole's clusters and friends-of-friends halos, numbered as the whole numbers them (by the lowest global id, else (piece, point)). Only regions that cross pieces are gathered; the rest are numbered by a sort over the pieces, so no rank holds every region. min_size counts each point once, where it is owned (meshes in pieces take it too) outliers(pds, ...) both tests over copies (ghost_points inside), the statistical test's mean and deviation over every piece's points; the pieces come back without the copies voxel_downsample(pds, size, keep=) the grid anchored at every piece's lower corner; each voxel's owned points brought to one piece by a sort over the pieces and reduced there in (piece, index) order. A centroid goes to the piece of its voxel's first point; "first" and "nearest" keep points on their own pieces deposit(pds, grid, field=None, ...) each piece deposits its owned points; the grids combine over every rank in piece order (sums and counts add, means divide them, extrema take the least or greatest). Every rank gets the whole grid's field; field is a name halo_catalog(pds, region="point_region", mass=, velocity=None, ...) each halo's owned particles sorted to one piece by label, in (piece, index) order, and catalogued there: a PartitionedDataSet of catalogues, halos in label order across them, mbp an index in piece mbp_piece

Pieces cut from a cloud in index order give the whole's answers bit for bit where the answer is reduced in point order (clusters' numbers, centroids, halo catalogues, including each MBP); in a periodic box, values measured through an image agree to a rounding, since an image's position is rounded once more than the whole's minimum-image offset.

docs.title: Adaptive mesh refinement
docs.text:
An AMRDataSet(levels, ratios=(), domain=None, world=None) is a block-structured AMR hierarchy, as VTK's vtkOverlappingAMR and AMReX's: levels, each this rank's boxes of a level (a PartitionedDataSet or a list of datasets), and ratios[l], the refinement from level l to l + 1, a whole number or one per axis. The hierarchy is in index space alone, as AMReX's: a box is a dataset of a StructuredTopology whose offset is its first cell's index in its level, and its geometry is anything structured -- an image, a rectilinear grid, a curvilinear grid -- since which cells a finer level covers is a matter of integer boxes. VTK's AMR holds images and (since 9.6) rectilinear grids; curvilinear boxes are Tack's.

amr.levels, amr.ratios, amr.domain, amr.dimension, amr.num_levels the levels (PartitionedDataSets), the ratios (three per level), level 0's cell-index box amr.boxes(level) every rank's boxes of a level, (n, 2, 3) cell-index boxes [lo, hi), gathered over the world when the hierarchy is made, as VTK's metadata and AMReX's BoxArray are replicated for level, box in amr this rank's boxes, coarsest level first marks made with the hierarchy: REFINEDCELL on cells a finer box covers; REFINEDPOINT on points at whose location a finer level has a point, so a coarse point on the edge of a refined region is one; DUPLICATEPOINT on points a lower-numbered sibling also holds. Every location and region is then owned once, at the finest level holding it. Marks given are recomputed; other bits are kept refused overlapping boxes in a level; a fine box that, coarsened, is not within its coarser level's boxes (proper nesting); a level's images off one lattice (one spacing and origin, axis-aligned: VTK's model); boxes with ghost cells; boxes of mixed dimension statistics(amr, name), entropy(amr, name, bins) over every box of every level, each region and location once per box every filter: contours, slices, clips and thresholds leave refined cells out (cracks at level boundaries remain); algorithms whose output is on the same cells (gradients, projections) compute there, refined data being valid amr_gaussian_pulse(dimension=3, ...) VTK's vtkAMRGaussianPulseSource: two levels, Gaussian-Pulse and Centroid on the cells ghost_cells(amr, layers=1, fields=None) each box grown by layers cells within its level's domain (amr.level_domain(level)), the ghosts marked DUPLICATECELL and DUPLICATEPOINT: a ghost a sibling box holds is its value, copied (AMReX's FillBoundary); one no sibling holds takes the coarser level's -- the coarse cell's value for a cell (injection), the coarse cell's corners by linear weights for a point (FillPatchTwoLevels) -- read from each value's owner; one neither holds is HIDDENCELL/HIDDENPOINT. A grid's ghost positions are filled the same way (an image's are its lattice), so rectilinear and curvilinear boxes grow too, a hidden point's position extrapolated along the grid. Ghosts a finer box covers are refined. amr.layers says how many update_ghosts(amr, *names) refreshes both kinds of ghost, and the points a box shares with a lower sibling, from their owners, after a filter: one tack.communication.Plan per kind, kept, and a kernel summing by weight probe(amr, where) each point evaluated in the finest level's cell holding it (refined cells hold nothing; on a level boundary the finer box wins), over every rank's boxes: a probe onto an image is the hierarchy resampled, as VTK's vtkAMRResampleFilter gives it (equal at every point VTK sets; VTK leaves points on the domain's upper faces unset) average_down(amr, name) in place, finest level first: each refined coarse cell the volume-weighted average of the fine cells over it, each refined coarse point the coinciding fine point's value (AMReX's average_down) interop vtk_to_dataset(vtkOverlappingAMR) gives an AMRDataSet (blocks placed by their vtkAMRBox); dataset_to_vtk(amr) a vtkOverlappingAMR when every box is an image or a rectilinear grid and each ratio is the same along every axis, else a vtkPartitionedDataSetCollection of a partitioned dataset per level. VTK's BlankCells marks the export as Tack does

Not here: crack-free contouring across levels, periodic domains, tagging and regridding, conservative interpolation (the vault's AMR proposal).

docs.title: Octrees
docs.text:
An OctreeDataSet(roots, tree, level, key, fields=None, mask=None, world=None, units=None) is a grid of octrees, VTK's vtkHyperTreeGrid with branching factor 2, stored as a linear octree for GPUs: roots the grid of root cells (an image or a rectilinear grid, 2D or 3D; root cell t, x fastest, is tree t), and every node of every tree, refined ones included, as its tree, its level (0 at the root) and its Morton key at that level (integer coordinates in the tree interleaved, x lowest, so a child's key is its parent's shifted by the dimension with its index, x fastest, below). Nodes are sorted in pre-order -- tree, key carried to the finest level, level -- so a subtree is one run. Each node's ancestors must be given, and a refined node all its children.

octree.tree, .level, .key, .marks the nodes, device arrays; marks REFINEDCELL on non-leaves, HIDDENCELL where masked octree.fields cell data: one value per node (dict of arrays) octree.is_leaf, .centers(), .measures(), .geometry() from the keys: which nodes are leaves, centres, volumes (areas), lower corners and sides octree.leaves() the leaves as an unstructured DataSet of voxels (pixels in 2D), cell c the c-th leaf, fields as cell data, hidden leaves HIDDENCELL; coinciding corners one point (sorted on the finest level's lattice), hanging ones kept probe(octree, where) each point's leaf values (one binary search of the keys carried to the finest level), valid 0 outside, on hidden leaves and off a 2D plane; over ranks, each point to the rank whose trees hold it OctreeDataSet.from_cells(roots, level, position, fields) from cells' levels and positions (whole octs, as RAMSES writes them), ancestors added with NaN values statistics(octree, name, weights=None, level=None), entropy(...) over the leaves (or one level's nodes), every rank's trees interop vtk_to_dataset(vtkHyperTreeGrid) (each tree's breadth-first descriptor read in one call, turned into keys) and dataset_to_vtk(octree); the mask as HIDDENCELL

Weighted statistics, for every kind of data: statistics(data, name, weights=...) with "volume" (cell measures, cell fields only) or a scalar field's name on the same entities. mean is sum(w x) / W, sum is sum(w x), the moments are sum(w (x - mean)^k), weight is W, the population variance m2 / W, the sample variance m2 / (W - sum(w^2) / W) (reliability weights, NumPy's aweights), and skewness and kurtosis take W for n. entropy(..., weights=...) shares each bin by the weights in it.

docs.title: Devices
docs.text:
A dataset is on the device its arrays are on, and it computes there: every algorithm, every derived entity (faces, edges, point links, groups, layouts), for_each, Set, CellLocator and the sources run and allocate on the dataset's device, whatever the default device is. Results stay on it.

  • data.device, data.topology.device, field.device, a_set.device: the device, a tack.Device. A structured topology holds no arrays, so it is on the device it was made for (device=, by default the default device when it was made).
  • A dataset's parts must share one device: a Field whose values are not on its topology's device is refused, and so is a dataset whose topology, geometry, fields or sets are on two (ValueError, "arrays on two devices"), when it is made and when an algorithm is given it.
  • data.to_device(device) copies it there: the topology from its arrays, each field in the same space, the sets by the same ids. What the topology derives is derived there afresh.
  • uniform_grid, rectilinear_grid, wavelet and tangle take device=; a rectilinear grid of device-array axes is on their device.
  • An implicit array is on the device of the arrays it holds: ConstantArray, UniformCoordinates and CartesianProduct take device= for the small arrays they store, to_device moves one, and one made from arrays on two devices is refused. One that holds no array (CountingArray, Function) belongs to no device.
with tack.device("cuda"):
    data = td.wavelet(20)                     # every array on the GPU
surface = td.contour(data, "RTData", 150.0)   # computed there, whatever the default
on_cpu = surface.to_device("cpu")

docs.title: Sets
docs.text:
A Set(data, on, ids) selects some of a topology's points, cells, faces or edges (on is "points", "cells", "faces" or "edges"; edge ids are those of topology.edges()). Its ids are kept sorted and unique, in the topology's id_dtype; an id outside the topology is refused when the set is made. flags() gives membership, 1 or 0 per entity.

  • Naming. data.sets maps names to sets of the dataset's own topology. Anything else is refused when it is put in: an array (wrap it in a Set), a set of another topology, or a name that is a domain's ("cells").
  • Builders return the set. boundary_faces(data) is a face set; name it to keep it: data.sets["boundary"] = boundary_faces(data).
  • Side sets. A face set is a side set: a boundary face has one side. Set.from_sides(data, cells, local_faces) takes (cell, local face) pairs, as Exodus side sets give them; local faces are numbered as the cell view numbers them. Which side was named is not kept.
  • Iteration. A cell, face or edge set's name is an iteration domain: for_each(kernel, data, "inlet", ...). A cell set runs over the cell groups' subgroups of its members, so field views and varying spaces work as on all cells. A point set is not a domain (points have no view): loop over its ids.
  • Carried through filters, by the maps that carry fields: an output entity is in a set when the input entity it came from is. Kept cells keep their sets (threshold, extract_cells), pieces of cells their cells' (contour, clip), and a face or edge set becomes a cell set where faces or edges become cells (extract_surface, extract_edges). A set of entities the filter makes anew -- interpolated points, faces derived afresh -- is left behind. Filters that keep the topology keep every set.

Open: boundary entities from readers mapped onto sets (Exodus side and node sets, MFEM boundary attributes).

docs.title: Partitioned datasets
docs.text:
A PartitionedDataSet(partitions, world=None) is a dataset in pieces: an ordered list of DataSets, as VTK's vtkPartitionedDataSet. Each piece is a whole dataset, with its own topology, numbering, geometry, fields, sets and device, and may have no cells. Iterate over it, index it (pds[i]) or take its length; pds.partitions is the tuple of pieces. Across MPI ranks it holds this rank's pieces, and world (a tack.communication.World, this process alone by default) is where the others are, for the algorithms that combine pieces.

  • Work on one piece takes the piece. Filters, analyses, selections and for_each take a DataSet, as everywhere else; loop over the pieces: for piece in pds: piece.fields["grad"] = td.gradients(piece, "T").
  • Only algorithms whose answer needs more than one piece take the partitioned dataset, and they name the field (a Field belongs to one piece's topology), which every piece must have:
  • statistics(pds, "T") takes each piece's moments on its own device and combines them pairwise (Pébay's update), so the result is the whole's up to rounding;
  • entropy(pds, "T", bins) bins the whole's range and sums each piece's histogram over it;
  • connected_components, outliers, voxel_downsample, deposit and halo_catalog on point clouds in pieces ("Point clouds in pieces").

Pieces with no values are skipped. Each piece counts only what it owns (below), so where every shared cell and point has one owner, the result is the whole's. Across MPI ranks each rank passes its own pieces, and the pieces' moments and histograms are gathered over pds.world and combined in the pieces' global order: the same bits however they are shared out, and as in one process. - split(data, pieces, ghost_layers=0) cuts a structured grid by index ranges, x fastest. pieces is a count, factored over the axes (each prime factor, largest first, cuts the axis whose pieces have most cells), or a tuple of counts, one per axis of the topology. Each axis's cells are shared out as evenly as they go, at least one per piece, and neighbouring pieces share the points between them. A piece keeps the geometry's kind (uniform coordinates with their origin moved, rectilinear axes cut, explicit points taken) and carries its block of every point, cell and L2 field and every set, as filters carry them; fields on faces or edges are left behind. ghost_layers adds that many layers of each neighbour's cells around a piece, as far as the grid goes, marked duplicates, as VTK's vtkGhostCellsGenerator adds them; filters need one (below). A point of several pieces' own cells is the first such piece's, x fastest, and a duplicate in the others, as are the points of the ghost layers; the input's own ghost marks come along. An unstructured mesh is partitioned by VTK (vtkRedistributeDataSetFilter) or by its host application. - ghost_cells(pds, layers=1, world=None, fields=None) gives each unstructured or polyhedral piece (all of one kind) a layer of its neighbours' cells, as VTK's vtkGhostCellsGenerator does, in one process (pieces on any devices) or across MPI ranks. Pieces neighbour where they share points at exactly the same position; a piece gains the cells of others that use a point it shares with them (DUPLICATECELL) and the points of those it lacks (DUPLICATEPOINT); a shared point belongs to the lowest piece holding it, and is DUPLICATEPOINT in the others. That is VTK's rule too: the cells, points, marks and values equal vtkGhostCellsGenerator's, and split's ghost layer's. Point and cell fields come along (fields chooses), and point and cell sets keep their members. Boundary points are matched by a sort of their positions over every piece (tack.communication.sort_by_key), and each piece sends each neighbour its cells around their shared points. layers=n grows each further layer from the points of the layer before, cells of any piece included, so pieces thinner than n cells are fine; two and three layers equal split's and vtkGhostCellsGenerator's. Structured pieces stay structured: pieces that tile a box of cells (each placed by its topology's offset, as split's and VTK's image pieces are) become their blocks grown by n cells, with their offsets, their values from the pieces that own them, and their coordinates grown with them (uniform, rectilinear, or explicit positions); the result is split's ghost layers exactly. - Global ids. data.global_ids is a tack.dataset.GlobalIds (or None), kept apart from the fields as the marks are: an i64 per point (points) and per cell (cells), either of which may be None, the same on every piece holding the entity and unique otherwise. vtk_to_dataset takes VTK's GlobalIds attributes as them, not as fields, and dataset_to_vtk writes them back (GlobalPointIds, GlobalCellIds, the names vtkGenerateGlobalIds gives); to_device moves them. Filters carry them where an output entity is an input entity (carry's Same and Take: kept points, kept or extracted cells, remove_ghosts), and what a filter makes (a contour's points, a clip's pieces, a surface's faces) has none, as in VTK. - generate_global_ids(pds, world=None) numbers the pieces' points and cells, as VTK's vtkGenerateGlobalIds: each piece its owned entities in its own order, after the pieces before it, and copies their owner's ids. Owners come from the ghost marks where there are any; a point several pieces hold unmarked (pieces without ghost cells share their boundary points) belongs to the lowest of them and is marked DUPLICATEPOINT in the others. On such pieces the ids and marks equal VTK's. On pieces with ghost cells VTK gives a point to the lowest piece holding any copy, ghost copies too, and remarks them; Tack keeps the owners the marks say, so an owner still holds every cell around its points. Points are copies when their positions are exactly equal, cells when their points' ids are; pieces from ghost_cells reuse its exchanges, and ghost_cells carries global ids into the ghost layer, matching points by them, where every piece has them. - probe(pds, where) with a partitioned source: each point goes to the lowest piece one of whose own cells (not a ghost) holds it, holding ahead of coming within the locator's tolerance, as one dataset ranks its cells; that piece evaluates it, and the values come back. The result equals probing the whole, points on faces pieces share included, with or without ghost cells (a point is evaluated in one cell). where is this rank's points (a dataset, an array, or a PartitionedDataSet, which gives one back); across MPI ranks every rank's points are probed over every rank's pieces. Built on tack.communication.Routing, which particles across pieces use too. - merge_pieces(pds, root=0, fields=None, device=None) gives the pieces back as one dataset, every owned cell and every point once, as VTK's vtkMergeBlocks after vtkRemoveGhosts: for writing one file, or for code that knows no pieces. Points are matched and numbered as generate_global_ids does; ghost cells go, hidden cells stay marked, the pieces' own global ids come along. Structured pieces that tile a box come back as that box's structured grid (split's input exactly, offset and coordinates included); other pieces as an unstructured dataset. Across MPI ranks the result is on root (None elsewhere). - update_ghosts(pds, *fields) copies the named point and cell fields' values on ghost points and cells from their owners, in place, for pieces ghost_cells or ghost_points made (they keep the exchanges as tack.communication.Plans). A filter that needs each entity's neighbours (project to points, point gradients) is right on what a piece owns and wrong on the ghost layer's rim; refreshing the ghosts in between makes a second such filter right too.

Ghost marks. Every cell and point that several pieces hold has exactly one owner; every other copy is a ghost. data.ghosts is a tack.dataset.Ghosts (or None), kept apart from the fields as the geometry is: a u8 per cell (cells) and per point (points), either of which may be None, holding VTK's vtkGhostType bits (Ghosts.DUPLICATECELL 1, REFINEDCELL 8, HIDDENCELL 32, DUPLICATEPOINT 1, HIDDENPOINT 2, and the rest, carried unread) and Tack's REFINEDPOINT 8, which VTK lacks. A duplicate is a copy of what another piece owns; hidden is data not valid there (a blanked cell); refined is data a finer AMR level supersedes (see "Adaptive mesh refinement"). Filters that make cells leave hidden and refined cells out (Ghosts.MASKED_CELLS); reductions leave out every skipped bit (SKIPPED_CELLS, SKIPPED_POINTS).

  • vtk_to_dataset takes a vtkGhostType array as the marks, not as a field, and dataset_to_vtk writes them back; split makes them; data.to_device moves them. Marks of the wrong length or type are refused when they are put in.
  • statistics and entropy leave out duplicate and hidden cells and points, on one dataset too, so each value counts once across all pieces. An L2 field goes by its cells' marks; a field on faces or edges, or of order 2, is refused on a dataset with marks until it is decided who owns those.
  • Filters process the ghost cells and carry the marks, as VTK does: what a piece makes near its edge is what the next step there needs (point normals, smoothing, a second filter that looks at neighbours). What a filter makes takes the owner of what it came from:
  • an output cell (a contour's triangles, a clip's pieces, a kept cell) its source cell's;
  • a kept point its own; a point on an input edge (a contour's, a clip's) the edge's; a point inside a cell (a clip's centroids) the cell's;
  • a surface face its cell's; a face two cells share, an edge, and a cell with no source cell (a vertex) the owner of its smallest point, smallest by position, so every piece holding it decides alike.

So over pieces with at least one ghost layer, the owned part of a filter's output is the whole's output, cell for cell and point for point, and statistics and entropy of the outputs are the whole's. Filters that keep the cells and points (warp, transform, cylindrical, spherical, shrink, as_polyhedra, as_polygons, probe's target) keep the marks as they are. - Pieces without ghost cells cannot tell what their neighbours make or keep from the cells, faces and edges they share: a contour point on a shared edge, a surface face on the cut, a shared point only a neighbour's kept cells use. Such a filter's output records that it lost the marks, and statistics and entropy refuse it with NotImplementedError naming the cause, rather than count shared values wrongly. Points chosen by their own values (threshold_points, extract_points, mask_points) keep them. Setting an output's ghosts clears the record. - Hidden cells are never processed: filters that make new cells or points (contour, slice, clip, threshold, extract_cells, extract_geometry, mask, extract_surface, extract_edges, triangulate, tetrahedralize) and the source of probe, advect and streamlines leave them out, as if they were not there. Faces or edges chosen by id, and a reused CellLocator, are refused on data with hidden cells. Outputs on the same cells keep their values there, marked. - remove_ghosts(data) takes out the duplicate and hidden cells and the points no remaining cell uses, as VTK's vtkRemoveGhosts: the last step before rendering, writing one file, or code that does not know ghost marks. The points kept keep their marks, and a point the piece owns stays even when only ghost cells used it, so reductions over the result are unchanged. A structured piece whose remaining cells are a block stays a structured grid.

pieces = td.split(td.wavelet(20), 8, ghost_layers=1)    # 8 image-data pieces
for piece in pieces:
    piece.fields["RTData_cells"] = td.project(piece, "RTData", td.Constant(piece))
s = td.statistics(pieces, "RTData_cells")               # the whole grid's
iso = td.PartitionedDataSet(td.contour(piece, "RTData", 160.0) for piece in pieces)
s = td.statistics(iso, "RTData")                        # the whole grid's isosurface's

packages/tack-vis/examples/44_partitioned_data.py runs all of it: pieces with ghost layers, their marks, work in a loop, reductions of the grid and of the pieces' isosurfaces checked against the whole, pieces spread over several GPUs where there are, and .vtpd files for ParaView.

Next (the partitioned-data proposal's later phases): more than one generated layer, and the algorithms that need more than ghosts (particles across pieces, probe of a partitioned source), on tack.communication.

docs.title: Kernels
docs.text:
@tack.kernel
def _jump(faces, values, out):
    for f in faces:
        c0 = faces.side_cell(f, 0)
        c1 = faces.side_cell(f, 1)                 # -1 on the boundary
        out[faces.entity_id(f)] = values[c1] - values[c0] if c1 >= 0 else 0.0

td.for_each(_jump, data, "faces", cell_values, out)

for_each(kernel, data, domain, *args):

  • domain is "cells", "faces", "edges" or the name of a cell, face or edge set.
  • It makes one launch per group. The kernel's first argument is the view of that group (for i in view). Each Field among args becomes its view for the same group, so u.value(i, pc) reads entity i. Other arguments are passed through unchanged.
  • There is no "points" domain. Point data, like any field's values taken one by one, is read by an ordinary kernel over field.values.
  • domain may also be a space: the kernel runs over its nodes, each once (data.node_views(space)), and takes arrays, not fields. A node view is an entity view -- points, edges, quad faces or cells -- whose entity i has node_count(i) nodes, each with node_dof(i, j) (where its value is in the space's values) and node_position(i, j) (where the geometry puts it):
@tack.kernel
def sample(nodes, values):
    for i in nodes:
        for j in range(nodes.node_count(i)):
            x = nodes.node_position(i, j)
            values[nodes.node_dof(i, j)] = x[0] * x[1]

space = td.H1(data, order=2)
values = tack.zeros((space.size,), data.dtype)
td.for_each(sample, data, space, values)

H1's nodes are its points and, at order 2, its edges' middles, its quad faces' centers and its hexahedra's and quads' interiors -- a shared node's position is the mean of its entity's points on a straight geometry, the geometry's own value on an order-2 one; L2's are each cell's corners (order 1) or parametric center (order 0); Constant's and values on cells' the parametric centers; values on points' the points. An L2 geometry gives a shared node no single position and is refused for them; on polyhedra, polygons and polylines only point nodes exist. interpolate is one such kernel.

What makes a group. On a shape-based topology, each shape is a group. A group is split further, on the device, by:

  • the spaces among the arguments that vary from cell to cell (an L2 with an order per cell), so each launch is specialized to one order;
  • any keys, such as SizeBuckets(topology, caps=(16, 32, 64, 128, 256)) on a polyhedral topology. That gives each launch a class constant MAX_SCRATCH, so that tack.local_array(dtype, cells.MAX_SCRATCH) has a size known at compile time.

Shape, order and size all go through this one mechanism. An algorithm that needs the groups itself uses data.launch_groups(domain, fields=(), keys=()), data.domain_view(domain, group) and field.view(group).

Fields are separate arguments. Views are not nested in a dataset object: each field is its own argument, viewed for the group being launched. A view is put together from mixins (entity kind, shape, geometry, incidence, space, storage), which share one namespace. A view refuses to build if two of them define the same name.

docs.title: What views offer
docs.text:
Views introduces them.

Every view supports for i in view and entity_id(i), the global id of the entity the loop is at. Names follow one rule per kind of answer:

  • a global id ends in _id: point_id(c, j), face_id(c, k), side_point_id(c, k, j);
  • a position ends in _position: corner_position(i, j), side_position(c, k, j), point_position(p) (by global id), and position(c, pc) at parametric coordinates;
  • a shape's local corner number ends in _corner: edge_corner(e, k), face_corner(f, k);
  • a count starts with num_: num_points, num_faces, side_num_points.

Cells. These methods work on every kind of topology, so face-based algorithms are written once:

Method num_faces(c) the cell's faces (codimension-1 entities) face_id(c, k), face_side(c, k) local face k's global id, and the side the cell is on side_num_points(c, k), side_point_id(c, k, j) local face k's points, walked outward from this cell side_position(c, k, j) that point's position
  • Shape-based cells add: the class constants NUM_POINTS, NUM_FACES, NUM_EDGES and DIMENSION; point_id(c, j); the geometry through corner_position(c, j), position(c, pc) and geometry_jacobian(c, pc); the shape's tables (parametric_point(j), edge_corner(e, k), face_corner(f, k), face_num_points(f), face_shape(f), shape functions); face incidence (face_orientation, face_position); and edges (edge_id, edge_sign). A face's corners go round it, a voxel's too.
  • Polyhedral, polygonal and polyline cells add num_points(c) and point_id(c, j) over the cell's distinct points, and point_position(p). Polyline cells add their chain in order: line_num_points(c), line_point_id(c, j).

Faces. num_points(f), point_id(f, j), corner_position(f, j), num_sides(f), and side_cell(f, s) / side_local(f, s) give the cell on side s and its local face number.

Edges. point_id(e, j), with the lower point id first, and corner_position(e, j).

Fields.

Field view Methods H1, L2, Constant value(c, pc), parametric_gradient(c, pc) at parametric coordinates; corner_value(c, j); the field's nodes, on cells with a reference element: NODES per cell, node k's value dof(c, k), its place in the array dof_index(c, k) and its parametric coordinates node_parametric(k) (Work at a field's nodes) Values at(i) SideTraces trace(f, s, j), value(f, s, pc)

docs.title: Algorithms and filters
docs.text:
Every algorithm is in tack.dataset.algorithms, one module each, and tack.dataset re-exports them all; Algorithms lists them by what they do, with their parameters. They share one set of conventions:

  • the dataset comes first: f(data, ...);
  • a field argument is a Field or the name of one of data's fields;
  • an algorithm that makes a new dataset takes fields= (all by default, a name, a list of names, or [] for none) and returns a DataSet;
  • an algorithm that computes a field returns a Field, and several fields a named tuple of them (cell_geometry, face_geometry, flow_quantities);
  • a summary returns a Python number (entropy), or a named tuple of them (statistics);
  • a selection returns a Set (boundary_faces, check_winding);
  • one name per operation, a variant a parameter (extract_surface defaults to the boundary; project moves a field into any space), and one parameter name per meaning (inside= keeps a region, value is a level, lower and upper a range);
  • filters that cut a mesh into a subset of its cells compact the points; extract_surface and extract_edges keep the input's points, so point ids stay valid. The point filters (mask_points, threshold_points, extract_points) are the point twins of mask, threshold and extract_geometry: the points as vertex cells, point fields carried and cell fields left behind;
  • nothing changes its input: a new dataset is new, and sets are kept by storing what boundary_faces returns.

Field arguments are checked against the input topology, including on empty datasets. A raw device array needs a Field(space, values) wrapper. A locator= must have been built for that same dataset; rebuild it after changing the geometry, as described under locating points below.

Numerical types. composite, dot and cross require matching input dtypes and retain that dtype. Use Cast(values, dtype) to convert explicitly. Algorithms that need fractional arithmetic (clip weights, statistics, magnitude and log_values) compute in f64 for f64 input, otherwise f32, converting integer values before arithmetic. statistics sums integer values exactly in f64 (to 2^53, without wrapping) and takes its moments in that floating precision; its extrema come from the original values. Converting wide integers may round values beyond the exact integer range of f32 (2^24) or f64 (2^53); use f64 input for greater precision on a backend that supports it. Integer magnitude and log_values therefore return floating point fields.

Empty supported filters return valid empty topologies and carry selected fields and sets by the same maps as nonempty filters; missing fields= names still raise KeyError.

In the table, "polyhedral" means PolyhedralTopology, "polygonal" PolygonalTopology and "polyline" PolylineTopology.

Shape-based Polyhedral Polygonal Polyline face_geometry (normals, areas), face_centers, cell_geometry (volume, area or length; centroid) yes yes yes yes cell_quality (scaled Jacobian, Jacobian ratio, condition, edge ratio, shortest and longest edge) yes (order 2 along its curved edges; a pyramid by its four tetrahedra) yes (by its fan tetrahedra) yes (by its fan triangles) edges only feature_edges (boundary, feature, non-manifold, manifold edges of a surface) yes (2D cells) no (a volume: extract_surface first) yes no edge_lengths, extract_edges yes yes yes no (no derived edges) boundary_faces, extract_surface yes (a 2D mesh's boundary: line cells; by default extract_surface passes a 2D mesh's cells through) yes (the surface is polygonal) yes (boundary: line cells; by default the polygons pass through) yes (vertex cells) jump and upwind_flux of cell data; net_flux, divergence, perot of face values yes yes yes yes threshold, extract_geometry, extract_cells, mask yes yes yes yes contour, slice, slice_plane yes (dimension= 3, 2 or 1 picks the cells of a mixed mesh, by default its highest; a 2D mesh's: line cells; lines': vertex cells; an L2 field or geometry gives each cell its own points; on segments, quads and hexahedra a field above order 1 or a curved geometry is cut on linear sub-cells, subdivision= steps along each axis or as many as tolerance= needs; elsewhere an order-2 H1 field is refused, since its corners alone would be contoured) yes (López, face-based) yes (line cells) yes (contour: vertex cells, of point data) clip yes (with an H1 geometry) yes (into polyhedra: faces clipped once, iso-polygons as caps) not yet not yet extract_points, threshold_points, mask_points yes yes yes yes implicit_values yes yes yes yes CellLocator, probe yes yes (in sub-tetrahedra; cells star-shaped from their cell point) yes (in triangles fanned from the cell point; star-shaped too) yes (on segments) advect, streamlines yes (2D and 3D cells; a curved geometry, a velocity of any order or L2) yes (in sub-tetrahedra;
