cells star-shaped from their cell point) yes (in triangles fanned from the cell point) no cell_centers, values_at_centers yes yes (at the cell point, the mean of its points; point and cell data) yes (likewise) yes (likewise) gradients(at="cells" | "points") of scalars or vectors, flow_quantities yes yes (Green–Gauss over each cell's faces, fanned from their points' means: exact for linear fields) yes (in the polygon's plane, Green–Gauss over its edges; 2D cells on shapes in their plane too) yes (zero) project between cell and point values yes yes (over each cell's distinct points) yes yes project into or from L2, H1 above order 1, SideTraces yes no no no side traces, and jump/upwind_flux of point data yes no no no

Where the table says "no", the algorithm needs a reference element and raises NotImplementedError saying so.

How fields carry through filters. Every filter that makes a new dataset (contour, slice, threshold, external faces and extract_surface, as_polyhedra, as_polygons) carries fields the same way, through tack.dataset.carry. The filter states how its output's entities come from the input's -- the same entity (Same), input entity ids[i] (Take), a piece of input cell ids[i] (Pieces), or a point between two input points (Interpolate) -- and one set of rules applies to every field:

Input field On the output point data (H1, values on points) through the point map; interpolated only if floating point H1 above order 1, a curved geometry at its order and nodes when whole cells are kept or taken (not pieces): each output cell's nodes are its source cell's; elsewhere its corner values, except on a solid's surface (extract_surface), whose nodes are the solid's, gathered at order 2 cell data (Constant, values on cells) through the cell map, keeping its kind L2 (DG) data copied cell by cell, each cell keeping its order, when whole cells are kept (not pieces) and the output has reference cells values on faces through the face map, oriented values negated where a face is turned; or onto the output's cells when they are input faces (a surface) values on edges through the edge map, given only where the edges are the input's (as_polyhedra) traces, anything without a map left behind

Provenance comes from the same rules: a cell field of the input's cell ids, data.fields["source"] = td.cell_ids(data) (an implicit counting array, nothing stored), reaches every output cell as the id of the input cell it came from -- kept, a piece of, or a face of -- and point_ids does the same for kept points. No filter needs an option for it.

What each filter gives:

Filter points cells faces edges threshold, extract_geometry, extract_cells, mask kept points kept cells kept faces, turned where needed (polyhedra) — contour, slice, slice_plane interpolated along edges pieces of the cut cells — — clip kept points, edge crossings and centroids pieces of the cut cells, whole kept ones — — extract_points, threshold_points, mask_points kept points, each a vertex cell — — — extract_surface the points the faces use, in order pieces (each face's cell); face values become cell values — — extract_edges the same points — (an edge has several cells) — the lines' cells: edge values become cell values as_polyhedra same same same same as_polygons same same — —

Every one of them takes fields=: all fields by default, a name or a list of names, or [] for none; a name the input lacks raises KeyError. A new filter states its maps and calls td.carry(data, out, points=..., cells=..., fields=fields). The maps, carry, keep_marks/drop_marks, visible, owned_values, Set.from_flags and td.units are public, so a filter of your own is written as the built-ins are (Filters of your own); test_public_filters.py rewrites built-ins with public names only and holds them to the originals.

Gradients. algorithms.gradients(data, field, at="cells") gives each cell's gradient at its parametric center; at="points" evaluates each cell's gradient at the point and averages over the cells around it, as VTK's vtkGradientFilter does (a pyramid's apex extrapolated from just below it, as vtkPyramid does). A vector field's gradient is 3k values per entity, row by row (d(u_i)/d(x_j) at 3i + j). flow_quantities(data, gradient) gives divergence, vorticity and the Q-criterion from a 3-vector field's, as a FlowQuantities named tuple. Cells below three dimensions get zero, and a cell of no volume NaN.

docs.title: Implicit functions
docs.text:
tack.dataset.Plane(origin, normal), Sphere(center, radius), Cylinder(center, axis, radius) (infinite), Box(lower, upper) (axis-aligned) and Planes(origins, normals) (the convex region below every plane: a frustum, a box at any angle; its planes are evaluated at the data's precision, as the others' numbers are). value(p) is negative inside, zero on the surface, positive outside, in VTK's and Viskores' forms -- quadrics for the sphere and cylinder, signed distances for the plane, planes and box -- so a slice by one lands on the same points as theirs.

Union(f, g, ...), Intersection(f, g, ...) and Difference(f, g, ...) combine functions as VTK's vtkImplicitBoolean does: the smallest value, the largest, and the first's or the rest's union's negated, whichever is larger. They hold their operands as nested device classes, so a kernel inlines the whole tree, and move them by an origin and match a Planes to the data as each operand would be.

Each is a @tack.device_class object whose parameters are instance values, so moving or resizing one compiles nothing anew; a kernel takes it as a template and calls f.value(p). Their parameters are world positions: on a dataset with an origin, each is moved by it in double precision (Origins and point clouds). Taking one:

algorithms.implicit_values(data, f) f at the geometry's values, a field in the geometry's space slice(data, f) where f is zero: a contour of those values extract_geometry(data, f, inside=True, boundary=False) whole cells inside (every point at or below zero) or outside, plus with boundary those f cuts extract_points(data, f, inside=True) the points inside or outside, as vertex cells

clip(data, by, value=0.0, inside=False) keeps the part of every cell where by -- point data or an implicit function -- is at or above value (below, with inside: inside an implicit function's region), cutting cells by Viskores' case tables (VisIt's): whole cells keep their shape (pixels and voxels become quads and hexahedra, as in VTK), cut cells become tetrahedra, pyramids, wedges and hexahedra (triangles and quads in 2D). The tables number a wedge's corners as VisIt does, mirrored from VTK's; Tack reads wedges through that order and writes wedge pieces back in VTK's, which taken directly would be inside out. Edge points are shared between cells; point data is interpolated onto them and onto the centroid points some cases add.

On an edge with an infinite or NaN value at one end, contour, slice and clip put the crossing at the finite end, and the fields carried to it take that end's values; interpolating would give NaN.

contour(data, field, value) takes a sequence of values too, and slice and slice_plane take one as value (the function's levels; for a plane, signed distances along its unit normal, so parallel planes): every value's contour in one dataset, made in one pass over the cells -- each cell compared with every value, emitting for those it crosses -- with each output cell's value in a cell field contour_value (of the field's type). Points are not shared between values. One value, not in a sequence, adds no field. For 10 values on 1M hexahedra the one pass took 38 ms against 80 for ten contours on an M1 Max's CPU (a loaded host); merging the larger output is most of what is left.

Where the isovalue equals a point's value, contour and slice take the crossings of every edge at that point to be the point itself, one output point shared by every cell there, with the point's own values (a value equal to the isovalue counts as above it). A triangle, polygon or line with two of its crossings at one point has no extent and is dropped (a polygon keeps its distinct points if three are left), as warp-simdata drops it. VTK and Viskores keep such cells and points, so their counts are higher where a level runs through mesh points (a plane through grid points, an isovalue some points have exactly); the areas agree.

extract_extent(data, extent, rate=1) keeps a box of a structured grid's points, every rate-th, as a structured grid of the same kind (VTK's vtkExtractGrid).

Without a function: extract_cells(data, cells), where cells is ids (a host array or an integer field), a cell Set of data, or the name of one in data.sets (cells keep their order, not the order given), mask(data, stride), threshold_points(data, field, lower, upper) and mask_points(data, stride), the last two as vertex cells.

docs.title: Field and geometry transforms
docs.text:
In tack.dataset.algorithms (and tack.dataset), in Viskores' conventions:

Function Result magnitude(data, f), dot(data, a, b), cross(data, a, b) a field in the same space convert(data, unit, field=None) the geometry, or a field, in another unit (Units) composite(data, f, g, ...) scalar fields of one space as one vector field log_values(data, f, base, min_value) the logarithm, values below min_value (default the smallest normal float) taken as it point_elevation(data, low, high, range) position along a line, clamped and mapped to range (VTK's elevation filter) point_ids(data), cell_ids(data) ids as implicit counting arrays: nothing stored warp(data, direction, scale, scale_by) the geometry moved along a vector field or a constant vector, optionally scaled by a scalar field transform(data, matrix) the geometry under an affine 4x4 or 3x4 matrix cylindrical(data, inverse), spherical(data, inverse) the geometry in cylindrical (r, theta, z) or spherical (r, theta, phi) coordinates, or back

Those that move the geometry return a dataset on the same topology with every field and set kept; on an L2 geometry each cell's own corners move.

docs.title: Refinement, statistics and sources
docs.text:
tetrahedralize(data) 3D cells as tetrahedra that meet face to face, as VTK's vtkDataSetTriangleFilter makes them: a structured grid's hexahedra in 5, the two mirror splits alternating with the parity of (i, j, k) in the whole grid (the topology's offset added); any other cell the cone from its corner of smallest point id -- global id, where the dataset has global ids -- over the faces without it, each quadrilateral face split from its own smallest corner, so neighbours split a shared face alike (hexahedron or voxel 6, wedge 3, pyramid 2), across the pieces of a partitioned dataset too. Viskores' fixed tables, used before, did not conform triangulate(data) 2D cells as triangles: quads and pixels in two, polygons in fans shrink(data, factor) each cell toward its centroid: an L2 geometry on the same topology, point data as L2 (Viskores and VTK give each cell its own points) statistics(data, f) a Statistics named tuple of Viskores' descriptive statistics: n, min, max, sum, mean, central moments, sample and population variance and deviation, skewness, kurtosis; of a PartitionedDataSet too (see Partitioned datasets) entropy(data, f, bins) Shannon entropy in bits of a bins-bin histogram over the values' range; refuses no values, fewer than one bin, and a range that is not finite (as numpy.histogram does); of a PartitionedDataSet too split(data, pieces, ghost_layers=0) a structured grid cut into a PartitionedDataSet, with ghost layers (see Partitioned datasets) remove_ghosts(data) data without its duplicate and hidden cells, keeping the points it owns (see Partitioned datasets) connected_components(data) which cells are connected through shared points, as VTK's vtkConnectivityFilter (all regions, colored) and Viskores' CellSetConnectivity: data with region on the cells and point_region on the points, numbered from 0 in order of their lowest cell (VTK's numbering); -1 for hidden cells and unused points; union-find on the device. Of a PartitionedDataSet too: regions numbered across every piece and rank, in order of their lowest global cell id where pieces have global ids (the whole's numbering for the whole's ids) merge_points(data, tolerance=0) coincident points made one, as VTK's vtkStaticCleanUnstructuredGrid and Viskores' CleanGrid merge them: points at most tolerance apart join, chains of them too (union-find through the point locator's bins, each set's root its smallest point whatever the order), and each set becomes its smallest point, keeping its position, point fields, marks and global id; the cells are the same on the merged points. For meshes written without merging their points, which must be merged before their pieces can be matched: the 512 pieces of a simulation's output, each storing a point about 2.6 times, merged piece by piece then numbered by generate_global_ids, give the merged mesh's 6,310,285 points. Unstructured, polyhedral, polygonal and polyline topologies; a polyhedral mesh's faces are matched again, so a face the pieces each stored once (OpenFOAM's processor boundaries) becomes one face with both cells ghost_cells(pds, layers=1, tolerance=0) unstructured pieces with a layer of their neighbours' cells, as vtkGhostCellsGenerator (see Partitioned datasets); with tolerance, pieces share points at most that far apart, for copies that differ in their last bits update_ghosts(pds, *fields) ghost values refreshed from their owners, in place, for pieces ghost_cells made merge_pieces(pds, root=0, tolerance=0) the pieces as one dataset, each cell and point once (see Partitioned datasets); tolerance as generate_global_ids takes it generate_global_ids(pds, tolerance=0) the pieces' points and cells numbered across all of them, as vtkGenerateGlobalIds (see Partitioned datasets); with tolerance (VTK's Tolerance), points of different pieces at most that far apart are one, and so are chains of them. Points a piece repeats within itself stay apart: merge_points merges them first. On a filter's output from pieces without ghost cells, which lost its marks, every point and cell is matched and the owners marked, so reductions take it sources.wavelet(extent, ...) VTK's and Viskores' wavelet (RTData) on a uniform grid sources.tangle(dims) Viskores' tangle cube (tangle) on [0, 1]^3

Tetrahedra and triangles are pieces of their cells (carry's Pieces): cell data goes to each, the points stay the same.

docs.title: Locating points, probing and advection
docs.text:
voxelize(data, grid, fields=None, samples=4) puts data on the voxels (cells) of an image: fraction, the share of each voxel the data covers, and each field's mean over it, as cell data, by samples probes a side per voxel (the same bits every run; batched); voxels the data does not reach are HIDDENCELL. It takes what probe takes (datasets, pieces, AMR hierarchies, octrees); with one sample it is the probe at the voxel centres.

CellLocator(data, density=1.0, levels=2) bins the cells' bounding boxes on a two-level grid over the dataset, as Viskores' CellLocatorTwoLevel does: a coarse uniform grid of about 32 cells a bin, each bin split into a uniform grid of leaves sized by its count, about 8 cells a leaf. A point is searched for among its leaf's cells, so a mesh graded toward a body in a large far field (the ONERA M6 wing's) is not all in a few bins. CellLocator(data, levels=1) bins the cells on one uniform grid of about density bins a cell instead, as Viskores' CellLocatorUniformBins and VTK's vtkStaticCellLocator do: on a small, even mesh a search there scans fewer candidates (6.6 a location against 12 on tack-examples' fire mesh), and on a graded one a few bins hold most of the cells. Pass it as locator=; both levels find the same cells. Where the search runs from the cells instead (cells a by-id search cannot read, or a fresh locator's first small query), the points are bucketed into a uniform grid of about density bins per cell. It records the topology, the geometry's values and their state when made; locator.serves(data) says whether it still locates in data's cells. probe, advect and streamlines take a locator for any dataset of the same topology and geometry, and refuse one whose positions Tack has written since (a kernel, fill or copyto into them). Given none, they use the locator the topology keeps (tack.dataset.locator.cached_locator), made once and again when the geometry changes or is replaced: repeated probes of a mesh build its bins once. Writes Tack does not make, through memory it shares (DLPack, export_memory, wrap_ptr), need a new locator. The state is a write count every array's storage keeps (DeviceBuffer.version, counted by host writes and by every launch that may store to it). locator.find(points) takes an (n, 3) array or a field of 3-vectors and returns Locations(cells, pcs, tets), a named tuple: each point's cell (a field of the dataset's id_dtype, -1 where none holds it), its parametric coordinates there, and tets, which is None except in polyhedra (below). A point counts as in a cell within 0.1% of the cell's bounding-box diagonal, as vtkProbeFilter's computed tolerance has it. Of the cells that hold the point the smallest id wins; a cell that only comes within the tolerance wins only where none holds it, so a point just inside one cell is not extrapolated in a lower-numbered neighbour. A cell holds a point within 1e-5 of its parametric domain (shapes.HOLD_TOLERANCE; of a sub-triangle or sub-tetrahedron in a fanned cell), so a point on a face, edge or vertex that cells share is held by all of them and goes to the smallest id: without the margin which cells held it was rounding noise, and the searches from the points and from the cells disagreed there. Advection ranks its cells the same way. The search runs from the points: one launch, each point testing the cells its bin may hold (cell_bins(), cells reached by id), and probe reads fields the same way, one launch per field. A curved geometry (H1 above order 1) and fields above order 1 or in L2 are read by id through each shape's own view, so a curved cell is inverted by its own map there as from the cells. Where cells cannot be read by id -- an L2 geometry, line or vertex cells -- it runs from the cells instead, each cell testing the points in the bins its box overlaps through its own view; so does a fresh locator's first query of fewer points than a quarter of its cells, sparing the cell bins until it is used again. Both rank candidates alike and give the same answer. The bins follow the geometry when the locator is built; build it again after moving the points.

A polyhedron has no parametric coordinates. Its faces are fanned into triangles from their face points (the mean of each face's points), and the triangles into sub-tetrahedra from the cell point (the mean of the cell's distinct points); point data is linear on each, taking the means of the values at those two points, so a linear field is exact and a face's two cells agree on it. On a polyhedral dataset find's tets is each point's sub-tetrahedron in its cell (i32, numbered face by face and edge by edge, -1 for none), and pcs its coordinates there, the weights of the face point and the edge's two points, which a field's view evaluates with tet_value(c, t, pc). The locator refuses a dataset with a cell that is not star-shaped from its cell point, whose sub-tetrahedra would overlap.

probe(data, where, fields=None, locator=None) evaluates data's fields at the points of where, as Viskores' Probe and VTK's vtkProbeFilter do. where is a dataset, which keeps its topology and fields, or an (n, 3) array, which becomes vertex cells. Each field becomes point data on where, alongside valid (1 where a cell holds the point, else 0 and the values are 0):

  • a field with a basis (H1, L2, Constant, values on points) is evaluated through it in the cell holding the point;
  • values on cells come from that cell;
  • anything else is left behind.

locator= reuses a locator built once for several probes.

Probing a dataset keeps its topology, geometry and id type, and samples its point positions (the corner values of an order-2 geometry). Host point input becomes vertex cells using the source's geometry precision and id width. Advection likewise preserves that geometry precision and id width.

Each shape's nearest_point(pts, x, pc) gives the point of a cell nearest x, as VTK's EvaluatePosition does: exactly for triangles and tetrahedra, by clamping the parametric coordinates for the others.

advect(data, field, seeds, step_size, steps, integrator="rk4", locator=None, tolerance=None, min_step=None, max_step=None, max_length=None) moves each seed through a steady velocity field -- point data, interpolated in the cell holding the particle, or cell data -- by fixed RK4 (or Euler) steps, as Viskores' ParticleAdvection does, or by RK45 steps that adapt (integrator="rk45": Cash-Karp, VTK's vtkRungeKutta45, with its rules: a step whose error estimate passes tolerance is tried again smaller, 0.9 h (err/tol)^-0.25, keeping its first stage; a step taken proposes the next, 0.9 h (err/tol)^-0.2, within [min_step, max_step]; one at min_step is taken whatever its error; a push out at a wall that moves the particle less than min_step ends it, SPATIAL_BOUNDS, as VTK's RK45 ends it out of its domain). A particle's step goes with it between a GPU's launches and from piece to piece. max_length stops a particle whose path has gone that far (in the length unit its last step lands on it). It returns the particles where they stopped, one vertex cell each, with steps, time and status. status holds Viskores' bits, ParticleStatus.SUCCESS, TERMINATE, SPATIAL_BOUNDS, TOOK_ANY_STEPS and ZERO_VELOCITY. streamlines(...) returns the paths, the seed first, as Viskores does: a polyline per seed that moved (a PolylineTopology), with seed on the cells and time on the points. A seed that took no step keeps its point and has no line.

The rules are Viskores':

  • a step is taken whole when every stage of it lies in the mesh;
  • a step that would leave the mesh is bisected to the boundary, and the particle is then pushed just outside by an Euler step from the last point inside (the bisection's bracket, grown until the locator finds no cell there, at most the way to the boundary again), ending with SPATIAL_BOUNDS; its time and path length count the way it went. Viskores pushes by the way to the boundary again, counting it once;
  • a particle stops after steps steps, outside the mesh, or at zero velocity;
  • a seed outside the mesh does not move and loses SUCCESS.

Going on. advect takes its own output as seeds: the particles go on from where they stopped, with their times and the steps they took (steps counts those too), and a particle that stopped outside, at zero velocity or after the new limit stays. Two calls of 20 and then 40 steps give 40 steps' particles exactly; a seed field comes along.

Over pieces. Given a PartitionedDataSet (and the field's name), advect and streamlines let particles cross from piece to piece, in rounds: each particle in flight goes to the lowest piece one of whose own cells (not a ghost) holds it, found from the pieces' boxes and their locators; each piece advances what it took; repeat until none is in flight. On pieces with ghost cells a particle stops after a whole step that ends in a ghost cell and the cell's owner goes on with whole steps, so the paths are the whole mesh's, up to rounding, wherever a step (step_size times the speed) fits in the ghost layer. Without ghost cells a particle crosses by the short step to the boundary and the push out, so it differs by about a step. Pieces whose shared faces are not one surface (a hexahedron's bilinear face against a polyhedron's fanned one, in a polyhedral="split" reading) leave slivers that no piece holds: a particle pushed into one goes on from where the push would have ended going the way to the boundary again, if a piece holds that, the move counted in its time and length and drawn in its stretch. advect returns a PartitionedDataSet of the particles on the pieces they stopped in (or left the domain from), each with a seed (its number among all the seeds); streamlines one of each piece's stretches of the paths, with seed and segment on the cells, each stretch after the first starting at a DUPLICATEPOINT, so every path's points are owned once. Pieces may be on any devices, or on MPI ranks, each rank passing its own seeds, numbered after the ranks before it; one process gives the same particles.

Each particle's whole path is one thread of one launch. Its stages locate it from the particle's side (CellLocator.cell_bins(), each bin's candidate cells) and reach the cell by id through the topology's flat arrays, the cell's type choosing its shape's inversion and interpolation. The kernel compiles only the shapes the mesh has. At 1M cells, 10,000 seeds and 200 steps it takes 0.27 s on 8 CPU threads and 0.33 s on Metal for hexahedra (0.34 s and 0.59 s for tetrahedra), against 2.1 s (1.6 s) for VTK's vtkStreamTracer on 8 threads.

A stage first tries the cell the particle was last found in, taking it only where it holds the point well inside (shapes.WELL_INSIDE, a thousandth of the cell, so no other cell of the mesh holds it and the search would give the same answer). A polyhedron is tried in its sub-tetrahedra, taken where one holds the point by the same margin, its four weights each at least a thousandth; it is the search's own call, so its sub-tetrahedron and coordinates are the search's. About one location in seven misses, mostly next to a face. On the AhmedML mesh's 21.5M polyhedra, 2,000 streamlines take 0.66 s on the CPU against 0.76, and 3.0 s on Metal against 6.0. advect(..., neighbors=True) and streamlines(..., neighbors=True) then try that cell's face neighbours, by the same rule, before the bins: a point that left its cell is mostly across a face (78% of the misses on the ONERA M6, 43-49% on the aneurysm), which a few cells' tests find where the bins test 50 to 100. Streamlines on the CPU take 1.5-2x less time there, the paths the same bit for bit. The table of neighbours (CellLocator.cell_neighbors(), six ids a cell) is built from the faces on first use and kept with the locator: 0.9 s and 210 MB for the aneurysm's 8.7M cells, 4.1 s and 1.1 GB for the M6's 46.9M. Only solid cells with a reference element walk to their neighbours: pyramids and surfaces search the bins as before, and polyhedra after their last cell.

docs.title: Interoperability
docs.text:
Function tack.interop.vtk.vtk_to_dataset(grid, dtype=tack.f32, polyhedral=None, orient=False, id_dtype=None, merge_points=None) a vtkUnstructuredGrid, vtkPolyData (as the unstructured grid of its cells; strips as their triangles), rectilinear grid or image (vtkImageData, as UniformCoordinates). Point data becomes H1, cell data Constant. A grid with polyhedra becomes polyhedral (polyhedral=True forces it); orient repairs inconsistent winding; merge_points (True or a tolerance) merges an unstructured grid's coincident points first tack.interop.vtk.dataset_to_vtk(data) back to VTK, polyhedra and polygons included (both) a vtkPartitionedDataSet and a PartitionedDataSet convert piece by piece (null pieces skipped); a vtkPartitionedDataSetCollection and a dict of names to PartitionedDataSets convert by vtkCompositeDataSet.NAME() ("block<i>" without one, "<name>#<i>" for a name taken) tack.interop.mfem.mfem_to_dataset(mesh, fields=None, dtype=tack.f32, id_dtype=None) an MFEM mesh, curved at order 2 too, with its grid functions tack.interop.mfem.mfem_field(data, mesh, gf, dtype=tack.f32) one grid function: H1 orders 1 and 2, L2 orders 0 and 1, scalars and vectors

Polyhedral formats such as CGNS arrive through VTK's readers. The CGNS reader's polyhedra can be inconsistently wound, so pass orient=True.

docs.title: Settled, and open
docs.text:
Settled by the prototype:

  • continuity follows from where values live;
  • fields are separate kernel arguments, and a domain view is flat: geometry and incidence are mixins, not nested templates, since geometry needs the cell's connectivity (templates may hold templates, which the implicit arrays use, but not refer back to their holder);
  • view methods follow one naming rule per kind of answer (ids, positions, corners, counts);
  • moving a field between spaces is one function, project;
  • sets know what they select, and filters carry them;
  • shape, order and size groups are one mechanism;
  • geometry is a field, kept apart from the named fields;
  • a field's values may be any array, explicit or implicit;
  • polyhedra are a separate path that shares the data model;
  • face values have an orientation where it matters.

Settled by the consolidation (2026-10-16):

  • one name per operation, a variant a parameter (extract_surface's faces, project's target space);
  • what each kind of algorithm returns: a filter a DataSet, an analysis a Field or a named tuple of them, a summary a number or a named tuple, a selection a Set;
  • one parameter name per meaning (inside=, value, lower/upper);
  • a dataset computes on its own device, and its parts share one.

The algorithm surface is settled as the core's is: a change to it is a decision, recorded in the CHANGELOG as breaking.

Open:

  • coefficient layout (DOF-fastest or cell-fastest);
  • filters on higher-order data (subdivide, rather than linearize);
  • clip on polyhedra, polygons and polylines;
  • locating points in polyhedra that are not star-shaped from their cell point (a solid-angle containment test);
  • a polyline topology's edges (its segments as global entities), and stitching contour lines into polylines.

docs.title: Dataset interoperability
docs.text: Use Connect Simulation Data for complete workflows. This catalog records format mappings and geometric restrictions.

docs.title: Reading and writing other formats
docs.text:
VTK unstructured grids. Linear cells read as the shapes above. A grid with polyhedra reads as a PolyhedralTopology, every cell a polyhedron of its faces, since one topology holds either shapes or polyhedra for now (a topology holding both is planned). For a large mesh that mixes them, read it with vtk_to_dataset(grid, polyhedral="split"): a PartitionedDataSet of two pieces over the same points, the shaped cells as themselves and the polyhedra as polyhedra, each point owned by one of them so reductions count it once (filters' outputs need generate_global_ids for that, or ghost cells: ghost_cells of the two with the shaped piece made polyhedral). A CFD mesh of 21M hexahedra and 508K polyhedra reads in under 5 seconds this way (with copy=False); read as polyhedra throughout, 27 seconds and 19 GB.

A mesh written per processor and put together without merging (OpenFOAM's foamToVTK of a decomposed case) repeats every point on a processor boundary. vtk_to_dataset(grid, merge_points=True) (or a tolerance in VTK's coordinates) merges them before anything else is read, as merge_points would after: the polyhedra's faces are matched once, so the boundary is the mesh's, and with polyhedral="split" each piece's owned points are decided on the merged points, so every point is owned once. Merging after a split reading is not the same: ownership was decided on the copies, and the pieces merged apart can disagree on it.

Cells whose corners are in the reverse of VTK's order -- inside out, with negative volumes and inward faces, as some converters write prisms -- are found on every read and named in a warning; vtk_to_dataset(grid, orient=True) turns them outward. Wedges are the usual case: VTK's documentation described the wedge's corner order the reverse of how its code (faces, parametric coordinates, Verdict's volume) has always used it, until March 2026, so writers that followed the documentation wrote every wedge inside out. Read as polyhedra, such cells make the faces they share refused, so a mesh with them needs orient=True there. Higher-order cells read as H1 fields of the grid's largest order, in any mix of shapes, dimensions and orders:

VTK cells Read as Lagrange (68-73: curve, triangle, quadrilateral, tetrahedron, hexahedron, wedge) equispaced H1 of their order Bezier (75-80) H1(basis="bernstein") quadratic edge, triangle, tetrahedron (21, 22, 24) H1 of order 2 quadratic quad, hexahedron, wedge (23, 25, 26: quad8, hex20, wedge15) serendipity, or the full order-2 space beside other cells biquadratic quad, triquadratic hexahedron, biquadratic-quadratic wedge (28, 29, 32) H1 of order 2 quadratic-linear quad and wedge, biquadratic-quadratic hexahedron (30, 31, 33) H1 of order 2 (exact: their spaces lie in it) biquadratic triangle (34), cubic line (35) H1 of order 3 (exact) quadratic, triquadratic, Lagrange and Bezier pyramids (27, 37, 74, 81), quadratic polygons (36) refused

dataset_to_vtk(..., higher_order=...) writes Lagrange, Bezier or VTK's classic quadratic cells.

VTK cell grids (vtkCellGrid, .dg files). These need a VTK newer than 9.7.1.

Cell grid basis Read as HGRAD C1, shared H1 order 1 (copied) HGRAD C1, per cell L2 order 1 (copied) constant Constant HGRAD C2, I2, A (any order), G (Gauss points), Bezier resampled by VTK onto Tack's equispaced space of that order: H1 shared, L2 per cell (exact) HCURL, HDIV, and pyramids' bases other than C1 left out, with a warning

dataset_to_vtk(data, cell_grid=True) writes C1 at order 1 and VTK's A basis above it.

MFEM. mfem_to_dataset reads H1 and L2 collections of any order (Gauss–Lobatto, equispaced, Gauss–Legendre and positive bases), MFEM's older collections, nonconforming (AMR) meshes, periodic meshes (an L2 geometry), and curved meshes. mfem_grid_function writes back.

Nonconforming meshes and T-junctions. A nonconforming mesh's hanging vertices are points of the finer cells, and its fields come with every value MFEM keeps per element, the constrained ones included, so the values on the two sides of a T-junction agree: contours, slices, clips, probes, gradients and subdivision are as on a conforming mesh. What Tack does not yet know is that a coarse cell's edge or face and the finer ones covering it are the same interface. faces() gives each of them one side, as if it were on the boundary, so boundary_faces, extract_surface, jump, upwind_flux, net_flux and other face-based algorithms treat T-junctions as boundary. On MFEM's ex6 star after refinement, 1280 of the 1450 one-sided edges are T-junctions. An octree's leaves (OctreeDataSet.leaves()) are the same.

See the Data Model reference for each function.

docs.title: Units and quantities reference
docs.text:
A field's values are numbers; what they measure is its unit. Tack keeps units on fields, not arrays: an array is storage and a field is meaning, so kernels, devices and implicit arrays never see a unit. A unit is a string such as "m/s", "K" or "Msun/kpc**3", kept in unyt's canonical spelling, so "m/s", "m*s**-1" and "m/s^1" are one unit. None is unknown, which is not the same as "dimensionless": nothing derived from an unknown unit is guessed.

The spatial unit is the geometry field's (data.unit), and the dataset's origin is in it.

docs.title: Where units come from
docs.text:
• Field(space, values, unit=); DataSet(..., unit=), uniform_grid, rectilinear_grid and point_cloud take unit= for the geometry, and point_cloud(..., units={name: unit}) for its fields. A geometry Field brings its own unit.
  • OctreeDataSet(..., units={name: unit}) (and from_cells): octree fields are arrays, so their units are a mapping; the spatial unit is the roots'.
  • The VTK interop reads and writes each array's UNITS_LABEL, the one unit VTK 9.7.1 keeps: on point and cell data, the points' array, a rectilinear grid's axes and a HyperTreeGrid's arrays and axes. VTK has nowhere to keep an image's spatial unit. A label that is no unit (VTK's labels are free text) is dropped with a warning; ^ is read as a power, as LLNL units and VTK write it.

Code units are scaled units, "3.0857e21*cm", which need no registry of their own. Besides unyt's units, Tack knows the US survey foot, ftUS (1200/3937 m): State Plane coordinates and older LiDAR use it, and it differs from the international foot by 2 parts per million, metres at survey coordinates.

docs.title: What keeps a unit
docs.text:
Filters carry fields through carry, so every field a filter takes along keeps its unit: clip, slice, threshold, extracts, contour (with contour_value in the contoured field's unit), tetrahedralize, shrink, warp, transform, probe, pieces, ghost cells, merging and to_device. So do the filters whose result is the same quantity: project, values_at_centers, traces, magnitude, voxel_downsample's means, SPH interpolation, and cell_centers and face_centers (positions, in the spatial unit).

Cylindrical and spherical coordinates give an unknown spatial unit, since an angle and lengths are no one unit.

docs.title: Derived units
docs.text:
Filters that compute a new quantity derive its unit from their inputs':

Filter Unit gradients the field's per spatial unit; flow_quantities' divergence and vorticity the gradient's, the Q-criterion its square jump the field's dot, cross the product of the two, by its SI name where it has one (N times m is J) composite the fields' one unit (two known units are refused) log_values a pure number, of a pure number (a dimensioned field is refused) cell_geometry measures in the spatial unit to the cells' dimension (m**3, m**2, m), centroids in it face_geometry, edge_lengths areas in the spatial unit to the faces' dimension (an edge's length on a surface), unit normals pure numbers; lengths in it net_flux, divergence, perot the flux's; it over the cells' measure; the faces' components' statistics Statistics.unit and weight_unit, and unit_of(name) for each number: the mean, extremes and deviations in the field's unit, the variances in its square, sum times the weights', skewness and kurtosis pure numbers deposit counts pure numbers, sums, means and extremes in the field's; per_volume over the cells' measure (1/m**3, kg/m**3) sph_density, sph_interpolate the mass per volume; the field's, times m / (rho L^d) (a pure number for consistent units) halo_catalog, outliers, point_normals masses in the mass field's, radii and centres and mean distances in the spatial unit; normals pure numbers advect, streamlines time in the spatial unit over the velocity's interpolate(..., unit=) what the caller says: a function's code does not say its unit

A difference of values with an offset zero -- degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit -- is in the absolute unit of the same size, kelvin or Rankine: gradients, jumps, variances and deviations. Such values are not multiplied (dot refuses them): convert to kelvin first. Labels, ids, flags and counts that are not quantities (region, cell_ids, outlier, neighbors) have no unit, and a result computed from a bare number -- upwind_flux's constant velocity, a mass given as one number, the potential's G -- is unknown.

docs.title: Quantities as parameters
docs.text:
A parameter in a unit takes a quantity: a string such as "10 cm", a pair (value, unit) (the value a number or an array), or a unyt or pint quantity. It is converted to what the parameter is compared with; a plain number is taken to be in that unit already, as before.

Parameter Converted to voxel_downsample's size; radius= of outliers, connected_components, point_normals, ghost_points; periodic= boxes; PointLocator's bin size and neighbors' radius; SPH smoothing lengths given as one number; the halo catalogue's softening; slice_plane's origin and distances the spatial unit threshold's and threshold_points' bounds, contour's values, clip's value by a field the field's unit, offsets included ("20 degC" on a field in kelvin) advect's and streamlines' step size the spatial unit over the velocity's a mass or density given as one number to SPH or the halo catalogue, upwind_flux's velocity none: the quantity brings its unit, so the result has one (mass=(1e10, "Msun") makes densities in Msun/kpc**3)

A quantity needs a unit to convert to: one given for a dataset or field of unknown unit is refused, as is one for an implicit function's values, which have none. A string that names a field (smoothing_length="h") is the field.

docs.title: Mismatches are refused
docs.text:
Positions compared or moved between datasets must be in one spatial unit, as they must be relative to one origin: probe's points, pieces of a PartitionedDataSet, the boxes of an AMRDataSet and an octree's probe refuse two known units, naming both and convert. An unknown unit cannot be checked, so it is not refused.

For conversion, see Connect Simulation Data.

docs.title: Visualization: filters you know
docs.text: Contour, slice, clip, threshold, gradients, probe, streamlines, statistics: Tack has the filters a VTK or ParaView user already knows, and they give VTK's results. They are written in Python on Tack's kernels, and they run on the CPU or a GPU, wherever the dataset lives. This page runs two of them, shows where the others are, and lists the conventions they all follow.

docs.title: Make a dataset and filter it
docs.text:
The example makes the image of VTK's wavelet source, computes the gradient of its field at the points, and extracts an isosurface. It needs nothing but Tack.

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")           # or "metal", "cuda", "hip", "level_zero"

data = td.wavelet(20)                    # an image of 41 x 41 x 41 points, field "RTData"
data.fields["gradient"] = td.gradients(data, "RTData", at="points")
surface = td.contour(data, "RTData", 157.0)

print(surface.num_cells, "triangles carrying", list(surface.fields))
# 25880 triangles carrying ['RTData', 'gradient']
assert surface.num_cells == 25880        # VTK's contour of the same image has as many

td.wavelet makes the same image as VTK's vtkRTAnalyticSource, with the point field RTData. A Tack dataset holds what a VTK dataset holds: a topology (how points join into cells), a geometry (the positions) and fields. VTK's point data is an H1 field of order 1, with one value per point, linear in each cell. VTK's cell data is a Constant field, with one value per cell.

Each filter takes the dataset and returns something new. gradients returns a field, and the example puts it in data.fields so that contour carries it onto the surface. contour returns a new dataset of triangles. If datasets, fields and filters are new to you, read the data model's first page before going on.

docs.title: Read and draw with VTK
docs.text:
Tack does not read most file formats, and it does not render. VTK does both, so a pipeline on your own data reads with VTK, filters with Tack, and writes or draws with VTK:

flowchart LR
    A["VTK reader"] -->|vtk_to_dataset| B["Tack dataset"]
    B --> C["Tack filters<br/>(on the dataset's device)"]
    C -->|dataset_to_vtk| D["VTK writer<br/>or renderer"]

vtk_to_dataset turns a VTK dataset into a Tack dataset. Its point data becomes H1 fields and its cell data Constant fields. dataset_to_vtk turns a result back. The contour above would become a vtkUnstructuredGrid of triangles, which a writer saves or a mapper draws. With copy=False the two share arrays instead of copying them. The VTK page shows the pipeline in code. It also covers partitioned and AMR datasets, higher-order cells, and Tack's filters as VTK algorithms in a VTK pipeline.

docs.title: Find the Tack filter for a VTK filter
docs.text:
Every filter is a function in tack.dataset, imported here as td. The table lists the VTK filters this part of the documentation covers, by task, with the page that shows each one. The algorithms reference has every algorithm's full signature and its Viskores counterpart.

VTK Tack Page vtkContourFilter, vtkFlyingEdges3D contour Extract vtkCutter slice, slice_plane Extract vtkTableBasedClipDataSet, vtkClipDataSet clip Extract vtkThreshold threshold Extract vtkExtractCells, vtkExtractGeometry extract_cells, extract_geometry Extract vtkExtractGrid, vtkExtractVOI extract_extent Extract vtkDataSetSurfaceFilter, vtkGeometryFilter extract_surface Extract vtkExtractEdges, vtkFeatureEdges extract_edges, feature_edges Extract vtkPolyDataNormals surface_normals Extract vtkGradientFilter gradients, flow_quantities Derive vtkCellSizeFilter, vtkCellCenters cell_geometry, cell_centers Derive vtkMeshQuality cell_quality Derive vtkIntegrateAttributes integrate Derive vtkCellDataToPointData, vtkPointDataToCellData project Derive vtkProbeFilter, vtkResampleWithDataSet, vtkResampleToImage probe Sample and trace vtkStreamTracer streamlines, advect Sample and trace vtkDescriptiveStatistics statistics, entropy Reduce vtkConnectivityFilter, vtkEuclideanClusterExtraction connected_components Reduce

Other tasks have pages of their own: point clouds and particles (VTK's vtkFiltersPoints), AMR and octrees, finite-volume fluxes, filters over pieces (vtkGhostCellsGenerator, vtkGenerateGlobalIds, vtkMergeBlocks), and steps over time (vtkParticlePathFilter, vtkStreaklineFilter, temporal statistics).

docs.title: What every filter has in common
docs.text:
Tack's filters follow one set of conventions, so what you learn on one applies to all of them.

  • The dataset comes first. A field argument is a td.Field or the name of one of the dataset's fields: td.contour(data, "RTData", 157.0).
  • Nothing changes its input. A filter that makes geometry returns a new dataset. One that computes a field returns a Field, and one that computes several returns a named tuple of them. A summary returns Python numbers. To keep a computed field with the dataset, put it in data.fields.
  • fields= chooses what the output carries. By default a filter that makes a dataset carries every field it can. Pass a name, a list of names, or [] for the geometry alone.
  • Filters run on the dataset's device. A dataset on a GPU is filtered on that GPU, and its result stays there. data.to_device("cuda") moves a dataset, as the devices page explains.
  • Parameters may carry units. A length, a time or a field value (a radius, a step size, a threshold's range) also accepts a quantity such as "10 cm", which is converted to the dataset's or the field's unit. A plain number is used as it is. Fields keep their units through filters (units).
  • Hidden cells are never processed. Cells that the dataset's ghost marks mark hidden are left out of every output. Summaries such as statistics also leave out the ghost copies that another piece owns.

docs.title: How Tack's filters differ from VTK's
docs.text:
The names and the results are VTK's, and Tack's tests hold its filters to VTK's output. Four things work differently:

  • Fields have a space, not only an association. A field may also jump between cells, as a discontinuous Galerkin solution does, and be of any polynomial order; filters use the field's own interpolation (fields, higher order).
  • Results do not depend on thread scheduling. Two runs on a device give the same bits.
  • Pieces are first-class. A filter given one piece computes that piece's share of the whole dataset's output (filters over pieces).
  • Your filters see the mesh as the built-in ones do, through public views, so they can be as fast (write a filter).

docs.title: How fast, against VTK
docs.text: On production data read with VTK's readers, on an Apple M1 Max's CPU, Tack's filters are mostly faster than VTK's on 8 threads: point gradients 14 to 33 times, isosurfaces 2.7 to 4.3 times. Not every filter is ahead: a slice of the ONERA M6 wing takes as long, and its outer surface slightly longer. On a GPU the filters are 11 to 2,269 times faster than VTK on the CPU. The performance page has every measurement, the machines and the versions.

docs.title: Adaptive data
docs.text:
An adaptive simulation refines its mesh where something happens, so its output holds the same region at several resolutions. Codes built on AMReX write block-structured AMR, and codes such as RAMSES write tree-based AMR. An analysis of either should use the finest data each region has and count every region of space once. Tack filters each box of an AMR hierarchy, adds ghost cells, averages fine data down to the coarse levels, resamples onto an image and reduces with weights. It also turns an octree's leaves into cells and probes them.

Tack has two adaptive models. An AMR dataset is levels of structured boxes, each level finer than the one before, as VTK's vtkOverlappingAMR. An octree is a grid of trees whose leaves are cells of different sizes, as VTK's vtkHyperTreeGrid. AMR hierarchies and octrees explains both, including the ghost marks that say which cells a finer level covers.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device(arch)

# VTK's AMR Gaussian pulse: a root image and two boxes refining it by 2.
amr = td.amr_gaussian_pulse(dimension=2, amplitude=1.0)
for level, box in amr:
    print(f"level {level}: {box.num_cells} cells")

# Each region of space counts once, at the finest level that holds it.
pulse = td.statistics(amr, "Gaussian-Pulse", weights="volume")
print(f"integral {pulse.sum:.4f} over an area of {pulse.weight}")

# Resample onto an image: each point from the finest box holding it.
image = td.uniform_grid((26, 26), origin=(-2.0, -2.0), spacing=(0.1, 0.1))
resampled = td.probe(amr, image)
assert resampled.fields["valid"].values.numpy().all()

level 0: 25 cells
level 1: 24 cells
level 1: 24 cells
integral 0.6633 over an area of 6.25

The integral counts each region once, at its finest level. The root image covers 6.25 square units, and the two fine boxes replace the parts of it they refine.

docs.title: The algorithms
docs.text: Task Algorithm Takes VTK or other counterpart Filter each box any filter, box by box a box the same filter on each block Grow each box by ghost cells ghost_cells AMR AMReX's FillBoundary, FillPatchTwoLevels Refresh ghost values update_ghosts AMR none Average fine data into coarse cells average_down AMR AMReX's average_down Probe or resample probe AMR, octree vtkAMRResampleFilter, vtkHyperTreeGridProbeFilter Summarize a field statistics, entropy AMR, octree vtkDescriptiveStatistics; Viskores' Statistics, Entropy Leaves as cells OctreeDataSet.leaves octree vtkHyperTreeGridToUnstructuredGrid

docs.title: Filter each box
docs.text:
An AMR dataset is not a dataset. It is a container of boxes, and iterating over it gives (level, box) pairs, coarsest level first. Each box is an ordinary dataset, so every filter runs on it. Filters leave out the cells a finer level covers, which the hierarchy marks REFINEDCELL. Their data are valid but superseded.

This hierarchy puts a refined box across the seam of two root boxes. The scalar's peak lies inside the refined region:

def box(lo, cells, spacing):
    """An image box of `cells` cells whose first cell is at index `lo` of its level."""
    corner = tuple(i * spacing for i in lo)
    points = tuple(n + 1 for n in cells)
    grid = td.uniform_grid(points, origin=corner, spacing=(spacing,) * 2)
    data = td.DataSet(td.StructuredTopology(points, offset=lo), grid.geometry.values)
    x = data.positions()
    f = np.exp(-((x[:, 0] - 4) ** 2 + (x[:, 1] - 4) ** 2) / 4)
    data.fields["f"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(f.astype(np.float32)))
    return data

# Two 4 x 8 root boxes, and a level-1 box across their seam (ratio 2).
amr = td.AMRDataSet([[box((0, 0), (4, 8), 1.0), box((4, 0), (4, 8), 1.0)],
                     [box((4, 4), (8, 8), 0.5)]], ratios=[2])

for level, piece in amr:
    refined = (piece.ghosts.cells.numpy() & td.Ghosts.REFINEDCELL) != 0
    print(f"level {level}: {piece.num_cells} cells, {refined.sum()} refined")

# The 0.5 contour lies where the fine box refines the roots,
# so only the fine box gives segments.
lines = [td.contour(piece, "f", 0.5) for _, piece in amr]
print([line.num_cells for line in lines], "segments")

level 0: 32 cells, 8 refined
level 0: 32 cells, 8 refined
level 1: 64 cells, 0 refined
[0, 0, 28] segments

The root boxes' contours are empty, because the 0.5 level lies where the fine box refines them. Each box keeps its offset, the index of its first cell in its level, which places it in the hierarchy. Its geometry may be an image, a rectilinear grid or a curvilinear grid.

docs.title: Add ghost cells and average down
docs.text:
A filter that reads each point's neighbours, such as point gradients, needs the cells around a box's edge. ghost_cells(amr, layers=1) grows every box by a layer of cells within its level's domain. Each ghost value comes from the best source the hierarchy has:

  • A ghost a sibling box holds is copied from it.
  • A ghost no sibling holds comes from the coarser level. A cell takes its coarse cell's value, and a point interpolates the coarse cell's corners linearly.
  • A ghost neither holds is hidden.

Positions are filled the same way, so rectilinear and curvilinear boxes grow as images do. update_ghosts(amr, "name") refreshes the ghost values after a filter changed the owned ones. average_down(amr, "name") puts the finer levels' data into the coarse cells and points they cover, in place:

grown = td.ghost_cells(amr)                  # every box a layer wider
for level, piece in grown:
    piece.fields["g"] = td.magnitude(piece, td.gradients(piece, "f", at="points"))
td.average_down(grown, "g")                  # refined points take the fine values
td.update_ghosts(grown, "g")                 # ghost values from their owners

average_down gives each refined coarse cell the volume-weighted average of the fine cells over it, and each refined coarse point the value of the fine point at its location. It runs finest level first, so a value reaches the coarsest level in one call. Call update_ghosts after it, since the ghost copies of the coarse values it changed are otherwise stale.

docs.title: Probe and resample
docs.text:
probe(amr, where) evaluates each point in the finest level's cell holding it. Probing onto an image therefore resamples the hierarchy, as VTK's vtkAMRResampleFilter does:

image = td.uniform_grid((65, 65), origin=(0.0, 0.0), spacing=(0.125, 0.125))
resampled = td.probe(amr, image)             # each point from the finest level
f = resampled.fields["f"].values.numpy()

Inside the fine box, the resampled values are exactly those of probing the fine box alone. valid is 0 where no box holds a point.

docs.title: Reduce with weights
docs.text:
statistics and entropy take an AMR dataset or an octree directly. They leave out refined cells and points, so each region of space counts once, at its finest level. They count values, though, and the cells of an adaptive mesh differ in size. The plain mean of a field weighs a small dense cell like a large empty one. weights="volume" weighs each cell by its measure, which gives the field's average over the domain. Then sum is the integral and weight the domain's measure, as the first example shows.

weights also takes a field's name. With a density field, a volume-weighted sum is a mass, and a field of mass per cell gives mass-weighted moments.

docs.title: Summarize an octree
docs.text:
An octree comes from a simulation reader as cells with levels and positions, or from VTK as a vtkHyperTreeGrid. OctreeDataSet.from_cells builds one from each cell's level and a position inside it, as a RAMSES reader or yt gives them, and adds the ancestors no cell gives. This octree refines one root cell to level 4 near a dense blob:

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Whole octs, as a RAMSES reader gives them: each cell's level and centre.
levels, centres = [], []


def refine(lo, size, level):
    mid = lo + size / 2
    if level < 2 or (level < 4 and np.linalg.norm(mid - 0.3) < 0.25):
        for child in range(8):
            offset = np.array([child & 1, (child >> 1) & 1, (child >> 2) & 1]) * size / 2
            refine(lo + offset, size / 2, level + 1)
    else:
        levels.append(level)
        centres.append(mid)


refine(np.zeros(3), 1.0, 0)
centres = np.array(centres)
rho = np.exp(-40 * ((centres - 0.3) ** 2).sum(axis=1))       # a dense blob
roots = td.uniform_grid((2, 2, 2))                            # one root cell, the unit cube
octree = td.OctreeDataSet.from_cells(roots, levels, centres, fields={"rho": rho})

plain = td.statistics(octree, "rho")
by_volume = td.statistics(octree, "rho", weights="volume")
print(f"mean {plain.mean:.4f}, by volume {by_volume.mean:.4f}, mass {by_volume.sum:.4f}")
leaf = octree.is_leaf
assert np.isclose(by_volume.sum, octree.fields["rho"].numpy()[leaf] @ octree.measures()[leaf])
assert np.isclose(by_volume.weight, 1.0) and plain.mean > by_volume.mean

The leaves of the refined region are small and dense, so the plain mean is far above the volume-weighted one. Reductions of an octree read its leaves. level= reduces the nodes of one level instead. is_leaf and measures() give each node's role and volume as NumPy arrays, for checks of your own.

docs.title: Turn octree leaves into cells and probe them
docs.text:
octree.leaves() gives the leaves as an unstructured dataset of voxels, or of pixels in 2D, with every field as cell data. Cell c is the c-th leaf in the nodes' order, np.flatnonzero(octree.is_leaf)[c]. Corners that coincide are one point, so the cells are connected. Corners on a finer neighbour's face stay hanging, as the tree has them. Every filter that reads cell data works on the result: threshold, cell_centers, extract_cells, probe.

probe(octree, points) gives each point the values of the leaf holding it, as VTK's vtkHyperTreeGridProbeFilter does. Values are constant over a leaf. valid is 0 outside the roots, on hidden leaves and off a 2D octree's plane.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Two root cells side by side; the first refined once, one of its children again.
roots = td.uniform_grid((3, 2, 2))
tree = [0] + [0] * 8 + [0] * 8 + [1]
level = [0] + [1] * 8 + [2] * 8 + [0]
key = [0] + list(range(8)) + [(7 << 3) | c for c in range(8)] + [0]
octree = td.OctreeDataSet(roots, tree, level, key,
                          fields={"level": np.array(level, np.float32)})

leaves = octree.leaves()
print(leaves.num_cells, "cells,", leaves.num_points, "points")
assert leaves.num_cells == 16
# 27 corners in the refined root, 19 more in its refined child, 4 more for the
# coarse root beside it, whose shared face's corners are already there.
assert leaves.num_points == 27 + 19 + 4

probed = td.probe(octree, np.array([[0.1, 0.1, 0.1], [0.9, 0.9, 0.9],
                                    [1.5, 0.5, 0.5], [3.0, 0.5, 0.5]]))
print(probed.fields["level"].values.numpy(), probed.fields["valid"].values.numpy())
assert list(probed.fields["level"].values.numpy()) == [1, 2, 0, 0]
assert list(probed.fields["valid"].values.numpy()) == [1, 1, 1, 0]

The octree constructor takes each node's tree, level and Morton key, as the octree model explains. A probe onto an image resamples the octree.

docs.title: Over MPI ranks
docs.text: The boxes of a hierarchy may live on several devices and several MPI ranks. Each rank passes its own boxes of each level and the world: td.AMRDataSet(levels, ratios, world=tc.World(comm)). The hierarchy gathers every rank's boxes when it is made. Its marks, ghost cells, average_down, probes and reductions then work across the ranks. An octree's ranks each hold whole trees. Its reductions combine every rank's leaves, and a probe sends each point to the rank whose trees hold it. Filters over pieces covers worlds and MPI.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• An AMR contour is one piece per box, and the pieces of different levels do not join at level boundaries. Crack-free contouring is not part of Tack yet.
  • An octree's leaves keep their hanging corners. Face-based algorithms treat a coarse-fine interface as boundary, since such faces are not yet paired.
  • An AMR dataset refuses boxes that overlap within a level, boxes not properly nested in the level below, image boxes off their level's lattice, and boxes that already have ghost cells.

docs.text:

docs.title: Derive quantities
docs.text:
Many questions about a simulation are about quantities it did not store: the gradient of a pressure, the vorticity of a flow, the volume and shape of each cell, the total mass in a region, a cell field seen at the points. Tack computes each of them with a filter that has a VTK counterpart: vtkGradientFilter, vtkCellSizeFilter, vtkMeshQuality, vtkIntegrateAttributes and vtkCellDataToPointData. Every result comes with its layout and its unit. A field can move between point and cell data in more than one way, and the last section helps you choose.

The filters here return fields or numbers, not a new dataset. Put a field in data.fields to keep it with the dataset, so that later filters carry it.

docs.title: Compute gradients and flow quantities
docs.text:
gradients(data, field) is VTK's vtkGradientFilter. By default it gives the gradient at each cell's centre. With at="points" it gives each cell's gradient at each point, averaged over the cells around the point, as VTK does. flow_quantities derives the divergence, the vorticity and the Q-criterion from a velocity's gradient.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 11), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2), unit="m")
x = data.positions()
data.fields["T"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(300 + 10 * x[:, 0]), unit="K")
rotation = np.stack([-x[:, 1], x[:, 0], np.zeros(len(x), np.float32)], axis=1)
data.fields["velocity"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(rotation, dtype=tack.vec3(tack.f32)),
                                   unit="m/s")

grad_T = td.gradients(data, "T")                         # one 3-vector per cell
at_points = td.gradients(data, "T", at="points")         # one per point
flow = td.flow_quantities(data, td.gradients(data, "velocity"))

print(grad_T.values.numpy()[0].round(3), grad_T.unit)              # [10. 0. 0.] K/m
print(flow.vorticity.values.numpy()[0].round(3), flow.vorticity.unit)  # [0. 0. 2.] 1/s
assert np.allclose(at_points.values.numpy(), [10, 0, 0], atol=1e-4)
assert np.allclose(flow.divergence.values.numpy(), 0, atol=1e-5)
assert np.allclose(flow.q_criterion.values.numpy(), 1, atol=1e-5)

The field may be point data (an H1 field of order 1), cell data (a Constant field), or a field of any order, continuous (H1) or discontinuous (L2). The gradient is computed through the field's own interpolation in each cell, and the geometry's Jacobian turns it into a gradient in space.

  • Layout. A scalar's gradient is a 3-vector. A vector of k components has 3k values, row by row: d(u_i)/d(x_j) is at 3 * i + j. That is VTK's and Viskores' layout of the gradient tensor, and what flow_quantities reads.
  • Units. The gradient's unit is the field's over the spatial unit: K/m above. A field or a dataset without a unit gives a gradient without one.
  • Higher order. at may also be an L2 space of the dataset: td.gradients(data, "u", at=td.L2(data, order=p)). That gives the gradient at every node of every cell, exactly, without the averaging that at="points" does. An order-p field keeps its detail this way.
  • 2D and degenerate cells. A 2D cell's gradient lies in its plane, as in VTK. Lines and vertices get zero, and a cell of no volume gets NaN.
  • Polyhedra. A polyhedron has no reference element, so its gradient of point data is computed by Green-Gauss over its faces. That is exact for a linear field.

flow_quantities returns a named tuple of three fields, divergence, vorticity and q_criterion, in the gradient's space: per cell from a cell gradient, per point from a point gradient. See the reference for gradients and flow_quantities.

docs.title: Other fields from fields
docs.text:
Smaller filters compute a field from fields pointwise. Each returns a field in its input's space, with a derived unit.

Tack Gives Viskores magnitude(data, field) each vector's length VectorMagnitude dot(data, a, b) the dot product of two vector fields DotProduct cross(data, a, b) the cross product of two 3-vector fields CrossProduct composite(data, *fields) scalar fields as the components of a vector CompositeVectors log_values(data, field) the logarithm, in any base LogValues convert(data, unit, field) a field, or the geometry, in another unit

dot, cross and composite need fields of one value type. VTK's vtkArrayCalculator has no counterpart: a formula of your own is a short kernel, as write a mesh algorithm shows.

docs.title: Measure cells
docs.text:
cell_geometry(data) gives each cell's measure (volume, area or length) and its centroid, as VTK's vtkCellSizeFilter does, as a named tuple of two cell fields. A 3D cell's volume comes from the divergence theorem over its faces, so it works on every shape, polyhedra included. A curved cell is measured by quadrature through its own map, so its volume is the curved cell's.

cell_centers(data) is each cell's parametric centre, as VTK's vtkCellCenters. It is not the centroid on a cell that is not affine, such as a skewed hexahedron. Use cell_geometry(data).centroid for the centroid.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 11), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2), unit="m")
cells = td.cell_geometry(data)
volume = cells.measure.values.numpy()
print(f"{volume.sum():.3f} {cells.measure.unit}")         # 8.000 m**3
assert np.isclose(volume.sum(), 8.0)
assert np.allclose(cells.centroid.values.numpy(), td.cell_centers(data).values.numpy())

faces = td.face_geometry(data)                             # each face's normal and area
assert np.isclose(faces.area.values.numpy().max(), 0.04)

On faces and edges, face_geometry gives each face's unit normal and area, face_centers each face's centroid, and edge_lengths each edge's length. Their fields live on the faces and edges that data.topology.faces() and edges() number. See the reference for cell_geometry and cell_centers.

docs.title: Measure cell quality
docs.text:
cell_quality(data, measures) says how well shaped each cell is: a dict of cell fields, one per measure. These are Verdict's definitions, as VTK's vtkMeshQuality uses them, and each measure is 1 on the ideal cell of its shape: an equilateral triangle, a square, a cube, a regular tetrahedron.

Measure What it says scaled_jacobian the worst corner's edges' determinant, the edges scaled to unit length: 1 ideal, 0 flat, negative inverted jacobian_ratio the least corner determinant over the greatest: 1 for every simplex, below 1 as a cell tapers condition the worst corner's condition number: 1 ideal, growing as the cell distorts edge_ratio the longest edge over the shortest min_edge, max_edge the shortest and the longest edge, in the spatial unit 
import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

mesh = td.tetrahedralize(td.uniform_grid((4, 4, 4)))
quality = td.cell_quality(mesh, ["scaled_jacobian", "condition", "edge_ratio"])
sj = quality["scaled_jacobian"].values.numpy()
print(f"scaled Jacobian {sj.min():.3f} to {sj.max():.3f}")   # 0.707 to 1.000

mesh.fields["sj"] = quality["scaled_jacobian"]
worst = td.threshold(mesh, "sj", -1.0, 0.75)                 # the cells to look at
assert np.isclose(sj.max(), 1.0) and np.isclose(sj.min(), 1 / np.sqrt(2))
assert worst.num_cells == np.count_nonzero(sj < 0.75)

The measures extend to every shape Tack has. Wedges and pyramids get every measure, and an order-2 cell is measured along its curved edges. Polyhedra and polygons are measured by the tetrahedra and triangles they are fanned into. Their Jacobian measures are then on the fan's scale, not the shape's: a cube stored as a polyhedron scores 0.58, not 1. Read them as a validity check (a positive scaled Jacobian means no fan tetrahedron is flat or inverted), and compare polyhedra with each other. The reference has the formulas and where VTK 9.7.1 differs.

docs.title: Integrate fields
docs.text:
integrate(data) gives the mesh's measure (its total volume, area or length) and the integral of each field over it, as VTK's vtkIntegrateAttributes does. It returns an Integrals of measure, measure_unit, values and units. A vector field's integral is a tuple.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 11), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2), unit="m")
x = data.positions()
data.fields["T"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(300 + 10 * x[:, 0]), unit="K")

totals = td.integrate(data, ["T"])
print(f"{totals.measure:.1f} {totals.measure_unit}, {totals.values['T']:.1f} {totals.units['T']}")
# 8.0 m**3, 2400.0 K*m**3
assert np.isclose(totals.measure, 8.0) and np.isclose(totals.values["T"], 2400.0, rtol=1e-6)
mean_T = totals.values["T"] / totals.measure            # the volume-weighted mean, 300 K
assert np.isclose(mean_T, 300.0, rtol=1e-6)

Each cell is integrated by Gauss quadrature through its own map, with enough points for the field's order and the geometry's. A field of any order on a curved mesh therefore integrates exactly, to rounding. Only the cells of the mesh's dimension count, as in VTK: a volume's integrals leave out its surface cells. Ghost copies are left out, and over a PartitionedDataSet the pieces are summed over every rank.

An integral is not a sum of samples. statistics gives the mean of the stored values, which on a graded mesh is not the volume-weighted mean that integrate gives (reduce explains the difference). See the reference.

docs.title: Move fields between point and cell data
docs.text:
project(data, field, space) makes a new field of field in another space of the same dataset. It covers VTK's vtkCellDataToPointData and vtkPointDataToCellData, and more. The common targets:

Target space Each value VTK td.H1(data) (point data) the mean of the source at the point, over the cells around it vtkCellDataToPointData td.Constant(data) (cell data) the source's average over the cell: its integral over the cell's measure td.Constant(data) with average="nodes" the mean of the source's values in the cell vtkPointDataToCellData td.L2(data, order=1) the source's values at the cell's corners 
import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 11), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2))
x = data.positions()
data.fields["T"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(300 + 10 * x[:, 0]))

per_cell = td.project(data, "T", td.Constant(data))          # each cell's average
per_point = td.project(data, per_cell, td.H1(data))          # back to the points
at_centres = td.values_at_centers(data, "T")                 # T at each cell's centre

print(per_cell.values.numpy()[:3])                           # [291. 293. 295.]
assert np.allclose(per_cell.values.numpy(), at_centres.values.numpy())
interior = (np.abs(x[:, 0]) < 0.9)                           # away from the ends
assert np.allclose(per_point.values.numpy()[interior], data.fields["T"].values.numpy()[interior])

The two averages into cell data differ in what they mean. The default, average="integral", is the field's true average over the cell, exact for any order and any curved cell. average="nodes" is VTK's mean of the values the cell stores. The two agree for a linear field on a tetrahedron or a box, but not on a pyramid, a distorted cell or a field of higher order.

Into point data, a continuous field comes across exactly, and where cells disagree (cell data, or a discontinuous field) each point takes their mean. Values on faces or edges have no interpolation, so they cannot be projected.

values_at_centers(data, field) evaluates a field at each cell's parametric centre through its interpolation. For a linear field that equals the cell average, as in the example. For higher-order fields it is a point value, not an average. See the reference for project and values_at_centers. The fields page explains spaces, and when each projection is the right one.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Precision. Filters compute in the dataset's precision, which vtk_to_dataset makes single by default. Jacobians and gradients are formed from differences of corners and values, never from absolute positions, so thin cells keep their short edges' accuracy in single precision. Where double precision matters, read the data with dtype=tack.f64 on a device that has it.

Singular corners. At the points, a cell whose Jacobian is singular at a corner (where two faces meet flat) has no gradient there. It is left out of that point's average, which is NaN only if no cell around the point is left. A pyramid's apex gets the gradient from just below it, as VTK's vtkPyramid does.

Cells without a reference element. On polyhedra, polygons and polylines, project moves only point data and cell data, one into the other. values_at_centers and cell_centers use the cell point, the mean of the cell's distinct points, which is where the cell's interpolation is fanned from. The polyhedra page explains why.

docs.title: Real data
docs.text: Tack's filters have been run on production simulations' output, read with VTK's readers, and checked against VTK's output: the ONERA M6 wing (46.9M tetrahedra and wedges), an aneurysm's blood flow (8.7M tetrahedra), the LANL wildfire (18.7M curvilinear cells), and 512 pieces of one simulation's output.
