docs.title: Extract parts of a dataset
docs.text: Most pipelines start by extracting the part of a dataset that matters: an isosurface, a cut through the volume, the cells in a range or a region, the outer surface. Tack has the extraction filters VTK has: contour, slice, clip, threshold, the cell extractors, and the surface and edge filters. Three of them can seem to answer one question, so the page starts by setting them side by side. The sections after it give each filter's main options and show how to choose the fields that come along.

docs.title: Keep, cut or intersect
docs.text:
The same scalar level can answer three different questions. The example makes the distance from the centre of a cube, r, and asks all three about the ball r <= 0.5.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((21, 21, 21), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
data.fields["r"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(np.linalg.norm(data.positions(), axis=1)))

sphere = td.contour(data, "r", 0.5)                # the level set: triangles
ball = td.clip(data, "r", 0.5, inside=True)        # cut cells: the part below 0.5
cells = td.threshold(data, "r", 0.0, 0.5)          # whole cells, every corner in range


def measure(d):
    return td.cell_geometry(d).measure.values.numpy().sum()


print(f"sphere area {measure(sphere):.3f}, ball volume {measure(ball):.3f}, "
      f"whole cells {measure(cells):.3f}")
# sphere area 3.102, ball volume 0.511, whole cells 0.304
assert abs(measure(sphere) - np.pi) < 0.05 * np.pi
assert abs(measure(ball) - 4 / 3 * np.pi * 0.125) < 0.05
assert measure(cells) < measure(ball)

r is an H1 field of order 1, which is point data: one value per point, linear along each cell's edges. The sphere approximates the true area π, and the clipped ball the true volume 0.524. The threshold keeps only the cells that lie wholly inside, so its volume is smaller. None of the three is wrong: each answers its own question.

  • contour: the sphere, a shell of triangles

  • clip: the ball, solid, its cut cells cut to the sphere

  • threshold: the whole cells inside, solid and blocky

Each is cut open at the plane y = 0 to show its inside, and colored by r (the script).

You want Filter Output Where a field takes a value contour triangles of a 3D mesh, lines of a 2D one Where an implicit function is zero, a plane say slice, slice_plane the same The part on one side of a level or a surface clip whole cells and pieces of cut cells Cells whose field lies in a range threshold whole cells Cells by id, by region or by box extract_cells, extract_geometry, extract_extent whole cells The outer surface, its edges, its sharp edges extract_surface, extract_edges, feature_edges faces as cells, edges as lines

docs.title: Contour a field
docs.text:
contour(data, field, value) is VTK's vtkContourFilter. A 3D mesh gives a surface of triangles, from VTK's case tables. A 2D mesh gives line cells, and a mesh of lines gives a vertex at each crossing. Point fields are interpolated onto the new points, and cell fields go to each triangle from the cell it came from.

value may be a list. All the levels are then made in one pass over the cells, and the cell field contour_value says which level each triangle belongs to:

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((21, 21, 21), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
data.fields["r"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(np.linalg.norm(data.positions(), axis=1)))

shells = td.contour(data, "r", [0.3, 0.6, 0.9])
levels = shells.fields["contour_value"].values.numpy()
print(shells.num_cells, "triangles at", np.unique(levels))
assert np.allclose(np.unique(levels), [0.3, 0.6, 0.9])

The main options:

  • merge_points (on by default) makes neighbouring triangles share their points, so the surface is watertight. A discontinuous field keeps its jumps: an L2 field's triangles share points only within each cell.
  • dimension (3, 2 or 1) chooses which cells to contour in a mesh of mixed dimensions. By default it is the mesh's highest. A mesh of tetrahedra and their boundary triangles gives the tetrahedra's surface, or with dimension=2 the triangles' lines. Cells of different dimensions are never mixed.
  • fields chooses the fields to carry (see Choose the fields that come along).

A cell with a NaN among its values makes no surface, so the surface stops at the cells that hold numbers. A cell field (Constant) has no level set inside its cells. To contour cell data, first project it to the points. The full signature is in the reference.

docs.title: Slice with a plane or a function
docs.text:
slice_plane(data, origin, normal) cuts the mesh with a plane, as VTK's vtkCutter does with a vtkPlane. slice(data, function) cuts it where an implicit function is zero. Both are contours of a function of position, so they carry fields as contour does and take its merge_points and fields. value sets the level, and a list of values gives parallel planes, or nested surfaces, in one pass.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((21, 21, 21), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
data.fields["r"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(np.linalg.norm(data.positions(), axis=1)))

section = td.slice_plane(data, origin=(0, 0, 0.05), normal=(0, 0, 1))
stack = td.slice_plane(data, origin=(0, 0, 0.05), normal=(0, 0, 1), value=[-0.5, 0.0, 0.5])
shell = td.slice(data, td.Sphere(center=(0, 0, 0), radius=0.5))

area = td.cell_geometry(section).measure.values.numpy().sum()
print(f"section area {area:.3f}, carrying {list(section.fields)}")
assert np.isclose(area, 4.0) and "r" in section.fields
assert np.allclose(np.unique(stack.positions()[:, 2]), [-0.45, 0.05, 0.55], atol=1e-6)

For slice_plane, value is a signed distance along the unit normal. The implicit functions are VTK's:

Tack VTK Negative td.Plane(origin, normal) vtkPlane behind the plane td.Sphere(center, radius) vtkSphere inside td.Cylinder(center, axis, radius) vtkCylinder inside td.Box(lower, upper) vtkBox inside td.Planes(origins, normals) vtkPlanes inside all the planes td.Union, td.Intersection, td.Difference vtkImplicitBoolean inside the combination

Each function is negative inside its region, zero on its boundary and positive outside, as in VTK. td.Difference(box, sphere) is the box with a ball taken out. The functions run on the device, as part of the filter's kernels. See the reference for slice and slice_plane.

docs.title: Clip by a field or a function
docs.text:
clip(data, by, value) keeps the part of the mesh where by is at or above value. by is a point field (or its name) or an implicit function, for which value is 0. With inside=True it keeps the part below instead. It works as VTK's vtkTableBasedClipDataSet does: cells wholly kept keep their shape, and cut cells become the pieces their case table lists. Point fields are interpolated onto the new points, and cell fields go to every piece of their cell.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 11), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2))
data.fields["x"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(data.positions()[:, 0].copy()))

half = td.clip(data, td.Plane(origin=(0.1, 0, 0), normal=(1, 0, 0)))   # keeps x >= 0.1
other = td.clip(data, "x", 0.1, inside=True)                          # keeps x <= 0.1
outside = td.clip(data, td.Sphere(center=(0, 0, 0), radius=0.5))      # keeps r >= 0.5

volume = [td.cell_geometry(d).measure.values.numpy().sum() for d in (half, other)]
print(f"volumes {volume[0]:.3f} + {volume[1]:.3f}")
assert np.isclose(volume[0], 0.9 * 4) and np.isclose(volume[1], 1.1 * 4)

The default side is the positive one, so clip(data, plane) keeps the side the normal points to, and clip(data, sphere) keeps the outside. Pass inside=True to keep the inside of a function's region. extract_geometry, below, is the other way round: it keeps the inside by default.

A polyhedral mesh is clipped into polyhedra: each cut cell becomes the polyhedron of its kept part, capped by its iso-polygons. Polygon and polyline meshes are not clipped yet. The full signature is in the reference.

docs.title: Keep cells whose field lies in a range
docs.text:
threshold(data, field, lower, upper) keeps the cells whose field lies in [lower, upper], with only the points they use, as VTK's vtkThreshold does. The cells keep their shapes and their order, and their points are renumbered in order.

  • For a cell field (Constant), the cell's one value decides.
  • For a point field, every corner must be in range by default. With all_points=False, one corner in range is enough (VTK's AllScalars off).
import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((21, 21, 21), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
data.fields["r"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(np.linalg.norm(data.positions(), axis=1)))

inside = td.threshold(data, "r", 0.0, 0.5)                       # every corner in range
touching = td.threshold(data, "r", 0.0, 0.5, all_points=False)   # any corner in range
print(inside.num_cells, "cells inside,", touching.num_cells, "touching")
# 304 cells inside, 792 touching
assert inside.num_cells < touching.num_cells
assert inside.positions().shape[0] == inside.num_points           # only the points used

The output is an unstructured mesh, even when the input is an image. See the reference.

docs.title: Extract cells by id, by region or by box
docs.text:
Three filters keep whole cells chosen another way. Each keeps only the points the cells use, and carries the fields as threshold does.

  • extract_cells(data, cells) keeps cells by id, as VTK's vtkExtractCells. cells is an array of ids, an integer field, a cell set, or the name of a set in data.sets. The cells keep their order in the mesh, not the order given.
  • extract_geometry(data, function) keeps the cells inside an implicit function, as VTK's vtkExtractGeometry: cells with every point at or below zero. With inside=False it keeps the cells outside, and with boundary=True it also keeps the cells the function's surface cuts.
  • extract_extent(data, extent, rate=1) keeps a box of a structured grid, as VTK's vtkExtractGrid and vtkExtractVOI. extent is a (low, high) pair of point indices per axis, both included, or VTK's flat (i0, i1, j0, j1, k0, k1). rate keeps every n-th point. The output is a grid of the same kind, so an image stays an image. A box one point thick is a grid of one dimension less.
import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((21, 21, 21), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1))

picked = td.extract_cells(data, np.array([0, 1, 2, 7999]))
ball = td.extract_geometry(data, td.Sphere(center=(0, 0, 0), radius=0.5))
cut = td.extract_geometry(data, td.Sphere(center=(0, 0, 0), radius=0.5), boundary=True)
corner = td.extract_extent(data, ((0, 10), (0, 10), (0, 10)))
coarse = td.extract_extent(data, ((0, 20), (0, 20), (0, 20)), rate=2)
layer = td.extract_extent(data, ((0, 20), (0, 20), (10, 10)))      # a plane: 2D

print(picked.num_cells, ball.num_cells, cut.num_cells, corner.num_cells, layer.num_cells)
assert (picked.num_cells, picked.num_points) == (4, 24)
assert ball.num_cells < cut.num_cells
assert isinstance(corner.topology, td.StructuredTopology) and corner.num_cells == 1000
assert coarse.num_points == 11 ** 3 and layer.num_cells == 400

The reference has extract_cells, extract_geometry and extract_extent.

docs.title: Extract the surface and its edges
docs.text:
extract_surface(data) is the outer surface of a mesh, as VTK's vtkDataSetSurfaceFilter. A 3D mesh's boundary faces become triangles, quads or polygons, wound outward. A 2D mesh is its own surface and passes through. The surface's points are the ones its faces use, renumbered in order, as VTK's geometry filter keeps them. Point fields come along at those points, and each face takes its cell's cell fields.

boundary_faces(data) gives the same boundary as a face set instead of a dataset. extract_surface(data, faces) makes a surface of any face set, or of the name of one in data.sets.

extract_edges(data) makes every edge a line cell on the same points, as VTK's vtkExtractEdges. feature_edges(surface) keeps the edges of a surface by how many cells meet there and at what angle, as VTK's vtkFeatureEdges:

  • boundary edges belong to one cell.
  • feature edges belong to two cells whose normals are at least angle degrees apart, 30 by default.
  • non-manifold edges belong to three or more cells.
  • manifold edges are the other edges of two cells. They are off by default.

The output's cell field kind says which kind each edge is (td.EdgeKind). feature_edges works on 2D cells, so a volume mesh's surface comes from extract_surface first.

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

box = td.uniform_grid((4, 3, 3))                      # 3 x 2 x 2 cells
surface = td.extract_surface(box)
edges = td.extract_edges(surface)
sharp = td.feature_edges(surface)                     # the box's 12 edges, in segments
kinds = sharp.fields["kind"].values.numpy()

print(surface.num_cells, "faces,", edges.num_cells, "edges,", sharp.num_cells, "feature edges")
assert surface.num_cells == len(td.boundary_faces(box)) == 2 * (6 + 6 + 4)
assert sharp.num_cells == 4 * 3 + 4 * 2 + 4 * 2 and (kinds == td.EdgeKind.FEATURE).all()
assert td.feature_edges(td.uniform_grid((4, 4))).num_cells == 12    # an open square's boundary

surface_normals(surface) adds normals to a surface, as VTK's vtkPolyDataNormals without splitting: a unit normal per cell as cell_normals, and one at each point as normals, the sum of its cells' normals made unit length. It first winds every connected region's polygons alike, as VTK's consistency option does. With weights="area", small slivers count for little in the points' normals.

The reference has extract_surface, extract_edges, feature_edges and surface_normals.

docs.title: Choose the fields that come along
docs.text:
Every filter on this page takes fields=. By default it carries every field it can. A name or a list of names selects fields, and [] keeps the geometry alone. An unknown name raises KeyError. A field you computed travels only if it is in data.fields.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((21, 21, 21), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
data.fields["r"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(np.linalg.norm(data.positions(), axis=1)))
data.fields["source_cell"] = td.cell_ids(data)       # a cell field: each cell's id

sphere = td.contour(data, "r", 0.5, fields=["source_cell"])
bare = td.contour(data, "r", 0.5, fields=[])
print(list(sphere.fields), list(bare.fields))
assert list(sphere.fields) == ["source_cell"] and list(bare.fields) == []

How a field travels depends on where its values live:

Field On the output point data (H1) kept at kept points, and interpolated along the edge at new points cell data (Constant) copied to each kept cell, or each piece or triangle of a cut cell L2 kept cell by cell where whole cells survive values on faces or edges kept where the filter keeps the faces, as extract_surface does, and otherwise left behind

Integer point fields are not interpolated: contour, slice and clip, which make new points, leave them behind, while threshold and the other filters that keep whole cells carry them. To keep labels through a cut, store them on the cells. td.cell_ids(data), as above, records which input cell each output cell came from, since the output's own cells are numbered afresh. Cell sets come through filters the same way: an output cell is in a set when the cell it came from was, and the set refers to the output's own cells.

docs.title: Cut higher-order fields and curved cells
docs.text:
A field above order 1, or a curved geometry, has level sets that bend inside each cell. contour, slice and slice_plane cut such a dataset on linear sub-cells of the cells the level can reach. By default each cell is cut into as many steps along each axis as the field's or the geometry's order, whichever is larger. Each new point is placed where the field itself takes the value, so the surface's points lie on the true level set whatever the number of steps. The steps decide only how finely the surface is faceted.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


@tack.func
def blob(x):
    return x.x * x.x * x.x - x.y * x.z + 0.5 * x.y * x.y


data = td.uniform_grid((5, 5, 5), spacing=(0.25, 0.25, 0.25))
data.fields["u"] = td.interpolate(data, blob, td.H1(data, order=3))

surface = td.contour(data, "u", 0.2)                   # 3 steps a cell, the field's order
p = surface.positions().astype(np.float64)
error = np.abs(p[:, 0] ** 3 - p[:, 1] * p[:, 2] + 0.5 * p[:, 1] ** 2 - 0.2).max()

whole, part = td.clip(data, "u", 0.2).partitions       # a PartitionedDataSet
print(surface.num_cells, "triangles, off the level set by", f"{error:.1e}")
print(whole.num_cells, "whole cells of order", whole.fields["u"].space.order,
      "and", part.num_cells, "linear pieces")
assert error < 1e-5 and whole.fields["u"].space.order == 3

  • Linear tetrahedra: each cut is flat within its cell

  • An order-4 field on straight hexahedra: the cuts bend inside the cells

  • Curved cells of order 3, the field of order 3 on them

The same field contoured on three kinds of cells. Where the field or the geometry is of higher order, the surface follows the level set inside each cell, not a straight line between the corners (gallery).

The options:

  • subdivision=n cuts each cell into n steps along each axis.
  • tolerance= chooses the fewest steps whose estimated error is within it, in the field's unit. Give subdivision or tolerance, not both.
  • exact=False places each point where the straight line between the sub-cells' values crosses the level, as a linear contour of the sub-cells would.

clip and threshold keep what they need not cut. Cells that lie wholly on the kept side stay as they are, curved and of their order. Only the others are cut into linear sub-cells. The result is a PartitionedDataSet of the two parts, whole cells first, and their shared points are owned once, so summaries over both parts count each point once. A dataset of straight cells and order-1 fields clips and thresholds into one dataset, as above.

slice and slice_plane cut a function of position, so only a curved geometry makes them subdivide. They follow it on segments, quads, hexahedra and voxels, and use the corners of other curved cells. The higher-order page explains the fields themselves.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Empty outputs are valid. A filter that finds nothing returns a dataset of no cells. Check num_cells before assuming there is geometry to draw.

Clips through mesh points. clip names its new points by the edges they lie on, as VTK's vtkTableBasedClipDataSet does. A clip exactly through mesh points, such as a plane through a layer of faces, therefore leaves a new point on top of the mesh point and cells of no volume between them, as VTK's does. td.merge_points merges the coincident points, as VTK's vtkCleanGrid does. contour and slice instead make such a crossing the mesh point itself, and drop the triangles that lose their area.

Cells without a reference element. Polyhedra, polygons and polylines have no parametric cell, so the filters treat them as the polyhedra page explains: a field is linear on the tetrahedra and triangles each cell is fanned into.

Filter Shapes Polyhedra and polygons Polylines threshold, extract_cells, extract_geometry yes yes yes contour, slice yes, and above order 1 on segments, quads, hexahedra, triangles, tetrahedra and wedges yes contour gives vertices clip yes polyhedra, into polyhedra, but not polygons yet not yet extract_surface yes yes the chains' ends

An order-2 H1 field on pyramids is refused by the cuts. Pyramids support order 1.

docs.text:

  • Filters over pieces: every filter here on a dataset in pieces, each piece computing its share of the whole's output.
  • Write a filter, when none of these does what you need.

docs.title: Finite-volume data and fluxes
docs.text:
A finite-volume code stores cell averages, cell-centred vectors, and normal velocities or fluxes through faces. To check its balances, you keep each quantity on the cells or faces it belongs to and compute with the faces' geometry. Tack's face algorithms read the two sides of a face, take jumps, upwind fluxes, net fluxes and divergences, and reconstruct cell vectors from face-normal components. With them you can check a simulation's balances in Tack, and write face kernels of your own in the same way.

The algorithms on this page work on every topology with faces: structured grids, unstructured meshes and polyhedra. VTK has no counterparts for them. In 2D a cell's faces are its edges, so a face's "area" is an edge's length and a cell's measure is its area.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Two hexahedra in a unit cube, with a cell average of density in each.
data = td.uniform_grid((3, 2, 2), spacing=(0.5, 1.0, 1.0), unit="m")
data.fields["density"] = td.Field(td.Constant(data), tack.array([1.0, 2.0], tack.f32),
                                  unit="kg/m**3")

# Density carried by a uniform wind of 0.3 m/s along x.
mass_flux = td.upwind_flux(data, "density", ((0.3, 0.0, 0.0), "m/s"))  # kg/s through each face
outflow = td.net_flux(data, mass_flux)                                  # kg/s out of each cell
rate = td.divergence(data, mass_flux)                                   # outflow per volume

print(outflow.values.numpy(), outflow.unit, "|", rate.values.numpy(), rate.unit)
assert np.allclose(outflow.values.numpy(), [0.0, 0.3])
assert np.allclose(rate.values.numpy(), [0.0, 0.6])

[0.  0.3] kg/s | [0.  0.6] kg/(m**3*s)

The first cell's inflow and outflow balance. The second cell sends out 0.6 kg/s through its boundary face and takes in 0.3 kg/s from the first.

docs.title: The algorithms
docs.text: Task Algorithm Gives Face normals and areas face_geometry fields on faces Face centroids face_centers a field on faces Cell volumes and centroids cell_geometry fields on cells The boundary faces boundary_faces a face set Both sides of each face project into SideTraces a field on faces A field's difference across each face jump a field on faces A field's upwind flux through each face upwind_flux an oriented field on faces Each cell's outward sum of face fluxes net_flux a field on cells Each cell's finite-volume divergence divergence a field on cells Cell vectors from face-normal components perot a field on cells

docs.title: Keep quantities where the simulation put them
docs.text:
A finite-volume code stores control-volume averages and forms balances from face fluxes. Tack keeps each quantity in the space that says where it lives, without converting it. Fields explains spaces. The ones finite-volume data uses are:

Simulation quantity Space Meaning A cell average Constant(data) one constant in each cell (cell data) A cell-centred value or vector Values(data, "cells") one value per cell, with no basis A face pressure, area or label Values(data, "faces") one value per face A normal component or an integrated flux Values(data, "faces", oriented=True) one value per face, positive along its normal

Constant says a value holds across its cell. Values records where a value belongs and nothing more. Neither turns an average into the point value of an unknown original field.

A value on faces is oriented when it changes sign with the face's normal. A filter that turns a carried face around, as threshold does when it keeps only a face's second cell, negates oriented values and leaves plain ones alone. A pressure, an area or a label is plain. The flag cannot check that an imported value has the right sign.

docs.title: Faces and their two sides
docs.text:
Every face has side 0 and, inside the mesh, side 1. Its normal points out of side 0. A face's flux is therefore positive out of its side-0 cell and negative out of its side-1 cell. A boundary face has side 0 alone. This is Tack's form of the owner and neighbour convention of codes such as OpenFOAM, though Tack's face order need not be the simulation's.

The examples from here on use two hexahedra of 0.5 by 1 by 1 metres:

# Two hexahedra in a unit cube, each 0.5 by 1 by 1 metres.
data = td.uniform_grid((3, 2, 2), spacing=(0.5, 1.0, 1.0), unit="m")

The geometry algorithms give what a balance needs:

# One density average per cell, kept as a constant in that cell.
data.fields["density"] = td.Field(td.Constant(data), tack.array([1.0, 2.0], tack.f32),
                                  unit="kg/m**3")
cells = td.cell_geometry(data)          # measure (volume) and centroid of each cell
faces = td.face_geometry(data)          # normal (out of side 0) and area of each face
centers = td.face_centers(data)         # each face's area centroid
boundary = td.boundary_faces(data)      # the faces with one side, as a face Set

cell_geometry gives volumes and volume centroids. Use these centroids in volume calculations. cell_centers is a different point: the centre of the reference cell, or a polyhedron's mean of points, which on a distorted cell need not be its centroid.

data.topology.faces() numbers the faces Tack derives. Before attaching a simulation's face arrays, map its face ids and orientations to these. An array of the right length does not establish the correspondence. A polyhedral topology built from explicit faces can keep the simulation's face order, provided its sides agree. Build meshes and fields shows how.

docs.title: Compute values on faces
docs.text:
A face kernel computes one value per face. for_each(kernel, data, "faces", ...) runs it over a view of the faces, and faces.entity_id(f) is the face's index into arrays over all faces. Each face has one writer, so no atomics are needed. This kernel computes a uniform velocity's normal component, its volumetric flux, and the flux of a second flow, u = (x, y, z), whose divergence is 3:

@tack.kernel
def normal_components(faces, normals, areas, centers, normal_velocity, volume_flux,
                      radial_flux, vx, vy, vz):
    for f in faces:
        e = faces.entity_id(f)                      # the face's id among all faces
        un = normals[e].dot(tack.vec3(vx, vy, vz))  # a uniform velocity's normal component
        normal_velocity[e] = un
        volume_flux[e] = un * areas[e]
        # A second flow, u(x, y, z) = (x, y, z), whose divergence is 3.
        radial_flux[e] = centers[e].dot(normals[e]) * areas[e]

num_faces = data.topology.faces().num_faces
normal_velocity = tack.empty((num_faces,), data.dtype)
volume_flux = tack.empty_like(normal_velocity)
radial_flux = tack.empty_like(normal_velocity)
velocity = (0.3, -1.2, 0.7)
td.for_each(normal_components, data, "faces", faces.normal.values, faces.area.values,
            centers.values, normal_velocity, volume_flux, radial_flux, *velocity)

oriented = td.Values(data, "faces", oriented=True)
data.fields["normal_velocity"] = td.Field(oriented, normal_velocity, unit="m/s")
data.fields["volume_flux"] = td.Field(oriented, volume_flux, unit="m**3/s")
data.fields["radial_flux"] = td.Field(oriented, radial_flux, unit="m**3/s")

Write a mesh algorithm explains views and for_each.

docs.title: Normal velocity and flux are different inputs
docs.text:
For a unit normal n_f, an area A_f, a velocity u_f and a density rho_f:

un_f = dot(u_f, n_f)    normal velocity        m/s
Q_f  = A_f * un_f       volumetric flux        m³/s
M_f  = rho_f * Q_f      mass flux              kg/s

perot takes the normal velocity un_f. net_flux and divergence take an integrated flux such as Q_f or M_f. None of them infers which an array holds, or multiplies by the area for you.

docs.title: Read both sides of a face: traces and jumps
docs.text:
A field with a basis, such as an H1 field (point data) or a discontinuous L2 field, has a value on each side of every face. Projecting it into SideTraces(data) evaluates each cell at its faces' corners. The two sides stay separate and line up point by point in the face's own order, as MFEM's double-valued face vectors do. jump(data, field) gives the difference at each face's centre, side 1 minus side 0, and zero on the boundary:

data = td.uniform_grid((3, 2, 2), spacing=(0.5, 1.0, 1.0), unit="m")
x = data.positions()
data.fields["density"] = td.Field(td.Constant(data), tack.array([1.0, 3.0], tack.f32))
data.fields["T"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array((x[:, 0] + 2 * x[:, 1]).astype(np.float32)))

sides = td.project(data, "density", td.SideTraces(data))   # each side's values on each face
density_jump = td.jump(data, "density")                     # side 1 minus side 0
T_jump = td.jump(data, "T")                                 # zero: T is continuous

The density has one nonzero jump, of magnitude 2, at the face between the cells. The continuous T has none. The sign of a jump depends on which cell is side 0, and its magnitude does not.

SideTraces holds eight values per face, two sides of up to four corners: value (face * 2 + side) * 4 + corner. Triangles leave the fourth slot unused, and boundary faces leave side 1 zero. Traces need 3D cells with a reference element. jump evaluates each side's basis at the face's centre, so a DG field's jumps are its own, of any order. Cell data is read from each side's cell directly, on any topology, polyhedral included.

docs.title: Check a cell and boundary balance
docs.text:
With s_cf +1 when cell c is side 0 of face f and -1 when it is side 1:

net_c = sum_f s_cf * Q_f
div_c = net_c / V_c

net_flux is the outward sum. divergence divides it by each cell's measure. An interior face adds equal and opposite amounts to its two cells, so the cells' outflows sum to the boundary's outflow:

net = td.net_flux(data, "radial_flux")             # each cell's outflow, m**3/s
divergence = td.divergence(data, "radial_flux")    # the outflow over the volume, 1/s

For u = (x, y, z) each cell of 0.5 m³ has a net outflow of 1.5 m³/s, a divergence of 3/s. The cube's boundary outflow is 3 m³/s. The uniform velocity's divergence is zero in both cells. Answers like these test the orientation and the area and volume factors, not only a plausible picture.

divergence of face fluxes is not flow_quantities' divergence, which is the trace of a field's gradient. Use the face-flux balance when the simulation supplies fluxes.

docs.title: Upwind fluxes
docs.text:
upwind_flux(data, field, velocity) is the flux of a field carried by a constant velocity, out of side 0 of each face: (v · n) * area * u. At an interior face u is the field on the upwind side, the side the flow leaves, evaluated at the face's centre as a DG advection scheme does. The result is an oriented, integrated face flux, ready for net_flux and divergence, as the first example shows. velocity is three numbers, or a quantity such as ((0.3, 0.0, 0.0), "m/s"), and the flux's unit follows.

A boundary face uses its one cell's value whichever way the flow goes, even for inflow. Prescribe your own boundary flux when that rule does not represent the simulation. upwind_flux is a helper for checks and analysis, not a finite-volume solver.

docs.title: Reconstruct a cell vector with Perot's method
docs.text:
C-grid models such as MPAS and ICON store each face's normal velocity. To show it at cells, perot(data, flux) reconstructs one vector per cell by Perot's method:

u_c = sum_f s_cf * A_f * un_f * (x_f - x_c) / V_c

Here x_f is the face's area centroid and x_c the cell's volume centroid.

velocity_at_cells = td.perot(data, "normal_velocity")   # normal components, not fluxes

Although the argument is named flux, pass the normal velocity in m/s, not a volumetric flux in m³/s: the method multiplies by the area itself. The result is a Values(data, "cells") field of 3-vectors in the input's unit. It reproduces a uniform vector exactly on cells with planar faces. It is first order and does not recover an arbitrary field. Perot's paper gives the method.

Probing and advection read cell values as constant over each cell. That is an interpretation for analysis. Projecting the vector to H1 averages the cells around each point, which smooths jumps and is not a conservative remap.

docs.title: Run and check
docs.text:
uv run python docs/examples/vis2_finite_volume.py --arch cpu

The program runs every check on the two hexahedra and again after as_polyhedra makes them polyhedra: volumes and centroids, the uniform velocity's reconstruction, the two divergences, the boundary balance, the upwind mass outflow, and the traces and jumps.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• On pieces, refresh the ghost values before anything that reads a neighbour's cell, and count each owned cell once when reducing. Filters over pieces shows both.
  • A coarse-fine face of an octree's leaves, a T-junction, counts as boundary for now, since such faces are not yet paired.
  • A cell of zero volume gives NaN from divergence and perot. A cell of a lower dimension than the mesh has no faces, and its net flux is zero.
  • Limiters, boundary conditions and conservative remapping belong to the numerical method, not to these helpers.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Write a mesh algorithm explains face and cell kernels.
  • Fields explains spaces, for choosing an interpolation or a higher-order representation.
  • Derive covers gradients and flow quantities from fields with a basis.

docs.title: MFEM, Warp and others
docs.text: Besides VTK, Tack exchanges data with two libraries directly. MFEM, the finite-element library, gives meshes and solutions of any order, curved and discontinuous; Tack reads them into its spaces without resampling them onto linear cells. NVIDIA Warp runs Python kernels on NVIDIA GPUs; Tack shares arrays with it, and datasets with its simulation-data library, warp-simdata. Data in either one goes through Tack's algorithms as it is, and the last section says where to go for other libraries. Tack's terms are in the glossary.

docs.title: Bring an MFEM solution into Tack
docs.text:
MFEM comes through PyMFEM, which Tack's interop extra installs (uv sync --extra interop, or pip install mfem). mfem_to_dataset takes an MFEM mesh and named grid functions on it:

import mfem.ser as mfem
import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td
from tack.interop.mfem import mfem_grid_function, mfem_to_dataset

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

mesh = mfem.Mesh.MakeCartesian2D(4, 4, mfem.Element.QUADRILATERAL, True, 1.0, 1.0)


class Cubic(mfem.PyCoefficient):
    def EvalValue(self, x):
        return x[0] ** 2 * x[1]


continuous = mfem.FiniteElementSpace(mesh, mfem.H1_FECollection(3, mesh.Dimension()))
u = mfem.GridFunction(continuous)            # H1 of order 3
u.ProjectCoefficient(Cubic())
discontinuous = mfem.FiniteElementSpace(mesh, mfem.L2_FECollection(2, mesh.Dimension()))
w = mfem.GridFunction(discontinuous)         # L2 (DG) of order 2
w.ProjectCoefficient(Cubic())

data = mfem_to_dataset(mesh, {"u": u, "w": w})
print(data.fields["u"].space, data.fields["w"].space)
# H1(order=3, basis='gauss_lobatto') L2(order=2, basis='gauss_legendre')

# The integral of x^2 y over the unit square is 1/6, from the order-3 field itself.
assert abs(td.integrate(data, "u").values["u"] - 1 / 6) < 1e-6

# And back to MFEM, the same values in MFEM's numbering.
back = mfem_grid_function(data, data.fields["u"], mesh)
assert np.allclose(back.GetDataArray(), u.GetDataArray(), atol=1e-6)

The mesh's elements become the topology, in VTK's corner order. Its element attributes become an integer Constant field, "attribute". Each grid function becomes a field in the space its collection matches:

MFEM collection Tack field H1 of order 1 H1 of order 1 (point data), one value per vertex L2 of order 0 Constant (cell data) L2 of order 1 L2 of order 1, each element's values at its corners H1 of order 2 and up, L2 of order 2 and up Tack's space of that order and basis a vector grid function a field of vectors, in either of MFEM's orderings

For orders 2 and up, Tack has MFEM's common bases: Gauss-Lobatto (MFEM's default for H1), Gauss-Legendre (its default for L2), closed uniform, and the positive (Bernstein) bases. On those, values are copied and permuted into Tack's numbering. Any other basis is evaluated at Tack's nodes, which is exact, since both spaces hold the same polynomials. Triangles, tetrahedra and wedges use Tack's equispaced nodes. Higher order explains the spaces.

mfem_grid_function(data, field, mesh) gives a field back as an MFEM GridFunction, its values permuted into MFEM's numbering. Keep the returned function's fes and fec attributes alive as long as it is used.

docs.title: Kinds of MFEM mesh
docs.text:
• Curved meshes. A mesh with nodes of order 2 or more gets a geometry of that order, an H1 field of positions. Filters see the curved cells: cuts are made on sub-cells, with each crossing on the field itself.
  • Periodic meshes keep their nodes per element, so the geometry is an L2 field. Cells on the two sides of the seam share points in the topology but sit apart in space.
  • Nonconforming meshes from adaptive refinement read with their hanging points as points of the finer cells. Their fields come with every value MFEM keeps per element, so values agree across each T-junction. Contours, slices, clips, probes, gradients and subdivision work as on a conforming mesh.
  • MFEM's numbering. mfem_to_dataset(mesh, fields, dofs="table") keeps an H1 field of order 2 and up, and a curved geometry, numbered as MFEM numbers them: its values as they are, in a space numbered by MFEM's element-to-DOF table. By default they are renumbered by entity, as Tack's own spaces are.

MFEM fields above order 1 on pyramids are refused: Tack has no such space on pyramids yet.

One limit matters for face-based algorithms. Tack does not yet know that a coarse cell's edge or face and the finer ones covering it are the same interface. faces() gives each of them one side, as if it were on the boundary. So boundary_faces, extract_surface, jump, upwind_flux, net_flux and other face-based algorithms treat T-junctions as boundary. On MFEM's ex6 star after refinement, 1280 of the 1450 one-sided edges are T-junctions.

The MFEM gallery runs MFEM's examples through Tack: curved tetrahedra and hexahedra of order 3, elasticity in H1 and DG, adaptive refinement, a curved surface, and DG advection on a periodic mesh. Its scripts are in docs/gallery/mfem_examples.py.

docs.title: Share arrays and datasets with Warp
docs.text:
Warp support is a prototype. Tack has a Warp device, tack.device("warp"), which runs Tack's kernels through Warp on Warp's default device: its first CUDA device, else its CPU. On it, a Tack array's memory is a wp.array, and Tack launches on the Warp stream a caller's wp.launch uses. So one program can run its own Warp kernels and Tack's filters on the same arrays. Install it with uv sync --extra warp, which adds warp-simdata; see Backends for what the Warp device lacks.

tack.interop.warp.from_warp and to_warp share arrays both ways, mapping Warp's vector and matrix types to Tack's (wp.vec3 and tack.vec(3, tack.f32)). Here Warp makes a field, Tack contours it, and Warp moves the contour's points:

import warp as wp

import tack
import tack.dataset as td
from tack.interop.warp import from_warp, to_warp


@wp.kernel
def sphere(field: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32), n: int):
    t = wp.tid()
    i, j, k = t % n, (t // n) % n, t // (n * n)
    p = wp.vec3(float(i), float(j), float(k)) - wp.vec3(float(n - 1) * 0.5)
    field[t] = wp.length(p)


@wp.kernel
def lift(points: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec3), out: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec3)):
    t = wp.tid()
    out[t] = points[t] + wp.vec3(0.0, 0.0, 100.0)


device = tack.device("warp")
n = 24
f = wp.empty(n ** 3, dtype=wp.float32)
wp.launch(sphere, n ** 3, inputs=[f, n])
with device:
    data = td.uniform_grid((n, n, n))
    data.fields["r"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), from_warp(f))   # Warp's memory, no copy
    iso = td.contour(data, "r", 8.0)
points = to_warp(iso.geometry.values)                         # a wp.array of wp.vec3
out = wp.empty_like(points)
wp.launch(lift, points.shape[0], inputs=[points, out])

Each side keeps the other's memory alive for as long as it is used. An array on another Tack device goes to Warp through DLPack, which waits for its queued launches. An implicit array has no memory, so to_warp stores its values first. Warp arrays have no read-only flag, so a read-only Tack array given to Warp can be written there.

to_simdata and from_simdata exchange whole datasets with warp-simdata. Image data, structured grids, polydata and unstructured grids (polyhedra included) map to Tack's topologies. NODE fields become H1 fields and ELEMENT fields Constant ones, and collections become PartitionedDataSets. Arrays that both store alike are shared. Several of warp-simdata's other models come across as they are, sharing their arrays: point clouds, surface meshes, OpenFOAM meshes, CGNS sections, EnSight parts, corner-point grids and FLASH data. The rest go through warp-simdata's own VTK conversion. to_simdata leaves behind what warp-simdata has no place for: ghost marks, global ids, sets, units and time. It writes positions as single-precision world positions, so far coordinates lose the precision Tack's origin kept.

docs.title: Other libraries
docs.text:
• PyTorch, CuPy, NumPy and anything with DLPack share arrays with Tack directly; see Share arrays. Wrap the shared array in a td.Field to give it a meaning in a dataset.
  • A simulation's own arrays, on the host or on its device, become a dataset through Connect simulation data.
  • ParaView reads what VTK writes; see VTK for writing files and for Tack's filters in VTK pipelines.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
• MFEM lists every element's corners in VTK's order, the prism included. MFEM's own VTK writer swaps a prism's corners, which turns such a prism inside out against VTK's convention; mfem_to_dataset reads the mesh directly and is not affected.
  • The full signatures are in the Data Model reference.

  • Higher order: the spaces MFEM's fields arrive in.

docs.title: Filters over pieces
docs.text:
Data often comes in pieces: a reader's partitions, a simulation's blocks, the share of each GPU or MPI rank. The analysis should still give the whole dataset's results, whether the pieces are on one process or on many ranks. Tack runs filters on each piece and combines the pieces only where an answer needs all of them. The sections below show what changes when filters run on pieces, how to add ghost cells and global ids, which algorithms combine the pieces, and how to merge the pieces back into one dataset.

Tack keeps each piece a whole dataset, and a PartitionedDataSet holds them, as VTK's vtkPartitionedDataSet does. Ghost marks say which cells and points of a piece another piece owns. Data in pieces explains the container, the marks and owners, and global ids. This page shows what the algorithms do with them.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device(arch)

whole = td.wavelet(10)                            # 21^3 points, 8000 cells
pieces = td.split(whole, 4, ghost_layers=1)       # a PartitionedDataSet

# Work on one piece takes the piece: loop over them.
surfaces = []
for piece in pieces:
    piece.fields["grad"] = td.gradients(piece, "RTData")
    surfaces.append(td.contour(piece, "RTData", 160.0))
surfaces = td.PartitionedDataSet(surfaces)

# Reductions take the pieces and count each cell and point once.
print(td.statistics(pieces, "RTData").n, "points over the pieces,",
      whole.num_points, "in the whole")
iso = td.contour(whole, "RTData", 160.0)
assert td.statistics(surfaces, "RTData").n == iso.num_points

9261 points over the pieces, 9261 in the whole

The four pieces hold more points than the grid, since neighbouring pieces share some and each has a layer of its neighbours' cells. Each shared point has one owner, and the reduction counts it there alone.

docs.title: What changes with pieces
docs.text:
Three rules cover every algorithm:

  • Work on one piece takes the piece. Filters, analyses and for_each take a dataset, as everywhere else, and you loop over the pieces. There is no wrapper that applies a filter to every piece, because the loop says what it does.
  • Algorithms whose answer needs every piece take the container. These are the reductions, extract_surface, probe, particle tracing, connected regions, the point-cloud algorithms of this page, merge_pieces, and the algorithms that make ghosts and global ids.
  • Filters carry the ghost marks to what they make, as VTK's filters do. With a layer of ghost cells, the owned part of a filter's output over all pieces is the whole's output, cell for cell and point for point.

The algorithms that take pieces are:

Task Algorithm VTK or Viskores counterpart Cut a structured grid into pieces split none Add layers of neighbours' cells ghost_cells vtkGhostCellsGenerator Add neighbours' points to point clouds ghost_points none Refresh ghost values from their owners update_ghosts none Drop a piece's ghost cells remove_ghosts vtkRemoveGhosts; Viskores' GhostCellRemove Number points and cells across pieces generate_global_ids vtkGenerateGlobalIds Merge the pieces into one dataset merge_pieces vtkMergeBlocks; Viskores' MergeDataSets Summarize a field statistics, entropy vtkDescriptiveStatistics; Viskores' Statistics, Entropy The whole's surface extract_surface vtkDataSetSurfaceFilter; Viskores' ExternalFaces Probe at points probe vtkProbeFilter; Viskores' Probe Trace particles advect, streamlines vtkStreamTracer; Viskores' ParticleAdvection, Streamline Label connected regions connected_components vtkConnectivityFilter; Viskores' CellSetConnectivity

docs.title: How filters carry ownership
docs.text:
Filters process the ghost cells too. What a filter makes takes the owner of what it came from:

Output Owner a cell: a contour's triangle, a clip's piece, a kept cell its source cell's a point a filter keeps its own a point on an input edge, such as a contour's crossing the owner of the edge's smallest point a point inside a cell, such as a clip's centroid the cell's a surface face the cell it is a side of a face two cells share, an edge, a vertex the owner of its smallest point

"Smallest" goes by position, so every piece holding a shared edge decides alike, with no communication. With a ghost layer, the piece that owns a point holds every cell around it, so its filters see what the whole would. That is why each piece's point gradients at its own points are the whole grid's in the first example. The ghost part of the output is what the next filter near a piece's edge needs.

docs.title: Reduce over the pieces
docs.text:
statistics(pieces, name) takes each piece's moments on its own device and combines them pairwise, in the pieces' global order. entropy(pieces, name, bins) sums each piece's histogram over the whole's range. Both count only what each piece owns, so the statistics of the pieces' isosurfaces are the whole grid's isosurface's.

extract_surface(pieces) gives the whole's surface, a piece each. A piece's own surface includes the faces it shares with its neighbours, since it cannot tell them from the boundary. Given the container, the faces two pieces hold are matched by their points and left out.

docs.title: Remove the ghosts at the end
docs.text:
Before rendering, writing one file, or handing a piece to code that does not know ghost marks, take the ghost output away:

finished = td.PartitionedDataSet(td.remove_ghosts(s) for s in surfaces)
print(sum(s.num_cells for s in finished), "triangles,", iso.num_cells, "in the whole")

remove_ghosts drops the duplicate and hidden cells and the points no remaining cell uses, as VTK's vtkRemoveGhosts does. The points it keeps keep their marks, so reductions over the result are unchanged. A point the piece owns stays even when only ghost cells used it. A structured piece whose remaining cells form a block stays a structured grid. dataset_to_vtk keeps the marks too, so pieces with ghosts can go to VTK as they are, and VTK leaves the ghosts out when it renders.

docs.title: Pieces without ghost cells
docs.text:
Without ghost cells, a piece cannot tell what its neighbours make on the cells, faces and edges they share. A contour point on a shared edge belongs to the owner of the edge's smallest point, and that piece may have no cell holding the edge. Tack does not guess. Such outputs record that they lost their marks, and reductions refuse them:

bare = td.split(whole, 4)                         # no ghost cells
cut = td.PartitionedDataSet(td.contour(piece, "RTData", 160.0) for piece in bare)
try:
    td.statistics(cut, "RTData")
except NotImplementedError as error:
    print("refused:", str(error).split(":")[0])
marked = td.generate_global_ids(cut)              # owners found by matching points
assert td.statistics(marked, "RTData").n == iso.num_points

surface = td.extract_surface(bare)                # the whole's surface, a piece each

generate_global_ids of the outputs marks them. It matches their points by position, so a point several pieces made belongs to the lowest of them. The marked outputs then reduce to the whole's. That costs one exchange of the outputs' points, where ghost cells cost a layer of cells in every piece before filtering.

What does not depend on neighbours works on pieces without ghost cells as they are:

  • reductions of the pieces themselves, and extract_surface of the container;
  • filters that keep the cells and points: warp, transform, cylindrical, spherical, shrink, as_polyhedra, as_polygons, and probe's target;
  • filters that choose points by their own values: threshold_points, extract_points, mask_points.

docs.title: Add ghost cells
docs.text:
split(data, n, ghost_layers=1) cuts a structured grid and adds the layer itself. Pieces from elsewhere, such as a partitioner, a reader or VTK's redistribution, get one from ghost_cells, as VTK's vtkGhostCellsGenerator would give them:

# Unstructured pieces without ghost cells, as a partitioner or a reader gives them.
plain = td.PartitionedDataSet(td.tetrahedralize(piece) for piece in bare)
ghosted = td.ghost_cells(plain)                   # one layer of neighbours' cells
deeper = td.ghost_cells(plain, layers=2)          # two, for two neighbour filters in a row

Pieces neighbour where they share points at exactly the same position. tolerance= matches points a little apart, for pieces whose copies of a shared point differ in their last bits. A shared point belongs to the lowest piece holding it. ghost_cells takes unstructured, polyhedral or structured pieces, all of one kind. Structured pieces stay structured, each its block grown by the layers. as_polyhedra makes shaped pieces polyhedral, for a reader that gives both kinds.

  • An image, split into eight structured blocks

  • Tetrahedra, extracted by octant

  • Hexahedra, wedges and pyramids, extracted by octant

Each mesh of a unit cube is cut into eight pieces, one an octant, and ghost_cells gives each piece one layer. The pieces are drawn pulled apart. A piece's own cells have its color, and its ghost cells are faint, reaching into the pieces around it.

A filter that needs each entity's neighbours is right on what a piece owns, but wrong on the rim of the ghost layer, whose neighbours the piece lacks. Before a second such filter reads those values, copy them from their owners:

for piece in ghosted:
    piece.fields["c"] = td.values_at_centers(piece, "RTData")         # a cell field
    piece.fields["p"] = td.project(piece, "c", td.H1(piece))          # back to points
td.update_ghosts(ghosted, "p")                    # the rim's values from their owners
for piece in ghosted:
    piece.fields["grad_p"] = td.gradients(piece, "p", at="points")    # right where owned

ghost_cells keeps its exchanges, so each update_ghosts is one copy per neighbour, not a new matching. Two layers (layers=2) avoid the refresh for two neighbour filters in a row, at the cost of more cells.

docs.title: Number points and cells across pieces
docs.text:
Each piece numbers its points and cells from 0. Global ids number them across all the pieces, the same id wherever a point or cell is held. VTK's GlobalIds arrays become them, and generate_global_ids makes them, as vtkGenerateGlobalIds does:

numbered = td.generate_global_ids(ghosted)
ids = numbered[0].global_ids.points               # i64, the same at a shared point

piece.global_ids.points and .cells are i64 arrays. Filters keep the ids of the points and cells they keep, such as threshold, extract_cells and remove_ghosts. What they make has none. With global ids on every piece, ghost_cells matches points by id rather than position, and connected_components numbers regions as on the whole dataset.

docs.title: Probe, trace and label across pieces
docs.text:
Three algorithms follow points or regions from piece to piece:

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
points = rng.uniform(-9.0, 9.0, (200, 3))
probed = td.probe(pieces, points)                 # each point from the piece holding it
regions = td.connected_components(pieces)         # one number per region, across pieces
seeds = rng.uniform(-5.0, 5.0, (20, 3))
paths = td.streamlines(pieces, "grad", seeds, 0.002, 100)   # each piece's stretches
  • probe(pieces, points) evaluates each point in the piece one of whose own cells holds it, and returns the values in your points' order. The values equal those of probing the whole. Ghost cells are not needed.
  • advect and streamlines hand particles from piece to piece. With a ghost layer wider than a step, the paths are the whole mesh's up to rounding. A particle that ends a step in a ghost cell goes to the cell's owner. Without ghost cells it crosses at the boundary by a shortened step. Each piece of streamlines' result holds the stretches it traced, and each stretch after the first starts at a point marked as a duplicate.
  • connected_components(pieces) labels cells connected through shared points, numbering each region once across all the pieces.

docs.title: Point clouds in pieces
docs.text:
A point cloud's pieces share no points, so a filter over a point's neighbours needs copies of the nearby points other pieces hold. ghost_points appends them, marked as ghosts: every point within radius of the piece, or exactly those among its owned points' k nearest. The neighbour filters of Points and particles then run per piece, and each owned point gets the whole's answer. Clustering, statistical outliers, voxel downsampling, deposits and halo catalogues need every piece, so they take the container:

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Clumps in a periodic box, and the same cloud cut into four pieces.
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
box = 10.0
x = np.concatenate([c + rng.normal(0.0, 0.3, (400, 3)) for c in rng.uniform(1, 9, (12, 3))]
                   + [rng.uniform(0.0, box, (2000, 3))]) % box
x = x.astype(np.float32)
whole = td.point_cloud(x, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0))
parts = np.array_split(x, 4)
pieces = td.PartitionedDataSet([td.point_cloud(part, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0))
                                for part in parts])

# Per piece, after copying in each owned point's 10 nearest from elsewhere.
ghosted = td.ghost_points(pieces, k=10)
normals = np.concatenate([td.point_normals(piece, k=10).fields["normals"].values.numpy()
                          [:len(own)] for piece, own in zip(ghosted, parts)])
expected = td.point_normals(whole, k=10).fields["normals"].values.numpy()
assert np.abs(normals - expected).max() < 1e-3

# Over the pieces: the whole's clusters, numbered as the whole numbers them.
groups = td.connected_components(pieces, radius=0.15, min_size=50, periodic=box)
labels = np.concatenate([p.fields["point_region"].values.numpy() for p in groups])
assert np.array_equal(labels, td.connected_components(
    whole, radius=0.15, min_size=50, periodic=box).fields["point_region"].values.numpy())
print(labels.max() + 1, "clusters")

A piece's own points come first in ghost_points' result, in their order, which is why [:len(own)] picks them. After a filter that is right only on a piece's own points, update_ghosts brings the copies' values from their owners: SPH densities before an interpolation that reads them, for instance. deposit of pieces gives every rank the whole grid, and halo_catalog of pieces a catalogue piece per piece. In a periodic box the copies across a face are images, moved by the box's side, so run per-piece filters on ghost_points' result without periodic.

docs.title: Merge the pieces into one dataset
docs.text:
merge_pieces gives the pieces back as one dataset, each cell and point once, ghosts dropped: to write one file, or for code that knows no pieces.

one = td.merge_pieces(pieces)                     # None on the other ranks
print(type(one.topology).__name__, one.num_cells, "cells")

StructuredTopology 8000 cells

Structured pieces that tile a box come back as one structured grid. Others give an unstructured dataset, numbered as generate_global_ids numbers it. Across MPI ranks the result is on the root rank, root=0 by default, and None elsewhere.

docs.title: Pieces from VTK
docs.text:
vtk_to_dataset turns a vtkPartitionedDataSet into a PartitionedDataSet, and dataset_to_vtk turns it back. VTK's filters cut an unstructured mesh with ghost cells, with no MPI needed:

from vtkmodules.vtkFiltersParallelDIY2 import (
    vtkGhostCellsGenerator,
    vtkRedistributeDataSetFilter,
)
from vtkmodules.vtkImagingCore import vtkRTAnalyticSource

import tack
import tack.dataset as td
from tack.interop.vtk import vtk_to_dataset

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

mesh = vtkRTAnalyticSource(whole_extent=(-10, 10, -10, 10, -10, 10))()
cut = (vtkRedistributeDataSetFilter(number_of_partitions=4,
                                    preserve_partitions_in_output=True)
       >> vtkGhostCellsGenerator(number_of_ghost_layers=1, build_if_required=False))
pieces = vtk_to_dataset(cut(mesh))                 # four unstructured pieces, marked
assert td.statistics(pieces, "RTData").n == mesh.number_of_points

VTK covers the conversions in full.

docs.title: Pieces on several devices
docs.text:
A piece is a dataset, so it can live on any device, and each piece's work runs where the piece is. Reductions reduce each piece on its own device:

# Spread the pieces over the GPUs there are, or keep them on the CPU.
gpus = [tack.device(f"cuda:{i}") for i in range(tack.device_count("cuda"))]
devices = gpus or [tack.device("cpu")]
spread = td.PartitionedDataSet(piece.to_device(devices[i % len(devices)])
                               for i, piece in enumerate(pieces))
print(td.statistics(spread, "RTData").mean)      # each piece reduced where it is

Data on devices explains where a dataset lives and how to_device moves it.

docs.title: Across MPI ranks
docs.text:
Over MPI, each rank holds its own pieces, and the container's world says where the others are. A world is a tack.communication.World, made from an mpi4py communicator or, without one, for this process alone. The algorithms that take the container then communicate. The per-piece loops do not change:

from tack import communication as tc

try:
    from mpi4py import MPI
    world = tc.World(MPI.COMM_WORLD)              # under mpiexec: every rank
except ImportError:
    world = tc.World()                            # this process alone

every = td.split(whole, 8, ghost_layers=1)        # or each rank reads its own
mine = td.PartitionedDataSet([every[i] for i in range(world.rank, 8, world.size)], world)
print(td.statistics(mine, "RTData").mean)        # over all eight pieces, on every rank

mpiexec -n 4 python script.py

The same script runs in one process and on many ranks. Tack imports no MPI module: you make the communicator, and mpi4py must be built against your MPI (uv sync --extra mpi). Results that sum over pieces add in the pieces' global order, so they have the same bits however the pieces are shared out. With an MPI that reads device memory, tc.World(comm, gpu_aware=True) sends device arrays without staging them through the host. Make the rank's device (tack.device("cuda:N")) before importing mpi4py.MPI, which starts MPI. MPI covers worlds and transports, and every algorithm here is written on the communication layer, so one of your own can be too.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Hidden cells. Filters never process cells marked hidden, since their data are not valid there. Every filter that makes cells or points leaves them out, and so do probe, advect and streamlines in their source dataset. Algorithms whose output is on the same cells, such as gradients and projections, still compute there, and the marks stay. Faces or edges chosen by id and a reused CellLocator are refused on data with hidden cells.

Fields the marks cannot place. An L2 field goes by its cells' marks. A field on faces or edges, or of order 2, is refused by reductions on a dataset with marks, since who owns those values is not decided yet.

Not here yet. Rebalancing pieces and asynchronous exchange are not planned for now.

docs.title: Steps over time
docs.text:
A simulation produces its time steps one after another, in situ or as a series of files. An analysis of them should receive each step once and keep only what it needs of earlier ones. Tack's temporal filters work that way. They keep running statistics over the steps, take time derivatives, carry particles through a velocity field that changes in time, and build pathlines and streaklines.

Tack keeps no series of steps. Each step is a dataset at its own time, data.time in data.time_unit, and every filter keeps that time on what it makes. Stateless filters, such as a contour or a threshold, treat each step like any dataset. Filters that need more than the current step are small objects, temporal filters, that you feed one step at a time. Their update(data) returns that step's output, and the object keeps what it needs of earlier steps. Coordinates, units and time explains a dataset's time and units.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

stats = td.RunningStatistics("T")       # per point, over the steps so far
rate = td.TimeDerivative("T")           # since the previous step

for step in range(5):
    # A simulation's step: its mesh, a temperature field and the time.
    data = td.uniform_grid((8, 8, 8), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1), unit="m")
    data.time, data.time_unit = 0.5 * step, "s"
    x = data.positions()
    temperature = 20.0 + 5.0 * np.sin(x[:, 0] * 3.0 + 0.4 * step)
    data.fields["T"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(temperature.astype(np.float32)),
                                unit="degC")

    summary = stats.update(data)        # the step, with T_mean, T_variance, T_min, T_max
    change = rate.update(data)          # the step with T_dt; None on the first step
    hot = td.threshold(summary, "T_max", 24.0, 30.0)      # filters as on any dataset

print(stats.count, "steps;", summary.fields["T_variance"].unit, change.fields["T_dt"].unit)
assert summary.time == 2.0 and change.fields["T_dt"].unit == "K/s"
assert np.all(summary.fields["T_min"].values.numpy() <= summary.fields["T_mean"].values.numpy())

5 steps; K**2 K/s

docs.title: The temporal filters
docs.text:
Filter What update(data) returns VTK or Viskores counterpart RunningStatistics the step with each field's mean, variance, minimum and maximum so far vtkTemporalStatistics TimeDerivative the step with each field's rate of change since the previous step none Advection the particles at the step's time vtkParticleTracer Pathlines a polyline per particle through its positions so far vtkParticlePathFilter; Viskores' Pathline Streaklines a polyline per seed through the particles it released vtkStreaklineFilter

extend_paths is a function, not an object. It joins one step's particles onto the paths so far.

Two rules hold for all of them. Feed the steps in increasing time. And feed every step through the same object, since the object is the memory between steps.

docs.title: Keep running statistics
docs.text:
RunningStatistics(fields) takes a name or a list of names. Each update adds the step's values, per point or per cell, and returns the step with four fields beside its own:

Field Meaning Unit <name>_mean the mean over the steps so far the field's <name>_variance the population variance the field's squared <name>_min, <name>_max the extremes so far the field's

The sums are kept on the device by Welford's method, in double precision where the device has it. Vector fields are taken component by component. count is the number of steps added. The variance of a field in degrees Celsius is in kelvin squared, since a difference of temperatures is in kelvin.

The filter keeps only its sums, so nothing of earlier steps is copied. The steps must be on one mesh. That means the same topology, or one of the same kind, sizes and arrays, as a simulation gives that builds a new dataset each step over the same mesh. A step on another mesh is refused. Remesh it onto the first step's mesh first, by probing onto it, say.

docs.title: Take time derivatives
docs.text: TimeDerivative(fields) returns the step with <name>_dt, the backward difference (value - previous) / (time - previous time) per point or cell. Its unit is the field's over the time unit, so a field in degrees Celsius gives kelvin per second. The first step has no previous one, and its update returns None. The steps must be on one mesh and in increasing time. Times in two units, such as seconds and then minutes, are converted.

docs.title: What a filter keeps of earlier steps
docs.text: A filter that needs an earlier step's values keeps a copy of them. In situ, a simulation's arrays often reach Tack without a copy, through DLPack, and the simulation overwrites them at the next step. A reference would then see the new values. copy=False keeps references instead, when you know the buffers are not reused between steps. Each filter keeps only what it reads: a field, and the positions where the mesh moves. An image's coordinates or a constant field, which nothing writes, are kept as they are.

docs.title: Carry particles through the steps
docs.text:
Advection(field, seeds) carries particles through a velocity field that changes in time. Each update moves every particle from its time to the step's time. The velocity between two steps is linear in time, from the previous step, which the filter keeps, to this one. The update returns the particles at their current positions: a point cloud at the step's time.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


def step(t):
    """A wind along x that strengthens with time: the simulation's step at t seconds."""
    data = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 2), spacing=(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), unit="m")
    data.time, data.time_unit = t, "s"
    v = np.zeros((data.num_points, 3), np.float32)
    v[:, 0] = 0.5 + 0.1 * t
    data.fields["v"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(v, tack.vec3()), unit="m/s")
    return data


particles = td.Advection("v", seeds=[[1.0, 5.0, 0.5], [1.0, 2.0, 0.5]], step_size=0.25)
paths = None
for t in range(6):
    if t == 2:
        particles.inject([[1.0, 8.0, 0.5]], time=2.0)    # a third particle, from 2 s
    now = particles.update(step(float(t)))              # the particles at this step's time
    paths = td.extend_paths(paths, now)                 # joined into polylines by seed

x = now.world_positions()[:, 0]
print(x, now.fields["release"].values.numpy())
# x(t) = 1 + 0.5 t + 0.05 t^2: exact, since the velocity is linear in time.
assert np.allclose(x[:2], 1 + 0.5 * 5 + 0.05 * 25, atol=1e-4)
assert np.isclose(x[2], 1 + (0.5 * 5 + 0.05 * 25) - (0.5 * 2 + 0.05 * 4), atol=1e-4)
assert paths.num_cells == 3

[4.75       4.75       3.54999995] [0. 0. 2.]

The particles' fields are:

Field Meaning seed each particle's number source the seed point it came from, or -1 release its release time time its current time status ParticleStatus bits, as advect gives them

seeds are released at the first step's time. inject(points, time=) releases more particles at any time from the last step's on. Without time, they are released at the last step's time. A particle released after the coming step waits for a step that reaches it. A time before the last step is refused, since that interval has been integrated.

The main options:

  • integrator is "rk4" (the default) or "euler".
  • step_size, in the steps' time unit, bounds each substep. By default there is one substep from step to step.
  • copy=False keeps a reference to the previous step instead of a copy.

The velocity at each substep is a probe of both steps' own meshes, so the mesh may change between steps. A particle that leaves the mesh stops where it last was, marked SPATIAL_BOUNDS. Times convert between the steps' unit and the velocity's, so steps in minutes with a velocity in metres per second work.

docs.title: Build pathlines and streaklines
docs.text:
A pathline is one particle's path through a field that changes in time. A streakline is the line through every particle released from one point over time, as dye released continuously traces it.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")


def step(t):
    """A swirl that speeds up: a simulation's step at time t (seconds)."""
    data = td.uniform_grid((21, 21, 3), spacing=(0.5, 0.5, 0.5), unit="m")
    data.time, data.time_unit = t, "s"
    x = data.positions().astype(np.float64) - [5.0, 5.0, 0.0]
    v = np.stack([-x[:, 1], x[:, 0], np.zeros(len(x))], axis=1) * (0.2 + 0.1 * t)
    data.fields["v"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(v.astype(np.float32), tack.vec3()),
                                unit="m/s")
    return data


seeds = np.array([[7.0, 5.0, 0.5], [5.0, 8.0, 0.5]])
pathlines = td.Pathlines("v", seeds, step_size=0.1)
streaklines = td.Streaklines("v", seeds[:1], releases=4)
for t in np.arange(0.0, 3.01, 0.5):
    data = step(t)
    if t == 1.0:
        pathlines.inject([[3.0, 5.0, 0.5]])          # released at the last step's time
    paths = pathlines.update(data)                   # every particle's path so far
    streak = streaklines.update(data)                # the line of the seed's particles

print(paths.num_cells, "paths,", paths.num_points, "points;", streak.num_points, "in the streak")
radius = np.linalg.norm(paths.world_positions()[:, :2] - [5.0, 5.0], axis=1)
assert np.allclose(radius[paths.fields["seed"].values.numpy() == 0], 2.0, atol=1e-3)
assert paths.num_cells == 3 and streak.num_cells == 1

Pathlines is Advection and extend_paths together. It takes Advection's arguments and returns the current pathlines every step: a polyline per particle, with seed and time on its points. A particle's first point stays alone, in no line, until the particle has moved.

  • Tetrahedra: the velocity linear in each cell

  • Order 3 on curved hexahedra

Each picture follows 16 particles through 60 steps of a swirl that changes in time, inside a unit cube. Each path is drawn as a tube colored by time. The gallery shows two more kinds of cell.

Streaklines(field, seeds, releases=1) releases releases particles at each seed every step, at times spread evenly over the interval since the previous step. It returns a polyline per seed through its particles still in the mesh, newest first, with source, release and time on the points.

extend_paths(paths, particles) stands alone. Given None or its last result, and an Advection's output, it appends each particle's new point and joins the points of each particle into a polyline by seed. Particles written to files step by step can be joined into paths afterwards this way.

docs.title: Steps in pieces
docs.text: A PartitionedDataSet streams piece by piece. Each piece keeps its own state, so every step must bring the same pieces, and the output is pieces too. Over MPI ranks each rank feeds its own pieces. The statistics and derivatives need nothing from other ranks. Advection over pieces probes each point on the rank whose cells hold it, so particles stay on the rank that released them. Filters over pieces explains pieces and ranks.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
How many particles. The particles live on the host in double precision. Each substep probes both steps for every particle. Point location runs on the device, but each probe is its own set of launches, so Advection and the line filters suit thousands of particles more than millions. For a steady field, advect and streamlines run every particle on the device, one thread each; see Sample and trace.

Pieces and hierarchies at one time. The pieces of a PartitionedDataSet and the boxes of an AMR dataset must share one time, in units that convert. An octree's time is its roots'.
