docs.title: Points and particles
docs.text:
Some data comes as points rather than cells: LiDAR and photogrammetry scans, or the particles of SPH, N-body and molecular dynamics codes. Most questions about such data start from each point's neighbours. Tack's point algorithms find those neighbours, mark noise, thin a cloud, estimate normals, put points on a grid, resample SPH particles and find dark matter halos. Each names its VTK or Viskores counterpart, so you can find the filter you already use.

A point cloud in Tack is a dataset whose cells are its points, one vertex cell each. Its fields are point data. How a cloud is stored, and how it keeps its precision far from zero through its origin, is explained in Particles and point clouds.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# A noisy scan of a tilted plane: 20,000 points, 30 stray returns above it.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
xy = rng.uniform(0.0, 10.0, (20000, 2))
z = 0.1 * xy[:, 0] + rng.normal(0.0, 0.01, len(xy))
z[:30] += 5.0
scan = td.point_cloud(np.column_stack([xy, z]), fields={"z": z})

marked = td.outliers(scan, radius=0.2, min_neighbors=3)    # adds "outlier", 1 for noise
clean = td.threshold_points(marked, "outlier", 0, 0)        # keeps the rest
thin = td.voxel_downsample(clean, 0.25)                     # one point per 25 cm voxel
oriented = td.point_normals(thin, k=10)                     # adds "normals"

print(scan.num_points, "->", clean.num_points, "->", thin.num_points, "points")
normals = oriented.fields["normals"].values.numpy()
assert scan.num_points - clean.num_points >= 30
assert np.median(normals[:, 2]) > 0.99                      # up, off the plane

20000 -> 19970 -> 1865 points

docs.title: The algorithms
docs.text:
Every algorithm here takes a point cloud and returns a new dataset or field. Most of them search each point's neighbourhood through a locator, a structure that bins the points so a search visits only nearby ones.

Task Algorithm VTK or Viskores counterpart Find the points within a radius, or the k nearest PointLocator vtkStaticPointLocator Mark noise outliers vtkRadiusOutlierRemoval, vtkStatisticalOutlierRemoval Keep the points whose field lies in a range threshold_points vtkThresholdPoints Thin to one point per voxel voxel_downsample vtkVoxelGrid Estimate surface normals point_normals vtkPCANormalEstimation Group points closer than a distance connected_components(radius=) vtkEuclideanClusterExtraction Count, sum, average or take extremes on a grid deposit Viskores' ParticleDensityNearestGridPoint, ParticleDensityCloudInCell SPH density sph_density none SPH resampling onto other points sph_interpolate vtkSPHInterpolator A catalogue of halos halo_catalog Viskores' cosmotools

extract_points and mask_points, VTK's vtkExtractPoints and vtkMaskPoints, also take point clouds; see the algorithms reference. Each algorithm here is deterministic. None of them sums with atomics, so the same input gives the same values on every run.

docs.title: Find neighbours with a point locator
docs.text:
PointLocator sorts a cloud's points into uniform bins. neighbors(radius) returns every point within a radius of each query, and nearest(k) the k nearest points, nearest first. By default the queries are the cloud's own points, each leaving itself out. Pass other points to query them instead.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
cloud = td.point_cloud(rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0, (5000, 3)))
locator = td.PointLocator(cloud)

offsets, ids = locator.neighbors(0.05)         # within 0.05 of each point
nearest, squared = locator.nearest(8)          # the 8 nearest, nearest first
probes = np.array([[0.5, 0.5, 0.5], [0.1, 0.9, 0.2]])
closest, _ = locator.nearest(3, probes)        # the 3 nearest to other points

offsets, nearest = offsets.numpy(), nearest.numpy()
print("point 0 has", offsets[1] - offsets[0], "neighbours within 0.05")
x = cloud.positions()
assert np.array_equal(nearest[0], np.argsort(((x - x[0]) ** 2).sum(axis=1))[1:9])

# Filters take the locator, so several of them bin the cloud once.
marked = td.outliers(cloud, k=8, deviations=2.0, locator=locator)

neighbors returns CSR arrays: the neighbours of query q are ids[offsets[q]:offsets[q + 1]]. nearest returns (m, k) arrays of ids and squared distances, with -1 where a cloud has fewer than k points. Query points given as a NumPy array are world positions.

A filter given no locator uses the one the dataset's topology keeps, so a chain of filters on one cloud bins it once. A locator records the positions it was built from and is refused once Tack writes to them. For kernels of your own, locator.grid() gives the bins as a device class.

docs.title: Mark and remove outliers
docs.text:
outliers marks points rather than removing them, as PDAL does. It adds outlier, a u8 point field that is 1 for noise. threshold_points(data, "outlier", 0, 0) keeps the rest, and the marks stay for inspection. It has two tests:

  • The radius test (radius and min_neighbors) marks a point with fewer than min_neighbors other points within radius, as VTK's vtkRadiusOutlierRemoval does. It adds neighbors, each point's count.
  • The statistical test (k and deviations) marks a point whose mean distance to its k nearest is more than deviations standard deviations above the mean of those distances, as PCL does. It adds mean_distance.

VTK's vtkStatisticalOutlierRemoval also removes points that many deviations below the mean, such as duplicates in dense spots. Tack marks only the far ones. The two agree on the mean distances.

docs.title: Thin a cloud to one point per voxel
docs.text:
voxel_downsample(data, size) keeps one point per occupied voxel of a grid with sides of size, anchored at the points' lower corner, as VTK's vtkVoxelGrid and PDAL's filters.voxeldownsize do. keep chooses the point:

keep The point kept Its fields "centroid" (default) a new point at the mean of the voxel's points floating-point fields averaged; integer fields, such as a classification, from the voxel's first point "first" the voxel's lowest-numbered point the point's own "nearest" the voxel's point nearest the centroid the point's own

Point fields come along, chosen by fields= as for every filter. Cell fields do not, since the output's cells are new.

docs.title: Estimate normals
docs.text: point_normals fits each point's neighbourhood and adds normals, unit vectors in the direction the neighbourhood spreads least, as VTK's vtkPCANormalEstimation does. The neighbourhood is the k nearest points or those within radius. A normal points toward viewpoint when you give one, otherwise along direction, which is up by default: the outside of terrain. A point with fewer than three neighbours, or whose neighbours lie on a line, gets a zero normal.

docs.title: Put points on a grid
docs.text:
deposit(data, grid, field, reduce=) sums points into an image, a dataset made by uniform_grid. With method="nearest" each point goes to the cell holding it, and the result is a cell field. With method="cic" (cloud in cell) each point is spread over the corners of its cell by trilinear weights, and the result is a point field. Without field it counts points. With a field, reduce is "sum", "mean", "count", or for "nearest" also "min" and "max". per_volume=True divides by each cell's volume, which turns counts or masses into densities.

The highest return in each cell of a LiDAR survey is a surface model, and the lowest ground return a terrain model:

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# A 100 m survey tile in UTM coordinates: sloping ground and a building.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
east, north = rng.uniform(0.0, 100.0, (2, 40000))
height = 0.02 * east + rng.normal(0.0, 0.02, len(east))
roof = (np.abs(east - 50.0) < 10.0) & (np.abs(north - 50.0) < 10.0)
height[roof] += 8.0
world = np.column_stack([east + 431000.0, north + 4580000.0, height + 120.0])
tile = td.point_cloud(world, fields={"z": world[:, 2]})
print(tile.origin)                                   # the tile's corner, in whole metres

# A 2D image of 2 m cells over the tile, moved to the tile's origin.
image = td.uniform_grid((51, 51), origin=(431000.0, 4580000.0), spacing=(2.0, 2.0))
image = image.rebased(tile.origin)
surface = td.deposit(tile, image, "z", reduce="max").values.numpy().reshape(50, 50)
print(f"roof {surface[25, 25]:.1f} m, ground {surface[5, 5]:.1f} m")
assert abs(surface[25, 25] - 129.0) < 0.2 and abs(surface[5, 5] - 120.2) < 0.2

A cell no point reaches holds 0 for counts and sums, and NaN for the other reductions. Points outside the image are left out.

The survey's coordinates are millions of metres from zero. point_cloud gives such a cloud an origin at its lower corner, so its positions keep millimetres in single precision. An image needs the same care, since its corner is stored in the geometry's precision too. rebased(tile.origin) moves the image's corner next to zero in double precision and keeps it an image. Coordinates, units and time explains origins.

docs.title: Resample SPH particles
docs.text:
sph_interpolate(particles, target) evaluates the particles' fields at a target's points by SPH kernel sums, as VTK's vtkSPHInterpolator does. Each particle j contributes (m_j / rho_j) A_j W(|x - x_j|, h_j) to a point x, out to its kernel's support. The target is any dataset (an image, a slice, another cloud) or an (n, 3) array of world positions. When a code writes no density, sph_density computes one, adding density to the particles.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Particles of equal mass on a jittered lattice filling the unit cube: density 1.
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
side = np.arange(0.0, 1.0, 0.05) + 0.025
x = np.stack(np.meshgrid(side, side, side, indexing="ij"), axis=-1).reshape(-1, 3)
x += rng.uniform(-0.005, 0.005, x.shape)
particles = td.point_cloud(x, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
                           fields={"h": np.full(len(x), 0.06), "mass": np.full(len(x), 0.05**3),
                                   "T": 300.0 + 10.0 * x[:, 0]})
particles = td.sph_density(particles)                           # adds "density"
inner = np.all((x > 0.2) & (x < 0.8), axis=1)
assert abs(np.median(particles.fields["density"].values.numpy()[inner]) - 1.0) < 0.02

image = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 11), origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
resampled = td.sph_interpolate(particles, image, fields=["T"], normalize=True)
T = resampled.fields["T"].values.numpy()
shepard = resampled.fields["shepard"].values.numpy()
print(f"coverage {shepard.min():.2f} at a corner, {np.median(shepard):.2f} inside")
p = image.positions()
inside = np.all((p > 0.15) & (p < 0.85), axis=1)
assert np.abs(T - (300.0 + 10.0 * p[:, 0]))[inside].max() < 0.05

The result also has shepard, the sum of (m / rho) W at each point. Near 1 the particles cover the point, and near 0 they do not. normalize=True divides by it, as VTK's Shepard processing does, which keeps a constant exact out to the particles' edge.

The main options:

  • kernel is "cubic" (the default), "quartic", "quintic" or "wendland", normalized in dimension dimensions. They are VTK's kernels, and the results agree with vtkSPHInterpolator to rounding.
  • smoothing_length, mass and density name point fields, h, mass and density by default. Each also takes one number for every particle.
  • periodic reaches across the faces of a periodic box.

sph_density takes the same options. Each particle's density sums over the particles within its own smoothing length's reach, itself included: the gather form, as SPLASH computes it.

docs.title: Find halos in a periodic box
docs.text:
A halo finder groups dark matter particles closer than a linking length. That is friends of friends, and in Tack it is connected_components with the linking length as radius. On a point cloud, whose cells are its points, connected_components(radius=) is Euclidean clustering, as VTK's vtkEuclideanClusterExtraction does. It adds point_region, each point's group, numbered from 0, or -1 for none. min_size drops groups of fewer points and numbers the rest again. halo_catalog then summarizes each group.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# Three halos in a periodic box of side 50, one across a face, and a background.
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
box = 50.0
centres = np.array([[10.0, 10.0, 10.0], [30.0, 25.0, 40.0], [49.5, 20.0, 20.0]])
clumps = [c + rng.normal(0.0, 0.4, (n, 3)) for c, n in zip(centres, (3000, 1500, 800))]
x = np.concatenate(clumps + [rng.uniform(0.0, box, (20000, 3))]) % box
v = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, x.shape)
particles = td.point_cloud(x, fields={"v": v}, origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0))

linking = 0.2 * box / len(x) ** (1 / 3)
groups = td.connected_components(particles, radius=linking, min_size=100, periodic=box)
catalog = td.halo_catalog(groups, mass=1.0e10, velocity="v", periodic=box)
counts = catalog.fields["count"].values.numpy()
print(catalog.num_points, "halos of", sorted(counts.tolist()), "particles")
assert catalog.num_points == 3 and counts.min() > 700

periodic is a box: its side, its three sides, or its two corners. Distances are then to a point's nearest image, so a halo across a face of the box is one halo. PointLocator, outliers, point_normals, connected_components and the SPH algorithms take periodic too.

The catalogue is a point cloud with one point per halo, at its most bound particle, or at its centre of mass with center="com". Its fields are:

Field Meaning halo, count, mass the label, the number of particles, their total mass com the centre of mass mbp, potential the most bound particle's index and its potential velocity, dispersion the mass-weighted mean velocity and the 1D velocity dispersion (with velocity=) radius the distance to the halo's farthest particle

mass is one number for every particle or a point field. The most bound particle is exact for every halo: large halos are pruned by bounds, not estimated. softening and G set the potential's softening length and gravitational constant.

docs.title: Point clouds in pieces
docs.text: A cloud split over ranks, or a survey cut into tiles, needs each piece's neighbours from the other pieces. ghost_points copies them in, and connected_components, outliers, voxel_downsample, deposit and halo_catalog take the pieces directly and give the whole cloud's answer. Filters over pieces shows how.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Reproducible sums. voxel_downsample, deposit, the SPH sums and halo_catalog add their terms in point order, so a run gives the same bits every time. Counts, minima and maxima are the same on every device. Sums agree to rounding, since a GPU may fuse a multiply and an add. Every distance that decides something, such as a voxel's nearest point or the k nearest, is computed alike on every device, so the same points are chosen everywhere.

Precision. The statistical outlier test's mean and deviation are taken in double precision on the host. point_normals cannot tell a strip about 4% as wide as it is long from a line in single precision, and gives it a zero normal.

Integer fields keep their type through point_cloud. A classification or an intensity stays an integer, while floating-point fields take the cloud's precision.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Particles and point clouds explains the model behind these algorithms.
  • Sample and trace probes meshes at points and traces particles through velocity fields.
  • Filters over pieces runs these algorithms on clouds split over ranks.

docs.title: Reduce: statistics and regions
docs.text: Some answers are a few numbers, not a new mesh: the range and mean of a field, how its values spread, how many separate regions a threshold leaves and how big each is. Tack's reductions compute them. statistics and entropy summarize a field, as VTK's vtkDescriptiveStatistics does, and a summary can be weighted by volume or mass. connected_components labels the connected regions of a mesh or a point cloud, as vtkConnectivityFilter does.

docs.title: Summarize a field
docs.text:
statistics(data, field) returns a Statistics of a scalar field's values: their count n, min, max, sum and mean, the central moments, the sample and population variances and standard deviations, the skewness and the kurtosis. It computes them as Viskores' Statistics filter does, with the moments taken about the mean in a second pass.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((21, 21, 21), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
r = np.linalg.norm(data.positions(), axis=1)
data.fields["r"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(r))

s = td.statistics(data, "r")
print(f"n {s.n}, range {s.min:.3f} to {s.max:.3f}, mean {s.mean:.4f}, "
      f"std {s.sample_stddev:.4f}, skewness {s.skewness:.3f}")
# n 9261, range 0.000 to 1.732, mean 1.0077, std 0.2909, skewness -0.364
assert s.n == data.num_points
assert np.isclose(s.mean, r.mean(dtype=np.float64), rtol=1e-6)
assert np.isclose(s.sample_variance, r.astype(np.float64).var(ddof=1), rtol=1e-5)

The numbers are Python floats, so the call waits for the device work it reads. Their definitions:

Name Is m2, m3, m4 the sums of (x - mean)^k sample_variance, population_variance m2 / (n - 1) and m2 / n sample_stddev, population_stddev their square roots skewness sqrt(n) m3 / m2^1.5, 0 for a constant field kurtosis n m4 / m2^2, not the excess kurtosis, and 0 for a constant field unit the field's unit, which mean, min and the others are in

Integer fields are summarized in floating point.

Ghosts are left out. Cells and points that the dataset's ghost marks mark as copies owned by another piece, or as hidden, are not counted. A PartitionedDataSet is summarized whole: field names a field every piece has, each piece reduces what it owns on its own device, and the parts are combined in the pieces' order over every MPI rank. The result is the same however the pieces are shared out among ranks. statistics also takes AMR datasets, counting each region of space once at its finest level, and octrees, counting their leaves (adaptive data).

See the reference for the full signature, and Statistics for every field it holds.

docs.title: Weight by volume or mass
docs.text:
statistics summarizes the stored values, each counted once. On a mesh whose cells differ in size, that is not the mean over the volume: a region of many small cells counts for more than a region of a few large ones. weights weighs each value:

  • weights="volume" weighs each cell by its measure. The field must be cell data (a Constant field), whose values belong to the cells. Point data is refused.
  • weights= a field's name weighs each value by that field, on the same entities. A density gives mass-weighted moments.

With weights, mean is sum(w x) / W, sum is sum(w x), and weight is W, the sum of the weights. The example's grid is fine near x = 0 and coarse toward x = 8:

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

axis = np.concatenate([np.linspace(0, 1, 11), [2.0, 4.0, 8.0]])   # graded along x
data = td.rectilinear_grid(axis, [0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0], unit="m")
data.fields["T"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(data.positions()[:, 0].copy()), unit="K")
data.fields["T_cell"] = td.project(data, "T", td.Constant(data))   # each cell's average

samples = td.statistics(data, "T")                                # the points, each once
by_volume = td.statistics(data, "T_cell", weights="volume")
print(f"mean of the samples {samples.mean:.3f} K, over the volume {by_volume.mean:.3f} K")
# mean of the samples 1.393 K, over the volume 4.000 K
totals = td.integrate(data, ["T"])
assert np.isclose(by_volume.mean, totals.values["T"] / totals.measure)
assert np.isclose(by_volume.weight, 8.0) and by_volume.weight_unit == "m**3"

The volume-weighted mean equals the integral over the measure, which integrate gives directly. With weights the population variance is m2 / W, and the sample variance treats the weights as reliability weights, as NumPy's aweights does.

docs.title: Measure how a field's values spread
docs.text:
entropy(data, field, bins=10) is the Shannon entropy, in bits, of the field's histogram: -sum(p log2 p) over the shares of the values in bins equal bins over their range, as Viskores' Entropy filter computes it. A constant field has entropy 0, and values spread evenly over 2^k bins have entropy k.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

values = np.random.default_rng(0).uniform(size=100_000).astype(np.float32)
cloud = td.point_cloud(np.c_[values, values, values])
cloud.fields["u"] = td.Field(td.H1(cloud), tack.array(values))

bits = td.entropy(cloud, "u", bins=8)
print(f"{bits:.3f} bits")                      # 3.000 bits: 8 equally full bins
assert abs(bits - 3.0) < 0.01

entropy leaves out ghosts, combines pieces and takes AMR datasets and octrees as statistics does. Over pieces, the bins span the whole dataset's range. weights works as for statistics: each bin's share is the sum of its weights over the sum of all of them. See the reference.

docs.title: Label connected regions
docs.text:
connected_components(data) finds which cells are connected through shared points, as VTK's vtkConnectivityFilter does with all regions extracted. It returns the dataset with two new fields: region on the cells and point_region on the points. Regions are numbered from 0 in the order of their lowest cell id. A point no cell uses, and a hidden cell, get -1.

To pick one region, threshold region:

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((21, 21, 21), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1))
x = data.positions()
to_nearer_centre = np.minimum(np.linalg.norm(x - [0.5, 0, 0], axis=1),
                              np.linalg.norm(x + [0.5, 0, 0], axis=1))
data.fields["d"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(to_nearer_centre))

blobs = td.threshold(data, "d", 0.0, 0.3)               # two separate balls of cells
labelled = td.connected_components(blobs)
regions, sizes = np.unique(labelled.fields["region"].values.numpy(), return_counts=True)
print(dict(zip(regions.tolist(), sizes.tolist())))      # {0: 48, 1: 48}

largest = regions[np.argmax(sizes)]
one_ball = td.threshold(labelled, "region", largest, largest)
assert len(regions) == 2 and one_ball.num_cells == sizes.max()

It runs on the device, by union-find over the cells and their points. The regions are the same on every device and every run, since each is numbered by its lowest cell.

docs.title: Cluster points by distance
docs.text:
With radius, points within that distance of each other are connected too. On a point cloud, whose cells are its points, that is Euclidean clustering, as VTK's vtkEuclideanClusterExtraction does it. With a linking length it is friends-of-friends halo finding. min_size gives the regions of fewer points the label -1, and numbers the rest again in the same order.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
points = np.concatenate([rng.normal(0.0, 0.05, (200, 3)),       # a cluster of 200
                         rng.normal(1.0, 0.05, (300, 3)),       # a cluster of 300
                         [[5.0, 5.0, 5.0]]]).astype(np.float32)  # a stray point
cloud = td.point_cloud(points)

clusters = td.connected_components(cloud, radius=0.1, min_size=10)
labels, sizes = np.unique(clusters.fields["region"].values.numpy(), return_counts=True)
print(dict(zip(labels.tolist(), sizes.tolist())))      # {-1: 1, 0: 200, 1: 300}
assert dict(zip(labels.tolist(), sizes.tolist())) == {-1: 1, 0: 200, 1: 300}

periodic= joins points across the faces of a periodic box, as a cosmology box needs. The points and particles page covers clustering and halo catalogues in full.

docs.title: Regions over pieces
docs.text: Over a PartitionedDataSet, regions are numbered across every piece of every MPI rank. Each piece labels its own cells, and pieces join the regions that meet at the points they share. With global ids on every piece, regions are numbered by their lowest global cell id, which is the whole dataset's numbering. Without them, they are numbered by their lowest (piece, cell). Filters over pieces explains pieces, ghost cells and global ids. See the reference.

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
Pieces give the whole's answer. Where every shared cell and point has one owner, as the ghost marks arrange, statistics over pieces equal the whole dataset's up to rounding. The order of combination is fixed by the pieces' order, not by which rank finished first.

Stored values, not functions. statistics and entropy count the values a field stores. For an H1 field of order 1 (point data), those are the point values. For a field of higher order, they are its node values, or a Bernstein basis's coefficients, and neither is a set of samples spread evenly over the cells. For integrals and true averages of any order, use integrate or project into cell data.

docs.text:
• Derive quantities: integrals, cell measures and the fields worth summarizing.
  • Points and particles: outliers, downsampling, deposits and halo catalogues.
  • Filters over pieces: how reductions combine pieces over MPI ranks.

docs.title: Sample and trace fields
docs.text: A field is a function of position, and many questions ask for its value somewhere the mesh stores nothing: along a line, at a sensor, on another grid. Others follow a velocity field: where do particles released here go? Tack's probe answers the first kind, as VTK's vtkProbeFilter and vtkResampleToImage do. It samples a dataset at points, onto another dataset, or onto an image. streamlines and advect answer the second, as vtkStreamTracer does, with a choice of integrator, step and device.

docs.title: Probe a dataset at points
docs.text:
probe(data, where) evaluates data's fields at the points of where, as VTK's vtkProbeFilter does. where is an (n, 3) array of points or another dataset. Each point is located in the cell that holds it, and each field is evaluated there through its own interpolation. The result is where with every field as point data, and a field valid: 1 where a cell holds the point, 0 where none does.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 11), origin=(-1, -1, -1), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2))
x = data.positions()
data.fields["T"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(300 + 10 * x[:, 0]))

points = np.array([[0.31, 0.2, 0.0], [-0.5, 0.1, 0.7], [5.0, 0.0, 0.0]])
samples = td.probe(data, points)
valid = samples.fields["valid"].values.numpy()
T = samples.fields["T"].values.numpy()
print(valid, T)                                   # [1 1 0] [303.1 295.    0. ]
assert list(valid) == [1, 1, 0] and np.allclose(T[:2], [303.1, 295.0])

line = td.uniform_grid((21,), origin=(-1, 0.1, 0.0), spacing=(0.1, 0, 0))   # a line of points
along = td.probe(data, line)                      # keeps the line's topology
assert np.allclose(along.fields["T"].values.numpy(), 300 + 10 * line.positions()[:, 0], atol=1e-4)

Check valid before reading a sample. A point outside the mesh gets 0 in every field, and 0 may also be a real value.

  • Tetrahedra: the field linear in each cell

  • Polyhedra: the field linear on each cell's tetrahedra

  • Order 4 on straight hexahedra

  • Order 3 on curved hexahedra, the plane's edge following them

Each picture probes the field cos 2πx + cos 2πy + cos 2πz of a unit cube's mesh onto a tilted image plane wider than the cube, colored by the field. The plane's points that no cell holds (valid 0) are left out, so its edge shows the mesh's boundary. The gallery describes the four meshes.

  • Points as an array become vertex cells, one per point. Their positions are world coordinates, converted in double precision.
  • A dataset keeps its own topology and geometry. Probing onto a line of points samples along the line, and probing onto an image (td.uniform_grid) resamples the mesh onto it, as VTK's vtkResampleToImage and vtkResampleWithDataSet do. A probed field replaces a field of the same name in where.
  • Cell data (a Constant field) is copied from the cell that holds the point. A field with an interpolation, such as point data (an H1 field of order 1) or an H1 or L2 field of any order, is evaluated in that cell. An integer field is rounded to the nearest integer, as VTK's probe rounds it.

Where a point lies in several cells, on a face or an edge they share, the lowest cell id wins. At a discontinuity this decides which side is sampled. It is not an average across the interface.

docs.title: Reuse the locator
docs.text:
Finding the cell that holds a point takes a locator, a search structure over the cells, as VTK's vtkStaticCellLocator is. Without one, probe uses the locator the dataset's topology keeps, so probing the same mesh again does not build it again. td.CellLocator(data) builds one you can pass to probe, advect and streamlines as locator=. It serves any dataset of the same cells and positions.

A locator follows the positions. After Tack writes them (a kernel, fill, copyto), the kept one is rebuilt, and one you built is refused, since its bins describe the old mesh. Positions changed through memory shared with another library are not seen, so build a new locator then.

probe also takes AMR datasets and octrees, as VTK's vtkAMRResampleFilter and vtkHyperTreeGridProbeFilter do (adaptive data), and datasets in pieces over MPI ranks (filters over pieces). See the reference.

docs.title: Put a mesh's fields on an image
docs.text:
Probing onto an image samples one point per image point. voxelize(data, grid) instead gives each voxel (a cell of the image) the share of its volume the data covers, as the cell field fraction, and each field's mean over that share. That is what a simulation's fields are on a uniform grid, for analysis or for machine learning.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

# A ball of tetrahedra, cut from a cube, with a temperature rising along x.
mesh = td.tetrahedralize(td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 11), spacing=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1)))
x = mesh.positions().astype(np.float64)
mesh.fields["r"] = td.Field(td.H1(mesh), tack.array(np.linalg.norm(x - 0.5, axis=1)))
mesh.fields["T"] = td.Field(td.H1(mesh), tack.array(300.0 + 10.0 * x[:, 0]), unit="K")
ball = td.clip(mesh, "r", 0.4, inside=True)

voxels = td.uniform_grid((6, 6, 6), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.2))
image = td.voxelize(ball, voxels, samples=6)
covered = image.fields["fraction"].values.numpy().sum() * 0.2 ** 3
volume = td.cell_geometry(ball).measure.values.numpy().sum()
print(f"covered {covered:.4f} of the ball's {volume:.4f}")
assert abs(covered - volume) < 0.02 * volume
assert image.fields["T"].unit == "K"

Each voxel is sampled at samples points along each axis (4 by default, so 64 in 3D), at the centres of its sub-voxels, through probe. So fraction is right to about one sample's share, and a mean is the samples' mean, not an integral. More samples cost more probes. Voxels the data does not reach are hidden. voxelize takes anything probe takes. See the reference.

docs.title: Trace streamlines
docs.text:
streamlines(data, field, seeds, step_size, steps) follows a steady velocity field from each seed, as VTK's vtkStreamTracer does. The result is one polyline per seed, with the cell field seed (which seed the path started from) and the point field time (when the particle reached each point). advect takes the same arguments and returns only where each particle stopped.

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 3), origin=(-1, -1, -0.1), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.1))
x = data.positions()
rotation = np.stack([-x[:, 1], x[:, 0], np.zeros(len(x), np.float32)], axis=1)
data.fields["velocity"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(rotation, dtype=tack.vec3(tack.f32)))

seeds = np.array([[0.5, 0, 0], [0, 0.75, 0]], np.float32)
paths = td.streamlines(data, "velocity", seeds, step_size=0.05, steps=20)
ends = td.advect(data, "velocity", seeds, step_size=0.05, steps=20)

lengths = td.cell_geometry(paths).measure.values.numpy()
print(paths.num_cells, "lines of length", lengths.round(3))     # 2 lines of length [0.5 0.75]
# The flow turns at unit angular speed, so time 1 is one radian round.
assert np.allclose(lengths, [0.5, 0.75], atol=1e-3)
assert np.allclose(ends.positions()[0, :2], [0.5 * np.cos(1), 0.5 * np.sin(1)], atol=1e-4)
assert np.allclose(ends.fields["time"].values.numpy(), 1.0, atol=1e-5)

The velocity may be point data, cell data, or a field of any order, on a straight or curved mesh. seeds is an (n, 3) array or a field of 3-vectors. A seed that cannot take a step, outside the mesh say, keeps a point in the output and makes no line.

  • Tetrahedra: point data, linear in each cell

  • Polyhedra: point data, linear on each cell's tetrahedra

  • Order 4: an H1 velocity on straight hexahedra

  • Order 3: an H1 velocity on curved hexahedra

Each picture traces 25 seeds through a swirl inside a unit cube, with integrator="rk45", step_unit="length" and max_length=1.4. The paths are drawn as tubes colored by time. The gallery has the script.

docs.title: Choose the step
docs.text:
By default step_size is a time step: each step integrates dx/dt = velocity over that time, so its length depends on the speed. step_unit="length" makes it an arc length along the path instead, as vtkStreamTracer steps by default. The particle then follows the velocity's direction, slow flow takes steps as long as fast flow, and steps * step_size is the longest path. Where speeds vary widely, length steps reach as far in far fewer steps. time on the points is the particle's time either way.

The integrator is "rk4" (fixed-step fourth-order Runge-Kutta, the default), "euler", or "rk45", which adapts the step as VTK's RK45 (Cash-Karp) does:

  • step_size is the first step.
  • A step whose error estimate exceeds tolerance (a distance, 1e-6 by default) is tried again, smaller.
  • Each step taken proposes the next, between min_step and max_step. By default they are a fiftieth of step_size and twice it, VTK's ratios.

Smooth stretches take long steps and sharp turns short ones. On a swirl at VTK's settings, rk45 takes about half of fixed RK4's points and lies as close to the path as VTK's RK45 does.

Two options end a path early, whatever the integrator. max_length stops a path that has gone that far. terminal_speed, in the velocity's unit, as in vtkStreamTracer, stops it at the first point where the speed is at or below that value, so a path stops where the flow does. A step size, a length or a speed may be a quantity such as "5 mm", converted to the dataset's units.

docs.title: Read why a particle stopped
docs.text:
advect returns a dataset of the particles where they stopped, one vertex cell each, with three point fields: steps (how many steps it took), time and status. status holds the bits of td.ParticleStatus:

Bit Means SUCCESS the particle was traced TERMINATE its path ended inside the mesh: its steps were done, it reached max_length, or a bit below ended it SPATIAL_BOUNDS it left the mesh TOOK_ANY_STEPS it moved at all ZERO_VELOCITY it stopped where the velocity is zero SLOW_SPEED it stopped at terminal_speed

Check status and time before treating a short path as a sign of slow flow.

advect also continues from its own output. Pass the returned dataset as seeds, and each particle goes on from where it stopped, with its time. The steps argument counts the steps taken before, so pass the new total:

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 3), origin=(-1, -1, -0.1), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.1))
x = data.positions()
rotation = np.stack([-x[:, 1], x[:, 0], np.zeros(len(x), np.float32)], axis=1)
data.fields["velocity"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(rotation, dtype=tack.vec3(tack.f32)))

seeds = np.array([[0.5, 0, 0], [0.9, 0.9, 0]], np.float32)
first = td.advect(data, "velocity", seeds, step_size=0.05, steps=20)
later = td.advect(data, "velocity", first, step_size=0.05, steps=40)    # 20 more

status = later.fields["status"].values.numpy()
print(later.fields["steps"].values.numpy(), later.fields["time"].values.numpy().round(3))
assert later.fields["steps"].values.numpy()[0] == 40
assert status[1] & td.ParticleStatus.SPATIAL_BOUNDS                  # the corner seed left

The full signatures are in the reference: streamlines, advect and ParticleStatus.

docs.title: At a wall
docs.text:
When a step would leave the mesh, advect and streamlines halve it until it stays inside, as Viskores' SmallStep does, then push the particle out along the velocity there. The path ends at the mesh's edge (SPATIAL_BOUNDS) only if that push leaves the mesh. At a no-slip wall the flow runs along the wall, so the particle stays in the fluid and goes on downstream.

VTK's vtkStreamTracer ends a line as soon as a step leaves the mesh, so near walls its lines stop sooner. In the wake of the AhmedML car body (72 seeds behind the body, length steps of 0.005), VTK ends 29 lines within 0.02 of the body and Tack 1. Tack's wake lines are longer, a median of 9.0 against 6.5. A terminal_speed does not make the two agree: at 5% of the free stream VTK still ends 22 lines by the body and Tack 6, because the flow where VTK's steps cross the wall is faster than that.

docs.title: Make tracing fast
docs.text:
Choose the device by the number of seeds. Each particle is one thread that takes all its steps. A few seeds therefore use a few threads of a GPU built for thousands, and one GPU thread is slower than a CPU core. Below a few thousand seeds the CPU is usually faster, and above, the GPU. On a 28-core AMD EPYC against an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada (ms, warm):

mesh seeds CPU CUDA aneurysm, 8.7M tetrahedra 25 8.4 32.0 2,000 57.2 75.8 20,000 871 331 ONERA M6 wing, 46.9M cells 17 41.7 84.4 1,024 92.9 149 16,384 1,190 108

For a few seeds on a mesh that lives on a GPU, trace on a CPU copy of it, data.to_device("cpu"). The locator is built where the mesh is.

Choose the locator by the mesh. The default locator bins the cells on two levels, as Viskores' CellLocatorTwoLevel does, so a mesh graded toward a body in a large far field is not crowded into a few bins. On a small mesh of cells of about one size, one uniform grid of bins holds fewer candidates a bin, as VTK's vtkStaticCellLocator does. Build it with levels=1 and pass it in.

Walk to the neighbours. neighbors=True tries the face neighbours of the cell a particle was last in before searching the locator. On large meshes this takes about half the time, for a table of face neighbours (six ids a cell) that the locator keeps. On surfaces and polyhedra it changes nothing.

Neither choice changes the result. Both locators find the same cells, and the walk finds the cell the search would, so the paths are the same, bit for bit:

import numpy as np

import tack
import tack.dataset as td

tack.set_default_device("cpu")

data = td.uniform_grid((11, 11, 3), origin=(-1, -1, -0.1), spacing=(0.2, 0.2, 0.1))
x = data.positions()
rotation = np.stack([-x[:, 1], x[:, 0], np.zeros(len(x), np.float32)], axis=1)
data.fields["velocity"] = td.Field(td.H1(data), tack.array(rotation, dtype=tack.vec3(tack.f32)))
seeds = np.array([[0.5, 0, 0], [0, 0.75, 0]], np.float32)

default = td.streamlines(data, "velocity", seeds, 0.05, 100)
uniform = td.streamlines(data, "velocity", seeds, 0.05, 100,
                         locator=td.CellLocator(data, levels=1))
walking = td.streamlines(data, "velocity", seeds, 0.05, 100, neighbors=True)
assert np.array_equal(uniform.positions(), default.positions())
assert np.array_equal(walking.positions(), default.positions())

docs.title: Details
docs.text:
rk45 and divergent flow. The adaptive integrator's step control makes yes-or-no choices. Where paths diverge, in a recirculation or at a wall, a change the size of rounding can send two runs, or two devices, along paths of different lengths, each within the tolerance. A looser tolerance makes that rarer.

Pieces. Over a PartitionedDataSet, give the field by name. Particles cross from piece to piece, over MPI ranks or not, and each piece holds the stretches of path it traced (filters over pieces).

Unsteady flow. advect and streamlines follow one steady field. Repeating them step by step does not trace a particle through a flow that changes in time. Pathlines and streaklines do that, on steps over time.

Supported cells. Probing and tracing take every shape, polyhedra (located in the tetrahedra they are fanned into) and polygons (in the triangles they are fanned into). Probing also takes polylines, on their segments, but tracing does not. A polyhedron or polygon must be star-shaped from the mean of its points, and the locator refuses one that is not.
